pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Kinked demand curves are most likely associated with which type of market structure?
new_option_b: Monopoly
new_option_c: Pure competition
new_explanation_en: Oligopolistic markets are characterized by a small number of competitors selling nondifferentiated products.  Kinked demand curves reflect the way competitors respond to any firm's attempts to increase market share or profitability.  The dotted black demand curve shows the hypothetical quantities demanded for a single oligopolist's product assuming naïve responses by competitors to different pricing strategies. The adverse outcomes likely confronting oligopolists are reflected in the red and blue segments of the kinked demand curve (DED).  Price cuts by one firm will likely be matched by competitors acting to defend their market shares.  The result is less elastic demand (ie, red demand curve segment, D) at price levels below the initial equilibrium (E). Competitor reaction is quite different if oligopolists attempt to increase profitability by raising prices.  The greater elasticity of demand (ie, the blue demand curve segment, D) at prices above the initial equilibrium results from competitors not matching a price increase.  Some of the price- raising firm's customers switch suppliers to avoid the price hike. The unit sales decrease after a price hike will proportionally be greater compared with the unit sales increase if prices were cut.  For example, whereas a 1% price cut might have resulted in a unit sales increase of 3%, a 1% price increase might cause a 5% decrease in unit sales. (Choice B)  A monopolist is the only seller in their market segment.  Monopolists are free to raise or lower price in search of profit maximization. (Choice C)  Firms in purely competitive markets are price-takers.  Each is so small relative to the total market that their actions cannot impact the equilibrium price; these firms therefore face flat (ie, infinitely elastic) demand curves.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Two firms, A and B, are the only manufacturers of Product X.  Each firm can choose whether to charge a high or low price for X; currently both charge a low price.  Each firm controls 50% of the market.  The table shows the expected profit (in USD) for both companies at both prices: Based on this information, the Nash equilibrium for these firms:
new_option_b: exists when A charges a high price and B charges a low price.
new_option_c: exists when A charges a high price and B charges a high price.
new_explanation_en: In an oligopoly, a Nash equilibrium refers to a set of optimal strategies by two (or more) market participants to maximize their profits.  Although it assumes that each participant acts in its own best interest, it also assumes that firms will consider the response of competitors to some action. For instance, a firm could try to increase profits by raising prices but may also consider the loss market share to competitors that do not raise their prices. In this question, Firm B always earns more when it sells at a lower price, so it has no incentive to sell at a higher price, regardless of Firm A's strategy.  Therefore, since A will act in its best interest, it charges a high price.  By doing so, A earns $350 instead of $200.  Therefore, a Nash equilibrium exists when Firm B sells at a low price and Firm A sells at a high price (Choice A).  Note that B earns less if it responds by charging a high price: it will earn either $375 (if Firm A charges a low price) or $380 (if A charges a high price).  Both are lower than what it earns by charging a low price ($390 if A charges a high price and $400 if A charges a low price). (Choice C)  Participants act in their own self-interest to maximize profits and do not adopt strategies that maximize the industry's profits to the detriment of their own profitability.  Although total profits are maximized when both firms charge a high price, in the absence of collusion, Firm B is better off charging a low price. Explain supply and demand relationships under oligopoly, including the optimal price and output for firms as well as pricing strategy

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: For a firm operating under perfect competition, the short-run supply function is best described as the:
new_option_b: marginal cost curve.
new_option_c: average total cost curve.
new_explanation_en: A firm's supply function reflects the quantities it will produce at various price (P) levels.  Profit-maximizing firms produce output such that the incremental costs of the last unit produced (ie, marginal cost [MC]) equals the revenue received for that unit (ie, marginal revenue [MR]). Under perfect competition, individual firms cannot affect equilibrium (ie, market) price—they are "price takers"—so they face perfectly elastic demand curves.  Therefore, the market equilibrium price is the firm's MR (ie, P = MR).  All else equal, starting from equilibrium, if demand: increases and the equilibrium price rises, firms increase output, despite a rise in MCs, if the increase in cost does not exceed the additional revenue, or decreases and the equilibrium price falls, firms decrease output, thereby reducing MC to the point that the cost of the last item produced is no longer greater than the revenue from that unit. In the image, the quantities of output (Q  and Q ) for two levels of demand (D  and D ) also reflect the market equilibrium prices under perfect competition, since P = MR.  The bolded portion of the MC curve indicates how output varies between those price levels, or in other words, the quantities the firm is willing to produce (ie, its supply function) over that price range. (Choice A)  Although the changes in variable cost are reflected in MC, it is the MC curve, not the variable cost curve, that is a firm's supply function. (Choice C)  The average total cost (ATC) curve indicates average costs per unit as output varies but does not reflect how output changes as prices change.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: An analyst gathers current price and cost information about a firm operating in a perfectly competitive market: Based only on this information, which of the following is the firm's optimal course of action in the long run?
new_option_b: Exit the market
new_option_c: Continue to operate as is
new_explanation_en: A firm's cost structure drives the decision to continue operating or exit the market.  In the long run, the focus is on the relationship between the market price and average (total) cost (ATC).  ATC is calculated as the total cost per unit, including fixed costs and variable costs, to produce a certain volume of units. In general, a firm should operate as long as it is earning at least a zero economic profit, which means price must equal or exceed ATC.  If price is below ATC, as in this scenario, the firm has essentially "locked in an economic loss" and should exit the market (see the exhibit). In the short run, the relationship between price and the average variable cost (AVC) (eg, labor, raw material) per unit is the decision driver. Typically, fixed costs are assumed to be irrelevant in the short run.  Therefore, as long as price is above AVC, the firm is covering some portion of fixed costs and is better off operating than shutting down.  However, in the long run, operating with price above AVC but below ATC is not sustainable (Choice C). (Choice A)  Firms operating in a perfectly competitive environment cannot raise their prices since any firm's individual demand curve is perfectly elastic and the firms will sell nothing at a price above the market price.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: For a duopoly (ie, two-firm market that is a special form of oligopoly) in equilibrium, which of the following choices best describes a characteristic of the Cournot assumption?
new_option_b: Firms cooperate to set output and price.
new_option_c: A firm's output is constant in the long run.
new_explanation_en: Oligopoly pricing theories Theory Description Kinked demand curve Compete on price Differentiate with advertising and branding Cournot assumption Firms act independently and simultaneously Equilibrium (ie, stable price and output quantity) Nash equilibrium No cooperation (ie, collusion) Firms act in their own best interest Stackelberg (ie, first mover) Firms act dependently and sequentially Leader (ie, top dog) sets quantity, others respond Collusion Firms cooperate to set quantity and price Firms act in the industry's best interest Oligopoly is a market structure in which a small number of firms sell similar products, with nonprice competition varying by market.  For example, many consumer goods companies compete by differentiating products through advertising and branding.  High barriers to entry typically protect existing firms from new entrants. Oligopolistic firms may adopt various pricing strategies.  Since the Cournot assumption supposes a competitive market, demand and marginal revenue curves are downward sloping (ie, firms are not price takers).  Supply and prices adjust naturally until, at long-run equilibrium, output quantity and price stabilize for each firm. (Choice A)  The Stackelberg (ie, first-mover) pricing theory, not the Cournot assumption, supposes that firms act sequentially, with the market leader moving first. (Choice B)  The Cournot assumption, applied to a duopoly (ie, two-firm market) in equilibrium, supposes that both firms act simultaneously and independently, without collusion (ie, cooperation), to determine production quantities to maximize profits.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: If a firm is currently breaking even, it is most likely producing at the point where average revenue is equal to:
new_option_b: average fixed costs.
new_option_c: average variable costs.
new_explanation_en: A firm breaks even when total revenues are equal to total economic costs, and the firm earns an economic profit of zero.  This condition holds for both perfect competition and imperfect competition (eg, monopolist competition, oligopoly, and monopoly). Economic profit is typically lower than accounting profit since economic costs include both accounting and opportunity costs (eg, owner's required return).  Thus, a company may earn a positive accounting profit even if the economic profit is zero or negative. The breakeven point can also be expressed as when average revenue per unit equals average total costs per unit, which also results in an economic profit of zero: (Choices B and C)  Firms incur both variable and fixed costs.  Operating at a price equal to average fixed costs or average variable costs would mean that the firm was taking in revenue equal to its fixed costs or variable costs, thus not covering total costs.  As noted, breakeven occurs when total revenue equals total costs.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Characteristics for three oligopoly markets are as follows: Based only on this information, which of the markets has the highest probability of successful collusion?
new_option_b: Market B
new_option_c: Market C
new_explanation_en: Collusion occurs when competing firms work together, either informally or by formal agreement (ie, a cartel), to maximize industry profits by reducing output and/or raising prices.  For example, airlines may agree to charge the same price for specific routes, or oil producers may set output quotas.  Collusion can be hard to maintain, however, as competitors have incentive to agree but then "cheat" and increase output and/or undercut the oligopoly price. Certain market characteristics tend to support successful collusion: A smaller number of firms means that coordination and monitoring are easier, and profits from any collusion will be divided among fewer firms. Where firms have similar cost structures, the firms face similar profitability hurdles, making it easier to agree on the oligopoly price. If products are homogeneous, the potential to compete through product differentiation is limited and collusion is more attractive. In this case, all four characteristics for Market A indicate a higher probability of successful collusion; only two characteristics of Market B and one of Market C suggest collusion would be successful (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A firm in a perfectly competitive industry increases production capacity, but then experiences an increase in its average total cost of production. To counteract the diseconomies of scale, the firm should most appropriately:
new_option_b: diversify into a different industry.
new_option_c: increase marketing expenditures.
new_explanation_en: Diseconomies of scale (ie, higher unit costs) typically result from a firm becoming too complex or too geographically dispersed to manage effectively.  Higher unit costs also can result from excessive capacity relative to demand.  This means that fixed costs are spread over small volumes. Average cost curves show the cost per unit at various levels of output.  Each short-run average cost (SAC) curve reflects a different level of fixed costs.  All possible SAC curves determine the long-run average cost (LAC) curve.  Decreasing returns to scale (ie, diseconomies of scale) are illustrated by the upward sloping portion of the LAC curve to the right of Q .  LAC is minimized at the level of capacity implied by SAC . The situation posited in the question implies a firm that has expanded excessively, reaching too large a scale of operations to manage effectively (SAC ).  The firm should scale down (eg, close or sell off factories) to achieve lower average costs per unit of output.  Inversely, a firm operating at a lower level of capacity (SAC ) could reduce costs (ie, realize economies of scale) by expanding. (Choice B)  Diseconomies of scale often result from excessive size or complexity.  Diversifying into other industries increases the complexity of operations and doesn't directly address the problem of excessive unit cost. (Choice C)  Increased marketing expenditures add to costs, exacerbating the problem of excessive costs.  Increased marketing might be a solution in market structures where prices can be raised but is not a viable alternative in a perfectly competitive market.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: In the short term, for a firm operating under perfect competition, the most appropriate point for a shutdown is when:
new_option_a: marginal cost falls below average total cost.
new_option_b: market price falls below average variable cost.
new_option_c: average total cost equals average variable cost.
new_explanation_en: From an economic perspective, a firm breaks even when total revenues equal total economic costs and economic profit is zero, or (per unit) when average revenue equals average total cost (ATC).  Total costs include both fixed and variable costs.  Marginal revenue (MR) is the additional revenue generated from selling one additional unit, and marginal cost (MC) is the cost of producing one additional unit. With perfect competition, the firm has a horizontal demand curve, and therefore MR and average revenue are both equal to the market price.  The breakeven point is when MR = ATC = MC; at this point, MR "covers" ATC, including fixed and variable costs. In the short term, fixed costs are sunk costs since fixed costs are independent of quantity produced.  If the price falls so that MR < MC, the firm can continue to produce as long as MR is greater than or equal to average variable cost (AVC): since variable costs are still covered, there is still some profit from production (Choice A).  However, if the price falls such that MR < MC < AVC, then the firm is not covering either its fixed or variable costs and should shut down. (Choice C)  AVC is a component of ATC and therefore will never be equal, no matter how many units are produced.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: In a perfect competition market structure, the industry demand curve is best described as:
new_option_b: perfectly price-elastic.
new_option_c: perfectly price-inelastic.
new_explanation_en: A perfect competition market structure has many sellers, all of whom sell an identical product.  Each seller's individual demand function (ie, demand curve) is perfectly elastic, meaning each can sell as many units of the product as it desires, but only at the market price.  No seller in this market structure has the power to change the price. Although each seller's own demand function in a perfectly competitive industry is perfectly elastic, this is not the case for the industry's demand function.  For nearly all products, as the price changes, the quantity demanded moves in the opposite direction, so the industry demand curve is negatively sloped. (Choice B)  A perfectly price-elastic demand curve is horizontal.  A perfectly elastic demand curve is the curve for each seller in a perfectly competitive industry. (Choice C)  A perfectly price-inelastic demand curve is vertical.  This means that there is a specific quantity demanded for the product that does not change, regardless of any change in price.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A firm operating in a perfectly competitive market has average variable costs of KRW 80,000 and average total costs of KRW 100,000.  The market equilibrium price is KRW 75,000.  Based only on this information, in the short run, the firm should most likely:
new_option_b: increase advertising.
new_option_c: continue to operate as is.
new_explanation_en: A firm's cost structure drives the decision to continue operating or exit the market.  In the short run, the relationship between price and average variable cost (AVC) is the decision driver.  AVC is the average variable cost per unit to make a product (eg, labor, raw material). When the market price (KWR 75,000) is below AVC (KWR 80,000), the revenue per unit does not cover the cost of production.  If the firm is not covering variable costs, it is also not covering any of its fixed costs, which strengthens the argument that it should exit the market. (Choice B)  Since firms operating in a perfectly competitive environment are price takers (face a horizontal demand curve) and sell products that are perfect substitutes for each other, increasing advertising will have no effect on units sold (or revenue per unit). (Choice C)  Continuing to operate is an appropriate short-run decision if the market price is at or above AVC.  In that case, the firm would be covering all variable costs and some fixed costs (eg, rent, interest payments) and is better off operating instead of shutting down.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: In perfectly competitive markets, each individual firm's demand curve is:
new_option_b: infinitely elastic.
new_option_c: perfectly inelastic.
new_explanation_en: Perfectly competitive markets are characterized by numerous competitors selling an undifferentiated (homogenous) product.  All firms are small relative to the total market for the product.  Each can sell as much as they could produce at the market (ie, equilibrium) price.  Additional output by one firm cannot impact the equilibrium price.  Consequently, each faces an infinitely elastic or flat demand curve. Nothing prevents a firm from cutting the price of its output; however, doing so would not benefit the company.  Unlike other industry structures, a firm operating in a perfectly competitive market could sell all it can produce at the market price.  Selling at a below-market price implies forgoing profits. (Choice A)  Unitary elastic refers to downward-sloping demand curves that reflect equal percentage changes in quantity and price (ie, a 1:1 ratio). Unitary elasticity means that the sensitivity of quantity demanded to changes in unit price varies across price levels.  Trade-offs between price and quantity are typical for firms operating outside of purely competitive industries.  Such firms can impact the demand for their product by raising or lowering price. (Choice C)  Perfectly inelastic or vertical demand curves imply that the quantity demanded is unaffected by price.  An example is demand for a drug that is currently the only effective treatment for a life-threatening disease.  Perfectly inelastic demand is not a likely characteristic of any market in the long run.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: If firms' supply curves can be used to determine the optimal, profit-maximizing price, those firms are most likely operating in:
new_option_b: perfect competition.
new_option_c: monopolistic competition.
new_explanation_en: A firm's supply function reflects the quantities it will produce at various prices.  All firms maximize profits at the level of output at which marginal cost (MC) = marginal revenue (MR); therefore, a firm's MC curve can be used to determine the optimal quantity of output.  In a market with perfect competition, where a firm has perfectly elastic demand (ie, it is a price taker) and price (P) = MR, MC can also be used to determine the price that maximizes profit (ie, price at which MC = MR = P).  Thus, the MC curve reflects the firm's willingness to supply and defines its supply curve. In other market structures, such as oligopoly, monopoly, and monopolistic competition, P ≠ MR due to inelasticity of demand.  The optimal price is determined by the demand curve, which reflects the inelastic demand.  Although MC can be used to determine the optimal quantity of output, the MC curve does not reflect the firm's willingness to supply at various prices and does not define the supply curve (Choices A and C). For a firm in perfect competition, long-run equilibrium means producing a quantity of output that minimizes the firm's average total cost, which equals the market price for its product.  At this level of output economic profit is zero, so Total cost = Total revenue, or Price per unit × Quantity of units sold = Average total cost per unit × Units sold. Under the monopoly and monopolistic competition structures, firms have some pricing power, but any new price must be offered to all customers; therefore, MR ≠ Change in price multiplied × Change in quantity sold.  Although the relationship between the average revenue and MR is similar under both structures, in general, the demand curve for monopolistic competitors is flatter (ie, more elastic).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A cheese producer competes by creating a differentiated, high-quality cheese that sells for a premium price in the very crowded local retail cheese market.  The market structure that this cheese producer operates in is best described as:
new_option_b: perfect competition.
new_option_c: monopolistic competition.
new_explanation_en: Monopolistic competition is a market structure characterized by numerous competitors selling differentiated products and by low barriers to entry.  These companies compete on price, quality, marketing, and/or location. Innovative products or strategies can allow firms in monopolistic competition to temporarily achieve above-average levels of profitability.  These above-average earnings are known as economic profits.  In monopolistically competitive markets, economic profits are quickly erased by the numerous existing competitors or by new competitors, allowed by the low barriers to entry. (Choice A)  Oligopolies have few competitors, deliver homogenous products (eg, crude oils), and have high barriers to entry. (Choice B)  Perfect competition markets are characterized by homogenous products, low barriers to entry, and firms with no control over the market price (ie, price takers).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Profit-maximizing monopolists most likely attempt to produce a level of output at which marginal cost equals:
new_option_b: marginal revenue.
new_option_c: average total cost.
new_explanation_en: Marginal cost (MC) is the increase in total expenditure for each additional unit produced.  Marginal revenue (MR) is the increase in total revenue for each additional unit sold.  Monopolists can offer products at a higher price, as demand allows, to increase total revenues, or at a lower price to expand unit sales.  If there is no ability to engage in price discrimination, the lower price must be offered to all customers.  MR accounts for the impact on total revenue of all units being sold at a new price. As shown in the image above, if monopolists produce and sell at quantities: between 0 and Q , MC is decreasing faster than MR, which increases profit margins and total profits. between Q  and Q , MC is increasing, which decreases profit margins; however, since MC is less than MR, total profits are still increasing. greater than Q , MC is greater than MR and total profits are reduced. Therefore, total profit is maximized at the level of production at which MC equals MR. (Choices A and C)  A marginal cost that equals either the average revenue or average total cost implies that production and sales levels are exceeding the profit-maximizing level of output (Q ).  Cutting prices to expand sales beyond Q would increase revenue by less than the additional costs, thus reducing total profit.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: The following data is for a firm operating under perfect competition: Quantity produced Total economic cost (€) 100 510 101 511 102 513 103 516 104 520 105 525 106 531 If the price per unit is €5, economic profits are maximized when the firm produces:
new_option_b: 105 units.
new_option_c: 106 units.
new_explanation_en: Under perfect competition, firms face a horizontal demand curve with the market price equal to marginal revenue.  The level of output that maximizes economic profit is also the economic breakeven, where marginal revenue (MR) equals marginal cost (MC) and average total cost (ATC): MR = MC = ATC.  At that point, production of: additional units would result in an economic loss, wherein MR < MC and ATC, and fewer units would result in a missed profit, wherein MR > MC. In this case, profit is maximized at 105 units, the point at which MR per unit (ie, €5 market price), MC, and ATC are all equal. Production data at a unit price of €5 Quantity produced Total cost MC per unit MR per unit ATC per unit 100 510 − 5 5.10 101 511 1 5 5.07 102 513 2 5 5.03 103 516 3 5 5.01 104 520 4 5 5.00 105 525 5 5 5.00 106 531 6 5 5.03 Note:  Although this question specifically addresses perfect competition, the condition that firms maximize profits when MR = MC applies to all market structures. (Choice A)  At 104 units of production, ATC per unit is the same as for 105 units (€5.00).  However, MC (€4) is less than MR (€5) and still rising, so the firm has not yet reached maximum economic profit. (Choice C)  At 106 units of production, both MC (€6) and ATC (€5.03) are greater than MR (€5), so the production of the 106th unit would result in an economic loss.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.01 Firms and Market Structures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: For a firm operating in perfect competition, which of the following statements is most accurate with respect to long-run equilibrium?
new_option_a: The firm can expect to earn zero economic profit.
new_option_b: Zero economic profit means that the firm generated an accounting loss.
new_option_c: The firm should produce goods at a level at which marginal revenue exceeds average total cost.
new_explanation_en: Economic profit is the difference between a firm's total revenue, which is price (P) × quantity sold (Q ), and its total cost, which is cost (C) × Q .  Total cost consists of accounting expenses plus opportunity costs; opportunity costs include the owner's expected return from the business. Any firm in a perfectly competitive industry should always produce the quantity of goods at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost.  In the short run, a firm can earn an economic profit; this is reflected in the yellow rectangle shown above.  However, since there are no barriers to entry in perfect competition, additional sellers are attracted by the potential economic profit and enter the industry. The increased supply from these new entrants causes the market price to fall to the point where marginal revenue, marginal cost, and average cost meet (Choice C).  The new equilibrium quantity is at Q', which represents the point at which TR equals TC and economic profit equals zero. (Choice B)  Economic profit equals accounting profit (ie, total revenue − accounting expenses) minus opportunity costs.  Opportunity costs include a rate of return to the business owner.  If economic profit equals zero, then the formula can be rearranged so that accounting profit = owner's return.  This means that accounting profit is positive, not negative.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.02 Understanding Business Cycles - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: The following table lists various economic indicators and the trend in each one over the past several months for an economy. Economic Indicator Trend Unemployment Record low Unit labor costs Modestly rising Industrial production growth Steadily higher Residential building permits Steady decline New orders for manufacturing Steady decline Long-term bond yields Declined 1% Short-term bond yields Stable This mix of economic indicators most likely forecasts near-term future economic:
new_option_b: acceleration.
new_option_c: deceleration.
new_explanation_en: Certain economic and financial measures have historically exhibited consistent patterns indicating the stage of the business cycle.  These economic indicators are characterized as leading, coincident, or lagging indicators. Leading indicators provide the most value to investment practitioners since they signal changes in real GDP several months to a year in advance.  Coincident indicators move largely in tandem with the economy, and lagging indicators trail changes in the economy by several months or quarters.  How specific indicators are classified will vary from country to country, but leading indicators that are consistent across most economies include: Interest rate spread Residential building permits/construction Stock market performance New manufacturing/machinery orders Business confidence/expectations In this scenario, all three leading indicators are indicating a period of economic deceleration or slowing growth in the coming quarters. Residential building permits and new orders for manufacturing have been in steady decline.  The interest rate spread is the difference between short-term rates and long-term rates.  A narrowing of the spread, as is the case here (ie, the yield curve flattened by 1%), implies economic deceleration.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: In an economy that operates under an exchange rate targeting policy, which of the following conditions is most likely?
new_option_a: The central bank is required to maintain a fixed policy interest rate.
new_option_b: Monetary policy can focus on internal rather than external considerations.
new_option_c: Target country inflation (deflation) is imported regardless of the effect on the domestic economy.
new_explanation_en: Monetary policy targets Stated policy target Long-run economic goal Country characteristics Inflation Fixed rate or range for specified price index Price stability leading to better long- run performance Larger, more developed economies Interest rates Target adjusted over business cycle Optimize across multiple goals (employment, GDP growth) Exchange rate Fixed rate or range versus target currency Stability versus economies of major trading partners Smaller, less developed with significant import/export sectors The goal of monetary policy is to optimize economic welfare, although central banks are given a variety of policy targets intended to attain that goal.  Central banks may have: One policy target (ie, single mandate) that guides all policy actions: A specific inflation target (eg, 2%) or a specified range An exchange rate target, which is a fixed level or band of values versus a major currency (eg, EUR) Multiple policy targets that seek an optimal balance among potentially conflicting goals: High employment GDP growth Stable prices Stable exchange rate When a country uses exchange rate targeting, its policies are designed to maintain an exchange rate target (or range) with another currency, usually from a larger and/or more stable economy.  As a result, if the target currency's economy experiences inflation or deflation, so does the economy that targets it. In this situation, since all policy actions must be aimed at maintaining the targeted currency exchange value, the targeting economy gives up monetary policy independence.  This may adversely affect both the targeting economy and its ability to address any adverse effects.  For example, exchange rate targeting may keep a central bank from exercising independent monetary policies based solely on domestic conditions, such as maintaining a fixed policy interest rate or adjusting monetary policy (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A demand curve for money is depicted in the graph below: Which of the following best explains the shape of the curve between M  and M ?
new_option_b: Policy rate of zero
new_option_c: Neutral rate of interest
new_explanation_en: There are limits to the effectiveness of monetary policy.  This is often true in a deflationary environment when the demand curve for money becomes horizontal (ie, infinitely elastic), as shown in the graphs above.  A liquidity trap occurs when the quantity of money continues to expand but fails to lower interest rates since economic agents would rather hold cash than borrow or lend.  At this point, monetary policy stops stimulating economic activity and loses its effectiveness. A central bank's monetary policy tools depend on others to implement them.  For example, a central bank can lower interest rates or reduce reserve requirements but cannot force anyone to borrow or lend.  A liquidity trap is an example of such ineffectiveness. The economist John Maynard Keynes is credited with coining the phrase "pushing on a string" to describe the limitations of monetary policy.  It is easy to visualize how pulling on a string can bring something closer and how pushing on a string has no effect since it crumples and goes nowhere.  In a liquidity trap, the central bank is effectively "pushing on a string." (Choice B)  Central bank policy is not constrained by the zero boundary; policy rates can and have been negative. The demand for money does not necessarily stagnate at a zero-bound policy rate. (Choice C)  The neutral rate of interest is the central bank's policy rate that neither slows nor accelerates economic activity and is not specifically associated with the money demand curve.0 Describe qualities of effective central banks; contrast their use of inflation, interest rate, and exchange rate targeting in expansionary or contractionary monetary policy; and describe the limitations of monetary policy

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Quantitative easing is operationally similar to which monetary policy tool?
new_option_b: Conducting open market operations
new_option_c: Increasing or decreasing the policy rate
new_explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Quantitative easing (QE) is operationally equivalent to buying securities through open market operations.  QE is pursued after other expansionary policies (eg, decreasing interest rates) have failed to return the economy to its potential growth rate.  QE is intended to prevent a recession from becoming a depression.  The differences between open market operations and QE are the scale of the purchases, the types of securities purchased, and the sellers. In the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, QE purchases were of unprecedented magnitude (multiple trillions of USD or similar values of EUR, GBP, and JPY).  Furthermore, whereas open market operations normally dealt in short-term government securities, QE purchases were often long-term government securities and securities of other issuers (eg, corporate bonds).  Also, many sellers were not from the usual group of banks and market makers. (Choices A and C)  Neither changing the reserve requirement nor adjusting the policy rate (also called the official interest rate or official policy rate) requires central banks to trade securities; therefore, neither is operationally similar to QE.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Large open market purchases of government securities by a central bank are used to decrease:
new_option_b: domestic inflation rates.
new_option_c: domestic currency's exchange value.
new_explanation_en: Monetary policy actions are typically used to affect one or more of the following domestic economic variables: GDP growth, inflation, interest rates, and/or currency value.  Monetary policies are either: expansionary, which are typically used to increase economic growth when it is below potential GDP or when the economy is in recession, or contractionary, which are typically used to reduce inflation expectations and often accompanied by policies that reduce expected GDP growth rates. A policy of central bank open market purchases of securities is an expansionary policy.  Such purchases increase commercial bank reserves, in turn leading to an increase in the money supply.  All else equal, this causes domestic interest rates to decrease and investors to invest in currencies with relatively higher interest rates, resulting in a decrease in the domestic currency's exchange value. (Choices A and B)  Open market security purchases are indicative of an expansionary monetary policy, which would be used to increase GDP growth rates and put upward pressure on domestic inflation.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following is least accurate regarding monetary policy tools?
new_option_a: Bank reserve requirements are independent of the central bank policy rate.
new_option_b: Banks typically increase base rates when the central bank increases the policy rate.
new_option_c: Bank reserve requirements increase when the central bank buys securities from banks.
new_explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Central banks use monetary policy tools to manipulate the money supply to achieve price stability.  When the economy is growing too fast and inflation is high, central banks will enact contractionary policies to reduce the money supply to moderate growth and inflation.  When the economy is growing slowly and inflation is muted, central banks will enact expansionary policies to increase the money supply to accelerate growth. Central banks use open market operations (ie, buying [selling] of securities from [to] banks) to manipulate the amount of bank reserves.  Banks reserves increase when the central bank buys securities from banks.  Conversely, bank reserves decrease when central banks sell securities. Note that the open market operations change the amount of bank reserves, and not the bank reserve requirement. (Choice A)  The bank reserve requirement and the central bank's policy rate are two separate monetary policy tools for influencing the amount of loanable money. (Choice B)  Central banks will typically lend to banks at the policy rate.  When policy rates change, banks will adjust their own base lending rates accordingly.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A country pursues tight fiscal policy and easy monetary policy for several years.  Which of the following are the most likely consequences for the size of the public and private sectors relative to the country's GDP?
new_option_a: Larger public sector and smaller private sector
new_option_b: Smaller public sector and larger private sector
new_option_c: No change in their relative sizes as both sectors would be equally affected
new_explanation_en: Economic activity is divided between the public sector (eg, government bureaucracy, the military) and private sector (eg, businesses, consumers). The private sector accounts for the bulk of economic activity in most countries.  However, the public sector accounts for a significant portion of GDP in most developed economies.  Since monetary policy and fiscal policy impact the economy through different channels, the specific policy mix may impact the two sectors differently. Tight fiscal policy (eg, lower government spending) may result in slower growth, if not outright shrinkage, of the public sector.  Easy monetary policy (eg, increased open market purchases) likely causes lower interest rates, stimulating expansion of the private sector through more consumer spending and business investment.  The mix of tight fiscal and easy monetary policy usually results in the private sector accounting for a larger proportion of GDP and the public sector a smaller proportion (Choices A and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following is least likely a function of a central bank?
new_option_b: Determine infrastructure spending
new_option_c: Manage foreign exchange and gold reserves
new_explanation_en: Typical roles of central banks Monetary roles Banking roles Manage money supply Implement monetary policy Manage foreign exchange and gold reserves Act as lenders of last resort Oversee the banking system Regulate the payment system Serve as government's and bankers' bank Fiscal policy (ie, government management of expenditures and receipts to affect economic growth) is executed by governments, not central banks.  Infrastructure spending is a fiscal policy tool used to provide public goods (eg, hospitals, schools) and stimulate economic activity. Central banks are responsible for monetary and banking functions.  For example, central banks manage foreign currency and gold reserves by buying/selling as needed to maintain liquidity and stabilize national currency (Choice C).  In addition, central banks regulate payment processing systems to ensure efficient financial transactions (Choice A).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following factors may limit the impact of expansionary monetary policy in a deflationary economy?
new_option_a: Short-term interest rates cannot be reduced to 0% by central banks.
new_option_b: Central bank policy may fail to induce banks to increase lending activity.
new_option_c: Central bank open market operations may be unable to sufficiently expand bank reserves.
new_explanation_en: Monetary policy impacts the real economy indirectly.  Central banks attempt to influence the direction of the real economy by manipulating bank reserves.  Expansionary monetary policies create excess bank reserves with the intent of expanding the money supply, resulting in lower interest rates and more rapid GDP growth. The money supply expands only if the banks use the reserves to make loans.  However, banks must expect to profit from making a loan. Furthermore, businesses normally borrow only if the loan proceeds can be profitably invested.  A weak economy undermines the incentives of both borrowers and lenders.  The inability of central banks to induce more lending activity can impede the transmission of monetary policy actions to the real economy. (Choice A)  Interest rates can be reduced below 0%.  Several major central banks (eg, Bank of Japan, European Central Bank) have pursued policies resulting in negative short-term interest rates. (Choice C)  Independent central banks generally face no limits on their ability to create excess reserves through open market purchases.  The US Federal Reserve created trillions of dollars of bank reserve in the attempt to foster economic recovery after the financial crisis of 2008.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following most likely limits a central bank's ability to implement effective expansionary monetary policy?  The central bank is unable to:
new_option_a: reduce the policy interest rate below the neutral rate.
new_option_b: increase the amount of excess reserves held by commercial banks.
new_option_c: increase businesses and consumers' willingness to hold bank deposits.
new_explanation_en: In a system of fractional reserve banking, banks hold reserves to back their deposits.  Central banks directly control commercial bank reserves but not the money supply.  To increase the money supply, the usual transition mechanism for expansionary monetary policy is: central banks create excess bank reserves by buying securities through open market operations or reducing reserve requirements for commercial banks; commercial banks use their excess reserves to make loans; borrowers use loan proceeds to make payments; and recipients of the payments deposit the money into their banks. The increase in deposits increases the money supply. However, the effectiveness of expansionary policy may be limited by businesses' and consumers' unwillingness to hold money in bank deposits (eg, when interest rates are low).  Furthermore, money in deposits is exposed to the bank's credit risk, which may in turn cause withdrawals from the bank.  This reduces the money supply and limits the effect of the expansionary policy. (Choices A and B)  Central banks face few limits on setting policy rates or creating excess reserves.  Central banks can pursue these policies to the extent they deem appropriate, so the inability to reduce the policy rate or increase excess bank reserves are not impediments to pursuing expansionary policies.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.04 Monetary Policy - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following central bank actions is most likely considered expansionary monetary policy?
new_option_b: Selling government bonds through open market operations
new_option_c: Holding the policy rate constant as the neutral rate falls below it
new_explanation_en: Monetary policy tools Tool Description Expansionary Contractionary Open market operations Trade securities (usually government securities) Buy securities Sell securities Policy interest rate Set interest rate used to signal markets Lower Raise Reserve requirements Set percentage of bank deposits held in reserves Decrease Increase Expansionary monetary policies are used to increase economic growth during periods of decline (eg, when output is below potential GDP).  For example, a central bank can implement an expansionary policy of increasing excess reserves in the commercial banking system by: making open market purchases, reducing reserve requirements, which turns some required reserves into excess reserves, or reducing the policy interest rate, which reduces the costs banks incur when borrowing reserves. Excess reserves encourage increased lending since banks can earn higher returns by making loans than by holding reserves.  This expands the money supply and lowers interest rates, leading to growth in borrowing, investment, and consumption, and thus an expanded GDP. (Choice B)  A central bank conducts open market sales to reduce its holdings of government bonds when implementing a contractionary monetary policy.  Commercial banks use reserves to purchase the bonds, which contracts the money supply. (Choice C)  A central bank holds its policy interest rate constant as the neutral rate of interest falls below the policy rate in order to tighten credit conditions.  This inaction by a central bank is contractionary, not expansionary.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.05 Introduction to Geopolitics - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Three geopolitical risks may affect a country's investment returns: Event Risk Likelihood Velocity Impact Size Impact Breadth A High High Moderate Discrete B Moderate High High Broad C High Medium Low Broad Within the context of a country's investment returns, based on only the above information, which event warrants the highest level of risk assessment?
new_option_b: Event B
new_option_c: Event C
new_explanation_en: Event risk Likelihood Velocity Impact size Impact breadth A High High Moderate Discrete B Moderate High High Broad C High Medium Low Broad Analysts evaluate geopolitical risks to gauge their potential impact on investment returns.  To do so, an analyst collectively assesses an event's: Likelihood (ie, probability of the event) Velocity of the impact (ie, how quickly the event may impact investment returns) Size and nature of the impact (ie, how large the impact may be, and its overall reach) In this scenario, Event B poses the most significant risk.  Even though it has only a moderate probability of occurring, its impact on the country's economy will be fast, intense, and broad-based if it occurs.  As an example, pandemics do not occur frequently, but when a pandemic occurs, its disastrous impact on an economy will be swift. (Choice A)  Although Event A has high probability and high velocity, its impact is moderate and discrete (ie, narrowly limited to one sector or to a few sectors).  Therefore, its threat is not as significant as Event B's. (Choice C)  Compared with Event B, Event C has lower impact and takes longer to move the market.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following trade policies is most appropriate for a country to enact if it is trying to reduce a large trade deficit?
new_option_a: Reduce import tariffs on raw materials and manufactured goods by an average of 50%.
new_option_b: Impose import quotas limiting foreigners to 20% of a domestic market in which imports constitute 5% of the market.
new_option_c: Negotiate a voluntary export restraint agreement with a country running a large trade surplus with the domestic economy.
new_explanation_en: Quotas, tariffs, and voluntary export restraints are the policies most commonly used to reduce trade deficits.  Imposing quotas or levying tariffs on imports directly impacts commercial counterparties.  Alternatively, agreements with foreign governments are used to restrain their firms from exporting to the domestic market.  Although the specific mechanisms of each policy differ, all restrict foreign sales in the domestic market.  All else constant, the trade balance is favorably affected as reduced imports shrink trade deficits or increase trade surpluses. Voluntary export restraints are negotiated with countries currently running large surpluses.  Foreign governments agreeing to constrain their exports will reduce domestic imports.  Effective voluntary export restraint agreements reduce trade deficits. (Choice A)  Reducing tariffs on raw materials and manufactured goods tends to make those foreign-sourced items less expensive.  Tariff cuts increase imports, which leads to higher trade deficits. (Choice B)  Import quotas normally reduce trade deficits.  Limiting foreign producers to a 20% market share in a market where foreign sales account for only 5% of sales is an ineffective way to reduce the trade deficit.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: An analyst has compiled the following information: Economic Model Coffee Price ($) Sugar Price ($) Country A Autarky 0.70 0.50 Country B Autarky 1.00 0.45 Country C Autarky 0.90 0.60 Country Z Open economy 1.10 0.40 Country Z is an open economy, trading at world prices, and does not currently trade with any of the other three countries.  Assuming equal consumption of both commodities, which country will benefit the most from a trading relationship with Country Z?
new_option_b: Country B
new_option_c: Country C
new_explanation_en: An autarky is a country that produces all goods and services consumed internally and does not trade with others.  An autarkic economy is considered a closed economy.  Domestic prices within a country are a function of its ability to produce those goods with only domestic resources and are known as the autarkic prices. Countries that do not place restrictions on imports and exports are known as open economies.  Open economies are said to practice free trade as they import and export at the world's price for goods and services (eg, Country Z). The further away the world price is relative to a country's autarkic price, the greater the potential trade benefit for the autarky.  A country's terms of trade benefit the most if world export prices are greater than its autarkic price and world import prices are less than its autarkic price since the country can achieve greater purchasing power. In this scenario, all the autarkies produce coffee below world price and sugar above world price. Thus, if all three traded with other countries, each would export coffee and import sugar.  The net terms-of-trade improvement would be greatest for Country A since it would sell (ie, export) coffee at the world price of $1.10 and buy (ie, import) sugar at the world price of $0.40, netting a $0.50 improvement. (Choices B and C)  The net terms-of-trade improvement for Country B is $0.15. For Country C, it is $0.40.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A country recently imposed a tariff on apples of €300 per metric ton.  The pre-tariff price for apples was €2,000 per metric ton.  The table below shows the quantity demanded and the quantity supplied by domestic producers, along with the pre- and post-tariff prices of apples: Pre-Tariff Post-Tariff Quantity demanded (metric tons) 200 150 Quantity supplied (domestic producers) 110 130 Price per metric ton €2,000 €2,300 The image below shows the market for apples in this country: The area labeled A in the image represents an increase in:
new_option_b: consumer surplus.
new_option_c: government revenue.
new_explanation_en: A tariff is one type of trade restraint.  It is a tax on imported goods that is usually paid by domestic consumers in the form of higher prices. Although tariffs are intended to protect domestic producers, they often lead to  inefficiencies in an economy's production and consumption functions. Area A in the diagram above represents an increase in the producer surplus.  This surplus is the sum of two components: The higher revenue for the pre-tariff quantity sold:  Before the tariff, domestic producers sold 110 metric tons of apples for €2,000 per metric ton.  They now sell those 110 metric tons for €2,300 per metric ton. The revenue generated from the additional quantity produced:  After the tariff, domestic producers increased their output from 110 to 130 metric tons. (Choice B)  The tariff results in an increase in producer surplus but it also causes a decrease, not an increase, in consumer surplus.  The decrease consists of the sum of areas A, B, C, and D in the diagram. (Choice C)  The government revenue from the tariff is the amount shown in area C in the diagram.  It represents the amount of imports (ie, the difference between the quantity demanded by domestic consumers and the quantity supplied by domestic producers) multiplied by the tariff.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A country that is a price taker in the international market imposes a per-unit tariff of €50 on imported mobile phones.  The table below shows domestic consumption, domestic production, and mobile phone prices before and after the tariff's imposition: Before Tariff After Tariff Domestic quantity demanded (thousands) 8,200 7,000 Quantity supplied (domestic suppliers) (thousands) 4,000 6,500 Price (per phone) €200 €250 The total deadweight loss (in €) from the imposition of the tariff is closest to:
new_option_b: 62.5 million
new_option_c: 92.5 million
new_explanation_en: A tariff is one type of trade restraint.  It is a tax on imported goods that is usually paid as a higher price for the goods and usually results in a loss to the net welfare of the economy.  Tariffs cause inefficiencies in both the supply and production functions of the economy; these losses are known as deadweight losses.  In the diagram above, the supply deadweight loss is Region B and the demand deadweight loss is Region D. Before the tariff, all suppliers had per-unit production costs of €200 or less.  The tariff caused the price to increase to €250 so domestic suppliers whose production costs were greater than €200 could now compete.  However, domestic supply increased (from 4 million to 6.5 million) while domestic demand decreased (from 8.2 million to 7 million), therefore the additional domestic supply represented a reallocation of resources to phones when those resources could have been better employed elsewhere in the economy, creating an inefficiency. The demand deadweight loss is evidenced from the reduced domestic demand after the tariff.  Consumers who might have spent more than €200 for a phone but would not spend €250 were excluded from the market. The deadweight loss is the sum of the areas of the triangles B and D: Compare types of trade restrictions, such as tariffs, quotas, and export subsidies, and their economic implications

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\2. Economics\2.06 International Trade - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A country initiating a free trade agreement with its major trading partners is least likely to experience:
new_option_a: a wider variety of goods available to consumers.
new_option_b: increased employment in industries facing import competition.
new_option_c: higher wages in industries that expand due to increased exports.
new_explanation_en: Most economists believe greater overall welfare is attained when countries engage in international trade rather than by attempting self-sufficiency in meeting domestic demand (ie, autarky).  The gains from international trade derive from each country concentrating on the production of goods it produces relatively more efficiently and trading for goods it produces relatively less efficiently.  Gains result from specialization and economies of scale. The gains from trade are not shared equally; there are winners and losers.  On one hand, industries expanding to meet export opportunities will benefit from higher prices, due to increased foreign demand, and their employees will benefit from greater job opportunities and higher wages (Choice C).  On the other hand, the industries' domestic customers must pay higher prices.  In addition, industries facing import competition will suffer domestic market share decline.  As such industries contract, they will employ fewer workers. (Choice A)  Increased trade results in greater consumer choice.  This is due both to imported goods competing with domestic suppliers and the introduction of previously unavailable products.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\3. Portfolio Management\10.04 Introduction to Risk Management - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A company decides to shift price risk by entering into an options contract to buy a commodity.  As a consequence, the company most likely:
new_option_a: pays a premium at contract initiation.
new_option_b: is obligated to purchase the commodity in the future.
new_option_c: will exercise the option and purchase the underlying if prices decline.
new_explanation_en: Risk shifting refers to using derivatives (eg, forward commitments, contingent claims) to modify risk by moving exposure to a counterparty. Options (ie, contingent claims) require the buyer to pay a premium; they create the right, but not the obligation, to exercise the option and buy the underlying commodity at the contract price. If the price of the underlying increases, the fixed exercise price shifts the risk to the option's seller, who must sell the commodity at the (lower) exercise price.  However, the buyer can take advantage of any subsequent price declines, as it can let the option expire and buy the commodity at the lower market price. (Choice B)  Forward commitments, not options, obligate both parties to complete the transaction in the future. (Choice C)  The company will likely exercise if prices increase, not decline, in the future.  The option's exercise price serves as an upper limit in that if the commodity price increases, the company will exercise the option and will avoid having to pay the higher market price.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\3. Portfolio Management\10.04 Introduction to Risk Management - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: The purpose of the risk budgeting process is most likely:
new_option_b: eliminating the need for hedging.
new_option_c: setting a target return percentage.
new_explanation_en: Risk budgeting is the process of allocating a pre-determined level of risk to activities (eg, assets, investments) based on their underlying risk characteristics.  Risk budgeting can use one-dimensional, or one-factor, risk metrics such as an appropriate beta, which measures risk compared to the overall market.  Or, it may use multi-dimensional, or multi-factor, risk metrics such as size (eg, market cap), profitability (eg, net income), and style (eg, value, growth). These metrics guide management in daily risk-return trade-off decisions and help identify projects or assets that add value and have the highest return per unit of risk.  The company may choose to do more risky activities than planned yet stay within the risk tolerance by hedging or using insurance. (Choice B)  Eliminating the need for hedging is not the purpose of risk budgeting.  Risk management, of which risk budgeting is a fundamental element, does not eliminate risk but can help manage it with tools, including hedging. (Choice C)  Risk budgeting does not project target return information.  Risk budgeting focuses on asset and investment risk characteristics and metrics in the context of the pre-determined risk tolerance.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\3. Portfolio Management\10.04 Introduction to Risk Management - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following statements about elements of the risk management framework is most accurate?
new_option_a: The company determines how frequently it monitors risk positions.
new_option_b: The risk infrastructure team is responsible for determining the risk budget.
new_option_c: The identification phase includes the assessment of whether risk positions align with the desired risk tolerance.
new_explanation_en: The elements (ie, phases) of the risk management framework incorporate the enterprise-wide spectrum of risk management activities and help management stay within the company's risk tolerance while pursuing strategic goals.  These elements can be summarized as follows: Leadership determines the overall strategic operating goals, risk budget, and risk tolerance. Management allocates capital to risky projects and manages daily operations. The risk infrastructure (eg, people, systems) gathers, measures, monitors, and reports risk positions. How frequently a company monitors its risk position may vary among entities and depends upon the size of the organization, available resources, and to what degree risk affects decision-making.  For example, a large multinational entity may opt for daily monitoring, whereas a smaller regional firm may choose monthly monitoring. (Choice B)  Leadership determines the company's risk budget during the risk governance phase.  In the context of risk management, risk infrastructure refers to the people and systems that support the implementation of risk management with data collection, measurement, monitoring, and reporting. (Choice C)  Assessing the current risk position's alignment with the company's risk tolerance is done in the monitoring phase, not the identification phase.  During the identification phase, the company analyzes risk drivers (eg, economic factors, industry's intensity of competition, specific company factors). Things to remember The risk management framework includes risk governance, risk infrastructure, policies and procedures, identification, measurement, monitoring, reporting, and strategizing.  Companies determine how often to monitor risk positions based on the size of the organization, available resources, and to what degree risk affects decision-making. Describe features of a risk management framework

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\3. Portfolio Management\10.04 Introduction to Risk Management - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following is the most appropriate risk management measure for an equity option contract?
new_option_b: Delta
new_option_c: Value-at-risk
new_explanation_en: Derivative risk metrics: the Greeks Delta Price sensitivity to change in the value of the underlying asset Gamma Rate of change in the derivative's delta Rho Price sensitivity to changes in interest rates Theta Price sensitivity to changes in the passage of time Vega Price sensitivity to changes in volatility in the underlying asset Derivatives include a variety of securities, such as futures, options, swaps, and forwards.  In portfolio management, derivatives are widely used as a risk management tool to hedge risks.  These risks can range from macro risks, such as changes in interest rates or a widespread equity market decline, to micro risks, such as reaction to an upcoming quarterly earnings report. Although using derivatives to hedge risk is common, derivatives come with their own unique set of risks.  These risks are quantified as delta, gamma, rho, theta, and vega, which collectively are known as the Greeks.  Delta is commonly viewed as being the most important risk metric of the Greeks since it reflects the sensitivity of a derivative's price to changes in the price of the underlying asset. (Choice A)  Beta measures the sensitivity of an asset's risk relative to market risk.  A stock or an asset that has a beta of 1.0 has the same relative risk as the market.  Beta risk would be more applicable to the underlying equity or an equity portfolio, not the option itself. (Choice C)  Value-at-risk attempts to quantify the probability of a minimum expected loss over a specific period.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\3. Portfolio Management\10.04 Introduction to Risk Management - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: If a company shifts the price risk of a commodity by purchasing a futures contract, then the company most likely:
new_option_b: pays an initial premium.
new_option_c: has no future obligations.
new_explanation_en: Risk shifting refers to using derivatives (eg, forward commitments, contingent claims) to modify risk by moving exposure to a counterparty. Forward commitments (eg, futures, forwards, swaps) do not require a premium payment at initiation but obligate both parties to complete the transaction in the future (Choice C). The futures contract specifies the price of the commodity in the future, and thus eliminates the price uncertainty and limits the risk for the company purchasing the commodity.  The risk is shifted to the counterparty in the futures contract. (Choice B)  Risk shifting can also be achieved by using contingent claims (eg, options).  In contrast to forward commitments, options require the buyer to pay a premium.  The advantage of paying the premium is that the buyer is granted the right, but not the obligation, to exercise the option.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\3. Portfolio Management\10.04 Introduction to Risk Management - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Risk governance is most effective:
new_option_a: when applied to both core and non-core business units.
new_option_b: after a significant unexpected event when actual data become available.
new_option_c: when mainly focusing on mitigating risks that threaten the company's viability.
new_explanation_en: Risk governance is a "top-down" process that begins with a company's leadership (eg, board of directors) and provides enterprise-wide risk management guidance.  Leadership is responsible for providing context and transparency regarding operating goals and risk tolerances and then authorizing managers to run daily operations based on this guidance.  Leadership also continually provides high-level supervision regarding alignment of current risks and risk tolerance. Risk governance is most effective when it is used to identify and anticipate risky events (ie, when applied proactively).  Prior planning and analysis protect the company from starting from a defensive position when a crisis occurs.  Risk governance also applies to portfolio management activities and to a company's overall business operations. (Choice B)  Effective risk governance is proactive, not reactive.  In the absence of historical data, risk can be modeled using hypothetical data. (Choice C)  Leadership involvement in risk governance should not have a narrow scope.  Leadership's guidance and continual supervision encompass enterprise-wide risk activities that go beyond the company's survival. Things to remember Effective risk governance is implemented proactively, enterprise-wide, and from the top down.  Leadership provides guidance on how risk management is incorporated into daily operations and establishes a link between strategic goals and their inherent risks. Define risk governance and describe elements of effective risk governance

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\3. Portfolio Management\10.04 Introduction to Risk Management - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Using derivatives to modify a company's currency risk is best described as which of the following types of risk modification?
new_option_b: Risk transfer
new_option_c: Risk prevention
new_explanation_en: Risk shifting uses derivatives (eg, forward commitments and contingent claims/options) to modify risk by moving risk to a counterparty.  For example, a company that needs to pay a foreign supplier in the future may lock in the exchange rate by entering into a futures contract with a counterparty.  Doing so shifts the risk of exchange rate movements from the company to the counterparty. (Choice B)  Using risk transfer implies that a company has chosen to take on a risk and then modify that risk by purchasing insurance.  This transfers most of the risk to the insurance firm.  The loss to the company is limited to the cost of the insurance policy and any associated deductible. (Choice C)  Risk prevention or risk avoidance refers to when a company chooses to not accept a risk.  Here, the company could avoid currency exchange rate risk by purchasing only from domestic suppliers. Things to remember Risk shifting refers to the use of derivatives (ie, forward commitments and contingent claims/options) to modify risk.  Other risk modification methods include risk avoidance or prevention, self-insurance and diversification, and risk transfer. Describe methods for measuring and modifying risk exposures and factors to consider in choosing among the methods

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\4. Corporate Issuers\4.03 Corporate Governance - Conflicts, Mechanisms, Risks, and Benefits - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following is most accurate with regard to a dual-class share structure?
new_option_a: Shareholders have voting power equal to their percentage of ownership.
new_option_b: It may grant founders superior voting control even if their ownership level falls below 50%.
new_option_c: It typically grants outside shareholders greater voting power than insiders and family members.
new_explanation_en: Normally, public companies have a share structure that grants each shareholder proportional voting power based on the number of shares held.  For example, a shareholder who owns 50% of the company controls 50% of the votes.  One exception to the general rule is a dual-class structure, where different share classes allow different numbers of votes per share (eg, Class A at one vote per share vs. Class B at two votes per share). A dual-class structure may create disproportional voting power relative to share ownership.  Insiders (eg, founders) commonly hold Class B shares, which grant them dominant voting control on important issues (eg, board elections or strategic decisions) even if their share ownership falls below 50%. (Choice A)  Shareholders have voting power equal to their percentage of share ownership only if all shares grant the same number of votes. Different share classes allow for different votes per share in a dual-class structure. (Choice C)  Class B shares are granted mainly to insiders and family members and not to outside shareholders; therefore, greater voting power is typically held by insiders and family members.
