new_question_en: A 10-year, zero-coupon bond is priced at 64.3928 per 100 of par value and is trading at a 4.50% yield-to-maturity using annual compounding. Assuming a 10-basis point change in yield-to-maturity, the approximate modified duration of the bond is closest to:
new_explanation_en: The solution requires determining the price of the zero-coupon bond twice: at the initial yield minus 10 basis points (price ) and at the initial yield plus 10 basis points (price ).  The price of a zero-coupon bond is the present value of its face amount.  After obtaining the two prices, use the formula in the first exhibit to calculate the approximate modified duration.  Be sure to enter the yield change in its decimal form (ie, 10 basis points = 0.10% = 0.001). The question specifies using a 10-basis point change in the bond's yield.  The choice of yield change is somewhat arbitrary.  Using too large or too small a yield change (eg, 100 basis points or 1 basis point) is likely to result in a less useful value for duration.  Typically, yield changes of between 5 and 25 basis points might be used.  The calculated value for duration will vary a bit depending on the basis point change being used. (Choice B)  9.62 results from calculating the price of the zero-coupon bond at only a 4.40% yield.  The difference between the price at a 4.40% yield and the initial price is divided by the initial price multiplied by 0.001. (Choice C)  10.00 is the Macaulay, not the modified, duration for the 10-year zero-coupon bond.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.10 Interest Rate Risk and Return - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: An investor with a 10-year investment horizon purchases a noncallable 10-year, 7% annual coupon bond.  The bond purchase price is 107.360087 per 100 of par value, with a 6% YTM.  The bond's annual modified duration is 7.180.  The duration gap at the time of the investment is closest to:
new_explanation_en: Bond investor exposure to reinvestment risk or price risk results from any divergence between intended investment horizon and a bond's Macaulay duration.  The difference is referred to as a duration gap and calculated as: Macaulay duration minus investment horizon.  A positive duration gap means the investor has greater exposure to price risk; a negative gap results in greater exposure to reinvestment risk. Since the bond's modified duration was provided, the Macaulay duration must be calculated before the duration gap can be determined.  Macaulay duration is found by multiplying the modified duration by 1 + YTM expressed as a periodic rate.  Since the bond in question is an annual coupon bond, the periodic rate is the same as the given YTM.  Since the duration gap is negative, the investor has exposure to reinvestment risk. (Choice A)  −2.82 results from subtracting the investment horizon from the bond's modified duration rather than its Macaulay duration. (Choice C)  0.00 would be the correct answer if the investor had purchased a zero-coupon bond.  Since zeros have a Macaulay duration equal to their maturity, buying a 10-year zero-coupon bond would result in the investment having a Macaulay duration equal to the investment horizon.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.10 Interest Rate Risk and Return - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: An investor with a 2-year investment horizon buys a 10-year government bond that pays a 3% annual coupon.  The resulting mismatch between the 10-year bond's duration and the investment horizon results in the investor having the greatest exposure to:
new_option_b: liquidity risk.
new_option_c: reinvestment risk.
new_explanation_en: A mismatch between an investor's holding period (or investment horizon) and a bond's Macaulay duration results in exposure to two types of interest rate risk: price risk and reinvestment risk.  An investment horizon that is longer than the Macaulay duration results in exposure to reinvestment risk.  An investment horizon shorter than the Macaulay duration creates price risk. A 10-year coupon bond will have a Macaulay duration of less than 10 years, but significantly longer than 2 years.  At the end of the investment horizon, the bond will still have 8 years until its maturity.  If the bond's YTM has increased or decreased by even a relatively modest amount (eg, 0.50%), the price change will be much greater than the reinvestment income on 2 years of coupon income. The duration mismatch can work to the investor's advantage.  If yields decline, the investor's 2-year horizon return will be greater than the bond's YTM at purchase.  However, the mismatch becomes a disadvantage for the investor if yields rise since the price decrease will exceed the additional reinvestment income. (Choice B)  Liquidity risk refers to the ability to convert an investment into cash at a price close to the bond's fair value.  The investment would not create significant exposure to liquidity risk since government bonds are typically more liquid than other fixed income securities. (Choice C)  Investors have exposure to reinvestment risk when their investment horizons are longer than the Macaulay durations of their bond holdings.

The question specifies using a 10–basis point change in the bond's yield.  The choice of yield change is somewhat arbitrary.  The calculated value for duration will vary somewhat depending on the basis point change used. pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\4. Corporate Issuers\4.05 Capital Investments and Capital Allocation - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: When making capital budgeting decisions, which of the following types of investment projects most likely allow management to have the highest level of confidence?
new_option_b: Replacement projects
new_option_c: New products and services
new_explanation_en: Categories of capital projects Rationale Decision considerations Replacement Worn, broken, or inefficient assets Most accurate cash flow projections, greatest certainty of decisions Expansion Add capacity for existing products Greater uncertainties over cost and revenues compared with replacement projects New products and services Research and development, and investment in products not yet offered by the company Greater uncertainties than expansion projects, most complex investment decisions Regulatory, safety, and environmental Driven by external party (eg, government, insurance company) Necessary to stay in business, not directly profit- driven like other categories Pet projects or high-risk investments Capital allocation error Overly optimistic projections, or failure to apply proper project analyses Profit-motivated capital budgeting decisions are classified as replacement projects, expansion projects, or introduction of new products and services.  Since replacement projects are projects that replace assets already in use, net cash flows can be estimated much more accurately compared to other capital budgeting decisions: Acquisition and operating costs:  Such assets have been purchased or constructed previously, and there is an operating history on which to base cost estimates. Revenues:  Previous period revenues and familiarity with the product market's competitive environment allow for better revenue estimates. More accurate cash flow estimates allow managers a higher degree of confidence regarding decisions on replacement projects compared to decisions on other types of projects. (Choice A)  Although expansion projects also imply an extension of previous investments, they entail more uncertainties than replacement projects.  There may be advantages and disadvantages related to the larger scale of operations and reactions of competitors that are difficult to quantify.  These factors cause expansion project decisions to be more complex. (Choice C)  Decisions to invest in new products or services are the most complex capital budgeting decisions since they have the greatest uncertainties regarding initial cost, operating expenses, and revenues.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\4. Corporate Issuers\4.05 Capital Investments and Capital Allocation - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following most accurately describes the opportunity cost of funds used in net present value (NPV) analysis of investment projects?
new_option_a: Company's average cost of debt capital
new_option_b: Expected return on comparable investment projects
new_option_c: Discount rate that results in projects having a zero NPV
new_explanation_en: Net present value (NPV) analysis evaluates investments based on the present value of a project's cash flows.  NPV is the difference between the present value of the cash outflows and inflows generated by the project.  The present values are the nominal cash flows discounted by the project's required rate of return (r). Investment in a project means forgoing the return that could have been earned from investing in other projects (ie, opportunity cost of funds). Therefore, companies require a return that is at least equal to the rate of return available from comparable projects, given that return also meets the investors' requirements. (Choice A)  A company's average cost of debt capital is inappropriate for valuing an individual project since the average cost is not based on the project's risk or required return. (Choice C)  The discount rate that results in projects having an NPV of zero is the internal rate of return (IRR).  IRR is an alternative capital budgeting method to NPV analysis.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\4. Corporate Issuers\4.05 Capital Investments and Capital Allocation - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A company plans to retool an automobile factory to produce a new model to replace the existing model.  Which of the following is most appropriately considered an opportunity cost?
new_option_a: Forgone revenue from the existing model
new_option_b: Interest expense on money borrowed to finance the project
new_option_c: Decline in sales of another model produced by the company
new_explanation_en: Capital budgeting considerations Description Impact on projected cash flows Sunk costs Costs previously incurred None Opportunity costs Forgone value of using an asset in its next-best use Reduce net cash flows by cash flow forgone Externalities Side effects of project Ignore if outside of company, adjust cash flows if inside company Using an asset in one activity often means forgoing its use in some other endeavor.  In capital budgeting, an opportunity cost is the net cash flow not realized from an asset being used in some alternative activity.  The net cash flows not received from the highest value alternate use of the asset are treated as an opportunity cost and subtracted from cash flows projected in the capital budgeting process. In this scenario, a company considers retooling the factory to produce a new model and discontinuing production of the existing model.  The revenue no longer earned on the discontinued model is an opportunity cost related to the introduction of the new model.  The net cash flows projected for the new model must be reduced by the net cash flows no longer earned on the discontinued model. (Choice B)  Financing costs are related to the opportunity cost of capital.  However, the opportunity cost of capital is not factored into the net cash flows from an investment.  Financing costs are related to the discount rate used to calculate the cash flows' present value. (Choice C)  Lost revenues on another model still being sold should be factored into incremental net cash flows.  However, this is an example of an externality—specifically, cannibalization—and not an opportunity cost.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\4. Corporate Issuers\4.05 Capital Investments and Capital Allocation - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A company's analyst made the following after-tax cash flow projections for two independent investments: Year 0 1 2 3 Project A −36,000 14,000 16,000 16,000 Project B −39,000 15,500 16,500 17,000 The cost of capital is the company's hurdle rate of 12.5%.  Based on the internal rate of return (IRR) approach, which of the following actions is most appropriate for the company?
new_option_b: Invest in Project B.
new_option_c: Invest in both Projects A and B.
new_explanation_en: HP 12c TI BA II Plus Using a financial calculator, the internal rate of return (IRR) for Projects A and B are 13.0% and 12.1%. When the IRR is at the respective rates above, the net present value (NPV) of each project is equal to zero (ie, the present value of cash inflows equals cash outflows). When evaluating projects under the IRR decision rule, a project should only be accepted if the IRR is above the hurdle rate, which is usually the firm's weighted average cost of capital.  Furthermore, if the projects are independent (ie, selection of multiple projects is allowed), choose all projects with an IRR above the hurdle rate.  If the projects are mutually exclusive (ie, selection of only one project is allowed), choose the project with the highest IRR. In this independent project scenario where multiple selections are allowed, only Project A should be selected since its IRR is above the hurdle rate.  Project A's IRR at 13.0% is greater than its WACC at 12.5%.

new_question_en: An analyst is evaluating the profitability of a five-year expansion project.  Which of the following should be used to value the project according to the principles of capital budgeting?

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\4. Corporate Issuers\4.05 Capital Investments and Capital Allocation - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A company is analyzing two mutually exclusive three-year projects with conventional cash flows: Cash Flows (£ millions) Year 0 1 2 3 IRR Project A −60 12 30 55 22.2% Project B −80 60 45 5 24.3% If the hurdle rate is 8% and there are no other cash flows, then based on the IRR and NPV criteria, the best investment decision is to invest in:
new_option_b: B only.
new_option_c: both A and B.
new_explanation_en: NPV and IRR criteria are commonly used to make capital investment decisions.  The general rule is to accept a project if: the project's NPV is positive or the project's IRR is greater than the required rate of return (ie, hurdle rate). For independent projects with conventional cash flows, the NPV and IRR lead to the same investment decision.  When a project has a positive NPV, IRR will always be greater than the project's required rate of return, and vice versa. IRR and NPV can produce conflicting rankings when projects are mutually exclusive (ie, the firm can accept only one project).  NPV is a better criterion than IRR since the NPV model: shows the amount of value added to the firm, whereas IRR shows only the rate of return, not the actual value added.  In this case, Project B has a higher IRR (24.3%) that translates into a lower NPV of £18.10 million (as per the calculations below).  The greater the NPV, the more value added to the firm. uses a more conservative reinvestment rate.  The discounted cash flow analysis implicitly assumes cash flows are reinvested at the discount rate, which is the required rate of return (for NPV) or the IRR.  Required rates of return are returns that could be earned on equivalent projects, so NPV reflects a more realistic reinvestment assumption. new_question_en: A project has the following forecasted annual cash flows (in ¥ billions): Year Cash Flow 0 −5 1 15 2 8 3 −20 Based on this information, which of the following discount rates will produce the lowest net present value (NPV)?
new_explanation_en: HP 12c TI BA II Plus The net present value (NPV) of an investment equals the present value of its forecasted net cash flows (ie, inflows minus outflows).  The discount rate used for calculating NPV is the required rate of return for investors, which accounts for the investment's risk. Typically, for projects with conventional cash flows (ie, one initial negative cash flow followed by positive future cash flows), lower discount rates will yield higher NPVs.  However, for projects with unconventional cash flows (ie, negative cash flows occurring beyond the initial period), the relationship between discount rates and the size of the NPV can vary. In this case, the investment has unconventional cash flows.  The lowest discount rate (6%) yields the lowest NPV (−¥0.52 billion) (Choices B and C).  This occurs because the sizable negative terminal cash flow generates the most negative present value when using the 6% discount rate; therefore, the NPV is reduced more than under the other two rates.

new_question_en: A company is building a new plant.  The NPV of the plant is projected to be €8 million if demand is high, and −€3 million if demand is low.  Both scenarios are equally likely.  The company has also secured a 1-year lease on some adjoining land, with an option to buy, to expand the facility if demand is high.  The costs of the lease and expected cash flows from the expansion option are: Option cost (1-year lease expense) 0.5 million Annual net cash inflows over 5 years (Years 2–6), if exercised 0.4 million Required rate of return 8% The value of the plant with the option (in EUR) is closest to:

new_explanation_en: HP 12c TI BA II Plus Real option classifications Real option type Flexibility offered to: Timing Delay an investment decision until more information becomes available (eg, project sequencing) Fundamental Undertake projects only when fundamentals of underlying asset are favorable (eg, oil refineries) Sizing Abandon a project (ie, abandonment option) Expand (ie, growth option) Price-setting Increase prices with demand Production-flexibility Change output volume Use alternative input Produce different output A real option arises during normal business activities or operations when management has some flexibility in the investment decision process.  Real options give management either: timing flexibility (ie, timing or fundamental options) or operational flexibility (ie, sizing options, pricing options, or production flexibility options). When evaluating investment projects, management should consider if there are any real options linked to a project, and the value that they add to the project. In this instance, the lease is a production-flexibility option that allows management to alter production capacity to manage demand-supply mismatches.  It will be exercised only when demand is high, of which there is a 50% probability.  The NPV of the plant with the option is calculated as the NPV without options, adjusted for the cost and value of the option, as follows: Step 1:  Determine the value of the plant without the option by summing the NPV under the different scenarios: Expected NPV = P (NPV ) + P (NPV ) = 0.5 (8.0 million) + 0.5 (−3.0 million) = €2.5 million Step 2:  Calculate the NPV of cash flows from the option if exercised: Step 3:  Determine the NPV of the plant with the option: = NPV without options − Cost of options + Value of options where the option's value accounts for the probability of high demand = 2.5 − 0.5 + 0.5(1.48) = €2.74 million (Choice A)  €2.50 million is the expected NPV of the plant without the option. (Choice C)  €3.48 million results from ignoring the probability that demand level might remain low, whereby the option would not have any additional value. new_explanation_en: HP 12c TI BA II Plus Common errors in capital allocation decisions Correct application Misapplication Drawback Project criterion NPV IRR IRR cannot be used with unconventional cash flows Assumes reinvestment at IRR Profitability measure Long-term performance Short-term performance Firms are incentivized to boost EPS and net income in the short term Discount rate Project's required return WACC Reflects the firm's risk, not the project's Cash flows Exclude sunk costs Include financing costs Include opportunity costs Mishandling costs Miscalculated NPV When making a capital investment decision, firms typically use the capital allocation process based on a cash flow analysis.  Common capital allocation errors include accounting for cash flows incorrectly and using the wrong discount rate. Cash flows incurred prior to the investment decision (ie, sunk costs) are not included in the analysis since they do not represent a cost of the project. Income that would be generated if the project is not pursued (ie, forgone income) is considered a direct cost (ie, opportunity cost) of the project and should be included. The discount rate should be the project's required return (not the company's WACC) since that return reflects the project's incremental risk rather than the company's total risk. In this scenario, the marketing campaign is a sunk cost, which should be excluded from the analysis; the forgone rental income is an opportunity cost and therefore should be included.  Thus, the project's annual net cash flows of CAD 220,000 (240,000 after-tax cash flows − 20,000 opportunity cost) would be discounted at the project's required rate of return (8.0%): Describe principles of capital allocation and common capital allocation pitfalls LOS

new_question_en: An analyst gathers the following information about a company: In 20X1, the company borrowed using a 20-year mortgage. In May 20X3, the company received cash for services to be delivered in 20X5. In November 20X3, the company purchased inventory and will pay suppliers in February 20X4. In 20X3, which of the following is most likely classified as a long-term liability?
new_option_b: The current portion of long-term debt
new_option_c: The debt payable from the inventory purchase
new_explanation_en: Liabilities are debts that a company owes to others.  Noncurrent liabilities are debts due in more than 12 months.  If a debt is due to be paid in 12 months or less, it is classified as a current liability. Unearned revenue is a liability recorded when a company receives cash in advance of the delivery of goods or services; only when the company delivers the goods can it consider the revenue earned.  In this scenario, since the company received cash in 20X3 and will not deliver the goods until 20X5, the time elapsed between cash received and delivery is greater than 12 months. (Choice B)  The current portion of long-term debt represents the amount of repayment due (in less than 12 months) in the current period, so it is a current, not a noncurrent, liability. (Choice C)  If a company buys inventory in the second half of the year and repays it in the first half of the following year, the debt is considered current, not noncurrent, since it is paid within 12 months.

new_question_en: An analyst gathers the following data: Which of the following companies most likely has the greatest ability to pay its current liabilities based on the quick ratio?
new_option_b: Company B
new_option_c: Company C
new_explanation_en: The quick ratio is a liquidity ratio that measures a company's ability to meet its short-term obligations (ie, due within a year).  It is a conservative liquidity measure because it includes only cash, marketable securities, and accounts receivable. In the context of calculating the quick ratio, marketable securities are considered short-term.  Inventory, excluded from the quick ratio, is a less liquid current asset as it takes longer to convert to cash.  Prepaid expenses are not included in the quick ratio since they are rarely converted to cash. Here, add the quick assets and divide this sum by total current liabilities.  Company C has the greatest ability to pay with a quick ratio of 0.778.

new_question_en: A company discloses its required depreciation expense for five years: 20X3–20X7 depreciation expense (in USD) 20X3 52,000 20X4 60,000 20X5 75,000 20X6 87,000 20X7 101,000 The company uses units of production to calculate depreciation expense.  Based only on this data, the company most likely expects an increase in:
new_option_b: net margin.
new_option_c: units produced.
new_explanation_en: The units-of-production depreciation method expenses an asset's cost based on its use during each period.  Depreciation expense is calculated by multiplying the units produced each year by the depreciable unit cost, which is calculated as the asset's depreciable value (ie, initial cost less salvage value) divided by the total number of units expected to be produced over the asset's life. The depreciable unit cost is constant since the asset's cost is known, and the salvage value and the total number of units expected to be produced are estimated at the beginning of the asset's life (Choice C).  Therefore, the only variable that can change the depreciation expense will be the actual number of units produced.  Using the units-of-production method, if the depreciation expense increases each year, the number of units produced is also expected to grow. (Choice B)  Net margin (ie, net profit margin) is a measure of profitability, and it increases only if profit increases or revenue decreases.  In this scenario, although production and COGS are expected to grow, that does not suggest the net margin will increase.

new_question_en: An investor is evaluating several callable bonds.  The investor believes short-term interest rates are likely to rise significantly, but intermediate and long-term rates will be stable.  Which of the following types of duration would be most appropriate for evaluating the risk of the bonds given the expected flattening of the yield curve?
new_option_b: Modified
new_option_c: Effective
new_explanation_en: Bond duration Type Measures Applicable bonds Macaulay Present-value-weighted average time to receipt of coupon and principal No embedded options Modified Percentage change in price for a given change in bond's yield-to-maturity No embedded options Effective Percentage change in price due to parallel shift of benchmark yield curve All Key rate Percentage change in price due to a shift within a portion of benchmark yield curve All Money Price change in currency units given a change in the appropriate yield or curve All Key rate duration is used to assess the impact on bond values of a movement of rates along a portion of the yield curve (eg, ten-year rate or from zero to three years to maturity).  This allows key rate duration to measure the impact of changes in the shape of the yield curve (ie, shaping risk) on the value of callable bonds. A callable bond has uncertain future cash flows since it may be called and retired before maturity.  Investors use effective duration to try to account for the cash flow uncertainty by assuming parallel shifts of the benchmark yield curve (Choice C). If short-term rates rise and the yield curve flattens as anticipated, a key rate duration calculated on such an assumption produces a better estimate of the bond's change in value.  Under such circumstances, a key rate duration more accurately assesses an issuer's incentive to call the bond and the future cash flow uncertainty. (Choice B)  Modified duration measures the sensitivity of a bond's price to a change in its yield-to-maturity.  Since it is based on a change in that single interest rate, modified duration cannot be used to assess the impact of a shift in rates over a portion of a benchmark yield curve.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.13 Curve-Based and Empirical Fixed-Income Risk Measures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Effective duration is the most appropriate duration measure for bonds with:
new_option_b: predictable cash flows.
new_option_c: a well-defined yield-to-maturity.
new_explanation_en: Effective duration estimates how much a bond's total price will change in response to a parallel shift of the benchmark yield curve.  Since effective duration uses the yield curve instead of the YTM, it is a more appropriate measure of interest rate risk for bonds that have embedded options, such as callable and putable bonds.  Those bonds have unpredictable cash flows due to the possibility of option exercise and thus lack a well-defined YTM. (Choices B and C)  For bonds that have predictable cash flows, and thus a well-defined YTM, interest rate risk can be measured using approximate modified duration, which is based on YTM.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\7. Fixed Income\7.13 Curve-Based and Empirical Fixed-Income Risk Measures - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Compared with analytical duration, empirical duration is the more appropriate measure to estimate the impact of benchmark interest rate changes for a bond portfolio of:
new_option_b: global high-yield corporate bonds.
new_option_c: highly rated European covered bonds.
new_explanation_en: Duration is a linear estimate of the change in a bond's price given a change in its yield. Analytical duration (eg, modified duration) estimates price and yield changes given a change in benchmark interest rates, based on current market information. Empirical duration estimates a bond's interest rate sensitivity using the correlations between benchmark yields and yield spreads based on historical data and statistical relationships with other factors (eg, credit, liquidity). Empirical and analytical duration will be very similar for bonds that have similar risks as benchmark securities, but will differ for bonds with considerable spread risk, such as credit, liquidity, or country risk, etc.  The more types of risk a bond is exposed to, besides interest rate risk, the more relevant its empirical duration will be.  Empirical duration is particularly useful in predicting price changes during periods of financial stress (eg, flight to quality), as correlations among risky assets increase dramatically. Global high-yield corporate bonds represent a wide variety of credit, country, and liquidity risks, in addition to interest rate risk, so empirical duration can be expected to be a more appropriate predictor of their prices than analytical duration. (Choices A and B)  US agency and highly rated (eg, AAA, AA+) European covered bonds carry little credit risk; therefore, both duration measures will be very similar.

new_question_en: An analyst gathers the following data on two companies: Selected financial information In EUR (millions) Company A Company B Inventory valuation method LIFO FIFO Revenue (20X9) 1,300 2,200 COGS (20X9) 800 1,500 Gross profit (20X9) 500 700 Inventory (20X9) 145 280 Inventory (20X8) 115 265 LIFO reserve (20X9) 20 LIFO reserve (20X8) 35 Neither company has reported inventory shortages or write-downs.  After the appropriate adjustments are made to compare the companies' financial data, Company A's inventory turnover is most likely:
new_option_b: the same as Company B's.
new_option_c: greater than Company B's.
new_explanation_en: Two steps are required to allow for a comparison between Company A and Company B: Convert Company A's financial information from LIFO to FIFO, and then calculate the inventory turnover of both companies. Since the two companies use different inventory valuation methods, Company A's inventory and COGS must be converted from LIFO to FIFO. This is achieved with the LIFO reserve, a required disclosure for a company using LIFO.  To convert Company A's ending inventory for a given period to FIFO, add the LIFO reserve for the same period to the inventory balance.  To convert COGS, add the amount of decrease in the LIFO reserve over the period to the reported COGS. The change in the LIFO reserve is calculated from a period's beginning and ending LIFO reserve.  The adjustments to Company A's financial data are as follows: After Company A's data is converted to FIFO, the inventory turnover for both companies can be calculated and compared.  Inventory turnover is the ratio of COGS to average inventory (ie, the average number of times that the company sells and replenishes its inventory during a period). Adjusted financials (FIFO) Company A Company B Revenue 1,300 2,200 COGS 815 1,500 Gross profit 485 700 Inventory (20X9) 165 280 Inventory (20X8) 150 265 Inventory turnover 815 / [(165 + 150) / 2] = 5.2 1,500 / [(280 + 265) / 2] = 5.5 Converting Company A's inventory and COGS to FIFO shows that the company has a lower inventory turnover than Company B (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.06 Analysis of Inventories - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A clothing retailer reporting under IFRS purchased merchandise for £500,000 at the beginning of the year.  Normally, the retailer could sell this inventory for £700,000, but now the estimated selling price is £510,000.  The cost of selling the inventory is £15,000.  Based on this information, the retailer's reported carrying value of inventory (in £ thousands) is closest to:
new_explanation_en: Inventory may lose value due to spoilage, obsolescence, or declines in selling prices.  Companies update their inventory values on the balance sheet to account for such events.  IFRS require companies to report the carrying value of inventory at the lower of historic cost and net realizable value (NRV).  The NRV equals the estimated selling price minus the cost of completing and selling the inventory. In this scenario, the estimated selling price is now 510 (in £ thousands).  The selling cost is 15, so the NRV is 495 (510 − 15).  Since the NRV is lower than the historical cost of 500, this inventory should be written down to the NRV of 495 on the balance sheet. (Choice A)  485 is the carrying value, not the selling price, less the selling cost. (Choice C)  500 is the historical cost of the inventory, but it is lower only if incorrectly compared to the selling price instead of the NRV.

new_question_en: A company reporting under US GAAP and using FIFO assesses its inventory's net realizable value as being €200,000 less than its carrying value.  The company records a write-down and increases COGS by €200,000.  In the subsequent period, a new assessment of the inventory's net realizable value is €250,000 higher than its revised carrying value.  The company's most appropriate action is to reduce COGS by:
new_explanation_en: Inventory write-downs and reversals When to write down When to reverse a write-down Maximum reversal US GAAP (FIFO, weighted average) Net realizable value < cost Reversals prohibited N/A US GAAP (LIFO, retail inventory) Market value < cost Reversals prohibited N/A IFRS Net realizable value < cost Net realizable value > carrying value Amount of write-down Inventory costs may decline due to spoilage, obsolescence, or reduced selling prices.  Companies reporting under IFRS and US GAAP using any inventory valuation method other than the LIFO and retail inventory methods must value their inventory at the lower of cost and net realizable value.  Net realizable value is the estimated selling price in the normal course of business less the costs to complete the sales of inventory. If the net realizable value of a company's inventory becomes lower than its cost, the company must write down the inventory to its net realizable value.  At the same time, the company must increase COGS by the same amount.  This becomes the inventory's new carrying value. Under US GAAP, reversals of write-downs are prohibited.  Therefore, in this scenario, the company should do nothing even though the net realizable value of its inventory rose above its carrying cost following the write-down.  It should not reduce COGS. Under IFRS, write-downs can be reversed in subsequent periods if net realizable value rises above the new carrying value.  However, a reversal cannot exceed the value of the write-down (Choices B and C).

new_question_en: A company that reports under US GAAP decides to change its inventory accounting from FIFO to LIFO.  The change on its financial statements is most appropriately disclosed:
new_option_a: retroactively, including a restatement of prior years' financial statements.
new_option_b: retroactively, without restating prior financial statements but disclosing the impact of the change to prior years' statements in footnotes.
new_option_c: prospectively, without restating prior financial statements but disclosing the impact of the change to prior years' statements in footnotes.
new_explanation_en: Disclosure requirements: change in inventory costing methods Change reporting method to: US GAAP IFRS LIFO Explain why LIFO is superior Apply prospectively No restatement of prior statements Not permitted Any other method Explain why new method is superior Apply retrospectively Restatement of prior financials Must justify change Apply retrospectively Restatement of prior financials Only US GAAP permit companies to use LIFO.  Switching from LIFO to any other method requires the company to explain why the new method is better than LIFO, and it must also restate prior financial statements as though it had used the new method in prior years (Choices A and B). One reasonable explanation for switching from LIFO to FIFO is that it improves comparability between IFRS and GAAP reporting companies. When switching to LIFO from another method, US GAAP require the company to treat the change prospectively.  It must disclose the reasons for the change but is not required to restate prior financial statements.  Although the CFA materials do not explain why no restatement is necessary, there is no need to retroactively adjust comparisons since IFRS companies cannot use LIFO.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.06 Analysis of Inventories - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A manager collects information on a company's inventory for a period: Per-Unit Inventory USD Original cost 105 Selling price 140 Selling cost 10 Completion cost 30 Replacement cost 96 Normal profit margin 7 The company uses LIFO to calculate COGS.  Based on only this information, under US GAAP, the per-unit value (in USD) for the existing inventory is closest to:
new_explanation_en: Inventory may lose value due to spoilage, obsolescence, or declines in selling prices.  Companies often update their inventory values on the balance sheet to account for such events.  US GAAP require companies to report inventory at the lower of historical cost or market value (MV). When a company reports under US GAAP and uses LIFO as its inventory costing method, MV is the current replacement cost subject to an upper and lower limit. The upper limit is the net realizable value (NRV), which is the selling price net of the costs to complete and sell the inventory.  In this scenario, NRV = Selling price − Selling cost − Completion cost, so NRV = 140 − 10 − 30 = 100. The lower limit is the NRV minus a normal profit margin.  In this scenario, the lower limit is NRV − Normal profit margin = 100 − 7 = 93. MV is always the middle number of the replacement cost (RC), upper limit, and lower limit when ranked in order: If RC > Upper > Lower, MV is the upper limit. If Upper > RC > Lower, MV is the RC. If Upper > Lower > RC, MV is the lower limit. In this case, the MV is the RC of $96 per unit since it is within the upper and lower limits and is lower than the historical cost of the inventory. (Choice B)  $100 is the upper limit for MV, which is capped at the upper limit only when RC exceeds the upper limit. (Choice C)  $105 is the company's historical cost.  The inventory's NRV is lower than its historical cost, so the NRV should be reported.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.06 Analysis of Inventories - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A company that reports under IFRS is valuing its year-end inventory.  It has collected the following information (in CHF millions): Historic cost 175 Replacement cost 165 Selling price 240 Cost to sell inventory 60 Based on this data, the inventory value (in CHF millions) reported on its balance sheet is closest to:
new_explanation_en: Inventory is initially recorded on a company's balance sheet at historic cost.  However, companies are required to regularly reassess this value.  If the inventory's value falls below its cost (eg, spoils, becomes obsolete, declines in selling price), the company must write down the inventory to reflect the new, lower value, which becomes the carrying value. IFRS require companies to report the carrying value of inventory at the lower of cost or net realizable value (NRV).  The NRV is the estimated selling price less the cost of completing and selling the inventory. In this scenario, the NRV of the inventory is CHF 180 million (240 − 60).  This is higher than the cost of 175, so no write down is taken and the inventory remains at 175. (Choice A)  165 is the replacement value, which is not used by IFRS in valuing inventory.  The replacement value is used by companies reporting under US GAAP and using LIFO or retail inventory methods when valuing inventory. (Choice C)  180 is the NRV, which is greater than the historical cost.  Since inventory is required to be valued at the lower of cost and NRV, the company would not be permitted to increase the value of its inventory above 175.

new_question_en: The credit protection buyer in a credit default swap most likely pays:
new_option_a: a series of payments in return for a promise of compensation if a credit event occurs.
new_option_b: a one-time premium for the right to benefit from an increase in a bond's credit spread.
new_option_c: the interest, principal, and appreciation on a specific bond in return for a fixed or variable rate.
new_explanation_en: A credit default swap (CDS) is a form of credit derivative.  The credit protection buyer makes a series of scheduled payments to another party, the credit protection seller, who provides protection against the credit risk posed by a third party.  In return, the credit protection seller pays a certain amount to the credit protection buyer only if the third party experiences a credit event.  A credit event includes bankruptcy and may include other events like debt restructuring or failure to make a scheduled payment.  A CDS is analogous to insurance paid for by the credit protection buyer. (Choice B)  A one-time premium for the right to benefit from an increase in a bond's credit spread describes a credit spread option, not a CDS. (Choice C)  Paying the interest, principal, and appreciation on a specific bond in return for a fixed or variable rate describes a total return swap.

new_question_en: The named third party of a credit default swap suffers a credit event that results in payment to the credit protection buyer.  The event is least likely to be which of the following?
new_option_b: A failure to make a scheduled payment
new_option_c: An involuntary restructuring of a debt contract
new_explanation_en: Credit default swaps (CDS) Credit protection buyer Makes periodic payments for life of contract Credit protection seller Pays cash settlement for credit event Credit events Declaration of bankruptcy Failure to make a scheduled payment Involuntary restructuring of debt contract Credit default swaps (CDS) are contingent claim derivative contracts that insure against credit losses on debt instruments of third parties. Credit protection buyers make a series of payments over the life of the CDS.  Credit protection sellers make a cash settlement payment to buyers only if a credit event occurs.  The reduction in an issuer's (ie, third party's) credit rating by a rating agency is not a common credit event in CDS contracts. (Choices B and C)  Both a failure to make a scheduled payment and an involuntary restructuring of a debt contract are common credit events.

new_question_en: A trader fails to meet a margin call on a long futures position, and before the position can be liquidated fast markets result in additional losses greater than the account balance.  The amount the trader owes the clearinghouse is most likely:
new_option_a: the full value of the futures contract.
new_option_b: the losses in excess of previous margin deposits.
new_option_c: zero, since losses are limited to the initial margin.
new_explanation_en: All losses on futures positions must ultimately be paid in cash.  As an indication of good faith, traders initiating futures positions meet an initial margin requirement in cash.  However, traders' losses are not limited to their margin deposits.  If futures prices move so rapidly that positions cannot be liquidated before losses exceed an account's value, then traders owe the clearinghouse any excess losses because, as counterparty, the clearinghouse has paid the gains to traders on the other side of the market as part of the regular daily settlement. The image above depicts a 12-point decline in the futures price, which results in a 12-point loss on a long position.  Since the original account value was the initial margin of 10, the loss exceeds the account value.  The trader is responsible to pay the account deficit (10 − 12 = −2) to the clearinghouse. (Choice A)  The full value of the contract is required at expiration only if the long party decides to buy the underlying asset rather than closing out the futures position before expiration. (Choice C)  Futures losses are not limited to traders' initial margin deposits since futures impose obligations on both counterparties, making them responsible for covering all position losses—even losses in excess of previous margin deposits.

new_question_en: Which of the following is least likely to be a feature of futures contracts?  Buyers and sellers:
new_option_b: negotiate the quantity of the underlying asset.
new_option_c: use a clearinghouse as their legal counterparty.
new_explanation_en: Features of futures contracts Contractual commitments Short (long) party obligated to sell (buy) underlying asset Exchange traded No over-the-counter trading of futures Clearinghouse Exchange clearinghouse as legal counterparty Standardized contracts Exchange sets all contract terms Margin requirements Cash deposits to cover losses on positions Daily settlement Gains and losses on open positions realized in cash daily Daily price limits Allowable price change from previous day's settlement price Futures contracts are standardized contracts: contract terms such as the quantity of the underlying asset or the contract expiration are established by the exchange where each contract is traded.  The buyers and sellers of futures cannot alter these terms.  Negotiated contract terms are a feature of over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives (eg, forward contracts). (Choice A)  Both the buyer and seller must meet margin requirements by depositing cash as a performance bond available to cover losses on their positions.  The margin requirements are set by the exchange where the contract is traded. (Choice C)  Although a futures contract is created by a trade between a buyer and seller, the exchange clearinghouse becomes the legal counterparty on the contract after the trade is initiated.

new_question_en: On the day of expiration, a European put option's underlying asset has a price of GBP 83.  The option's exercise price is GBP 76, and the put buyer paid GBP 3 to purchase the option.  The payoff to the put buyer is closest to:
new_option_b: GBP 0
new_option_c: GBP 7
new_explanation_en: A European put option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell an underlying asset at the exercise price on the date of the option's expiration.  If the market price is less than the exercise price, then the put buyer has the right to sell the underlying asset at a higher price than the existing market price.  The difference between the exercise price and the market price is the put buyer's payoff. If the market price is not lower than the exercise price, then the put buyer will not exercise the option, and there is no payoff.  Therefore, the put buyer's payoff is the greater of (exercise price – market price) and zero. In this scenario, the put's exercise price at expiration is GBP 76, and the value of the underlying is GBP 83.  The payoff is the greater of (76 – 83) = GBP −7 and zero, so the payoff is GBP 0. (Choice A)  GBP −3 is the put buyer's profit, which equals the payoff minus the amount paid to purchase the option: (0 – 3) = GBP −3. (Choice C)  GBP 7 is the result of subtracting the exercise price from the value of the underlying asset.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: If a put option holder exercises the option, the original put option seller:
new_option_a: is obligated to sell the underlying asset.
new_option_b: is obligated to buy the underlying asset.
new_option_c: has the right to buy the underlying asset.
new_explanation_en: Exercise of option contracts Calls Puts Buyer (long) Right to buy underlying asset Right to sell underlying asset Seller (short) Obligation to sell underlying asset Obligation to buy underlying asset Options are contingent claims that give contract holders the right to trade the underlying asset at a specified price on a future date.  An option holder does not have to exercise the trading rights.  However, if that right is exercised, the original contract seller is obligated to take the other side of the resulting trade. Buyers (ie, holders) of put options acquire the right to sell the underlying asset at the option's strike price.  If the put option holder exercises that right, the seller of the put option is obligated to buy the underlying asset. (Choice A)  Sellers of call options have the obligation to sell the underlying asset if the call option holder exercises the right to buy. (Choice C)  Buyers of call options have the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying asset.

new_question_en: Which of the following derivatives is most likely to require periodic payments equal to the net difference between its two payment streams?
new_option_b: Credit default swap
new_option_c: Forward rate agreement
new_explanation_en: Interest rate swaps are forward commitment derivatives in which counterparties exchange periodic payment streams based on interest rates. In a fixed-for-floating swap (eg, plain vanilla), one party pays a fixed interest rate on a notional principal amount based on a given currency, while the counterparty pays a floating rate calculated on the same notional principal amount and currency.  Payments are made at pre-established dates during the swap's life. With plain vanilla swaps, it is common that each party owes a different amount on each payment date, so by convention the payments are netted and the party with the greater obligation pays the difference between the two payments.  This difference between the two payments for the period is the cash due. (Choice B)  Credit default swaps require only the credit protection buyer to make periodic payments over the life of the swap.  The credit protection seller pays only if there is a default event. (Choice C)  In a forward rate agreement (FRA), a single payment is made by one party to the other when the FRA matures.

new_question_en: An investor sells a European put with a strike price of EUR 100 for EUR 5.  At expiration, the underlying stock is trading at EUR 90.  Based only on this information, the investor's profit (in EUR) is closest to:
new_explanation_en: A European put option gives its buyer (ie, long put) the right, but not the obligation to sell an underlying asset at the exercise price (ie, strike price) on the expiration date.  The option seller (ie, short put) sells this right and collects a premium (ie, price of the option contract).  The seller will be forced to buy the stock at the strike price if the put is exercised by the buyer. If at expiration the price of the stock is greater than the exercise price, the option will expire with no value and the seller's profit is the option premium.  The premium received is always the maximum profit for a seller of an option contract. If at expiration the price of the stock is less than the exercise price , the buyer will exercise the option and the seller's profit will be the option premium less the difference between the stock price at expiration and the exercise price. (Choice B)  If the investor had sold a call (ie, short call) with a strike price of EUR 100, the profit would be EUR 5 at expiration. (Choice C)  A profit of EUR 15 inappropriately assumes a gain of EUR 10 on the put position plus the premium received of EUR 5.

new_question_en: Payments of gains and losses on futures contracts are most likely made:
new_option_b: only at expiration.
new_option_c: as negotiated by the counterparties.
new_explanation_en: Forward commitment derivatives Futures Forwards Swaps Trading venue Exchange-traded Over-the-counter Over-the-counter Legal counterparty Exchange clearinghouse Contract counterparty Contract counterparty Contract terms Standardized Negotiated Negotiated Gain/loss realization Daily settlement At expiration Periodically (eg, semiannual) Futures, forwards, and most swaps are forward commitment derivatives that involve an exchange of contractual obligations between the counterparties.  Gains and losses on each derivative are settled at different frequencies. Futures gains and losses are paid as they are marked to market, and they are settled daily.  Positions are valued based on the day's closing price.  Any change in value from the previous day results in a cash deposit (ie, gains) or withdrawal (ie, losses). Forward contracts are settled at expiration (Choice B).  The short party must sell the underlying asset to the long party at the agreed price set at contract initiation.  The gain (loss) for the counterparties is the difference between the agreed price and the market price of the underlying. Forward commitment swaps are settled at a negotiated frequency (eg, semiannually) (Choice C).  On designated payment dates, the counterparties transfer cash equal to the difference between the value of the payment series (eg, fixed versus floating) that each is obligated to pay. Daily settlement of futures is designed to minimize counterparty credit risk by avoiding the build-up of unrealized gains and losses.  When settlement occurs only periodically or at expiration, underlying price movements can result in large unrealized gains and losses.  The larger one party's unrealized gain is, the greater its credit risk exposure to the counterparty that must make good on its loss.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.02 Forward Commitment and Contingent Claim Features and Instruments - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following best describes the maximum potential gains and losses on a short put at expiration?
new_option_b: Limited gains and unlimited losses
new_option_c: Unlimited gains and unlimited losses
new_explanation_en: The maximum gain for option sellers (ie, shorts) is limited to the option premium from the option sale and occurs when the option is out of the money.  In such cases, put holders will not exercise their right to sell since the underlying could be sold at the higher market price. If the option is in the money, put holders will exercise their right to sell the asset at the higher strike price, and the short put is obligated to buy the asset at the higher price.  The short put's loss at exercise is the difference between the strike price and the market price, and if that difference is greater than the premium received when the option was sold, the seller has a net loss.  As the underlying asset price decreases, the put seller faces increasing losses.  However, since underlying asset prices cannot fall below zero, the maximum loss is limited. (Choice B)  Short calls have limited gains and unlimited losses.  Call sellers' gains are limited to the premium received.  Potential losses are unlimited since losses increase as underlying asset prices increase, with no theoretical limit. (Choice C)  No asset or derivative has unlimited potential gains and losses.  Short option maximum gains are always limited.

new_question_en: The margin deposits required to hold futures contracts are best described as:
new_option_b: contract premiums.
new_option_c: performance bonds.
new_explanation_en: Futures margins Performance bond or good-faith deposit Money in account to cover losses on trades Initial margin requirement Smallest performance bond needed to initiate a position Maintenance margin requirement Minimum performance bond allowing a position to be held Taking long or short positions in futures requires traders to meet a margin requirement.  Futures margins are referred to as performance bonds or good-faith deposits.  The money in the account indicates traders' willingness and ability to satisfy their contractual obligations, including paying for losses on positions.  Readily available funds are necessary since futures are settled daily, so losses must be covered with cash immediately after every trading session. Futures margins should not be confused with equity margin accounts.  An initial deposit to buy equity securities on margin is effectively a down payment, with the balance due to the seller covered by a loan.  Futures margins are not down payments (ie, no money is paid to the futures contract seller) and no loan is necessary to complete the transaction (Choice A).  Both buyers and sellers of futures contracts must meet a margin requirement. (Choice B)  Premiums are paid when buying call or put options, but futures contracts cost nothing since their initial value is zero.

new_question_en: Options are most likely considered contingent claims due to:
new_option_a: sellers paying a premium that depends on future actions.
new_option_b: buyers having a right, but no obligation, to trade the underlying asset.
new_option_c: uncertainty regarding the counterparty's ability to meet contractual obligations.
new_explanation_en: Derivative contract comparison Forward commitments Contingent claims Contract Exchange of obligations Conveyance of rights Counterparties Both obligated to perform Buyer has the right, but no obligation, to exercise; seller's obligation is contingent on exercise Cost at initiation Usually no cost to either party Buyer pays premium to seller Examples Futures, forwards, most swaps Options, credit default swaps, total return swaps Contingent claims are derivatives that give holders the right to trade the underlying asset at a specified price at a future date.  Contract holders do not have to exercise that right, but if they do the original contract seller is obligated to take the other side of the trade that results from the exercise.  For a contingent claim, sellers must fulfill their obligations contingent on the contract holders exercising their rights. Contingent refers to the counterparties exchanging a right for an obligation.  This is unlike forward commitments, in which both buyers and sellers exchange obligations that each must fulfill. (Choice A)  Contingent claim sellers receive a premium for granting contract buyers specified rights. (Choice C)  Counterparty credit risk is the uncertainty that a counterparty will fulfill its obligation under a derivative contract.  The presence or absence of counterparty credit risk is not a factor in determining whether a derivative is considered a contingent claim.

new_question_en: For a trader with no positions in the underlying asset or related options, the maximum gain on a short call is best described as:
new_option_b: the premium received.
new_option_c: the strike price less the premium received.
new_explanation_en: Call options are derivatives that give: buyers (ie, long position) the right, but not the obligation, to buy the underlying asset at the exercise (ie, strike) price and sellers (ie, short position) the obligation to sell the underlying asset at the exercise price if the call buyer decides to exercise the right to buy. Options have asymmetric payoff profiles.  The greater the underlying price increase above the exercise price, the greater the gain to the call buyer and loss to the call seller. In contrast, if the underlying price is at or below the exercise price (ie, the option is at the money or out of the money), the call buyer will not exercise and the option's value is zero.  No matter how far below the exercise price the asset's value is, the buyer's loss is limited to the original cost of buying the option.  Since the most the call buyer can lose is the premium paid, the maximum profit to the call seller is the premium received. (Choice A)  The call option seller's potential loss is unlimited since there is theoretically no limit to the underlying asset's appreciation. (Choice C)  The put option seller's maximum loss is the option strike price less the premium received.

new_question_en: If the value of a patent has been impaired, the impairment is most appropriately accounted for:
new_option_b: only in the footnotes to the financials.
new_option_c: on both the balance sheet and income statement.
new_explanation_en: Impairment of intangible assets with a finite life Impairment test done only when significant events warrant analysis Accounting treatment essentially the same as for tangible assets Impairment reduces the value of the asset on the balance sheet Impairment flows through the income statement and into net income Intangible assets with a finite life (eg, patents) are amortized over time and can become impaired under certain circumstances.  Testing for impairment occurs irregularly and only when significant events warrant additional scrutiny. If an asset is deemed impaired, it is written down using an impairment charge that flows through the income statement, reducing net income in that period (Choice A).  The write-down also reduces the asset's carrying value (ie, historical cost minus accumulated amortization) on the balance sheet. (Choice B)  The footnotes are likely to include additional information regarding an impairment charge, but the impairment will definitely be reflected in the balance sheet and income statement.

new_question_en: A company capitalized a ¥120 million equipment purchase at the beginning of this year and will use straight-line depreciation with zero salvage value and a three-year useful life.  The company generates ¥200 million in revenue every year, and the tax rate is 25%.  If depreciation and taxes are the only expenses, and based only on this information, the second year's ending financial results most likely show:
new_option_b: ¥80 million in net PPE.
new_option_c: ¥120 million in cash from operations.
new_explanation_en: Capitalizing an asset purchase initially reports the full asset cost on the balance sheet and subsequently allocates that cost to the income statement as depreciation expense over the asset's useful life.  This allows the income statement to reflect the cost of using the asset more accurately in each period of its use. When the company capitalizes a purchase, the purchase price is reported on the balance sheet upon initial recognition.  In this situation, each year's depreciation expense of ¥40 million, or (¥120 million purchase price − 0 salvage value) / 3 years, is reported on the income statement. Since revenue is ¥200 million for Year 2 and ¥40 million in depreciation is the only expense, pretax income equals ¥160, and 25% of pretax income equals ¥40 million. (Choice B)  ¥80 million is the net PPE at the end of the first year.  Since historical cost (ie, gross PPE) is ¥120 million, and accumulated depreciation after two years is ¥80 million, net PPE equals ¥40 million at the end of the second year. (Choice C)  ¥120 million is the net income for the second year, not cash from operating activities.  To derive cash from operations for the second year, ¥40 million of depreciation (ie, noncash charge) is added back to net income.

new_question_en: A company buys a patent from a technology firm.  If the patent purchase is not a part of a business combination, then the total cost of acquiring the patent is most likely:
new_option_a: recorded at fair value on the balance sheet.
new_option_b: expensed immediately on the income statement.
new_option_c: allocated to fair value and goodwill on the balance sheet.
new_explanation_en: Treatment for intangible assets Acquisition method Treatment of costs Purchased on a stand-alone basis Fair value of assets capitalized on balance sheet Developed internally through research and development Research costs expensed immediately on income statement Development costs capitalized on balance sheet if product is developed for internal use (US GAAP) or has demonstrated technical feasibility (IFRS) Acquired through a business combination (eg, merger) Fair value of assets capitalized on balance sheet Additional goodwill created on balance sheet Intangible assets (eg, patents, trademarks, software) lack physical form and grant the holder exclusive rights to future benefits.  These assets can be obtained through a standalone purchase, the acquisition of another company, or internal development. The means of acquiring an intangible asset determines whether its costs are capitalized or expensed.  If capitalized, the total purchase cost of the asset appears on the balance sheet and is subsequently amortized on the income statement over its useful life.  If expensed, the entire purchase cost immediately reduces net income for the period on the income statement. In this scenario, the patent is a standalone purchase (ie, without a business combination), so the total purchase costs are capitalized on the balance sheet at fair value.  Alternatively, acquiring the patent through a business combination (eg, merger) would create goodwill (Choice B)  If the patent is developed internally, research costs are expensed. (Choice C)  There is no goodwill in this scenario since goodwill results only from business combinations.

new_question_en: At the beginning of this year, a company purchased electronic goods that cost €120,000 and chose to expense the purchase instead of capitalizing it.  The electronics have a useful life of 3 years with zero salvage value, and the company uses straight-line depreciation.  The company reports €300,000 in revenue each year and is taxed at 25%.  There are no other expenses aside from the purchase cost and corporate tax.  Based only on this information and compared to capitalizing the asset, expensing the asset most likely results in:
new_option_a: net PPE that is €120,000 lower in the current year.
new_option_b: net income that is €60,000 lower in the current year.
new_option_c: cash from operations that is €100,000 higher in the current year.
new_explanation_en: Expensing or capitalizing an asset purchase impacts the company's financial results differently each year, but the cumulative impact to net income and total cash flow under both methods is the same over time.  In this scenario, when the company expenses the asset, the full cost of €120,000 is reported on the income statement this year.  Subtracting €120,000 from revenue of €300,000 results in pretax income of €180,000, which yields €135,000 of net income after deducting €45,000 of taxes. Had the company capitalized the asset, at initial recognition €120,000 would be reported on the balance sheet as a long-term asset.  At year-end, €40,000 of depreciation (ie, €120,000 purchase price less 0 salvage value over 3 years) is reported as depreciation expense on the income statement and reduces pretax income to €260,000, which yields €195,000 in net income after subtracting €65,000 in taxes.  Therefore, expensing the asset would result in net income that is 135,000 − 195,000 = €60,000 lower in the first year. (Choice A)  €120,000 lower net PPE results from not subtracting depreciation of €40,000.  Net PPE at year-end is €80,000. (Choice C)  Cash from operations (CFO) is actually €100,000 lower when the asset is expensed.  This is because expensing the entire purchase cost reduces net income in the first year, which also reduces CFO.

new_question_en: A company reports under US GAAP and provides the following information on its equipment: Metric $ Carrying amount 31,000 Expected future cash flows Undiscounted 28,000 Present value 26,500 Fair value if sold 22,000 Cost to sell 2,500 Due to an impairment charge, the carrying value of the machine is closest to:
new_explanation_en: Impairment charges are recognized when an asset's carrying amount, measured as historical cost minus accumulated depreciation, is greater than its recoverable value.  US GAAP defines the recoverable amount as simply the undiscounted expected future cash flows.  In this case, the carrying amount ($31,000) exceeds the recoverable amount ($28,000). The impaired asset is written down to a new carrying value with a new depreciation schedule.  Under US GAAP, the asset would be written down to fair value (ie, value if sold [$22,000]).  This fair value estimate becomes the new carrying amount. In contrast, IFRS defines the recoverable amount and the new carrying value as the greater of the asset's fair value less costs to sell the asset ($22,000 − $2,500) or the discounted future cash flows ($26,500) that the asset is expected to generate (Choices A and C).

new_question_en: An analyst has collected the following information on a technology company that reports financial results using US GAAP: 20X7 $ thousands Gross profit 25,000 Research and development expenses (5,000) Depreciation and amortization expenses (4,000) Total equity (beginning of year) 100,000 Total equity (end of year) 120,000 Tax rate 25% The company amortizes intangible assets over a five-year period using straight-line depreciation.  Assume that the company can elect to either expense or capitalize its research and development costs.  If it had capitalized all research and development costs in 20X7, its return on equity for 20X7 would be closest to:
new_explanation_en: A company that expenses research and development (R&D) costs shows higher expenses and lower taxes and net income than a company that capitalizes those costs.  Capitalizing R&D expenses means that the company removes $5 million in expenses from its income statement. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) rises from $20 million to $25 million. However, capitalization also increases the company's noncurrent intangible assets by $5 million.  The company amortizes its intangible assets over five years, so amortization expense rises by $1 million in 20X7.  The overall result is an increase in both pretax income (from $16 million to $20 million), and after-tax (net) income (from $12 million to $15 million). Return on equity (ROE) = net income ÷ average equity.  The table below shows the adjustments to net income and equity from the company's capitalization of its R&D costs ($ thousands): (Choice A)  10.9% is the company's original ROE (ie, expensing rather capitalizing R&D costs). (Choice C)  14.1% results from correctly removing the R&D expense from the income statement but neglecting to account for the additional amortization expense.

new_question_en: A company maintains a defined benefit plan for its employees.  It recently determined that its employees' life expectancy has increased, which will increase the company's pension liability.  The amount of the increased liability can only be estimated.  Under US GAAP, the company most appropriately reports the increased liability on its financial statements:
new_option_a: in the footnotes only, since it cannot determine the amount of increase.
new_option_b: as part of other comprehensive income and amortizes the increase over time.
new_option_c: as part of other comprehensive income but does not amortize the increase over time.
new_explanation_en: Treatment of defined benefit (DB) plan items for IFRS and US GAAP IFRS US GAAP Income statement Increase in service costs Pension liability – interest expense Pension surplus – interest income Increase in service costs Pension liability – interest expense Expected return on plan assets Other comprehensive income (OCI) Actuarial gains/losses (not amortized over time) Difference between actual return on plan assets and return included in net income Actuarial gains/losses (amortized over time) Past service costs Determining the amount of a company's future defined benefit (DB) plan obligation involves making estimates based on actuarial assumptions for cost variables such as life expectancy during retirement.  Changes to these assumptions cause the company to increase or decrease its future obligation.  These changes translate into gains or losses in the period when the change occurs. IFRS and US GAAP both require the company to recognize the gain or loss in other comprehensive income (OCI), but they differ in how the company treats the OCI item in subsequent years.  US GAAP require the company to amortize the gain or loss ratably over time.  The effect of amortization is that reported pension expense is more consistent from year to year.  IFRS do not permit this "smoothing" technique. (Choice A)  Estimates of pension liability based on variables such as life expectancy are examples of actuarial assumptions.  Both IFRS and US GAAP permit use of actuarial assumptions to determine the amount of pension expense that companies can recognize. (Choice C)  IFRS do not permit amortization of pension items included in OCI.  Those items remain in OCI until the company recognizes the gain or loss.  This typically causes a company reporting under IFRS to show more variability in year-to-year pension expense.

new_question_en: The impact on a lessor's financial statements in the first year of a lease that was newly classified as a sales-type lease rather than a direct- financing lease is most likely higher:
new_option_b: return on equity.
new_option_c: depreciation expense.
new_explanation_en: A finance lease removes the leased asset from the lessor's balance sheet and treats the lessee as the owner.  This means that the lessee, not the lessor, depreciates the asset; therefore, the lessor's depreciation expense decreases rather than increases (Choice C). A finance lease also assumes that the lessee "purchased" the asset with funds borrowed from the lessor.  The purchase "price" is the present value of the lease payments.  For the lessor, this creates an asset (eg, lease receivable) that replaces the leased item; therefore, the lessor's total assets are unchanged.  Leverage is defined as assets divided by owners' equity, and since the numerator does not increase, leverage does not increase (Choice A). US GAAP (but not IFRS) further classify a finance lease as either a direct-finance or a sales-type lease.  When the present value of all lease payments equals the asset's carrying value at the beginning of the lease, the lease is a direct-finance lease.  When the payments' present value exceeds the lessor's carrying value at commencement, the lease is a sales-type lease. With a sales-type lease, the lessor recognizes the difference between the present value and carrying value as a gain in the first year of the lease.  This gain increases the lessor's net income.  Return on equity (ROE) equals net income divided by owners' equity, so ROE is higher with a sales-type lease than with a direct-finance lease.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following is least likely to affect the value of a derivative instrument relative to the price of the underlying asset?
new_option_b: Replication of the derivative position
new_option_c: Expected rate of return on the underlying asset
new_explanation_en: Derivative pricing concepts Arbitrage-free Traders take advantage of any mispricing of derivatives Riskless strategies are created from offsetting positions in derivatives and underlying assets Strategies are pursued until risk-free profits are eliminated (ie, no-arbitrage pricing) Replication Derivatives can be created synthetically from underlying and risk-free assets Equivalent positions must have the same expected returns Risk-neutral Derivative price reflects the value of the replicating strategy Riskless positions are created from long/short derivatives and replication strategies Riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return; cash flows are discounted at the risk-free rate Expected rates of return on the underlying asset are used for valuing assets, but not for pricing derivatives.  Since derivative prices are derived from the price of the underlying asset, a derivative's price level is affected by the underlying's expected return.  However, the price of a derivative relative to the underlying's price is based on arbitrage and replication, so the price difference between the derivative and the underlying is not affected by the asset's expected return. Derivative positions can be replicated by combining positions in the underlying with the risk-free asset.  Positions that are economically equivalent should trade at prices that result in equal returns.  If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer be earned (Choices A and B). This arbitrage-free pricing means that risk aversion by investors has no effect on derivative pricing.  Therefore, derivative pricing is described as risk-neutral pricing.  Since arbitrage positions are riskless, risk-neutral pricing is the basis for valuing derivatives.  The expected rate of return on the underlying has no influence on the price of a derivative relative to the underlying asset.

new_question_en: An asset has a spot price of CNY 48 and its one-year cost of carry is CNY −1.20.  If the risk-free rate is 3%, the forward price of the asset is closest to:
new_explanation_en: The owner of an asset pays the holding costs and receives the benefits of holding the asset.  In contrast, a forward contract allows its holder to buy the underlying asset in the future for a predetermined price, so the contract owner does not experience any benefits or costs of the asset prior to purchase.  The cost of carry is the net value of the costs and benefits of holding the asset.  If the costs outweigh the benefits, the cost of carry is negative.  If the benefits are greater than the costs, the cost of carry is positive. To calculate the forward price of an asset, subtract the future value of the cost of carry from the future value of the spot price.  Find the future value by compounding at the risk-free rate.  In this scenario, the asset's spot price is CNY 48, T = 1, the risk-free rate is 3%, and the cost of carry for one year is CNY −1.20.  Substitute to calculate the forward price: (Choice A)  CNY 48.20 is the result of disregarding the sign of the cost of carry, which in this scenario is negative. (Choice B)  CNY 49.20 is the result of failing to take the future values of the spot price and the cost of carry before subtracting.
