pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: In May of this year, a farmer sells wheat forward for delivery in August.  If the spot price of wheat increases, the value of the contract to the farmer most likely:
new_option_b: remains the same.
new_option_c: increases.
new_explanation_en: An owner of an asset is exposed to the risk that the commodity price will fall between now and when it is sold.  Selling an asset forward means that the seller commits to deliver that asset at a future date for a guaranteed price.  Selling forward eliminates the seller's price risk, but it also means that the seller does not benefit if the asset's spot price is higher than the contracted price when the contract expires. Although the price the farmer receives at expiration is guaranteed, the relative value of the contract varies prior to expiration depending on how spot prices of the underlying asset change.  At expiration, the value of the contract is the difference between the spot price and the forward price. Prior to that time, the contract's value is the difference between the asset's current spot price and the present value of the forward price. Any gain to one party from a change in the forward contract's value is exactly offset by the other party's loss.  In this example, any increase in spot wheat prices prior to expiration causes the contract's value to increase to the long party.  As the farmer is short, an increase in the contract's value represents a loss. (Choice B)  The price that the farmer receives at the contract's expiration does not change, but the value of the contract changes as the underlying asset's price changes. (Choice C)  The value of any contract to the short party increases only if the price of the underlying asset decreases.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following is a limit to potential arbitrage opportunities?
new_option_b: Assets trading in different markets
new_option_c: Accuracy of derivative pricing models
new_explanation_en: Limits of arbitrage Transaction costs Capital constraints Cost of capital Inability to short Assuming market efficiency, if arbitrage opportunities exist, investors will earn riskless profits until prices adjust and arbitrage-free pricing is achieved.  However, specific conditions can prevent some investors from taking advantage of an arbitrage opportunity. For example, investors might encounter the following obstacles: Transaction costs may be too high. Access to the extremely large sums of capital required to scale the opportunity may not be available. The cost of capital to exploit the pricing discrepancy may be too high. There may be regulatory or transactional constraints on the ability to short certain assets. (Choice B)  The trading of assets in different markets does not limit arbitrage.  The fundamentals of arbitrage are based on the concept of simultaneously buying a security (eg, domestically listed foreign stock) in one market and selling an economically equivalent security in another market (eg, foreign stock in its local market). (Choice C)  Derivative pricing models are based on the fundamentals of arbitrage pricing and replication and can accurately identify mispricing. However, limitations of arbitrage affect an investor's ability to eliminate the identified pricing discrepancy and earn riskless profits.

new_question_en: Compared with a forward contract on the same underlying asset, when interest rates are positively correlated to futures prices, the futures price is most likely:
new_option_b: the same as the forward price.
new_option_c: higher than the forward price .
new_explanation_en: One difference between a forward contract and a futures contract relates to the daily mark-to-market process for futures contracts.  Each day's change in the futures price generates a gain for one side and an identical loss for the other.  The exchange deducts the losses from the loser's accounts and transfers them to the winner's accounts.  The winner reinvests the daily cash flows, which generates interest income. The graph above shows the advantage of holding a futures contract rather than a forward contract.  Both contracts expire in one year and have a forward price of $25.  It is assumed that the underlying asset increased by $0.10 per day.  The gain on the underlying asset was $36.50 for both contracts but reinvesting the cash flows from the daily mark-to-market of the futures contract generated nearly $1 in interest. When interest rates and asset prices are positively correlated, rising prices create gains for the long futures holders, which in turn can be invested at higher interest rates.  This is disadvantageous to sellers of futures contracts.  To induce participants to take short futures positions, the futures price must be set higher than for a forward contract, which does not settle gains and losses each day. (Choice A)  Futures prices are lower than forward prices when interest rates are negatively correlated to futures prices. (Choice B)  When interest rates are constant, futures prices and forward prices are the same in most cases.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: When creating a synthetic position, owning a share of stock of a publicly traded company is best replicated by:
new_option_a: buying a risk-free bond and selling a futures contract on the stock.
new_option_b: buying a risk-free bond and buying a futures contract on the stock.
new_option_c: selling a risk-free bond and selling a futures contract on the stock.
new_explanation_en: Replication combines an asset and a derivative to form a portfolio that is economically identical to a completely different asset.  Buying a share of stock and selling a stock futures contract produces the same economic result as buying a risk-free bond.  Logically, this makes sense: The stock/futures contract portfolio guarantees the price the investor receives (ie, eliminates price risk), so the portfolio's expected return is the risk-free interest rate.  Rearranging terms, buying a share of stock is equivalent to buying a risk-free bond and buying a stock futures contract. Replication is necessary to enforce the principle that a derivative's price must relate to the price of its underlying asset so that no arbitrage opportunities are created.  In this question, the stock/futures portfolio and its synthetic equivalent (eg, the risk-free bond) both generate the same risk-free return, so they must be priced the same.  If not, an investor can earn an arbitrage profit. (Choice A)  Buying a risk-free bond and simultaneously selling a stock futures contract replicates a short position in the underlying stock. (Choice C)  Shorting the stock and the futures contract replicates a short position in the risk-free bond.

new_question_en: A stock has a spot price of £120 and pays dividends over the next year that have a present value of £5.71.  Assuming there are no other costs or benefits of holding the asset and a risk-free rate of 5%, the 1-year forward price (in £) of the stock is closest to:
new_explanation_en: Investors can own an asset in the future either by buying it today or buying a forward contract to acquire the asset in the future.  Arbitrage pricing guarantees that forward prices differ from spot prices by the net cost of carry for the underlying asset until the forward expiration.  A forward contract's price is increased by any costs avoided and reduced by any benefits foregone by holding the forward contract rather than the asset. For the arbitrage pricing to hold, a forward price must equal: the future value of the spot price [S  (1 + r) ] less the future value of any benefits (eg, dividends) [−γ (1 + r) ] plus the future value of any costs [θ (1 + r) ]. In this scenario, the forward price equals the future value of the spot price less the future value of the dividend: F(T ) = 120 (1.05)  − 5.71 (1.05)  = 120 (Choice A)  £114 results from subtracting the future value of the dividend from the current spot price. (Choice C)  £132 results from adding, rather than subtracting, the future value of the dividend from the future value of the spot price.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: The costs of holding an asset exceed the benefits.  At inception, the price of a forward contract on the asset is most likely:
new_option_b: equal to its spot price.
new_option_c: greater than its spot price.
new_explanation_en: Forward price versus spot price Forward < Spot Costs < Benefits Forward = Spot Costs = Benefits Forward > Spot Costs > Benefits By buying a forward contract rather than the underlying asset, an investor avoids the costs, but also forgoes any benefits, of holding the asset. Forward contracts are usually initiated at a value of zero; therefore, the forward price differs from the spot price by the net cost of holding the underlying asset until the forward contract's expiration. The net holding costs are referred to as the cost of carry, or just the carry. The costs of holding the underlying: always include the opportunity cost of the money used to purchase the asset and may include additional expenses such as storage or insurance. The benefits of holding the underlying may include: monetary benefits such as dividends or interest and/or a nonmonetary benefit referred to as a convenience yield. When the costs of holding the asset are greater than the benefits, the forward price is greater than the spot price by the net amount saved by holding the forward and not incurring the net costs of holding the underlying (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: All else being equal, for a one-year forward contract initiated six months ago, an increase in the storage costs of the underlying asset implies that the contract's value to the long party most likely:
new_option_b: remains the same.
new_option_c: increases.
new_explanation_en: At expiration, the long party will buy at the forward price and can sell at the spot price.  The forward contract requires the long party to buy the asset in the future, which means the party cannot hold the asset now.  As a result, the value of the contract is increased by the present value of the asset's holding costs and is reduced by the present value of the asset's forgone benefits.  Therefore, the forward contract's value at any time prior to expiration is equal to (spot price − present value of forward price + present value of costs − present value of benefits). In this hypothetical scenario, the storage cost of holding the asset increased since contract initiation.  Suppose that at the end of May, the present value of the forward price is 102, the spot price is 100, the present value of the benefits is 1, and the present value of the storage costs is 6.  Then the value of the forward contract is 100 − 102 + 6 − 1 = 3.  If instead the storage costs were 8, the value of the forward contract would be 100 − 102 + 8 − 1 = 5.  However, the forward price remains fixed throughout the life of the contract. Therefore, for the long party in a forward contract, all else being equal, if the storage costs of the underlying asset increase, the value of the forward contract increases (Choices A and B).

new_question_en: On the day a forward contract is initiated, the spot price of the underlying asset is greater than the forward price.  This implies that the future value of the asset's benefits is most likely:
new_option_a: less than the future value of the costs of holding the asset.

new_explanation_en: The long party in a forward contract forgoes the benefits and avoids the costs of holding the underlying asset by purchasing that asset in the future, rather than the present.  To calculate the forward price: subtract the future value of the asset's benefits and add the future value of the costs of holding the asset to the future value of the spot price. Therefore, if the forward price of the asset is less than the spot price, the future value of the benefits of holding the asset must be greater than the future value of the costs. For example, suppose the spot price on a one-year contract is 100, the risk-free rate is 3%, the present value of asset costs is 2, and the forward price is 99.  In that case, the future value of the benefits of holding the asset must be greater than the future value of the costs (6.06 > 2):

new_question_en: Arbitrage-free pricing of forward contracts is most likely when the difference between the forward and spot prices reflects the underlying asset's:
new_option_b: price volatility.
new_option_c: expected return.
new_explanation_en: Taking a position in a forward contract avoids the costs and forgoes any benefits of taking an equivalent position in the underlying asset.  However, economically equivalent positions should trade at prices that result in equal returns.  If the condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust and the risk-free profits can no longer be earned.  With the arbitrage-free (ie, no arbitrage) pricing, the forward and spot price difference should reflect the cost of carry. Cost of carry, sometimes expressed as carry, is the net cost of holding (ie, carrying) a position in the underlying asset or commodity until the expiration of the related forward contract.  Cost of carry reflects the net of the following: Costs:  Charges for storage, insurance, or financing the underlying position Benefits:  Income (ie, dividends or interest) or convenience yield from holding the underlying (Choices B and C)  An asset's price volatility and expected rate of return affect an asset's price, not the difference between the asset's spot and forward prices.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following is the least likely reason for spot prices to be higher than a futures price?
new_option_b: Convenience yield
new_option_c: Increased asset supply
new_explanation_en: The owner of an asset can eliminate (ie, hedge) future price risk by selling a futures contract, which obligates the owner to sell the asset for a guaranteed price when the contract matures.  Eliminating risk also limits return, so the seller should earn the same return as a risk-free investment.  Any different return results in an arbitrage opportunity; therefore, the futures price is equal to the spot price compounded at the risk- free rate. The futures price is adjusted by storage costs and convenience yield.  Storage costs reduce the hedged position's return below the risk-free rate, so adding storage costs makes the return equal to the risk-free rate.  Conversely, the owner may earn a convenience yield from the underlying asset.  The convenience yield produces a return greater than the risk-free rate, so subtracting the convenience yield makes the return equal to the risk-free rate. (Choice B)  If the underlying has neither storage costs nor a convenience yield, the futures price is always greater than the spot price.  Storage costs increase this difference.  The asset's spot price can exceed the futures price only when the convenience yield exceeds storage costs. (Choice C)  The price of an asset fluctuates based on supply and demand.  An asset's price tends to move in the same direction as demand, while price and supply move in opposite directions.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.04 Arbitrage, Replication, and the Cost of Carry in Pricing Derivatives - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: All else being equal, an increase in an asset's convenience yield implies that relative to the spot price, the forward price most likely:
new_option_b: remains the same.
new_option_c: increases.
new_explanation_en: The forward price reflects the value of buying an asset in the future; the spot price reflects the value of holding the asset now.  The market sets the forward price based on three factors: the spot price, the costs of holding the asset, and the benefits of holding the asset.  Owning the forward contract means avoiding the costs and forgoing the benefits of holding the asset.  Therefore, the costs' future value is added and the benefits' future value is subtracted to determine the forward price. As new forward contracts are written each day, the forward price of contracts on the asset fluctuates due to changes in the three factors.  If the spot price of the asset increases or if the costs of holding the asset increase, the forward price of the asset increases on new contracts: If the benefits of holding the asset increase, the forward price decreases: A convenience yield, normally associated with a commodity, is the value of the nonmonetary benefits of holding an asset.  Since the convenience yield is a benefit of holding the asset, if it increases, the forward price of the asset decreases relative to its spot price for new contracts written on the asset (Choices B and C).

new_question_en: Derivative pricing most likely assumes investors are:
new_option_b: risk averse.
new_option_c: risk seeking.
new_explanation_en: Derivative pricing concepts Arbitrage-free Traders take advantage of any mispricing of derivatives Riskless strategies are created from offsetting positions in derivatives and underlying assets Strategies are pursued until risk-free profits are eliminated (ie, no-arbitrage pricing) Replication Derivatives can be created synthetically from underlying and risk-free assets Equivalent positions must have the same expected returns Risk-neutral Derivative price reflects the value of the replicating strategy Riskless positions are created from long/short derivatives and replication strategies Riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return; cash flows are discounted at the risk-free rate Investors can create riskless positions by combining an underlying asset (eg, long a bond) with related derivatives (eg, short bond futures). Since such strategies expose them to no risk, investors are assumed to be risk neutral when pricing derivatives (Choice C). Similarly, derivative positions can be replicated by combining positions in the underlying with the risk-free asset.  Positions that are economically equivalent should trade at prices that result in equal returns.  If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer be earned.  This arbitrage-free (ie, no-arbitrage) pricing means that risk aversion by investors has no effect on derivative pricing (Choice B).

new_question_en: Derivative pricing uses the assumption of risk neutrality since derivatives:
new_option_b: are expected to return the risk-free rate.
new_option_c: are priced at a discount to the underlying asset to offset the derivatives' greater risk.
new_explanation_en: Derivative pricing concepts Arbitrage-free Traders take advantage of any mispricing of derivatives Riskless strategies are created from offsetting positions in derivatives and underlying assets Strategies are pursued until risk-free profits are eliminated (ie, no-arbitrage pricing) Replication Derivatives can be created synthetically from underlying and risk-free assets Equivalent positions must have the same expected returns Risk-neutral Derivative price reflects the value of the replicating strategy Riskless positions are created from long/short derivatives and replication strategies Riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return; cash flows are discounted at the risk-free rate Replication and arbitrage are the foundations of derivative pricing.  Investors can replicate assets by combining positions in derivatives and the risk-free asset.  Economically equivalent positions should trade at prices that result in equal returns.  If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer be earned.  Therefore, derivatives trade at arbitrage-free prices. Under these pricing conditions, investors can create riskless positions (eg, long stock index and short stock index futures), which earn a risk-free rate of return.  The ability to create riskless positions and arbitrage-free pricing means that risk aversion has no role in derivative pricing. Therefore, investor risk neutrality is assumed in derivative pricing. (Choice B)  Since a long or short position in derivatives is not risk free, its expected returns would not be equal to the risk-free rate.  Risk-free securities (eg, government T-bills) have expected returns equal to the risk-free rate. (Choice C)  Derivatives can trade at either a discount or premium to the underlying and still be fairly valued.  Any difference between underlying and derivative prices reflects cost of carry arbitrage pricing, not an adjustment for the relative riskiness.

new_question_en: An analyst gathers the following information on two 18-month forward contracts, each for a different underlying asset: Asset X Asset Y Present value of benefits of owning asset 9.17 1.94 Present value of costs of owning asset 11.57 4.34 Spot price 157.939 157.939 Forward price 167.120 ? If the risk-free rate is 2.8%, the forward price of Asset Y is most likely:
new_option_a: less than the forward price of Asset X.
new_option_b: equal to the forward price of Asset X.
new_option_c: greater than the forward price of Asset X.
new_explanation_en: An investor can own an asset in the future (ie, at time T) by: buying the asset now at the spot price S  and holding it until time T, or entering into a forward contract now to purchase the asset at the forward price F (T) at time T. An investor who buys the asset now and holds it until time T incurs the costs and benefits of holding the asset.  An investor who instead goes long the forward contract avoids the costs and forgoes the benefits of holding the asset. This is reflected in the relationship between the futures price and the spot price, specifically in the carrying cost, since including the term −(γ − θ)(1 + r)  = (−γ + θ)(1 + r)  is equivalent to describing the forward price as "equal to the future value of the spot price minus benefits plus costs." In this scenario, it is not necessary to use the formula since the net cost of carry associated with each contract is the same: −(γ − θ) = −(1.94 − 4.34) = −(9.17 − 11.57) = 2.40 Since all other relevant variables are equal for each asset (as given), the two contracts have the same forward price.  The forward price for Asset Y can be calculated as: (Choice A)  Reversing the costs and benefits in the formula for the forward price results in incorrectly calculating a forward price for Asset Y that is lower than Asset X. (Choice C)  Using the present value of the benefits of Asset Y of 1.94 in the formula for the forward price incorrectly as a negative number results in a forward price for Asset Y that is greater than Asset X.

new_question_en: Which of the following combinations best replicates a long risk-free asset position?
new_option_a: Long asset and short risk-free bond
new_option_b: Short asset and long a forward contract
new_option_c: Long asset and short a forward contract
new_explanation_en: The no-arbitrage price for a forward contract that has no holding period benefits or costs is the future value of the spot price, which is compounded at the risk-free rate to the forward expiration to account for opportunity cost.  Positions in any two of the three instruments (ie, underlying asset, forward contract, andrisk-free bond) can be combined to replicate the third instrument. A combination of positions that earns a risk-free rate is the synthetic equivalent of a risk-free asset.  A long position in a risk-free bond is replicated by simultaneously: buying an asset (−S ), and selling a forward contract [+F (T)]. Selling a forward contract against a long position in the underlying asset eliminates price risk from the position and locks in a certain return to expiration equal to F (T) − S .  When no-arbitrage pricing conditions hold, the position earns a certain (ie, risk-free) rate of return, making it the equivalent of a risk-free asset. (Choice A)  Long asset and short risk-free bond (ie, borrowing) is equivalent to buying a forward contract. (Choice B)  Short asset and long a forward contract is equivalent to shorting the risk-free bond.

new_question_en: Arbitrage-free pricing of derivatives most likely results in using a discount rate equal to:
new_option_a: zero due to the inability to earn arbitrage profits.
new_option_b: the risk-free rate since riskless positions should earn a risk-free rate of return.
new_option_c: the underlying's required rate of return since the derivative's expected returns must be the same.
new_explanation_en: Derivative pricing concepts Arbitrage-free Traders take advantage of any mispricing of derivatives Riskless strategies are created from offsetting positions in derivatives and underlying assets Strategies are pursued until risk-free profits are eliminated (ie, no-arbitrage pricing) Replication Derivatives can be created synthetically from underlying and risk-free assets Equivalent positions must have the same expected returns Risk-neutral Derivative price reflects the value of the replicating strategy Riskless positions are created from long/short derivatives and replication strategies Riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return; cash flows are discounted at the risk-free rate Derivative positions can be replicated by combining positions in the underlying with the risk-free asset.  Economically equivalent positions should trade at prices that result in equal returns.  If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer be earned.  Arbitrage-free pricing means that investor risk aversion has no impact on derivative pricing.  Therefore, derivative pricing is described as risk-neutral pricing. By combining positions in the underlying asset (eg, long bond) and the derivative (eg, short bond futures), investors can create riskless positions.  Since riskless positions earn a risk-free rate of return, the expected payoffs are discounted at the risk-free rate when pricing derivatives. (Choice A)  An absence of arbitrage profits means derivatives are fairly priced relative to the underlying asset.  In that case, taking offsetting positions in the derivative and an appropriate replication strategy earns the risk-free rate of return, resulting in the risk-free rate (not zero) being the appropriate discount rate. (Choice C)  An asset's required rate of return is appropriate for valuing assets but not for pricing derivatives.  Derivative prices are derived from their underlying asset's price, based on arbitrage and risk-neutral pricing; therefore, the asset's required rate of return is not the appropriate discount rate.

new_question_en: An analyst suspects a company of manipulating its financials.  A trend that could most likely be a warning sign is:
new_option_a: declining inventory turnover over multiple periods.
new_option_b: receivables decreasing as a percentage of total revenue.
new_option_c: a net-income-to-cash-from-operating-activities ratio consistently below 1.
new_explanation_en: Common warning signs of accounting manipulation Frequent reporting "surprises" "Nonrecurring" items that consistently appear in multiple periods Unusual levels of receivables, payables, inventory turnover, operating cash flow, net income, profit margins Underestimating warranty expenses that are "restated" in subsequent periods Useful lives for long-term assets that are different than industry average Related-party transactions Heavy emphasis on pro forma (non-GAAP, non-IFRS) earnings Financial reporting standards (eg, IFRS, US GAAP) give companies discretion and flexibility over the financial information they present, which can result in companies manipulating their financials.  Analysts must stay alert for warning signs of manipulation, which should be analyzed further. One potential warning sign is a declining inventory turnover ratio over multiple periods.  The inventory turnover ratio provides an indication on how efficiently a company is managing its inventory.  Although a declining ratio may simply be due to poor inventory management, it may also signal that the company is purposefully not recognizing obsolescence to avoid write-downs in the current period.  However, this could result in inventory write-downs in future periods. (Choice B)  Receivables that are increasing as a percentage of total revenue may result from poor credit management or indicate aggressive accounting policies to recognize revenue early, such as "channel stuffing" (ie, delivering product to distributors ahead of customer demand). (Choice C)  A net-income-to-cash-from-operating-activities ratio consistently above 1 may be a warning sign of lower quality financials or manipulation.  While this trend may be due to the cyclicality of the business, it could also indicate that the company is using aggressive accounting policies to recognize revenue early or defer expense recognition.

new_question_en: Which of the following circumstances would least likely result in a company issuing financial reports considered to be of low quality?
new_option_a: The company is experiencing an exceptionally strong period.
new_option_b: Earnings are volatile from period to period due to a competitive industry.
new_option_c: The CEO wants to sell the company at a large premium to its current stock price.
new_explanation_en: Low-quality financial statements refer to statements that may be incomplete, biased and/or contain errors.  The CFA Institute identifies three conditions that often lead to low-quality statements: motivation, opportunity, and rationalization.  Both incorrect answers illustrate situations in which a company's decision makers could be motivated to present their company's financial situation in a way that distorts the true picture. Management can be motivated by career or compensation concerns to reduce earnings volatility (Choice B).  One way to manage earnings volatility is to create reserves that management can draw on when needed to "smooth" earnings from period to period.  A company with less volatile earnings in a volatile environment could be perceived as a superior investment, which in turn could lead to management having better job security and compensation. Similarly, a CEO's motivation for wanting to sell the company (Choice C) could be related to compensation.  Many senior executives receive some of their compensation in company stock.  Selling the company at a substantial premium directly benefits them, and companies with high earnings tend to command a higher price in takeovers.  This could lead to choices that boost current earnings but prove to be unsustainable in the long term. By contrast, a company having a strong period has no need to further enhance earnings.  It would want to issue high quality statements so that users would trust that the earnings are "real."

new_question_en: Adjusted EBITDA most accurately:
new_option_a: may exclude the impact of equity-based compensation.
new_option_b: may be impacted by the choice of depreciation method.
new_option_c: is commonly prepared under the same methodology across firms.
new_explanation_en: Management often presents pro forma (non-GAAP) financial measures, alongside US GAAP (or IFRS) measures, to convey its own interpretation of company performance.  Certain non-GAAP measures, such as adjusted EBITDA, may exclude the impact of noncash (eg, equity- based compensation) or transitory (eg, litigation charges) items. Adjusted EBITDA varies across companies and often excludes the impact of equity-based compensation, acquisition-related charges, impairment, lawsuits, and gain or loss on disposal of assets or extinguishment of debt. These management adjustments (ie, addbacks) are meant to normalize reported earnings (eg, net income) by eliminating the impact from nonrecurring items.  However, management often justifies weak reported earnings by showing a reconciled schedule to a higher adjusted EBITDA.  Therefore, analysts should apply some scrutiny to these measures. (Choice B)  Depreciation method does not impact adjusted EBITDA since EBITDA measures earnings before depreciation. (Choice C)  The method for calculating adjusted EBITDA is unique to every firm and subject to management discretion.

new_question_en: An analyst gathers the following information on two competitors, concerning their differences in accounting methods. Company 1 Company 2 Classification of investments held indefinitely Available-for-sale Trading securities Composition of intangible assets Majority consists of goodwill No goodwill Depreciation method on fixed assets Straight line Accelerated To facilitate proper financial comparison, the analyst should most appropriately:
new_option_a: adjust Company 2's gross book value of fixed assets.
new_option_b: reduce Company 1's net income for fair value investment gains.
new_option_c: reduce Company 1's amount of intangible assets by its goodwill balance.
new_explanation_en: Common analyst adjustments Category Issue Adjustment Investments Available-for-sale vs. trading securities classification Adjust net income and/or other comprehensive income Inventory Comparing different cost methods (FIFO, LIFO, weighted average, specific ID) Adjust COGS and inventory balance Fixed assets Straight-line vs. accelerated depreciation methods Adjust depreciation expense and fixed assets' net book value Goodwill Significant M&A growth vs. internal organic growth Adjust book value of intangible assets for goodwill M&A = mergers and acquisitions. Analysts often compare companies that use different accounting methods and/or rely on distinct assumptions and estimates when preparing financial results.  Differences between IFRS and US GAAP may also distort comparison.  Analysts often adjust financial statements for such differences and/or requirements to facilitate "apples-to-apples" comparisons. In this scenario, Company 1's intangible assets include significant goodwill, while Company 2 has no goodwill.  Goodwill results purely from mergers and acquisitions activities and represents the purchase premium over an acquired company's fair value of net identifiable assets. Although goodwill is periodically tested for impairment, its value is subjective (ie, based on what the acquirer paid) and may overstate the acquirer's assets.  Therefore, an analyst should adjust Company 1's book value of intangible assets for better comparison with Company 2. (Choice A)  Net book value, not gross book value of fixed assets, should be adjusted when comparing companies that use different depreciation methods.  Gross book value represents the historical purchase price and remains constant.  Net book value is gross book value adjusted for accumulated depreciation. (Choice B)  Company 1 appropriately classifies investments that are held indefinitely as available-for-sale.  Fair value gains bypass net income and flow directly into other comprehensive income.  Thus, no adjustment to Company 1's net income is necessary.

new_question_en: Which of the following reporting practices is most likely considered aggressive accounting?
new_option_a: Presenting pro forma earnings per share (EPS) that are lower than reported EPS.
new_option_b: Capitalizing, instead of expensing, in-process research and development (R&D) costs.
new_option_c: Using the criteria of available-for-sale securities, rather than trading securities, to treat bond investment gains.
new_explanation_en: Aggressive accounting vs. conservative accounting Aggressive Conservative Capitalizing costs Classifying investments as trading securities Presenting better pro forma results than IFRS or GAAP results Expensing costs Classifying investments as available- for-sale securities Presenting pro forma results close to IFRS or GAAP results Accounting choices affect the quality of a company's financial results.  Aggressive accounting choices tend to inflate financial performance (eg, earnings, cash flow) in the current period but may understate performance in future periods.  Conservative choices typically understate performance in the current period but may enhance future performance. Capitalizing (instead of expensing) in-process research and development (R&D) costs in a reporting period assigns those costs to an asset on the balance sheet.  They are then amortized periodically as an expense on the income statement.  The capitalization of a cost will produce: higher net income in the current period since the entire cost is not expensed immediately, but lower net income in future periods since the remaining cost is expensed over time. Therefore, capitalization is an aggressive accounting choice.  R&D costs should be capitalized only when the product is reasonably certain to generate future revenue and is no longer considered to be in process. (Choice A)  Pro forma earnings typically include numerous management adjustments (ie, add-backs) that cause them to differ from reported earnings (ie, those under GAAP or IFRS).  In general, management presents pro forma earnings that are higher than reported earnings and therefore considered aggressive. (Choice C)  When bond investments are treated as available-for-sale securities, any gains in fair value are included in other comprehensive income on the balance sheet instead of going directly to net income (earnings).  Therefore, this treatment is a conservative choice.

new_question_en: Which of the following is least likely to increase financial reporting discipline?
new_option_a: Auditor reports included as part of the auditing company's consulting services
new_option_b: Debt covenants that require the current ratio to be at or above a minimum figure
new_option_c: Regulations that enforce disclosure but do not require management to certify financial statements
new_explanation_en: Primary mechanisms that enhance financial reporting discipline Regulators Recognize and enforce disclosure standards applicable to all companies Auditors Opinions that statements comply with standards and fairly present the company's finanical condition Investors Features such as debt covenants create special financial reporting requirements to aid creditors Many jurisdictions require a company's statements to be audited by an independent auditor.  An unqualified (ie, "clean") auditor's opinion does not guarantee the statements' accuracy, but it certifies that the statements comply with accounting standards and present the company's results fairly.  The prospect of a poor auditor's opinion can induce a company to produce high-quality statements since market repercussions from a poor report are severe. The company being audited pays the auditor's fee.  By itself, that does not impugn an auditor's independence and objectivity.  However, an auditor that bundles auditing with other services as part of overall engagement is not "independent."  Earning compensation from other services may cause an auditor to provide a lenient audit opinion to preserve those additional compensation sources. (Choice B)  Investors or creditors may have legally enforceable rights against a company that violates the terms of an investment contract.  An example is a lender that can accelerate payment of the loan if the borrower violates a debt covenant. (Choice C)  Regulations often impose penalties on a company if its financial statements contain material misstatements or omit certain information.  The possibility of penalties tends to enhance reporting discipline, regardless of whether the regulations require management to attest to the information's accuracy.

new_question_en: A company reports a significant increase in earnings per share (EPS) for fiscal year 20X8.  An analyst examining the annual financial statements determines that the increase arises mostly from sales of noncore fixed assets.  The statements are GAAP-compliant in all respects, and the footnotes provide significant details about the sales.  The financial statements most likely represent:
new_option_a: high-quality financial reporting and financial earnings.
new_option_b: high-quality financial reporting but low-quality financial earnings.
new_option_c: low-quality financial reporting but high-quality financial earnings.
new_explanation_en: Financial reporting can be evaluated from two perspectives.  The first is the quality of the reporting itself.  High-quality reporting is characterized by providing enough information to allow a user to make an informed decision about a company's valuation and desirability as an investment. High-quality reports consistently comply with accounting standards, provide more (rather than less) information, and use conservative accounting choices. The second perspective is the quality of the earnings the company reports.  A high-quality report does not necessarily mean that the earnings are also of high quality.  High-quality earnings result from activities that produce sustainable and recurring earnings.  Earnings that result from asset sales are unsustainable. The company in this question produces reports that appear to be of high quality (ie, complying with applicable accounting standards, detailed footnotes).  However, the reported earnings are not of high quality due to unsustainable earnings from asset sales. (Choices A and C)  The reporting quality is high, but the earnings quality is low.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: High-quality financial earnings are least likely characterized by:
new_option_b: sustainable and robust sources of revenue.
new_option_c: conservative estimates of useful lives for noncurrent assets.
new_explanation_en: High-quality financial earnings are characterized by sustainability over future periods.  The quality of reported earnings tends to be positively correlated to the quality of the financial statements that chronicle those earnings.  Companies with conservative accounting policies tend to generate high-quality earnings more often than companies with more aggressive reporting methods.  The same applies for companies that make unbiased accounting choices. Pro forma statements are one characteristic of aggressive reporting.  They selectively present limited information that makes current earnings appear stronger than might otherwise be justified.  The selective nature of the information calls into question whether the earnings are sustainable.  Pro forma presentations do not comply with either US GAAP or IFRS. Choosing shorter useful lives for noncurrent assets represents a conservative accounting choice (Choice C).  The shorter lives result in higher depreciation expense each year.  The increased expense means lower earnings.  Also, shorter useful lives implicitly signal the company's intent to invest in its infrastructure to foster future earnings growth. (Choice B)  Revenue is the primary driver of earnings.  Robust and sustainable revenues tend to result in consistent, high-quality earnings.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.10 Financial Reporting Quality - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following accounting choices would most likely artificially enhance reported results in the current period?
new_option_a: Expensing, rather than capitalizing, long-term asset purchases
new_option_b: Decreasing future benefit projections for a goodwill impairment assessment
new_option_c: Changing revenue recognition criteria from Free on Board (FOB) destination to FOB shipping
new_explanation_en: Under both IFRS and US GAAP, revenue can be recognized when the risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred to the buyer.  When goods are in transit: under Free on Board (FOB) destination, ownership transfers to the buyer when the shipped goods are received.  Therefore, the seller can recognize revenue only when the goods arrive at the customer's destination. under FOB shipping point, ownership transfers to the buyer upon shipment.  Therefore, the seller can recognize revenue when the goods are shipped. For a seller, switching shipping terms from FOB destination to FOB shipping will change the timing of when the goods' ownership is transferred, thus changing when revenue can be recognized.  It effectively allows a seller to recognize revenue earlier, which results in more reported revenue for the current period.  Therefore, management sometimes uses this tactic to enhance reported revenue for a period. (Choice A)  Expensing, rather than capitalizing, an asset purchase will increase operating expenses for the current period, thus lowering profits. Expensing an asset purchase is a conservative choice. (Choice B)  Decreasing future cash benefit projections in a goodwill impairment test will more likely lead to a write-down; therefore, it is a conservative choice.

new_question_en: A company sells a homogeneous product and many of its sales are on credit.  An analyst is reviewing the company's financial statements for the past three years.  Which of the following would an analyst least appropriately consider to be a warning sign concerning the company's financial reporting?
new_option_a: Inventory turnover has declined each year over the period.
new_option_b: The company routinely recognizes revenue using bill-and-hold arrangements.
new_option_c: The ratio of cash flow from operations to net income is consistently more than 1.0.
new_explanation_en: Common warning signs of accounting manipulation Frequent reporting "surprises" "Nonrecurring" items that consistently appear in multiple periods Unusual levels of receivables, payables, inventory turnover, operating cash flow, net income, profit margins Underestimating warranty expenses that are "restated" in subsequent periods Useful lives for long-term assets that are different than industry average Related-party transactions Heavy emphasis on pro forma (non-GAAP, non-IFRS) earnings Both GAAP and IFRS allow managers discretion over the financial information they are required to present and over how it is presented.  Analysts must be vigilant to detect managers' manipulation of financial statements which may reduce the quality of the financial statements and/or the company's earnings, even if such manipulation is not so extreme as to be criminal conduct. Analysts should pay close attention to the ratio of cash from operations (CFO) to net income.  Sales on credit (ie, new accounts receivable) are included in a company's net income.  Receivables must be converted to cash to pay expenses.  Not converting receivables to cash may indicate that the company is recognizing "sales" that are illusory (and thus cannot be converted to cash), which is an accounting impropriety.  A ratio of at least 1.0 indicates that CFO is keeping pace with net income; a ratio of consistently less than 1.0 likely constitutes a warning sign. (Choice A)  Inventory turnover (ie, the ratio of COGS to average inventory) measures how quickly a company sells its inventory.  If this ratio is decreasing, it may signal that the company has poor inventory management or that its inventory is becoming obsolete.  Declining inventory turnover is a warning sign. (Choice B)  A bill-and-hold arrangement is an agreement for a sale today with delivery deferred to a subsequent period.  The seller improperly recognizes the revenue today despite not delivering the goods.  Consistently using bill-and-hold transactions to recognize revenue is a warning sign.

new_question_en: A manager collects the following information (in USD) on a company that reports under US GAAP: The company has no inventory at the beginning of the year and 100 units in inventory at the end of the year.  Management is under pressure to meet its year-end earnings target and is considering changing its accounting methods.  Which change in inventory costing method is most likely to increase earnings?
new_option_b: Periodic weighted average to LIFO
new_option_c: FIFO to periodic weighted average
new_explanation_en: LIFO vs. FIFO: impact on financial statements Inventory costs COGS Profit LIFO Increasing Higher Lower Decreasing Lower Higher FIFO Increasing Lower Higher Decreasing Higher Lower Analysts should be aware of how a change in accounting methods or estimates can be used to manage or manipulate earnings.  Even when permitted by accounting standards, such a change should be interpreted in the context of the company's performance. When inventory costs are rising, changing inventory valuations to FIFO lowers COGS and increases earnings, since, under FIFO, the first (lowest cost) purchases flow into COGS.  LIFO, however, uses the last purchases (highest cost) to value COGS, and under the periodic weighted average (PWA) method, the average purchase cost flows into COGS. Using the COGS formula, there are 100 units sold (0 + 200 − 100 = 100) during the period; the value of the units sold depends on the inventory costing method used.  To determine which change in accounting method increases earnings the most, first find COGS using each method. Then find the difference in inventory costing methods; a decrease in COGS increases earnings. Switching from LIFO to FIFO saves the company USD 29,000 in reported expenses and increases earnings, whereas the other changes increase COGS and decrease earnings (Choices B and C).

new_question_en: An analyst compiles the following information about a company: 20X2 20X3 ROE 16.7% 17.2% Total asset turnover 1.06 1.07 Leverage 1.53 1.61 Based on only this information, the most appropriate conclusion is that:
new_option_a: return on assets increased and net profit margin increased.
new_option_b: return on assets decreased and net profit margin increased.
new_option_c: return on assets decreased and net profit margin decreased.
new_explanation_en: A company's ROE measures the level of profit, as measured by net income, the company can generate with the equity invested by shareholders. DuPont analysis breaks down ROE into its component factors to understand which elements are driving the company's returns. The first level of DuPont analysis separates ROE into the return on assets ratio (ROA) and the leverage ratio.  ROA is then broken down into the net profit margin and total asset turnover ratios.  This process separates ROE into three elements: Profitability, measured by the net profit margin ratio Efficiency, measured by the asset turnover ratio Leverage, measured by the leverage ratio Those elements can be broken down by additional levels of DuPont analysis. In this scenario, the company's ROA is determined from the ROE and leverage ratios as follows: ROE = ROA × Leverage ROA = ROE / Leverage ROA = 0.167 / 1.53 ≈ 10.9% ROA = 0.172 / 1.61 ≈ 10.7% Between 20X2 and 20X3, the company's ROA declined from 10.9% to 10.7% (Choice A).  The calculated ROA can be used to determine the company's net profit margin as follows: ROA = Net profit margin × Total asset turnover Net profit margin = ROA / Total asset turnover Net profit margin = 0.109 / 1.06 ≈ 10.3% Net profit margin = 0.107 / 1.07 = 10.0% 20X2 20X3 20X2 20X3 Between 20X2 and 20X3, the company's net profit margin declined from 10.3% to 10.0% (Choice B).

new_explanation_en: Return on common equity (ROCE) gauges the amount of residual net income (after accounting for preferred dividends) generated relative to common equity.  Preferred dividends are subtracted from net income since common shareholders receive distributions only after preferred shareholders receive their dividends.  Greater ROCE ratios suggest that a company is more effective in using common equity to generate a return for common shareholders. ROCE should not be confused with ROE (return on equity).  ROE measures the return for all equity investors (preferred and common) and is calculated as net income / average total equity. (Choice B)  5.18% results from failing to subtract preferred dividends from net income.  ROCE measures return for common shareholders only, so distributions to preferred shareholders (ie, preferred dividends) should be taken out. (Choice C)  6.18% results from incorrectly using EBIT, instead of net income, in the calculation.  EBIT measures profits before interest and taxes, which reduce income available to common shareholders.

new_question_en: An analyst calculates the following data for the year ending 20X9. Using DuPont analysis, the firm's return on equity (ROE) is closest to:
new_explanation_en: Return on equity (ROE) measures the profitability generated per unit of equity invested.  Simply defined, ROE is the ratio of net income to average shareholders' equity.  DuPont analysis subdivides ROE into five underlying components: tax burden, interest burden, profitability, efficiency, and leverage.  Each component gauges a different aspect of financial performance that contributes to ROE; that detail helps the company focus efforts at improvement. ROE can be calculated as the product of the company's return on assets (ROA) and leverage since profitability can be enhanced through leverage.  ROA, the ratio of net income to assets, can be expressed as the product of net profit margin, a measure of profitability, and asset turnover, a measure of efficiency. (Choice A)  15.1% is the product of net profit margin and average total assets less the tax rate.  The tax burden has already been factored into the net profit margin, so it is inappropriate to deduct it again. (Choice C)  25.2% occurs by inappropriately dividing ROA by the debt-to-equity ratio.

new_question_en: Which of the following is the best use of ratio analysis for a company?

new_explanation_en: Insights gained from financial ratio analysis Comprehension of: Helps in assessing: Internal economic relationships Projected free cash flow Current financial status Ability to expand and pay debts Management's strategy execution Reliance on management's claims Peer and time-series analysis Absolute and relative performance Ratio analysis entails reviewing a company's activity, leverage, profitability, and valuation ratios.  Detecting important economic connections between different ratios is crucial in making economic decisions; the ratios alone are just statistics regarding a company's performance. Analysts seek connections between ratios from time-series or cross-sectional analyses.  A company's efficiency may impact its profitability, which in turn affects its valuation.  Analysts must use inferences from ratio analyses to form independent judgments.  They then use these judgments to arrive at economic conclusions (eg, creditworthiness, stock price). (Choice A)  Historical profitability ratios show the company's ability to generate profit, but since profit is different from cash flow, these ratios are not useful in determining the company's creditworthiness. (Choice B)  The current year's liquidity ratios are data that may indicate the company's ability to pay short-term debts.  Only a comprehensive evaluation of all ratios over time can provide an understanding of the company's overall performance, not just its liquidity.

new_question_en: An analyst gathers the following information on two companies: ($ millions) Company A Company B Cash 100 120 Short-term marketable investments 40 25 Accounts receivable 40 55 Inventory 100 120 Current liabilities 255 275 Based on this information, compared to Company B, Company A most likely has a higher:
new_option_b: quick ratio.
new_option_c: current ratio.
new_explanation_en: Analysts use liquidity ratios to assess a company's ability to meet short-term obligations, based on some measure of current assets available to fund current liabilities.  Three common liquidity ratios are the current ratio, quick ratio, and cash ratio, which differ in how they measure available current assets.  The denominator of each ratio is current liabilities, but their numerators are as follows: Current ratio:  cash, short-term investments, accounts receivable, inventory, and prepaid expenses Quick ratio:  assets that can be "quickly" liquidated (ie, cash, short-term investments, accounts receivable) Inventory is excluded since it typically takes longer to convert to cash. Prepaid expenses are also excluded since typically they cannot be converted to cash. Cash ratio:  only cash and short-term investments, the most liquid of current assets This makes the cash ratio the most conservative of the three measures with respect to a company's ability to satisfy its current liabilities.  In this scenario, Company A has a higher cash ratio than Company B since Company A has more cash and short-term marketable investments relative to its short-term obligations.

new_explanation_en: Analysts can use integrated financial ratio analysis to gauge a company's performance over time in terms of its activity or efficiency, liquidity, solvency, profitability, and valuation. Activity ratios measure how efficiently a company uses its assets. Liquidity ratios measure how well a company can cover its short-term obligations with cash or assets that are easily converted to cash. Solvency ratios measure a company's ability to satisfy its long-term obligations. Profitability ratios measure a company's return on sales and return on investments. Valuation ratios measures a company's stock price relative to its fundamentals. In this scenario, solvency, as measured by debt-to-equity (Debt / Equity) and debt-to-EBITDA (Debt / EBITDA), has been improving.  The downward trend in both ratios indicates that the company has lowered its outstanding debt relative to its equity and EBITDA. (Choice B)  Efficiency (ie, activity), as measured by working-capital turnover (Sales / Net working capital) and fixed asset turnover (Sales / Fixed assets), has worsened.  Both ratios are trending down over time, indicating that the company has become less efficient at using its assets to generate sales. (Choice C)  The stock price has become less expensive over time relative to company fundamentals, as indicated by the decreasing price-to-book (P/B) and price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios here.  This suggests that the investors pay less for the stock relative to the company's earnings and book value.

new_explanation_en: Fixed asset (FA) turnover measures how efficiently a company generates revenue with its net FAs (ie, gross FAs less accumulated depreciation).  FAs are used over the long term and typically consist of property, plant & equipment (PPE) and intangible assets. High FA turnover may indicate that a company is using its FAs efficiently to generate sales (eg, operating machines near capacity). Low FA turnover may indicate that a company is not using its FAs efficiently (eg, there is excess capacity) or that the assets are relatively new, and therefore net FA is high due to little depreciation. In this question, divide 20X9 revenue by the average net FA to calculate FA turnover. It should be noted that income statement items (eg, revenue) reflect what happens throughout a period, whereas balance sheet items (eg, net FAs) reflect the balance at the end of the period.  In most ratios that mix an income statement item with a balance sheet item, the balance sheet item is averaged to better capture changes throughout the period.  Therefore, FAs are averaged to better reflect the level of FAs throughout the year. Operating margin measures ability to further cover operating expenses such as marketing or research and development. new_question_en: An analyst collects the following annual data for a company: Which of the following best describes how the company's efficiency compares with the industry?
new_option_a: The company has a receivable turnover that is better.
new_option_b: The company has more effective inventory management.
new_option_c: The company produces less revenue for a given asset level.
new_explanation_en: Activity ratios measure how efficient a company is and indicate its operational performance.  Days of inventory on hand (DOH), an activity ratio, indicates management's effectiveness in overseeing its inventory.  DOH is the average number of days it takes a company to convert inventory (eg, current assets) into revenue. The ratio is calculated as the number of days in the period divided by the company's inventory turnover (COGS/average inventory).  Lower DOH suggests that management has a lower drain on company assets and generates revenue more quickly.  Here, it has more effective inventory management than its peers since its DOH is less than the industry average (25.42 < 29.77). (Choice A)  Using the days of sales outstanding formula, the company's receivable turnover of 8.09 (45.10 = 365 / receivable turnover) is lower than the industry's of 12.13 (30.09 = 365/receivable turnover).  Its receivable turnover is worse, not better than the industry average.  If the days of sales outstanding (DSO) is lower than the industry average, so is the receivable turnover since they are effectively the same; DSO converts turnover into a time measurement. (Choice C)  Total asset turnover is a ratio that measures a company's overall efficiency; a higher ratio means the company is more efficient at generating revenue for a given level of assets.  The company produces more revenue for a given asset level than its peers since its total asset turnover is greater (1.20 > 1.15) than the industry average.

new_question_en: An analyst completes the following DuPont analysis on two companies: Compared with Company Y, Company X mostly likely has a:
new_option_a: lower ROE and is more efficient.
new_option_b: higher ROE and has a higher profit margin.
new_option_c: higher ROE and a higher proportion of debt.
new_explanation_en: DuPont analysis entails decomposing ROE into five components.  In this case, multiply the five components together to find the ROE of Companies X and Y, which are 16.20% and 15.55%, respectively.  Company X has a higher ROE despite its lower profitability (0.10 vs. 0.18) and efficiency (0.90 vs. 1.20) compared with Company Y's.  Company X has greater leverage (ie, proportion of debt) than Company Y (3.00 vs 1.20), which is why Company X's ROE is greater than Company Y's (Choices A and B). Leverage is a gauge of solvency as measured by the company's assets relative to its average total equity.  The higher the ratio, the more the company finances its assets with debt.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.11 Financial Analysis Techniques - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A company uses LIFO to determine the valuation for inventory and reports the following under US GAAP: The company discloses that its LIFO reserve in 20X7 was $277 and in 20X6 was $450.  If the company used FIFO instead of LIFO for its inventory valuation, then over the last year, the company's current ratio most likely:
new_option_b: remained the same.
new_option_c: increased.
new_explanation_en: Companies that use LIFO (last-in, first-out) to value inventory often report lower inventory and higher expense than companies that use FIFO (first- in, first-out).  Under US GAAP, companies that use LIFO must report the difference between inventory under LIFO and FIFO as the LIFO reserve. When preparing comparisons between companies that differ in their use of LIFO and FIFO inventory valuation, add back the LIFO reserve to convert LIFO inventory to FIFO. In this case, to find the company's current ratio as it would be under the FIFO method, add the LIFO reserve to current assets (inventory is a part of current assets). The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities.  Using current assets adjusted for FIFO, the current ratio decreases year over year from 5.33 to 5.04. (Choice B)  The current ratio would have remained the same with no adjustment for differences in the accounting method. (Choice C)  The current ratio would have increased by subtracting the LIFO reserve from current assets.  To adjust for differences between LIFO and FIFO, add the LIFO reserves to inventory.  This increases current assets.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.11 Financial Analysis Techniques - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: An analyst compiles the following data from a company's financial statements: SAR millions 20X6 20X5 20X4 Revenue 1,600 1,400 1,300 Net income 200 100 100 Current assets 550 500 500 Total assets 2,150 1,700 1,600 Current liabilities 350 300 300 Total debt 1,100 800 800 Total liabilities 1,350 1,000 900 Based on only this information, the change in which of the following ratios from 20X5 to 20X6 most likely would be considered an improvement to profitability or solvency?
new_option_b: Return on equity ratio
new_option_c: Financial leverage ratio
new_explanation_en: Financial ratios can be useful indicators of a company's health and performance and therefore are used extensively in financial analysis.  Ratios typically require context, either comparing them to other companies or to the same ratio in prior periods. In this scenario, the level of debt affects all three ratios.  The debt-to-equity ratio and financial leverage ratio both measure a company's leverage. Greater proportions of debt increase a company's leverage, causing both ratios to increase.  Debt also increases a company's interest expense, causing its net income and return on equity (ROE) to be more sensitive to changes in operating income. ROE is a profitability ratio that measures the return (ie, net income) earned by a company's equity shareholders.  Higher ROE ratios indicate a higher rate of return for each dollar of equity invested.  In this scenario, equity must be calculated before calculating ROE.  Liabilities are used to calculate equity since a company's shareholders have claims on its assets only after all obligations (eg, debt, accounts payable) have been paid. Steps 20X6 20X5 Calculate year-end equity: Assets − Liabilities Equity = 2,150 − 1,350 = 800 Equity = 1,700 − 1,000 = 700 Equity = 1,700 − 1,000 = 700 Equity = 1,600 − 900 = 700 Calculate average equity Equity = (800 + 700) / 2 = 750 Equity = (700 + 700) / 2 = 700 Calculate ROE: Net income / Average equity ROE = 200 / 750 = 26.7% ROE = 100 / 700 = 14.3% The company's ROE increased from 14.3% in 20X5 to 26.7% in 20X6, indicating an improvement of profitability. (Choice A)  The company's debt-to-equity ratio increased from 1.14 in 20X5 to 1.38 in 20X6, indicating a decline in solvency. (Choice C)  The company's financial leverage ratio increased from 2.43 in 20X5 to 2.69 in 20X6, indicating a decline in solvency.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.12 Introduction to Financial Statement Modeling - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Three manufacturers dominate the canned fruit market and buy fruits from a fragmented market of many farmers.  However, a large agricultural distributor enters the fruit market, sourcing the fruits from the farmers, which forces the manufacturers to buy directly from the distributor.  Based only on this information and on Porter's framework, which of the following forces is most likely weakening the manufacturers' competitive position?
new_option_b: Rivalry among incumbents
new_option_c: Bargaining power of suppliers
new_explanation_en: Porter's five forces: Effects on prices, costs, and profitability Pricing power is limited when… Threat of substitutes Substitutes exist Switching costs are low Rivalry among incumbents Industries are fragmented and have Limited growth High exit barriers High fixed costs Identical products Bargaining power of suppliers* Supplier is greater in size than buyer Demand is relatively inelastic No alternatives are available Bargaining power of customers The market is fragmented Products are nonstandardized Switching costs are low Threat of new entrants The threat of new entrants is high (eg, low barriers to entry) *Bargaining power of suppliers affects the prices of input costs. Porter's five forces framework is commonly used to assess how the competitive environment of an industry can affect prices and costs.  This methodology gives analysts valuable insights when forecasting revenues and margins. The bargaining power of suppliers denotes the level of influence or leverage that suppliers have when negotiating prices, terms, and conditions.  Suppliers may have stronger bargaining power in an industry when, for example: There are few suppliers, and each is greater in size than the firms in the industry Suppliers offer differentiated or specialized products or services There are no readily available substitutes and/or the costs to switch suppliers are high In this situation, the entrance of a large agricultural distributor, an intermediary that consolidates the manufacturers' supply sources, increases the bargaining power of suppliers and weakens the manufacturers' leverage when buying inputs (ie, fruits). (Choice A)  The threat of new entrants refers to new competitors entering the canned fruit market and directly competing with the food manufacturers.  However, the agricultural distributor is a supplier, not a competitor. (Choice B)  Rivalry among incumbents relates to the competitive landscape (eg, price competition, number and size of competitors, and product differentiation) in the food manufacturers' market of canned fruits.  There is no change in the intensity of competition between the three food manufacturers.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.12 Introduction to Financial Statement Modeling - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: At the beginning of the fiscal year, a CEO provides optimistic annual EPS guidance, citing strong government-sector demand.  Throughout the year, unforeseen tariffs significantly increase raw material costs.  The CEO declines to revise forecasts, stating that the company's solid fundamentals should be able to offset gross margin compression. Based only on this information, which of the following biases does the CEO least likely exhibit?
new_option_b: Illusion of control bias
new_option_c: Representativeness bias
new_explanation_en: Behavioral biases affecting analyst forecasts and their remedies Bias Description Remedy Overconfidence Having unjustified faith in own capacity and abilities Review past forecasts, assess relative accuracy Apply scenario analysis Illusion of control Overestimating own ability to control forecast accuracy Restrict number of model variables and expert opinions Conservatism Being reluctant to incorporate  new information (eg, anchoring) Regular review of models by an investment team Flexible models, fewer variables Representativeness Classifying new data based on past views or experience (eg, base-rate neglect) For base-rate neglect, consider both outside and inside information Confirmation Selecting data that confirm beliefs and discarding conflicting data Seek different perspectives (eg, neutral or negative opinions) Behavioral biases often lead to forecasting errors.  Analysts should recognize that biases exist and account for these biases in their analyses. Conservatism bias (eg, anchoring) occurs when individuals are reluctant to update a prior forecast to reflect new information. Illusion of control bias occurs when individuals overestimate their ability to control an outcome. Representativeness bias occurs when individuals form opinions based on past experiences or known classifications, dismissing the specifics of the current situation. In this scenario, the CEO exhibits conservatism in upholding the optimistic prior forecast in spite of contradictory evidence of rising costs (Choice A).  The CEO also exhibits illusion of control by thinking the company can maintain its EPS through its solid fundamentals (Choice B).  However, these actions are insufficient to clearly indicate representativeness since there is no indication of the CEO applying past beliefs or known classifications to conclude that the tariffs will not affect EPS.
