new_option_c: contraction risk.
new_explanation_en: Auto loan asset-backed securities: prepayment dynamics Securitized by Amortizing auto loans and leases Nonrecourse loans Subject to prepayment risk due to Changes in interest rates Early loan payoff Vehicle ownership change Sales and trade-ins Repossessions and resale Insurance proceeds for destroyed autos Auto loan asset-backed securities (ABS) are securitized by amortizing, nonrecourse loans, which are prone to prepayments.  Prepayment risk is normally associated with changing interest rates, but auto loan ABS are also impacted by other factors.  There are two forms of prepayment risk: contraction risk and extension risk. Contraction risk is most acute when interest rates fall and lead to refinancing (eg, mortgage, auto loan), which pay loans off early.  More prepayments than expected shorten the life of the ABS, resulting in a reduction in the final maturity. Extension risk occurs when interest rates increase; higher rates result in slower prepayments than expected and lengthen the security's life (Choice B). Auto loan ABSs have other elements that affect the speed of prepayments not directly tied to interest rates, which exposes investors to more contraction risk. Examples include: borrowers who choose to pay the loan early sales and trade-ins repossessions and resales insurance proceeds for destroyed vehicles (Choice A)  Balloon risk refers to a risk of partially amortizing and interest-only loans that have balloon payments due at the end of the loan. Balloon payments are unusual for auto loans and therefore are not a risk for holders of auto loan ABS.

new_question_en: If covered bondholders do not receive payments as scheduled and the bond has a soft-bullet redemption regime, the bond default is most likely:
new_option_a: delayed, and final maturity is extended.

new_explanation_en: Covered bond redemption regimes If fund sponsor defaults: Hard bullet Default triggered; payments accelerate Soft bullet Default delayed; final maturity date extended Conditional pass- through Pass-through mode triggered only if bonds are not retired at original maturity date A type of asset-backed security (ABS), a covered bond is secured by collateral consisting of a pool of loans (eg, auto loans, home mortgages). Interest and principal payments on ABS depend exclusively on the timely payment of the interest and principal on the underlying loans. Unlike other ABS, covered bonds offer an additional layer of protection since bondholders have dual recourse, which allows a claim on both the issuer and the cover pool (ie, underlying pool of loans).  Other kinds of ABS are typically issued by a special purpose entity so that the issuer remains bankruptcy remote. If payments on covered bonds are not received as scheduled, stipulations in the issuing documents (ie, loan covenants) called redemption regimes determine how the bonds are impacted.  The three types of covered bond redemption regimes are as follows: Hard bullet:  Bond default is triggered and all payments are due immediately.  This is the typical treatment for bonds of all types in the event of issuer default (Choice B). Soft bullet:  Bond default is delayed and payments continue on the original schedule.  The issuer's failure to pay does not trigger default since the maturity date is extended (eg, to 12 months).  A failure to pay principal and interest on the new, extended maturity date will trigger default. Conditional pass-through:  Bond default is not triggered and payments continue on the original schedule.  If payments are not fully satisfied at maturity (ie, conditional), the bond is converted to pass-through mode, in which payments are funneled directly from the underlying pool to bondholders until the original expected cash flow payments are met (Choice C).

new_question_en: A mortgage-backed securities (MBS) issuer is concerned that interest rates will soon fall, so it structures tranches with various maturities to mitigate prepayment risk.  This most likely describes:
new_option_b: credit tranching.
new_option_c: floating-rate tranching.
new_explanation_en: Time tranching example Tranche Average life (years) A 5.2 B 12 C 16 D 22 Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) are bonds created by bundling residential or commercial mortgage loans.  The principal repayments and interest provide cash flow to MBS investors.  To attract investors with different levels of risk tolerance or time preferences, MBS may be structured as multiple classes or tranches, which create different cash flows and therefore risk exposures for investors. One risk borne by MBS investors is prepayment risk.  When interest rates fall, borrowers may accelerate repayment of principal, either in part or in full.  This phenomenon (ie, contraction risk) reduces the maturity of the MBS and future cash flows to investors. To mitigate prepayment risk for certain MBS investors, issuers structure different bond classes with different maturities.  Known as time tranching, this redistributes prepayment risk by allocating all principal payments, including all prepayments, to the tranches with shorter expected maturities first.  Once the shorter-lived tranches are retired, the principal payments are allocated to tranches with longer expected maturities. (Choice B)  Credit tranching addresses default risk, which refers to the possibility that the borrowers of loans serving as collateral may default, either in part or in full. (Choice C)  Floating-rate tranches are created by combining fix-rated collateral with floating-rate instruments.  Floating-rate tranches are not designed to mitigate prepayment risk.

new_explanation_en: Asset-backed securities are bonds created from securitizing cash-generating assets, such as residential mortgages or credit card receivables. As the schematic above shows, the assets are bundled and sold to a special purpose entity (SPE) that uses them as collateral for bonds.  The cash flows from the loans pay the bonds' interest and principal.  Residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) are a type of ABS. One type of risk that RMBS present to bondholders is default risk.  This refers to the possibility that borrowers of the loans serving as collateral default, either in full or in part.  Since the cash flows from the collateral are the primary source of payments for the bonds, defaults can significantly impact the bondholders' expected returns. Some securitization structures attempt to mitigate the risk of defaults through credit tranching.  Instead of issuing only one class of bonds from the securitization, a credit-tranched structure uses multiple classes.  Subordinate classes are the first to absorb losses caused by defaults in the collateral, which shields senior classes from some default risk. (Choices B and C)  Extension risk and contraction risk are two types of prepayment risks.  Securitizations may offer different classes of bonds that allow investors to determine how much prepayment risk they want to be exposed to; this is known as time tranching.

new_explanation_en: Futures vs. forwards: similarities and differences Futures Forwards Contractual obligations Long obligated to buy and short obligated to sell at expiration Contract pricing = Spot price [1 + (net cost of carry)] Contract terms Standardized Negotiated Legal counterparty Clearinghouse Trade counterparty Gain/loss realization Settled daily in cash Settled at expiration Futures and forward contracts have some similar features but also several distinct differences.  Both are derivatives that place the same obligations on their contract counterparties.  Also, futures and forward prices both reflect arbitrage pricing.  Futures and forwards differ in several respects. Determination of contract terms:  Forward contract terms are negotiated by the buyer and seller.  Futures contract terms are standardized by the exchange where the contracts are traded. Legal counterparty:  Forwards are bilateral contracts between the original buyer and seller, whereas futures trades involve a clearinghouse that functions as the counterparty to both the buyer and the seller. Timing of gains and losses:  Forward contract gains and losses are settled at expiration.  Futures gains and losses are realized daily through mark-to-market valuation. (Choice B)  Futures and forwards impose the same obligation on their respective counterparties.  Both require the long party to buy and the short party to sell the underlying asset at expiration. (Choice C)  Futures and forward prices on otherwise equivalent contracts are usually the same since they are based on the same arbitrage- pricing relationship.  Consequently, futures and forwards almost always result in approximately the same amount of gains and losses.

new_question_en: For the general partner in a private equity or venture capital fund, which of the following waterfall distribution methods is most advantageous compared to the others?
new_option_b: Deal-by-deal.
new_option_c: Whole-of-fund.
new_explanation_en: Alternative investments (eg, private equity, venture capital, real estate) often have a waterfall distribution framework for paying out returns/profits.  Generally, limited partners (ie, LP investors) receive distributions equal to their initial capital outlay plus profits up to the hurdle rate; the general partner (GP) is then paid a performance fee.  At this point, unless the limited partnership agreement contains a catch-up clause, distributions and profits are split proportionately between the GP and LPs. Waterfall distribution methods are classified as either: deal-by-deal (American style) or whole-of-fund (European style). The timing of performance fee payments makes deal-by-deal waterfalls more advantageous to the GP since each deal is evaluated as each investment is exited.  This allows the GP an opportunity to receive performance fee cash flows earlier (eg, annually) than under the whole-of-fund method. (Choice A)  In deal-by-deal waterfalls, a clawback provision would likely be included in the partnership agreement to protect the LPs by restoring the profit split if subsequent investments in the portfolio do not earn performance fees.  This provision "claws back" the performance fee already paid to the GP and is not to the GP's advantage. (Choice C)  A whole-of-fund waterfall pays the GP based on the performance of the entire fund.  This delays payment of performance fees until the end of the fund's life (eg, 7–8 years), which is not to the GP's advantage.

new_question_en: At year-end, a private equity fund has returned 10% and has an 8% hurdle rate and a 20% performance fee with a catch-up clause.  Based on only this information, the performance fee earned by the general partner is closest to:
new_explanation_en: In alternative investments such as private equity and venture capital, once a fund's hurdle rate is reached, a catch-up clause allows the general partner (GP) to receive all subsequent distributions until the agreed-upon profit split occurs per the limited partnership agreement (LPA). Additional profits are then split proportionately (eg, 80/20). In this scenario, the fund's annual performance is 10%, which exceeds the 8% hurdle rate; thus, the GP earns a performance fee.  The catch-up clause combined with the 20% performance fee entitles the GP to the entire 2% profit above the 8% hurdle rate (ie, 20% of the 10% return). After this point, all profits are split (ie, 80/20 profit split) per the LPA since the GP is "caught up." (Choices A and B)  In this same scenario without a catch-up clause, the GP would have received a 20% performance fee on the 2% return above the hurdle rate, which is 0.40% (ie, 20% of 2%) of the fund's total profits.  This would be the minimum performance fee in this situation.

new_question_en: An analyst gathers the following data: Selected Data Bond price 100 Coupon rate 6% Risk-free rate 4% The bond has exactly 10 years until maturity and pays coupons annually.  There are no other costs or benefits while holding the bond.  A 1-year forward contract created with an initial value of zero most likely has an agreed-on price:
new_option_b: equal to 100.
new_option_c: greater than 100.
new_explanation_en: A forward contract price has an initial value of zero if the value of holding the forward contract (and not holding the asset until some future date) is equivalent to the value of holding the asset now and accruing any costs or benefits of having the asset in the meantime. If there is a net cost to having the asset now, then the forward price is greater than the spot price, and the net cost is the difference in the forward price and the spot price. If there is a net benefit to having the asset now, then the forward price is less than the spot price by the value of the net benefit derived from holding the asset. F  = S  (1 + r)  − C (1 + r) F  =  Forward price today C = Bond coupon payment S  = Spot price today T = Time to expiration r = Risk-free rate (opportunity cost of capital) In this scenario, the only holding cost is the opportunity cost of capital, which is the risk-free rate of 4%.  The benefit of holding the bond is the coupon of 6% that is paid in 1 year.  The net benefit of holding the underlying asset is the difference between the bond's 6% coupon and the 4% risk-free rate (ie, 2%). The bond and bond-forward contract are equivalent positions, so their prices imply the same return until the forward's expiration.  For that condition to hold, the forward contract price must be less than the spot price by the net benefit of holding the bond rather than the forward contract (Choices B and C). Explain how the value and price of a forward contract are determined at initiation, during the life of the contract, and at expiration

new_question_en: The seller of a forward rate agreement (FRA) is most likely trying to:
new_option_b: hedge a future borrowing rate.
new_option_c: speculate on rising interest rates.
new_explanation_en: A forward rate agreement (FRA) is a forward contract on an interest rate.  FRAs have a reference interest rate (, eg, a 60-day LIBOR) in place of an underlying asset.  The counterparties are locking in the FRA rate on a hypothetical loan for the term implied by the reference rate, to be initiated at the expiration of the FRA. A loan is not originated through the FRA.  Rather, a cash settlement occurs between the buyer (ie, long side) and the seller (ie, short side) at contract expiration.  The payment equals the difference between the current reference rate and the rate set in the FRA, discounted over the term of the hypothetical loan.  At expiration: Seller pays buyer if the reference rate is greater than the FRA rate Buyer pays seller if the reference rate is less than the FRA rate Lenders often sell FRAs to lock in (ie, hedge) their effective interest rate on future loans.  A lender who is hedged with an FRA will not benefit if rates increase, since the FRA buyer must be paid the value of the reference rate increase.  However, the hedged lender is protected from rate declines since the FRA buyer pays the lender the value of any reference rate decrease (Choice B). (Choice C)  Since FRA sellers gain from declining interest rates, a short FRA position is not used to speculate on rising interest rates.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\8. Derivatives\8.05 Pricing and Valuation of Forward Contracts and for an Underlying with Varying Maturities - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: If the benefits of holding an asset are greater than the cost of holding it, futures contracts on the asset most likely trade at prices:
new_option_b: equal to the spot price.
new_option_c: above the spot price.
new_explanation_en: Futures price = Spot price + Cost of holding underlying − Benefits of holding underlying Derivative pricing is based on the no-arbitrage principle (ie, arbitrage-free pricing).  This means that economically equivalent positions should trade at prices that result in equal returns.  If that condition does not hold, arbitrage occurs until prices adjust so that risk-free profits can no longer be earned. Futures price − Spot price = Cost of holding underlying − Benefits of holding underlying Benefits < costs Futures > spot Benefits > costs Futures < spot Benefits = costs Futures = spot Taking a long position in futures avoids the costs and forgoes any benefits of holding the underlying asset.  For equivalent positions (eg, long stock = long stock futures + long a risk-free bond) to earn equal returns, futures and spot prices must differ by the net cost of holding the underlying asset until the expiration of the futures contract.  When the benefits of holding the asset are greater than the costs of holding it, there is added value in holding the asset, so futures prices are below the spot price and not equal to or above it (Choices B and C). The net cost of holding a position in the underlying asset or commodity is called the cost of carry.  The carry, as it is sometimes called, reflects the net of: costs—charges for storage, insurance, or financing the underlying position, versus benefits—income (ie, dividends or interest) or convenience yield from holding the underlying.

new_question_en: A corporate borrower plans to close on a bank loan in 30 days, when the loan terms will be finalized.  The interest rate on the loan is tied to 90- day LIBOR.  Based on only this information, which of the following transactions most appropriately hedges the company's interest rate risk?
new_option_a: Long 30-day forward rate agreement (FRA) on 90-day LIBOR
new_option_b: Long 90-day forward rate agreement (FRA) on 90-day LIBOR
new_option_c: Long 120-day forward rate agreement (FRA) on 90-day LIBOR
new_explanation_en: A forward rate agreement (FRA) is a forward contract in which the underlying is not an asset, but a reference interest rate (eg, 90-day LIBOR).  A party planning to borrow in the future can buy an FRA to hedge against an increase in interest rates, and potential lenders can sell an FRA to hedge against a decrease in interest rates.  To be most effective, the FRA's: expiration should align with the initiation of the future loan, and its reference rate should align with the reference rate of the loan. In this scenario, the buyer is hedging against higher 90-day LIBOR rates in 30 days, when the terms of the loan will be finalized.  Therefore, a long 30-day FRA on 90-day LIBOR is the most appropriate contract to hedge the risk (Choices B and C).

new_question_en: A portfolio consists of a protective put position.  For put-call parity to hold, a portfolio of equal value most appropriately consists of a call with the same strike and expiration as the put and:
new_option_b: a long position in the underlying asset.
new_option_c: a short position in the underlying asset.
new_explanation_en: Put-call parity describes an arbitrage-pricing relationship between the prices of a European call and put that have the same strike price and expiration.  Put and call options can be used to create portfolios that produce identical payoffs. Arbitrage based on put-call parity ensures that the put and the call are fairly valued relative to each other at all times.  The equivalent portfolios variant of put-call parity, as shown in the image above, illustrates the pricing relationship between a protective put and a fiduciary call.  Both portfolios have the same value at expiration, and since European options are exercisable only at expiration, they also have the same value any time prior to expiration. A protective put is created by combining an option with a long position in the underlying asset. A fiduciary call portfolio combines a call option with a zero-coupon bond that has a face value equal to the options' strike price. In other words, the market value (ie, price) of the bond in the fiduciary call equals the present value of the strike price (ie, face value) discounted at the risk-free rate. (Choice B)  A long asset, long call position is not equivalent to a protective put and is not a portfolio of put-call parity. (Choice C)  A short position is not a component of put-call parity but can be used to create synthetic positions through replication.

new_question_en: A trader analyzes a European put and call, with the same strike price and expiry, on a stock that pays no dividend.  The trader notes that put-call parity does not hold: The price of a protective put is greater than the price of a fiduciary call.  To profit from this condition, the trader would most appropriately:
new_option_a: buy the stock, go long the put, and write the call.
new_option_b: sell short the stock, go long the put, and write the call.
new_option_c: sell short the stock, write the put, and go long the call.
new_explanation_en: If put-call parity holds, the price of a protective put is equal to the price of its corresponding fiduciary call, where the protective put and fiduciary call include put and call options with the same strike price and expiry that are written on the same underlying asset. In this scenario, the price of the protective put is greater than the price of the fiduciary call, which means that the price of the put option plus the underlying stock price minus the call price is greater than the present value of the strike price: To profit from this arbitrage opportunity, the trader must buy low and sell high.  The trader should sell short the stock, sell (write) the put, and go long (buy) the call (Choices A and B).  Note that the trader must borrow the stock to sell it short.  The resulting funds are equal to (p + S − c), which is deposited into an account earning the risk-free rate. At expiry (time T), the price of the stock has changed from S to S , and either: S  ≥ X, so the put option expires worthless.  The trader exercises the call option to purchase the stock at the strike price X. S  < X, so the call option expires worthless.  The put option is exercised, forcing the trader to purchase the stock at the strike price X. In either case, the trader returns the borrowed stock that was sold short.  Also at time T, the amount (p + S − c) that was invested at the risk-free rate has grown to (p + S − c)(1 + r)   Since at the time of the initial arbitrage: p + S − c > X(1 + r) it follows that at expiry: (p + S − c)(1 + r)  > X Therefore, the trader's net position at expiry is positive: (p + S − c)(1 + r)  − X > 0

new_question_en: For European options, the difference between put-call parity and put-call-forward parity is most likely that the forward contract:
new_option_b: replaces the strike price of the call option.
new_option_c: is combined with a risk-free bond to replace the asset.
new_explanation_en: Put-call parity forms the foundation of put-call-forward parity.  Put-call parity asserts that a protective put and fiduciary call constructed with European options on the same underlying asset and with the same strike price and expiration have the same payoff; therefore, at any time prior to maturity the values of the protective put and fiduciary call are equal. In put-call-forward parity the protective put portfolio is created by replacing the underlying with an equivalent synthetic asset (S).  The synthetic asset consists of a long forward contract and a risk-free zero-coupon bond with a face value equal to the asset's forward price. Entering into a forward contract costs nothing, so the value of the synthetic asset at Time 0 is simply the zero-coupon bond's present value. At expiration, the value of the maturing zero-coupon bond could be used to purchase the underlying asset by exercising the forward contract. (Choice A)  The forward contract does not replace the risk-free bond.  In fact, it requires the addition of a risk-free bond to the protective put portfolio. (Choice B)  The forward contract is part of the protective put portfolio, not the fiduciary call portfolio.  Therefore, the forward contract does not replace the strike price of the call option.

new_option_b: is exploited by selling the protective put and buying the fiduciary call.
new_option_c: is exploited by buying the protective put and selling the fiduciary call.
new_explanation_en: Put-call-forward parity describes the relationship between a European call and put option on the same underlying.  Each option has the same expiration date and exercise (strike) prices.  In put-call-forward parity, each option is a component of separate portfolios.  The call option is part of a portfolio known as a fiduciary call, and the put option is part of a protective put: Fiduciary call Protective put Long position in a European call option on underlying Long position in a zero-coupon bond that matures on option's expiration date with a face value equal to option's strike price Long position in a European put option on underlying Long position in a forward contract on underlying Long position in a zero-coupon bond that matures when both the option and forward expire, with a face value equal to the forward price Holding a long position in a forward contract and a zero-coupon bond with a face value equal to the forward price replicates owning the stock. In put-call-forward parity, the payoff is the same for both portfolios when all the derivative instruments expire, regardless of the underlying asset's price at that time.  Since the payoffs are identical, the portfolios must have the same value or else an arbitrage opportunity exists. Using the information in this question, and assuming a discount period of one year, insert the numbers to derive the values of the fiduciary call and protective put portfolios: The protective put is worth more than the fiduciary call, so there is an arbitrage opportunity (Choice A).  To exploit this, the investor would sell the protective put by selling the put option, the forward contract, and the zero-coupon bond, which would result in an inflow of €106.  At the same time, the investor would buy the fiduciary call, which would mean buying the call option and the zero-coupon bond, for a net outflow of €105.24.  The arbitrage profit is €0.76. new_explanation_en: Typical hedge fund fee structure Fee Basis for calculation Specific details Management Assets under management (AUM) Typically 1%−3% of AUM annually Does not depend on fund's profitability Always calculated before incentive fee Performance or incentive Annual returns Can be net or gross of management fee Can be subject to hurdle rate and/or high-water mark Hedge funds typically charge both a management fee and an incentive fee.  The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the total value of the fund's assets (ie, assets under management, or AUM).  It is assessed each year regardless of whether the fund earned a profit or incurred a loss.  In this question, the fund's management fee is ¥500 million, calculated as follows: The incentive fee is based on the fund's profits.  It can also be subject to a hurdle rate and/or a high-water mark.  Since this fund's incentive fee is net of the management fee, AUM is adjusted by subtracting the management fee from AUM before calculating the incentive fee.  This fund's adjusted ending AUM is ¥24.5 billion, which exceeds the high-water mark of ¥23 billion, so the fund is entitled to an incentive fee. If a hurdle rate applies, then the incentive fee is based on the profits in excess of the hurdle rate.  This means that the high-water mark is adjusted upward by multiplying it by (1 + hurdle rate).  After making the necessary adjustments, the fund's profits on which the incentive fee is based are ¥350 million, as shown below: The incentive fee is 20% × ¥350 million, or ¥70 million.  Adding the incentive fee to the management fee results in a total fee of ¥570 million.

new_question_en: The seed investor of a three-year-old hedge fund that invests in high-yield private placements requests a redemption of £20 million.  Fund details are listed below: Fund assets £50 million High-water mark £51 million Fee structure 2% and 20% Redemption notice period 2 weeks Lockup period 1 year Hurdle rate 2% Average annual returns since inception 1.5% Number of positions 20 Which of the following is the most likely outcome?

new_explanation_en: Effect of redemptions on hedge funds Poor performance often results in redemptions. A drawdown below the high-water mark is often a catalyst for redemptions. Large redemptions often cause forced selling, leading to further losses. Redemption notice periods help insulate a hedge fund from withdrawals. Lockup periods commit investors to a minimum investment period. The redemption is most likely catastrophic for this hedge fund for the following reasons: The redemption (£20 million) represents 40% of assets, making it difficult for the fund to continue executing its strategy. The fund has performed poorly, on average not even hitting its hurdle rate, and assets under management are currently valued below the high-water mark. Like other areas of asset management, fees have decreased, even for the hedge fund industry.  The 2-and-20 structure, common in the past, is now considered high for all but the most successful firms. The two-week redemption notice period is not long enough to result in an orderly disposition of assets since the fund is concentrated (only 20 positions) in illiquid assets (high-yield private placements) (Choice B). This relatively large redemption will create a negative feedback loop: The fund will be forced to sell assets, most likely creating losses and poor performance that will result in more redemptions, more asset sales, even poorer performance, and eventual liquidation. (Choice C)  As the seed (ie, initial) investor, this investor has been with the fund since its inception three years ago and is no longer restricted by the lockup period.

new_explanation_en: Hedge funds charge a management fee and an incentive fee.  The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the total value of the fund's assets under management (AUM).  It is assessed each year regardless of profitability. The incentive fee is levied against the fund's annual gains, subject to certain conditions.  It is calculated either gross or net of the management fee.  The net calculation subtracts the management fee from AUM to arrive at an adjusted AUM that is used to calculate the fund's profits. The high-water mark represents the value of AUM, net of fees, at any time during the fund's existence.  To earn an incentive fee, the fund must exceed the high-water mark, the base from which the fee is calculated. The hurdle rate is the minimum profit that the fund must earn (usually annually) before it receives an incentive fee.  The hurdle rate can either be "soft," meaning that the incentive fee is calculated based on the entire profit, or "hard," meaning that the incentive fee is based on only the excess profit above the hurdle rate. In this scenario, the fund generated net returns in 20X5 of 18.9% ( = (29.725 – 25) / 25 ), above the soft hurdle rate of 6%, and eclipsed the high- water mark of $27 million.  Therefore, the fund earned an incentive fee of 10% of profits, net of the management fee on average assets of $27,500,000: 0.10 × (29,725,000 − 27,000,000) = $272,500.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.02 Alternative Investment Performance and Returns - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A hedge fund had the following attributes during 20X3: Management fee 1.5% Incentive fee 15.0% Soft hurdle rate 5.0% High-water mark $200 million Beginning assets $191 million Ending assets $216 million If the management fee is calculated on ending assets and the incentive fee is based on net returns, the return (%) to the investor for 20X3 is closest to:
new_explanation_en: Typical hedge fund fee structure Fee Basis for calculation Specific details Management Assets under management (AUM) Typically 1%−3% of AUM annually Does not depend on fund's profitability Always calculated before incentive fee Performance or incentive Annual returns Can be net or gross of management fee Can be subject to hurdle rate and/or high-water mark An investor's hedge fund return is calculated net of fees.  Hedge funds often levy both a management fee and an incentive fee.  The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the fund's total assets under management (AUM) and is assessed regardless of profitability. The incentive fee is calculated as a percentage of profits, either net (ie, after deducting) or gross (ie, before deducting) of management fees. An incentive fee is often contingent on profits being greater than a hurdle rate and/or AUM being higher than the high-water mark.  The threshold for this hedge fund to earn an incentive fee is contingent on exceeding the 5% soft hurdle rate and the high-water mark of $200 million.  Since this fund has a soft hurdle rate, the incentive fee will be applied to the entire gain above the high-water mark. The fund's return for the year is calculated as follows (AUM and profits in $ millions): (Choice A)  9.7% is the investor return by assuming no high-water mark. (Choice C)  10.8% is the investor return assuming a hard hurdle rate of 5%.  A hard hurdle rate increases an investor's return, as the incentive fee is earned only on returns at or above the hurdle rate, not the entire gain.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.03 Investments in Private Capital - Equity and Debt - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A company targeted for a private equity leveraged buyout (LBO) is most likely to be a:
new_option_a: public company with a depressed stock price.
new_option_b: private company with significant intangible assets.
new_option_c: private company that is efficiently managed and operated.
new_explanation_en: Characteristics of attractive LBO target companies Depressed/undervalued stock price Agreeable management and shareholders Inefficient operations Robust and predictable cash flow Low leverage Unencumbered physical assets A leveraged buyout (LBO) occurs when a private equity (PE) firm purchases a controlling majority of the outstanding shares of a private or public company and the purchase is financed with a significant amount of debt.  The borrower is the company being acquired, not the PE firm.  The company's assets serve as collateral for the loan, and its cash flows pay the interest and principal on the debt. Due to the highly leveraged nature of the transaction, prudent company selection is critical to an LBO's success.  Acquirers look for firms that can: service the debt financing, improve their performance, and increase their value. Public companies are often the target of an LBO.  By targeting companies with a depressed stock price (ie, undervalued stock), the PE firm can structure the deal at a premium to the current market price, thus enticing existing shareholders to sell while still paying less than intrinsic value for the company.  Once the company's performance improves and its value increases, the company is sold again in the public markets or to strategic buyers. (Choice B)  Intangible assets are difficult to appraise and use as collateral.  Unencumbered physical assets (ie, not intangible assets) that can be used as loan collateral make a company more attractive as an LBO target. (Choice C)  PE firms add value by improving the efficiency of inefficiently managed companies, thus raising their value.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.03 Investments in Private Capital - Equity and Debt - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following best describes a characteristic of private equity?  Private equity funds:
new_option_b: can invest in public or private companies.
new_option_c: are more liquid than traditional investments.
new_explanation_en: Types of private equity (PE) strategies Type Characteristics Leveraged buyout Public company is converted to a private company Purchase price financed through debt and equity Target’s assets collateralize the debt and its cash flows service the debt Venture capital Usually invests in start-up companies with high growth potential Investments can be equity, debt, or both Development capital Typically involves mature companies PE financing allows company to expand Distressed investing PE fund buys debt or companies in bankruptcy or in default on debt Assumes that company can be turned around with new management Private equity is a type of alternative investment that encompasses both direct investment and indirect investment through private equity funds. Investments may be made in: private companies, as in venture capital investing; or public companies, with the goal of taking them private. Investments in private companies range from seed capital for startups and other early-stage companies to mezzanine financing to prepare a company planning for its initial public offering.  Investments in public companies typically entail leveraged buyouts to take large companies private. (Choice A)  Private equity funds are typically actively managed.  Funds are often actively involved with the companies they invest in, which can include replacing management, combining companies to realize synergies, or providing support functions.  Managers' goals are to help small companies grow and help poorly managed companies improve their operations and strategy to grow their investments. (Choice C)  Private equity investments are significantly less liquid than traditional investments (eg, stocks, bonds).  For private equity funds, investments often take years to realize any gains.  Investors in private equity funds often face lockup periods and redemption fees, making these investments illiquid.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.03 Investments in Private Capital - Equity and Debt - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Which of the following best describes a characteristic of an attractive leveraged buyout target company?
new_option_b: Unencumbered physical assets
new_option_c: High level of operating efficiency
new_explanation_en: A leveraged buyout (LBO) occurs when a private equity (PE) firm purchases effectively all the outstanding shares of a publicly traded company using equity capital and a significant amount of debt (often 80% or more of the transaction value).  PE firms raise money through investment funds with the intention of completely acquiring businesses. Due to the highly levered nature of the transaction, selecting a company with the right attributes is critical to an LBO's success.  One of an LBO's defining characteristics is that the transaction is structured so that the borrower is the company being acquired.  Therefore, having unencumbered physical assets that can be used as loan collateral is one factor that makes a target more attractive.  Other attractive characteristics include: an undervalued stock price, agreeable management and shareholders, inefficient operations, robust and predictable cash flow, and low leverage. Once the restructuring is complete, the company is sold in public markets or to strategic buyers at a price that constitutes a substantial return on the PE investors' original equity investment. (Choice A)  A cyclical profitability profile presents the risk of being unable to service the considerable amount of debt used to fund the transaction. (Choice C)  PE firms search for opportunities with the potential to cut costs or improve operating efficiency.  Therefore, a company that is already operating at a high level of efficiency is not an ideal LBO target.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.03 Investments in Private Capital - Equity and Debt - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Due to its position within a company's capital structure and its convertibility into common equity, which of the following types of debt is most commonly associated with leveraged buyouts?
new_option_b: Payment in kind
new_option_c: Contingent convertible
new_explanation_en: Mezzanine financing Used in Characteristics Leveraged buyout (LBO) Hybrid security structure issued in place of straight high-yield debt Equity conversion optionality or attached warrants Subordinate to all other forms of debt financing High coupon rate Venture capital Used as bridge financing to sustain a company backed by private venture capital until it receives proceeds from an upcoming initial public offering "Mezzanine" commonly refers to an intermediate floor in a large building (eg, hotel), above the ground floor but below the second floor.  The term mezzanine financing is figurative and refers to a hybrid type of financing within a company's capital structure, positioned between common equity and debt.  Key characteristics of debt in mezzanine financing include: high coupon rates, the most junior (ie, most subordinated) debt tranche, and hybrid securities that are convertible into common equity. A leveraged buyout (LBO) occurs when a private equity firm purchases the outstanding shares of a publicly traded company.  Mezzanine debt is the riskiest source of debt capital in these transactions, but it can provide a significant benefit to investors if the common equity increases in value. In venture capital, mezzanine debt is used to bridge the target company's cash needs until proceeds from an initial public offering (IPO) are received.  The ability to convert the debt into common equity once the IPO occurs is the primary attraction for investors. (Choice B)  A payment-in-kind (PIK) bond allows the issuer to pay coupon interest in cash or in additional bonds (ie, in kind).  PIK bonds are often used to fund LBOs but are not convertible into common equity. (Choice C)  Contingent convertible bonds (CoCos) are not used in LBOs.  Financial institutions issue CoCos since the bonds are classified favorably for regulatory capital purposes (ie, as equity).  Automatic conversion can occur when the issuer suffers losses that cause owner's equity on the balance sheet to fall below minimum regulatory requirements.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.03 Investments in Private Capital - Equity and Debt - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: If venture capitalists are investing in a company by providing funds to initiate commercial production, which of the following best describes the company's financing stage?
new_option_b: Seed
new_option_c: Angel
new_explanation_en: Venture capital financing Financing Characteristics Formative stage Divided into angel financing, seed stage, and early-stage financing Angel financing is from friends and family; venture capital (VC) funds begin to invest with seed stage Financing is through common and/or preferred stock Company's management retains control but fund receives equity interest Later stage Financing used to expand operations and/or marketing Management transfers control to VC VC finances company both by purchasing company's equity and by lending to it Mezzanine stage Provides funding until the company completes an initial public offering Venture capital (VC) is a type of private equity investing that focuses on very young companies.  VC funds provide financing at three general stages of a company's existence: the formative stage, the later stage, and the mezzanine stage.  The earliest investment in the company is done in the formative stage.  The formative stage consists primarily of a minority equity investment in the company that helps it with product development and allows management (typically the company's founders) to retain control. Formative-stage financing can be subdivided into: Angel investing—Angel investors, who are usually friends and family of the company's founder(s), provide equity capital, rather than VC funds.  This is often done only in the beginning, idea stage of the business (Choice C). Seed-stage financing—Seed capital provides funds that take an idea to a new level by financing market research, product development, and marketing.  This is typically the first stage when VC funds are invested in a company (Choice B). Early-stage financing—An early-stage investment allows the company to begin commercial production by providing the necessary funds to bring the product to market.  This is the last round of formative-stage financing.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.03 Investments in Private Capital - Equity and Debt - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A feature of mezzanine debt is that it most likely:
new_option_b: is used for funding early-stage companies.
new_option_c: offers more stable returns than direct lending.
new_explanation_en: Private debt generally refers to nonbank entities (eg, a private debt fund, an investment firm's private debt arm) lending money to private institutions.  It can be broadly classified into four categories. Direct lending:  private firms raise capital to lend directly to borrowers Mezzanine debt:  subordinated debt typically used for acquisitions or buyouts Venture debt:  lending for start-up companies that have low or negative cash flow Distressed debt:  purchases of debt of mature companies facing financial problems Mezzanine debt provides capital in the form of subordinated debt, which has higher risk.  Investors are typically compensated for this risk through a combination of higher interest rates and features like conversion rights, in which investors have the right to convert the debt to equity under specified conditions. (Choice B)  Venture debt is generally used to fund start-ups and early-stage companies.  Mezzanine debt typically is used for acquisitions and buyouts. (Choice C)  Direct lending is associated with relatively lower risk and more stable returns than mezzanine debt, which tends to be riskier with more volatile returns.

new_question_en: An investor is seeking an alternative investment that offers historically low correlation with global equities, relatively low volatility, and current income.  Which of the following most appropriately meets these requirements?
new_option_b: Managed futures
new_option_c: Publicly listed real estate investment trust
new_explanation_en: Farmland and timberland investments Farmland Timberland Common to both Sources of returns Commodity prices Lumber prices Harvest quantities Land price changes Investment attributes Possibly ESG Regular income Harvest inflexibility; at least annual harvest cycle ESG-friendly Long new growth cycle Harvest flexibility Inflation hedge Low correlation with traditional assets Can hedge with futures Investment vehicles Publicly traded REITs Direct purchase, but for largest investors only Private investment funds ESG = environmental, social, and governance REIT = Real estate investment trust The three sources of return on farmland are harvest quantities, commodity prices, and land prices.  Farmland provides a consistent income stream as the crops are harvested, and is considered an inflation hedge since it offers investors exposure to commodity and land prices. Relative to global equities, attributes that make farmland a desirable investment include low correlations, low annualized volatility, and comparable rates of return. (Choice B)  Managed futures provide diversification benefits to a typical portfolio, but the returns tend to be volatile. (Choice C)  Publicly listed real estate investment trusts have high correlations to global equities and exhibit high volatility.

new_question_en: In a floating-rate mortgage on a commercial real estate property, the lender's risk compared to the borrower's risk is best described as:
new_option_b: interest rate risk.
new_option_c: the loan-to-value ratio.
new_explanation_en: The loan-to-value ratio is one of the most common risk assessment tools used by mortgage lenders.  This ratio divides a loan's current value by the current appraised property value and reflects the size of the lender's investment relative to the borrower's investment. Since the property is generally the only collateral for the loan, the loan-to-value ratio is especially important in the loan risk assessment process and ultimately determines the amount of risk (ie, potential for capital losses) assumed by the lender.  A common initial loan-to-value ratio in commercial real estate is 65%–80%, meaning that the borrower has equity in the property of 35%–20%.  The greater the ratio, the greater the lender's risk. (Choice A)  Spread risk refers to the impact on a bond's price from changes in credit spreads, which are not directly relevant here. (Choice B)  In this case, the loan is a floating-rate mortgage, which neutralizes interest rate risk for the lender.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.04 Real Estate and Infrastructure - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: An investor seeking to benefit from the appreciation of commercial real estate would most appropriately buy:
new_option_b: mortgage real estate investment trusts.
new_option_c: commercial mortgage-backed securities.
new_explanation_en: Pooled real estate investments Sources of return Description Residential MBS Loan (mortgage) income Secured by property Pools of single-family residential mortgage loans Commercial MBS Loan (mortgage) income Secured by property Pools of commercial/multi-family residential mortgages Equity REITs Rental income Property appreciation Stable income on portfolio of commercial properties Mortgage REITs Loan (mortgage) income Secured by property Portfolio of residential and/or commercial MBS MBS = mortgage-backed securities; REITs = real estate investment trusts. Publicly traded, pooled real estate investments are usually structured as real estate investment trusts (REITs) or mortgage-backed securities (MBS).  There are two types of REITS: equity REITs and mortgage REITs. Equity REITs purchase (ie, own the equity in) commercial real estate. MBS and mortgage REITs invest in real estate–related debt. The benefits of property appreciation accrue primarily to the property owners.  Of the choices, only equity REITs own commercial real estate and realize the full benefit of property appreciation. (Choice B)  Mortgage REITs hold portfolios of MBS.  As holders of interests in pools of debt instruments, mortgage REITs are owed a share of the principal and interest of the loan pools; however, they do not participate in property appreciation. (Choice C)  Commercial MBS (CMBS) are interests in single pools of commercial mortgages.  CMBS holders have a claim on the interest and principal of the pooled mortgages, but they do not share in property value gains.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.05 Natural Resources - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: An analyst observes that a commodity's forward curve is in backwardation.  This situation most likely implies:
new_option_b: negative collateral yield.
new_option_c: convenience yield exceeds storage costs.
new_explanation_en: An investor who owns a physical commodity (eg, copper) incurs storage costs until the commodity is used or sold.  However, that investor also accrues benefits (eg, immediate availability) from directly owning the commodity; the benefit that offsets storage costs is the convenience yield.  In contrast, an investor who owns a futures contract on the same commodity incurs no storage costs until the contract matures and delivery is accepted, but no convenience yield is accrued. All else equal, a commodity's futures prices are higher than the spot price by the cost of holding the commodity, which prevents arbitrage. Therefore, the typical forward pricing structure for physical commodities is an upward-sloping forward curve (ie, futures prices > spot prices); in that case, the market is said to be in contango. A downward-sloping forward curve (ie, futures prices < spot prices), known as backwardation, results from the convenience yield exceeding storage costs.  Backwardation often indicates bottlenecks in supply or delivery in the spot market. (Choice A)  Roll yield is the return (positive or negative) that occurs when a contract nears expiration and the futures price converges with the spot price.  Backwardation results in a positive roll yield. (Choice B)  Collateral yield is a component of a futures contract's price return and should always be positive.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.05 Natural Resources - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A portfolio manager is seeking an alternative investment to diversify a pension portfolio.  If the investment is actively managed, liquid, and a variant of a global macro strategy, it is most likely a:
new_option_b: merger arbitrage fund.
new_option_c: managed futures fund.
new_explanation_en: Managed futures Features Actively managed futures trading Absolute return focus Subset of global macro approach Benefits Low/negative correlation to traditional assets Potentially strong performance during equity market corrections High liquidity Risks Use of substantial leverage Sustained periods of relative underperformance Managed futures (MF) are alternative investments that actively trade a variety of futures contracts (eg, commodity, interest rate, foreign exchange).  MF use short-term, trend-following strategies; are absolute-return oriented; and are most commonly associated with global macro investing.  Global macro is an investing strategy based on anticipating moves in macro factors (eg, interest rates, government policy, foreign exchange).  The primary attraction for MF investors is the low-to-negative correlations with traditional asset classes and high levels of liquidity. MF funds are similar in structure to hedge funds and often have comparable incentive fee structures based on fund performance.  As with numerous hedge fund strategies that have gone mainstream, many MF products are available in a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund format (ie, "liquid alts"). (Choice A)  A market-neutral strategy consists of buying undervalued stocks and shorting overvalued stocks to create a portfolio that is immune to market-level risks and is zero-beta.  Market-neutral portfolios do not employ global macro tactics. (Choice B)  Merger arbitrage pairs merger partners in long and short positions.  It is an event-driven, bottom-up strategy and does not use a global macro approach.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.05 Natural Resources - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: When a commodity's futures prices are in contango, its forward price curve most likely has:
new_option_b: a positive roll yield.
new_option_c: little to no convenience yield.
new_explanation_en: Slope of the futures curve Contango Backwardation Futures price > spot price May result if No convenience yield or Convenience yield < storage costs Futures price < spot price May result if Convenience yield > storage costs An investor who owns a physical commodity (eg, wheat, copper) incurs storage costs until the commodity is used or sold.  In contrast, an investor who owns a futures contract on the same commodity incurs no storage costs until the contract matures and delivery is accepted. All else equal, to prevent arbitrage, a commodity's futures prices are set higher than the spot price by the cost of holding the commodity.  An upward-sloping futures curve (ie, futures prices > spot prices) is the typical forward pricing structure for physical commodities.  This structure is called contango. Convenience yield, which offsets the storage costs, is the benefit the investor receives from directly owning the commodity (eg, immediate availability).  Contango results if the convenience yield is less than the storage costs, which is usually the case.  When the futures contract is in contango, there is little to no convenience yield (ie, benefit) to owning the commodity directly. (Choice A)  Backwardation has a negatively sloped (ie, downward-sloping) forward price curve since the futures price is less than the spot price. (Choice B)  Roll yield is the return (positive or negative) that occurs when the contract nears its expiration and the futures price converges with the spot price.  The roll yield for a forward price curve in contango is negative since the futures price is moving toward the lower spot price.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\9. Alternative Investments\9.05 Natural Resources - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A hedge fund that concentrates on midstream oil and gas investments is most likely to invest in:
new_option_b: drilling companies.
new_option_c: plastics manufacturers.
new_explanation_en: Categories of alternative investing in the oil and gas sector Category Characteristics Upstream Exploration and extraction Drilling and oil field services companies Midstream Refining and processing Gasoline, heating oil, and jet fuel refineries Downstream Makers of end-user goods from refined petroleum products Plastics and chemicals manufacturers Commodity investing focuses on physical resources, which include energy-related products like coal and crude oil.  In addition to gaining direct exposure to commodities through futures contracts, alternative investment vehicles also invest in the companies that mine and refine those products. In the oil and gas sector, companies are divided into three broad categories.  Upstream companies explore for and extract the basic product, such as crude oil.  Midstream companies refine the crude oil into gasoline, kerosene, and heating oil.  Downstream companies create other products or services (eg, tires, retail gas stations) from the refined commodity. An oil and gas sector hedge fund that focuses on midstream companies most likely invests in a gasoline refinery.  A drilling company is an upstream company (Choice B), and a plastics manufacturer is an example of a downstream company (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Hashimoto, CFA, is a personal wealth advisor at a large brokerage firm that offers fee-based, tiered client services to all clients.  The firm has just published an updated and in-depth analysis of a global oil producer.  The analysis notes that the firm is changing its recommendation on the oil company's stock from "sell" to "buy," despite an announcement that the producer is cutting its dividend amid greater volatility in the global oil markets.  Hashimoto writes a one-page summary of the analysis, which omits any mention of the recommendation change.  Hashimoto sends the in-depth analysis to Ueda, who is his largest client by assets under management.  She receives the highest level of the firm's tiered services.  He sends only the brief summary to his client Yamaguchi, who has a smaller account and receives a lower tier of service.  He decides not to send anything to a third client, Fujita, who is retired and dependent on the income from her small portfolio, and who receives the lowest tier of service. With respect to Standard III(B) on Fair Dealing, Hashimoto most likely violated the Standard by not distributing:
new_option_a: the recommendation change to Yamaguchi only.
new_option_b: the in-depth analysis to both Fujita and Yamaguchi.
new_option_c: the recommendation change to both Fujita and Yamaguchi.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities." Standard III(B) Fair Dealing focuses on a Member's and Candidate's responsibility to treat all clients fairly, specifically in terms of information distribution and investment actions.  Advisers must distribute information on a change in recommendation so that each client has an appropriate and fair opportunity to act on the information. In this case, Hashimoto has an obligation to inform all clients about the change of recommendation, regardless of whether it is accompanied by more detailed research and analysis.  Although the investment seems unsuitable for Fujita, and both Fujita and Yamaguchi receive lower tiers of service, they should both be informed of any change in the recommendation and be given an opportunity to act (Choice A). (Choice B)  Differentiated client services based on fees or levels of client activity are fair if they are offered to all clients.  In this case, Hashimoto has not violated the Standard by sending one client a more detailed analysis, since that client has chosen to receive a higher level of service. However, all clients should be notified of the recommendation change.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Donota Rosa, CFA, currently works with her best friend and supervisor Maria Danek, CFA, at Broadwick Investment Partners (BIP).  BIP is a private equity firm with award-winning funds.  Each of BIP's funds has a $20 million investment minimum for new investors.  After working with Danek for two years, Rosa leaves BIP to start her own firm.  Six months later, Danek helps Rosa by convincing BIP's management to waive the $20 million investment minimum exclusively for Rosa's clients, but the exclusivity will last for only one month.  Rosa clearly remembers how well BIP managed its funds and, based on her memory, is convinced it is an ideal investment for clients.  Grateful for this assistance and to meet the one-month deadline, she quickly jumps at the opportunity and immediately recommends BIP's funds.  With respect to the Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis, does Rosa most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, since she has a personal relationship with Danek.
new_option_c: Yes, since she relies on her memory to make an investment decision.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must: Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments, making investment recommendations, and taking investment actions. Have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action." Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis requires members and candidates to exercise diligence and thoroughness when making investment decisions.  While there is no exact policy or procedure that the Standard demands, appropriate and diligent research must be completed. Here, Rosa believes that the funds of Broadwick Investment Partners (BIP) are an ideal investment based on her memory and experience while working at BIP.  However, BIP may have changed its investment process or the funds' underlying securities over the last six months; based on current research, she might have a different investment recommendation. To comply with the Standard, regardless of limited time or personal relationships, Rosa must exercise diligence by conducting her own thorough review of the funds.  Memory or past experiences are inadequate justifications and are not reasonable bases to make investment decisions (Choice A). (Choice B)  Rosa does not violate the Standard by having a personal relationship with another investment manager.  While Danek does assist Rosa, Rosa must do her own work in making an investment recommendation.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Bernard Logan, CFA, manages a small-cap growth exchange-traded fund (ETF) for Firefly Capital.  Logan's boss is concerned that the ETF's trading volume is low compared to that of peers.  He directs Logan to determine which of the firm's largest investors the ETF would be suitable for, and then ask those investors to agree to purchase fixed amounts of the ETF at regular intervals over the next month.  Investors that agree to do so will pay reduced commissions.  The boss expects that the larger number of trades will support market liquidity for the ETF and create greater interest among potential investors, which will benefit the existing clients who invest in the ETF.  The boss asks that Logan not disclose this arrangement to the general investing public.  To comply with Standard II(B) Market Manipulation, Logan's best course of action is to:
new_option_a: suggest Firefly disclose the agreements before proceeding.
new_option_b: proceed with his boss's request without disclosing the agreements.
new_option_c: tell his boss that such agreements violate the Standards even if they are disclosed.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits activities by Members or Candidates that distort securities prices.  Manipulation can occur through: information-based activities (eg, spreading false rumors) and transaction-based activities (eg, exaggerated trading between two accounts). The key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is that the Member or Candidate must intend to deceive market participants that rely on market information.  If the Member's or Candidate's intent is to deceive investors, the Standard is violated.  Intent is inferred from the circumstances on a case-by-case basis. In this scenario, Logan's boss has the intent of making market participants believe the ETF's liquidity is greater than it really is by distorting trading volume, which would be a violation of the Standard (Choice B).  Once the agreements with Firefly Capital's largest customers have ended, liquidity is likely to fall. However, disclosing the agreements provides information that investors need to interpret market data and make informed decisions.  Therefore, Firefly may make such agreements with customers without violating the Standard provided the agreements are disclosed (Choice C).  To comply with the Standard, Logan should educate his boss on or remind his boss about the Standards and suggest disclosing the agreements.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Haley Jarwin, CFA, lives in Country Z.  She recently joined a new investment bank located in Country X.  Country X's securities require that the laws of a client's home country shall govern if the client is not located in Country X.  Jarwin is assigned to work on a large IPO for a client that is located in Country Y, whose securities laws are less strict than those of Country X.  Jarwin believes some of the client's confidential financial information is fraudulent and may be evidence of criminal activity.  Country X's laws require that she report her suspicions to securities regulators, but Country Y's laws prohibit reporting unless the client is first requested to remedy the fraud and refuses to act.  Country Z has no laws that apply to this situation.  Under Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, Jarwin's least appropriate course of action is to:
new_option_a: report the fraud to the Country X regulators.
new_option_b: do nothing since Country Z has no laws that apply.
new_option_c: request that the client amend the financial information so that it is not fraudulent.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities.  In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation…." Investment professionals often work with clients located in different countries with laws and regulations that might conflict with local laws. Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law mandates that Members and Candidates resolve conflicts that arise when laws of different countries require different actions in a given situation. In the CFA Code and Standards, the basic rule for "choice-of-law" issues is that the Member (or Candidate) must always adhere to the strictest given law.  However, if the Code and Standards impose stricter requirements than the law of the Member's home country or the country where the Member is doing business, the member must follow the Code and Standards. In this scenario, Countries X and Y both require her to take some action, so she would not be acting appropriately by doing nothing even though her own country's laws are silent on the issue (Choices A and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Hella Flosadottir, CFA, resides in Country A and works for an investment bank located there.  Her clients include a pension fund located in Country B.  Flosadottir routinely checks the monthly statements of all her clients, and the statement for the pension fund leads her to suspect that somebody may be embezzling from the fund.  However, the statement does not contain enough information for her to be sure that embezzlement is occurring.  The relevant laws of each country are shown below: Country Requirements of country's laws Comparative strictness to Code and Standards Country A Notify client of possible embezzlement Less strict Country B Notify police in Country B More strict To comply with Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, which of the following is Flosadottir's most appropriate action?
new_option_a: Contact the police in Country B
new_option_b: Advise the client of the possible embezzlement
new_option_c: Inform her firm's compliance officer of the situation
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities.  In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation...." Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law prescribes how Members and Candidates resolve conflicts when the applicable laws of a jurisdiction conflict with behaviors required by the CFA Institute Code and Standards.  The general rule is that Members and Candidates must adhere to the stricter of: the laws and regulations in their home country and the Code and Standards. In this scenario, the laws of Hella Flosadottir's country (Country A) are less strict than both the Code and Standards and the laws of Country B. Country B's laws are stricter than the Code and Standards, so Flosadottir's most appropriate action is to contact the Country B police. (Choices B and C)  Country A's laws would require Flosadottir to notify the client; the Code and Standards require her to seek guidance from her firm's compliance officer.  However, since both options are less strict than the laws of Country B, Country B's laws apply.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Latha Mani, CFA, manages an index fund with a small-cap growth mandate.  The fund is owned by Alpha Investments and has thousands of investors.  Mani's primary duty of loyalty is to:
new_option_b: operate the fund to its mandate.
new_option_c: Alpha Investments' shareholders.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their client's interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires Members and Candidates to be loyal to their clients and to use prudence and care when making investment decisions on a client's behalf.  This first step is properly identifying the client.  For Members and Candidates in an advisory role, the client is the service's investors or beneficiaries.  In cases where the Member or Candidate is a fund manager, the client is not an investor or beneficiary but the investment fund and its mandate. In this scenario, Latha Mani manages an index fund with a specific mandate.  Although the fund has investors, those investors may enter and exit the fund of their own accord.  Mani is not their advisor and therefore does not owe them her loyalty (Choice A).  Mani must be loyal to managing the fund to its mandate since investors have made investment decisions based on the expectation of using Mani's fund to gain exposure to small cap growth stocks.  Deviating from that mandate would breach clients' trust. (Choice C)  Although Mani owes loyalty to her employer and its shareholders, clients or fund investors take precedence before employers. Therefore, Mani's primary duty of loyalty is owed to managing the fund to its mandate.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Grace Kim, CFA, has been an adviser to clients at Keundon Investments for 10 years.  Kim negotiates with Keundon to cut back her hours to 20 per week (from 50) to allow her to manage her father's care.  Kim agrees to give up her advising role and work in the firm's back office.  She will be paid 25% of her usual salary, but she hopes to eventually return to full-time advising.  Kim informs clients of her new role and that they will have a new adviser at the firm.  The next day, one of her clients offers to pay her to confidentially review any recommendations he receives from another adviser, as he trusts her judgment.  To comply with Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements, which of the following actions is most likely required of Kim?
new_option_b: Accept the offer and inform her employer in writing
new_option_c: Obtain written permission from her employer before accepting the offer
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements notes that third-party, additional compensation is allowed.  However, if the arrangement could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with the employer, the Member or Candidate must obtain written permission from all parties involved. In this case, continuing her advising activities could reasonably be seen as presenting a conflict with Kim's agreed-upon, diminished role at the firm.  Kim would be required to obtain written permission from both the client and her employer. (Choice A)  Kim's duty of loyalty does not require her to refuse the offer; she may accept it if she first obtains written permission from all parties. (Choice B)  Merely informing her employer is not quite enough; Kim must get the employer's written permission as an involved party before she can accept the offer.
