pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Kathy Lee Wayne, CFA, is a portfolio manager who supervises a team at a large investment firm.  Since the firm has adopted CFA Institute Code and Standards, Wayne assumes its compliance policies and procedures are adequate for monitoring her team.  During her annual performance review, her supervisor tells Wayne that annual bonuses will be based only on hitting investment performance targets "no matter what it takes."  Wayne replies, "That sounds fine.  I'll let my team know, and my team will hit its targets!"  Some months later, a member of Wayne's team admits to falsifying reports in order to make it appear that the team hit its performance targets.  During the subsequent internal investigation, investigators conclude that Wayne did not participate in the falsification and could not be expected to have been aware of it.  According to Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, which of the following best describes how Wayne has not complied with recommended practice?
new_option_a: Only by failing to detect her employee's unethical activity
new_option_b: Only by readily accepting the incentive structure of the firm
new_option_c: Both by failing to detect her employee's unethical activity and by readily accepting the incentive structure of the firm
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Recommendations for compliance with the Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors acknowledge that a supervisor may not be able to dictate the ethical standards, culture, or compliance efforts of an entire firm, but should work with management to encourage the adoption of effective compliance tools.  One effective compliance tool is an incentive structure that supports ethical behavior. Here, Wayne should have recognized the firm's incentive structure as not supportive of ethical behavior and, in fact, perhaps as actually encouraging unethical behavior.  She should have brought this weakness to her supervisor's attention rather than accepting it without question. The guidance for Standard IV(C) is very clear that failing to detect unethical behavior does not mean that the supervisor violated the Standard or ignored its recommendations.  However, in this case, there is no evidence that Wayne ever investigated the firm's policies and procedures to determine if they were adequate to prevent the type of unethical behavior that occurred.  As a Charterholder, Wayne cannot assume, without investigation, that the existing policies are sufficient.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Zhao Fen, CFA, is an independent investor.  She holds a large position of Formula Industries, a lightly traded stock with low liquidity, in one of her two personal accounts.  If Zhao wishes to exit the position, which of the following would most likely violate the Standards?
new_option_a: Using an intermediary to sell the position outside of the market to avoid price impacts.
new_option_b: Selling her holdings as one position, which would likely cause a large drop in the price.
new_option_c: Trading the stock between personal accounts to attract interest from other market participants.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits activities by Members or Candidates that deceive market participants by distorting securities prices or volumes.  Manipulation can occur through: information-based activities (eg, issuing false or misleading information) and/or transaction-based activities (eg, exaggerated trading between two accounts). The Standard does not prevent the use of legitimate trading strategies, even if they cause price movements or are designed to purposefully limit the impact on the market.  The key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is intent: if the strategy is intended to deceive investors, it violates the Standard. In this scenario, if Zhao Fen traded Formula Industries stock between her personal accounts, it would give market participants a false impression of higher trading volume since the trading is not done between unique market participants.  Deceiving participants through transaction-based manipulation violates the Standard. (Choice A)  Using an intermediary (eg, block house) to sell the position outside the market or break the order into smaller batches is a legitimate trading strategy.  This practice aims to reduce a sale's impact on the market, but the resulting trades are done with other market participants and therefore do not violate the Standard. (Choice B)  While selling all the holdings in one position might drive down the price, Zhao may do so without intending to manipulate market participants; therefore, it is not the action most likely to violate the Standard.  The Standards do not require Members or Candidates to disadvantage themselves to uphold market integrity, so this strategy can be used if cash is needed quickly.

In this scenario, the laws of Hella Flosadottir's country (Country A) are less strict than both the Code and Standards and the laws of Country B. Country B's laws are stricter than the Code and Standards, so Flosadottir's most appropriate action is to contact the Country B police. pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Andrei Ostrovsky, CFA has been employed as an advisor at Bolshoi Investments Inc. (BII) for several years.  His employment agreement does not include a "noncompete" clause or termination policies.  Ostrovsky decides to leave BII and start a new advisory firm.  Prior to giving notice to his employer, Ostrovsky spends a few weekends setting up his new office.  There he "connects" with as many of his clients as he can on social media, which is easy as he knows their names.  Before leaving BII, he does not mention his departure from BII or his plans for his new firm to any client, on or off social media.  One day after leaving BII, he posts a notice on a social media site that he has left BII and that he would be happy to continue to advise his former clients at his new firm.  With regards to Standard IV(A) Loyalty, has Ostrovsky most likely violated the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, by soliciting business from BII's clients
new_option_c: Yes, by "connecting" with BII's clients while still employed by BII
new_explanation_en: "In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer." Standard IV Duties to Employers addresses the Member or Candidate's responsibilities as an employee.  Standard IV(A) Loyalty notes that Members and Candidates must try to protect the interests of their employer and avoid actions that may harm those interests. Before leaving an employer, a Member or Candidate must follow its policies and procedures for notifying clients and must not make any attempt to solicit clients for another firm.  After leaving an employer, the Member or Candidate can solicit former clients as long as the contact information used is not the property of the former employer. In this case, Ostrovsky did not mention either his departure from BII or his future plans to his BII clients before leaving BII, and he did not use BII's proprietary data to contact them, so he has not violated the Standard (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Elise Berger, CFA, is sell-side analyst for Brick Wall Bank (BWB).  Based on BWB's process, Berger sends her research reports through email to all clients simultaneously.  BWB's largest client, Standard Capital, offers to pay higher commissions to BWB for follow-up phone calls from Berger when she releases new research.  BWB and Berger agree to this arrangement.  Berger plans to offer this deal only to BWB's next nine largest clients since only they do enough business with BWB to afford the new service at the new, higher level of commission.  Which of the following best describes Berger's options under the Code and Standards?
new_option_a: Offer the higher level of service as planned
new_option_b: Not offer different levels of service to her customers
new_option_c: Offer the higher level of service only if it is offered to all clients
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities." Standard III(B) Fair Dealing requires Members and Candidates to treat all clients fairly when recommending investments or undertaking investment actions on their behalf.  Members and Candidates must ensure their investment recommendations are disseminated in a way that provides all clients the fair opportunity to act on every recommendation. However, "fair" does not mean "equal."  The Standard allows firms and analysts to offer higher levels of service to clients willing to pay a premium (Choice B).  These services: must not disadvantage or negatively affect other clients and must be disclosed and available to all clients and prospective clients. In this scenario, Berger plans to offer the higher level of service (ie, follow-up calls) only to Brick Wall Bank's (BWB's) ten largest clients.  Since she does not plan to offer this service to other clients, she violates the Standard.  Although other clients do not currently do enough business with BWB to afford the service, they might wish to do more business with BWB or pay higher commissions if the additional service were offered to them (Choice A).  Not disclosing the service to them gives them no choice.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Kalim Emara, Level I CFA Candidate, works for a national nonprofit charity and is responsible for investing the organization's surplus funds. Due to the recent retirement of the charity's chief financial officer, Emara has been assigned to temporarily take on some additional responsibilities regarding management accounting and internal auditing.  These additional responsibilities have reduced the amount of time Emara can devote to investment research.  To comply with the equity allocation guidelines of his organization's investment policy, Emara invests in a popular broad- based equity index fund without performing any specific evaluation of the fund. Emara is also an activist with a community group that opposes a regional hospital's plan to close down its local emergency services.  Emara has been arrested twice while participating in weekend protests of the hospital's plans. Based on this information, has Emara most likely violated Standard I(D)?
new_option_b: Yes, by engaging in illegal activity that led to his arrest.
new_option_c: Yes, by failing to research the broad-based equity index fund.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence." Standard I(D) Misconduct is primarily concerned with the professional activities of a Member or Candidate, which covers all conduct that may negatively impact the Member's or Candidate's trustworthiness, reputation, or ability to perform their duties.  Examples include acts that involve lying, cheating, theft, fraud, or other dishonest behavior.  However, violations of Standard I(D) are not limited to actions specifically prohibited by the Standard. Failure to take appropriate action or lack of sufficient effort may also constitute a violation.  However, there are other Standards that specifically address Emara's adding the broad-based equity fund (eg, V(A) – Diligence and Reasonable Basis; III(C) – Suitability).  Standard I(D) addresses fraud and misconduct that erode public trust in the profession.  Nothing in Emara's actions suggests that he committed fraud or deception, and asserting that Emara also violated Standard I(D) is an overbroad reading of the Standard (Choice C). (Choice B)  Being arrested and jailed for acts of civil disobedience does not in itself constitute a violation of Standard I(D).  In this case, Emara's protest activities are a form of civil disobedience that does not reflect poorly on his professional capacities.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Joanna Krakowski, CFA, is the chief compliance officer (CCO) at Universal Investment Managers (UIM).  Krakowski recently hired John Smith, CFA, as a compliance manager.  Smith will report directly to Krakowski, who believes the current compliance systems and procedures are adequate. As Smith settles into his new position, he discovers numerous deficiencies including outdated software, excessive manual processes, a compliance manual that has not been updated in four years, and inadequately trained and understaffed compliance personnel. Smith meets with Krakowski to address these shortcomings, as he does not believe he can adequately perform his duties given the circumstances.  Krakowski informs Smith that there is no money in the budget for new software or additional employees.  Smith's most appropriate action is to:
new_option_a: improve the compliance program using his best efforts, given his duty is to his employer.
new_option_b: decline his supervisory responsibilities in writing until the compliance systems are improved.
new_option_c: immediately submit a written resignation from UIM, since the compliance program is deficient.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise employees to encourage behavior that complies with local laws, rules established by their firms, and the Code and Standards.  They also must take reasonable steps to detect and prevent violations.  A Member or Candidate who encounters an inadequate compliance system should bring the shortcomings of the system to the attention of the company's managers and make recommendations for corrective actions. Any Member or Candidate who cannot perform supervisory responsibilities due to these shortcomings should decline to accept supervisory responsibility, in writing, until the compliance system is improved and allows for adequate controls.  Accepting a supervisory role when the compliance system is inadequate would not allow the Member or Candidate to adequately monitor compliance by subordinates, and thus would violate the Standard. (Choice A)  Smith has a duty to his employer to improve the compliance program using his best efforts but must decline the supervisory responsibilities of the job until the firm has committed to investing appropriate resources into the compliance program. (Choice C)  The Standard does not require the Member or Candidate to resign but to decline the supervisory responsibilities of the job until the compliance program is sufficiently improved.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: When a firm possesses material, nonpublic information about a stock, the least appropriate policy is a suspension of all:
new_option_a: risk-arbitrage activity in the stock by the firm.
new_option_b: market-making activity in the stock by the firm.
new_option_c: personal trading in the stock by firm employees.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II Integrity of Capital Markets discusses the member's and candidate's responsibility to protect the integrity of the capital markets. Standard II(A) focuses specifically on the use of material nonpublic information. Trading with material nonpublic information ("insider trading") threatens market integrity, which relies on all market participants having fair access to information and no participant having the advantage of using information that is not widely available.  The table below is a quick reference for determining whether Standard II(A) is violated: When a firm has material nonpublic information about a stock, it must try to ensure that trading does not violate the Standard.  A ban on all trading in the stock is not always necessary or advisable.  For example, if a firm acts as a market maker or dealer for a certain security, suspension of market making may signal that the firm has material nonpublic information and, in effect, expose that information.  Market-making activities may continue but should be restricted to taking passive, counterparty positions in unsolicited trades. (Choice A)  Risk-arbitrage activity (proprietary trading, as when a firm establishes positions for its own profit) should be suspended since there is great potential for illegal gains. (Choice C)  The stock should be placed on a "restricted" or "watch" list, and employees should not trade the stock for their personal accounts. Personal trades should be reported periodically and monitored for insider trading activity.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Ching Liu, CFA, investor relations manager at Emerald Software (ES), arranges a video conference call with a small group of sell-side analysts to discuss confidential company developments.  On the call, Liu tells the analysts that ES has decided to selectively disclose information to give the analysts time to think about the company developments before they are publicly announced in two days.  Liu then tells the analysts that the company had a disagreement with its auditors over revenue recognition policies and as a result, ES has changed auditors. Bo Wang, CFA, is an analyst on the call and immediately recognizes the negative implications this will have for ES.  Wang believes a potential accounting scandal will not only drive down the stock price, but will motivate customers to switch to Ruby Software (RS), ES's largest competitor. Later that day, Wang calls his best clients and recommends purchase of RS without mentioning ES.  Numerous clients act on this recommendation. According to Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information, it is most likely that:
new_option_b: only Liu violated the Standard.
new_option_c: only Wang violated the Standard.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information requires Members and Candidates to abstain from investment actions if they have material nonpublic information (MNI).  Trading on or acting on MNI erodes the public's trust in the fairness of the capital markets.  MNI can come from many sources, and a Member or Candidate must evaluate information to decide whether it is MNI before acting on it. Selective disclosure (eg, analysts on a conference call, corporate insiders) does not necessarily make information public.  In this question, Ching Liu and ES intentionally disclosed information and gave the analysts the timeline of when that information would be publicly disseminated.  This type of selective disclosure is not a violation of the Standard (Choices A and B). However, by agreeing to be part of the select group receiving the information, Bo Wang has a duty to keep this information confidential until it is released publicly by the company.  Even though Wang did not directly disclose the MNI, he violated the Standard by using his knowledge of MNI to influence others to act based on this information.  Acting on MNI is not limited strictly to that company's securities (eg, ES), any trading based on MNI is a violation of the Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Long Ming often places her taxable account trades with Jiang Bai, CFA at Pheng Securities, Inc.  Ming asks Bai for retirement advice.  Bai has no experience in giving retirement advice but does have a preexisting relationship with Insights Financial Planning (Insights) and refers Ming to Insights.  After reviewing Insights' suggested retirement plan, Ming speaks with Mao Yi, CFA at Insights and is considering signing a client contract.  As part of the referral arrangement between Pheng and Insights, Yi would direct Ming's retirement account trades to Bai instead of her firm's preferred broker.  According to Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, which of the following must disclose the referral arrangement to Ming before she signs the contract?
new_option_b: Bai and Yi
new_option_c: Pheng and Insights
new_explanation_en: Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." Under Standard VI(C), Members and Candidates must notify their employers, existing clients, and prospective clients of benefits or costs for client referrals.  Disclosing referral arrangements allows employers and clients to determine if objectivity is compromised and to identify costs. Members and Candidates must properly disclose referral arrangements before clients sign up for a service that confers the benefits (eg, revenue, income).  Before Long Ming signs new contracts, both Mao Yi and Jiang Bai, as parties to the arrangement, must disclose to Ming the details of the referral arrangement between them (Choice A). (Choice C)  The Standard requires Members and Candidates, not their firms, to disclose referral fees to clients.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Jingyi Yu, Level II CFA candidate, is a portfolio manager at an investment firm.  Recently, she has been advising clients to purchase shares of Shanghai Guangfu Health Technology (SGHT), and most of her clients have added the stock to their portfolio.  Yu is purchasing an apartment and plans to sell some of her personal portfolio, which includes SGHT stock, for the down payment.  Although the size of her position in SGHT is not material and her clients will not be disadvantaged by her trade, she is concerned about taking investment action that conflicts with her investment advice to clients.  If Yu's sale of SGHT stock complies with regulatory requirements, which of the following statements best describes her responsibilities under Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions?
new_option_a: Yu may sell shares of SGHT after informing her clients.
new_option_b: Yu should avoid selling SGHT stock for the down payment.
new_option_c: Yu may sell shares of SGHT for the down payment without notifying clients.
new_explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is intended to avoid inherent conflicts of interest that arise from placing personal investing decisions over interests of clients or employers.  However, the Guidance for the Standard acknowledges the possibility that personal circumstances might cause members or candidates to make investment decisions different from their firm's current recommendations. For example, members and candidates may sell a stock to raise funds for a down payment on a home, even if the firm is recommending a buy on that stock.  These transactions may occur if clients are not disadvantaged and the investment action complies with regulatory guidelines.  If the transaction complies with the Standard, it is irrelevant whether the member or candidate realized a gain from it. (Choices A and B)  Yu's sale of SGHT shares for a down payment complies with Standard VI(B).  There is no requirement for Yu to inform her clients before selling SGHT for the down payment.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Violeta Constantin, CFA, is an analyst at a company that has not adopted GIPS but has adopted the Code and Standards as its ethical guidelines.  The firm is preparing a report on its performance.  To comply with Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, Constantin should most likely advise the firm to:
new_option_a: disclose that results are reported gross of fees.
new_option_b: base results on a single, representative account.
new_option_c: exclude terminated accounts in performance results.
new_explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that this information is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation addresses the importance of communicating fair, accurate, and complete performance information.  The Standard recommends applying the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) to performance reporting.  If a firm has not adopted GIPS, then it should ensure that clients receive a fair, accurate, and complete report. For example, firms should make disclosures that lead to a more complete explanation of results, such as whether results are reported gross of fees or net of fees.  To be complete and accurate, reports should include terminated accounts (Choice C) and report the results of a weighted composite of similar portfolios, instead of a single, representative portfolio (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: The compliance manual for West Tech Investing (WTI) was developed to suit the needs of the firm and clients.  Excerpts from the personal securities transactions section of the policy include: Equity initial public offerings (IPOs) – Employees may participate in IPOs.  Prior approval is required only for offerings that present a potential conflict of interest. Private placements – Preclearance is required for the initial placement. Restricted list – The firm maintains a restricted list, and no employees involved in the investment decision-making process may trade the securities on the restricted list without prior approval. Participation in investment clubs – Employees are prohibited from joining investment clubs. Which of the company's policies is most likely in conflict with the recommended procedures for compliance in Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions?
new_option_b: Equity IPO participation
new_option_c: Investment club participation
new_explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions is intended to avoid inherent conflicts of interest that arise from placing personal investing decisions over client or employer interests.  One source of an actual or potential conflict of interest is personal participation in equity initial public offerings (IPOs). Personal participation in any equity IPO may appear to deprive clients of attractive investment opportunities.  The guidance for the Standard recommends that firms require preapproval (ie, preclearance) before employees participate in any equity IPOs, even if there is no potential conflict. Other recommended procedures include: Restrictions on private placements Establishment of blackout periods/restricted lists Reporting requirements Disclosure of policies regarding personal investments (Choice A)  WTI's restricted list policy follows the Standard's recommendations as it applies to individuals involved in the investment decision- making process. (Choice C)  The Standard allows firms to tailor personal investment policies to meet their own criteria—for example, by prohibiting certain activities such as investment clubs.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Javier del Monte, CFA, is an adviser for an asset management firm.  Five years ago, he was hired by Leonora Gomez to manage the investments of the Ochula Industries Employee Pension Fund.  Gomez, chief financial officer of Ochula Industries, is a trustee of the fund.  All employees are beneficiaries of the fund, except for company management, who receive stock options in lieu of pension participation.  During a routine review of fund performance, Gomez tells del Monte to have the fund buy a position in the publicly traded stock of Brazos Industries (BI). "That company is a disrupter," she notes, "and the stock price is about to soar."  Del Monte thoroughly and carefully analyzes this proposed change to the fund's allocation and concludes that the stock would be a good addition to the fund.  Del Monte confers with his boss, who advises him to "keep the customer happy—remember that Gomez is also a big personal client of our firm—so, go ahead and invest in BI; Gomez will be flattered."  To comply with Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, the most appropriate reason for del Monte to have the fund invest in BI stock is:
new_option_b: his employer advises it.
new_option_c: it is a good addition to the fund.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standards III(A-E) detail a member's or candidate's duties to clients.  According to Standard III(A), those duties include loyalty, prudence, and care when making decisions in the interests of clients.  The client's interests must always come first, even before the interests of employers, colleagues, or self.  However, in order to put the client's interests first, the client must be properly identified. The client is the party who receives the benefits and bears the risk of the assets under management.  The client is not defined as the party who hires the asset manager or adviser.  When assets are owned in trust, as in a pension plan, the trust's or pension plan's beneficiaries—those who receive the benefits and bear the risks of the investment—are the clients.  The plan trustees, despite hiring the asset manager, are not the clients. In this case, the fund's beneficiaries are the participating current and retired employees.  The fund is managed for their benefit, and it is to them that del Monte owes his loyalty.  Since, after thorough analysis, del Monte believes that the stock is a good investment to make for the fund, it would be appropriate for him to invest in the stock. (Choice A)  With regard to this fund, Gomez is not del Monte's client, although she is a trustee of the fund and a personal client of his firm.  His duty of loyalty is not to her but to the fund's beneficiaries. (Choice B)  Del Monte owes his primary duty of loyalty to his client, the fund's beneficiaries, before his own employer.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: James Wilson, CFA, is an unemployed equity analyst.  To keep his investing skills sharp while he looks for a job, he created a free investing blog, "Investing with the Wizard," which issues market commentary and specific investment ideas under the pseudonym "Investing Wizard."  In the blog's description, he states that "the author of this blog, Investing Wizard, is a CFA charterholder."  Does Wilson's conduct comply with Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA designation, and the CFA Program?
new_option_b: No, since he identifies the pseudonym as a CFA charterholder.
new_option_c: No, since he uses a pseudonym that implies extraordinary abilities.
new_explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B), Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program, requires the use of the author's full name in connection with the use of the CFA designation.  The Standard prohibits using a pseudonym or fictitious name in association with the CFA designation. Wilson violated the Standard by identifying his pseudonym, "Investing Wizard," as a CFA charterholder.  Note that using a pseudonym itself is not a violation of the Standards, but that pseudonym cannot be identified as a CFA charterholder (Choices A and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Frieda Simon, CFA, is a financial adviser at TCT Advisers.  One of Simon's clients, Anton Krause, offers to include her on a trip to his vacation home in Australia once his portfolio reaches €1 million to celebrate the milestone.  Krause also offers to pay her expenses for the trip.  Simon accepts both offers and does not disclose the agreement to TCT since the compensation is not monetary.  Another client, Karla Mayer, proposes a €500 bonus for Simon in any year that Mayer's portfolio achieves a return of 10% or higher.  Simon mentions this offer over lunch with her boss, who says, "That's a great offer.  I approve."  Based on this verbal approval, she accepts Mayer's offer.  Simon most likely violates Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Agreements with respect to:
new_option_b: the bonus from Mayer.
new_option_c: both the trip from Krause and the bonus from Mayer.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires Members and Candidates to obtain written permission before accepting compensation from third parties (eg, clients) for services rendered.  Compensation from third parties can create, or be reasonably viewed as creating, a conflict of interest with an employer's interest.  The Standard applies to both monetary and nonmonetary (eg, gifts, benefits) compensation. In this scenario, both the paid trip from Anton Krause and the annual bonus from Karla Mayer require prior written approval from the respective clients and from Frieda Simon's employer since both gifts come from third parties.  Simon received no approval for the trip and only verbal approval for the bonus, so she violates the Standard with both arrangements (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Munira Alam, CFA, is a financial adviser for Rahmi Hadi.  Hadi reads a report about Force Gaming Inc. (FGI) and calls Alam to purchase the stock.  After thorough research, Alam concludes that FGI is too risky for the parameters of Hadi's investment policy statement (IPS), although the amount of the proposed purchase would have only a minimal effect on his overall portfolio.  She calls Hadi to inform him about the risk.  Hadi acknowledges Alam's warning but insists that FGI stock be added to his portfolio, even if the IPS must be modified.  To comply with the Standards, Alam should:
new_option_a: purchase FGI based on Hadi's request.
new_option_b: cease her advisory relationship with Hadi.
new_option_c: refuse to purchase FGI for Hadi's portfolio.
new_explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must: b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. c. Judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio." Standard III(C) Suitability addresses the adviser's responsibility for assessing the suitability of investments for each client.  This responsibility entails researching a client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance.  These form the building blocks of the client's investment policy statement (IPS) and determine the suitability of proposed investments. Clients sometimes wish to make investments that do not align with their IPSs.  In such a case, the Member or Candidate should discuss the proposed investment with the client before making the trade, explaining why the investment diverges from the IPS.  If the investment has minimal impact on the portfolio, the Member or Candidate can purchase the investment without modifying the IPS after receiving the proper client approval, subject to the firm's guidelines. In this scenario, Munira Alam may purchase Force Gaming Inc. (FGI) stock for Rahmi Hadi's portfolio since she educated him on the deviation between the stock's risk profile and the IPS and received Hadi's acknowledgment that the position is inconsistent with his current IPS. (Choice B)  Alam would have to consider ceasing her advisory relationship with Hadi only if the unsolicited trade were material to Hadi's portfolio and he refused to update his IPS. (Choice C)  Alam does not have to refuse to purchase FGI stock even though it does not align with Hadi's IPS.  Since the trade will be immaterial to Hadi's portfolio, Alam only needs to educate Hadi and have him acknowledge that the trade is inconsistent with his IPS.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Gaurav Khatri is taking the Level I CFA exam.  During the break between sessions of the exam, he considers some questions he struggled with in Session 1 but cannot remember all the details.  He decides to bring a piece of blank scratch paper from his car into the exam room.  During Session 2, Khatri writes a few key words from difficult questions on the scratch paper so that he can confirm the calculations later at home. However, he does his math for the exam on writing materials provided by the proctors.  After the exam, he returns these writing materials with his math to the proctors but he keeps the scratch paper containing the key words.  Khatri violates Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs:
new_option_b: only by taking his notes from the exam room.
new_option_c: both by using scratch paper and taking his notes from the exam room.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) mandates that Members and Candidates maintain the reputation, integrity, validity, and security of CFA Institute's exams and programs.  The Standard prohibits behavior that would compromise the public's confidence in the level of merit needed to achieve a CFA charter. Each Candidate taking a CFA exam must adhere to the Candidate Agreement, which prohibits cheating and misconduct on any CFA Institute exams.  This includes any violation of the policies or practices of test administration. In this scenario, Gaurav Khatri violates the Standard by using paper brought from outside the exam room.  Candidates are allowed to write only on the materials provided by CFA Institute for taking notes and doing math.  Scratch paper brought from outside the exam room cannot be tracked, which compromises the security and integrity of the exams.  Khatri further violates the Standard by taking the scratch paper with notes about the exam out of the testing room (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Fatima Hakem, CFA, is a trader at Lakefront Capital.  On Monday, Hakem receives a report from Saad Murad, one of Lakefront's research analysts, who adds Global Materials to his list of most recommended stocks based on the company receiving government approval for a new gold mine.  Murad's report was simultaneously sent out to clients that morning based on Lakefront's best practices.  On Wednesday, Hakem receives an order from one of her largest clients.  The client wants to sell positions in the metals and mining industry, including its position in Global Materials, in order to rotate into the technology sector.  To comply with Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, Hakem's most appropriate action would be to:
new_option_a: place the client's order since the report was already disseminated.
new_option_b: refuse the client's order since it conflicts with Murad's recommendation.
new_option_c: inform the client of Murad's change in recommendation before placing the order.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities." Standard III(B) Fair Dealing requires Members and Candidates to treat all clients fairly when recommending investments or undergoing investment actions on their behalf.  Analysts who prepare investment recommendations must ensure that their opinion is disseminated in a way that provides all clients a fair opportunity to act on the recommendation. However, not all clients receive and consume new recommendations right away, which may lead them to make investment decisions they otherwise would not have made.  Therefore, when an analyst changes a recommendation, clients who place orders contrary to the new recommendation should be advised of the change. In this scenario, Fatima Hakem should inform the client about the change in recommendation on Global Materials since the client's order is contrary to Saad Murad's recommendation.  Placing the order before informing the client violates the Standard since it is Hakem's responsibility to confirm that the client received the most recent recommendation (Choice A).  Since the report was sent out only two days earlier, it is reasonable to assume the client may not have seen it.  Once the client is advised of the recommendation, however, Hakem is obligated to fulfill the client's request (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Chang Xue, CFA, is hired as an associate research analyst by Phoenix Capital, where she helps her senior analyst in writing research reports. After several months, Chang notices that her senior analyst receives material nonpublic information during discussions with management of covered companies.  She suspects this information is sometimes used to change the recommendations on those companies, although the specific information is not disclosed in the research reports. Acting on material nonpublic information is against the law in the country where Phoenix operates, but since the report does not disclose any material nonpublic information, Chang is not sure what to do.  She brings this up to Li Tengfei, the chief compliance officer for Phoenix.  Li tells Chang that she would not be found guilty of breaking the law since no information is disclosed in the report, so she should continue to assist in writing the reports.  To best comply with the Standards, Chang should:
new_option_a: dissociate from her role collecting data for her senior analyst.
new_option_b: do nothing since she is not the person using material nonpublic information.
new_option_c: do nothing since she received approval to continue from the firm's compliance officer.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities.  In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation.  Members and Candidates must not knowingly participate or assist in and must dissociate from any violation of such laws, rules, or regulations." Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires Members and Candidates to understand the laws of all countries where they reside and do business in order to know if their actions may contribute to violations.  If an action that a Member or Candidate assists with is believed to be a violation, the Member or Candidate should notify a supervisor or the firm's compliance department to stop the action.  If the violation continues, the Standard requires the Member or Candidate to dissociate from the action. When there is doubt if an action is a violation, the Member or Candidate should seek advice of legal counsel or compliance personnel. However, this advice does not absolve the Member or Candidate from potential violations of the Standard if the action is illegal.  Members and Candidates are still required to know local laws and report on or dissociate from violations, if necessary (Choice C). In this scenario, Chang has already brought the potential violation to the attention of the firm's compliance department.  Based on the Standard, Chang's next step should be to dissociate from the activity. (Choice B)  Although Chang is not the person using material nonpublic information, she is still required to report on or dissociate from violations, if necessary.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Deshawn Walker, CFA, and Jevon Glover, MD, grew up together and remain close friends today.  Walker is a manager at Primary Partners Associates (PPA) and works on the Small Cap Sciences Fund, which focuses on health-care securities with great upside potential.  Glover recently left his medical practice and now works for a sell-side securities firm where he is researching Cancer Advances Corp. (CAC), a company that uses artificial intelligence to design cancer drugs.  CAC has yet to become profitable, but Glover feels optimistic based on its pipeline.  He strongly suggests that Walker take a position in CAC since he expects the company to outperform.  Walker conducts thorough due diligence and concludes that CAC is riskier than its peers but also that the company could see significantly higher returns if regulators approve certain drugs. Therefore, he deems CAC appropriate for the Small Cap Sciences Fund. Regarding the purchase of CAC stock for the fund, Walker will most likely comply with Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts if he:
new_option_a: adds an insignificant position in CAC to the fund, so disclosure is unnecessary.
new_option_b: explains to Glover that he cannot buy CAC since a conflict of interest exists between them.
new_option_c: adds a significant position in CAC to the fund after he informs PPA of his relationship with Glover.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." When a conflict interferes with a member's ability to conduct unbiased investment evaluations, the member's employer must be informed of the conflict to comply with Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts. For example, a member who feels pressured by personal loyalty to a friend may be impeded from making impartial decisions and acting in the employer's best interest.  Therefore, to comply with the Standard, Walker must disclose his relationship with Glover to Primary Partners Associates (PPA).  Walker may subsequently purchase Cancer Advances Corp. (CAC) since, after performing due diligence, he believes the company is appropriate for the fund. (Choice A)  Since a conflict of interest exists between them, Walker must disclose his relationship with Glover before purchasing shares of CAC for the fund, regardless of the size of the transaction. (Choice B)  A conflict of interest, if resolved, does not necessarily result in the prohibition of behavior.  Since Walker believes CAC is suitable for the fund, once his relationship with Glover is disclosed and PPA has no objections, the purchase can be made.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Rhianne Bridges, CFA, oversees a group of junior equity analysts for an asset management firm.  Some of the analysts are charterholders or candidates for the CFA designation, and others are not.  Bridges discovers that Frank Parsons, an analyst who is neither a member nor a candidate, has accepted tickets to a sporting event from a client without first advising her or the firm.  Parsons' action constitutes a violation of CFA Institute's Code and Standards concerning disclosure of additional compensation.  Bridges reports the incident to her supervisors and warns Parsons not to do this again.  However, a month later, Parsons accepts tickets to a sold-out concert from a different client, again without notifying Bridges or the firm.  Has Bridges most likely violated Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors?
new_option_b: No, since Parsons does not need to follow the Code and Standards.
new_option_c: No, since she told Parsons not to repeat the conduct and reported it to her supervisors.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires members and candidates who supervise employees to take reasonable steps to ensure those employees, even employees who are not members or candidates, comply with the Code and Standards.  Therefore, Bridges must comply with the Standard with respect to all the employees she supervises, not just charterholders and candidates (Choice B). Although Bridges warned Parsons not to accept tickets from clients without first getting clearance and notified her supervisors of the initial incident, these steps alone are insufficient to comply with the Standard (Choice C).  CFA Institute's guidance for Standard IV(C) also requires that supervisors take appropriate steps to ensure that the prohibited conduct does not recur.  These steps can include: investigating thoroughly to assess the extent of the violation(s), restricting and/or monitoring the employee's activities, and considering changes to existing procedures to prevent future violations.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: For CFA Institute Members and Candidates, which of the following best describes an action that violates the Code and Standards?
new_option_a: Delegating supervisory duties to subordinates who are not charterholders
new_option_b: Accepting supervisory responsibility if the compliance system is inadequate
new_option_c: Failing to detect violations despite instituting an effective compliance system
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise employees to encourage behavior that complies with local laws, rules established by their firms, and the Code and Standards.  They also must take reasonable steps to detect and prevent violations.  A Member or Candidate who encounters an inadequate compliance system should bring the shortcomings of the system to the attention of the company's managers and make recommendations for corrective actions. Any Member or Candidate who is prevented from carrying out supervisory responsibilities due to these shortcomings should decline in writing to take on supervisory responsibility until the compliance system is fixed and is allowing for adequate controls.  Accepting a supervisory role when the compliance system is inadequate would not allow the Member or Candidate to promote compliance by subordinates and thus would violate the Standard. (Choice A)  Under Standard IV(C), supervisors who supervise large numbers of employees can delegate supervision.  The employee to whom those supervisory responsibilities are delegated does not have to be a CFA charterholder. (Choice C)  Supervisors should make a reasonable effort to detect unethical behavior.  However, failing to detect such behavior does not imply a violation of the Standard as long as the supervisor ensures that a proper compliance system is in place.  In such a case, the system may need to be reviewed.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Ivan Petrovich, CFA, manages the Emerging Markets Private Equity Fund.  Twelve of the fund's 87 holdings may go a week or more without a quoted price.  Petrovich believes that this is normal for some private equity holdings, so when reporting performance he uses the last available market price for the holdings that do not price daily.  According to Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, Petrovich should:
new_option_a: provide only GIPS-compliant performance reports to potential clients.
new_option_b: inform current and potential clients about the fund's pricing methodology.
new_option_c: remove unpriced securities from the fund's public performance reports.
new_explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation stipulates that Members and Candidates must use credible performance data to assess performance and present a fair and complete report.  Therefore, Members and Candidates must disclose information that can help clients evaluate a firm's performance.  In this scenario, if Ivan Petrovich does not inform clients about the fund's pricing methodology, he violates the Standard. (Choice A)  Petrovich is not required to show potential clients only GIPS-compliant reports.  Firms may elect to comply with GIPS, but Standard III(D) does not require GIPS compliance. (Choice C)  Since reports must be as complete as possible, excluding some securities would violate the Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Maria Garcia, CFA, is a sell-side analyst at Sharp Brokerage.  Garcia is preparing a research report on Kicks, Inc., a popular athletic shoe manufacturer.  Sharp Brokerage is a market maker in Kicks, Inc. Garcia is familiar with Kicks as she was on the investment banking team at a former employer that brought Kicks public two years ago.  Garcia also has a childhood friend who is now a professional athlete and occasionally receives free Kicks apparel. According to Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, the research report should most appropriately disclose:
new_option_a: Garcia's history with Kicks' initial public offering.
new_option_b: Garcia's friendship with the professional athlete.
new_option_c: that Sharp Brokerage is a market maker of Kicks.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts aims to protect employers and clients by promoting transparency, allowing them to evaluate whether a Member or Candidate is acting independently and objectively when offering investment advice or recommendations.  When a conflict can be reasonably viewed as interfering with a Member's or Candidate's ability to conduct unbiased investment evaluations, the employer and clients must be informed on all pertinent details of the conflict. In this instance, it is the broker/dealer (ie, Sharp Brokerage) who must notify clients that the firm is a market maker in the securities included in the report.  This disclosure alerts the client that the firm may have a potential conflict in that it likely holds shares of Kicks in its own account for market-making purposes. (Choice A)  Garcia's involvement in the IPO of Kicks two years ago with a previous employer does not create an ongoing or perpetual conflict. Garcia does not have a disclosable relationship with the company currently. (Choice B)  The fact that Garcia has a friend who is a professional athlete who occasionally receives free Kicks apparel is too tangential (indirect) and minor to cause a conflict.

Meyer was tasked with this assignment as she is the most qualified to do the analysis, but she personally believes the insurance portfolio should not invest in energy companies for environmental reasons.  After considering all factors, in her final report to the committee, Meyer recommends not investing due to the considerable risk involved. new_option_b: disassociate herself from the report, as it does not align with her personal beliefs.
new_option_c: disassociate herself from the report, as it does not reflect her true investment opinion.

new_question_en: Himari Sato just got home from taking Level I of the CFA exam.  She goes onto a popular online forum and writes, "Just got back from Level I. Definitely a hard exam, much harder than I expected based on my studying, but I think I passed!  However, I still disagree with CFA Institute's policy of providing ranges for the weights of each subject on the exam.  Just tell us what to expect!  I studied way too hard for derivatives, but the number of questions was at the bottom of the range.  I wasted so much time on this."  Sato violated the Standards by:
new_option_a: disagreeing with CFA Institute's exam policies.
new_option_b: expressing an opinion on the difficulty of the exam.
new_option_c: providing information about topics tested on the exam.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs mandates that Members and Candidates maintain the reputation, integrity, validity, and security of CFA Institute exams and programs.  The Standard prohibits behavior that would compromise the public's confidence in the level of merit needed to achieve a CFA charter. Candidates taking the exam must sign the Candidate Pledge, which identifies behaviors that are prohibited before, during, and after the test. These behaviors include: giving or receiving information about the exam before or during the exam, and providing information about the exam to others after the exam, including broad topic areas tested, until it is publicly released by CFA Institute. In this scenario, Himari Sato violates the Standard by disclosing information about the exam.  Even though she did not disclose information about specific questions, she did disclose that the number of questions about derivatives was at the bottom of the given range.  Learning this could give those who have not yet taken the exam an unfair advantage. (Choice A)  The Standard allows Members and Candidates to share opinions that disagree with CFA Institute policies (eg, allowing only two types of calculators) and stances on key issues (eg, advocacy articles). (Choice B)  Members and Candidates are allowed to share opinions about the exams or CFA Institute as long as the opinions do not reveal specific information about the exams.

new_question_en: Jacqueline Dumont, CFA, is an adviser to high-net-worth clients.  For over 20 years, she advised Marc and Denise Paraguet, who divorced three years ago.  As a condition of the divorce, all of their joint accounts were closed, and their assets were divided between them.  After the divorce was settled at the end of 20X1, Denise Paraguet remained Dumont's client for one year, then ended their advisory relationship and moved her investments to another firm.  Marc Paraguet, who remains a client of Dumont's, recently asked Dumont for information about Denise's investment activities during 20X2, when she was still Dumont's client.  To comply with Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, which of the following is Dumont's best course of action?
new_option_a: Share the information since Marc is her client.
new_option_b: Do not share the information since Denise was her client.
new_option_c: Share the information since Denise is no longer her client.
