pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Ajay Patel, CFA, is a financial adviser for Eclipse Financial.  At a party, Patel discusses financial advisory services with Nira Jain.  Jain asks Patel to be her adviser, but Patel states that he cannot accept new clients.  Patel recommends Eclipse and states that he has faith in all the company's advisers.  Jain agrees to become a client of Eclipse if Patel agrees to meet with her quarterly over dinner, paid for by Jain, to discuss her portfolio allocation.  Which of the following best describes Patel's options under the Code and Standards?
new_option_b: Patel can accept the offer but then must disclose it immediately to Eclipse in writing
new_option_c: Patel can accept the offer only after disclosing it in writing to Eclipse and receiving approval in writing
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires Members and Candidates to obtain written permission when third-party, additional compensation agreements could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with their employers.  Permission must be received from all parties before the agreement can be accepted.  The Standard applies to both monetary and nonmonetary (eg, gifts, benefits) compensation. In this scenario, accepting Jain's offer to pay for quarterly dinners to discuss portfolio allocation could be perceived as a conflict of interest since Patel's actions can be perceived as giving Jain preferential treatment.  His advice could be viewed as favoring Jain over his own clients and may run counter to advice given by Eclipse's other advisers.  To comply with the Standard, Patel would be required to obtain written permission from both Jain and Eclipse before accepting the offer so Eclipse can monitor his actions. (Choice A)  Patel is not required to reject the offer so long as he obtains written permission from all parties involved so his employer can monitor for conflicts. (Choice B)  Informing Eclipse after accepting the offer is a violation of the Standard.  Patel must receive permission before agreeing so Eclipse can decide if the agreement presents a conflict.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Naomi Jorgensen, CFA, a broker at Belton Financial, Inc., currently has a sell rating on Alpha Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (API) due to its lackluster pipeline of therapeutics.  Derek DiGravio, CFA, an investment banker at Belton, is helping API with its next round of funding and believes that if API receives an additional cash infusion, it will be very successful.  DiGravio suggests to Jorgensen that she should reconsider her rating.  To comply with Standard I(B) Independence and Objectively, Jorgenson's best course of action is to:
new_option_b: rate API only as a hold until corroborating public information is available.
new_option_c: update clients with publicly available information but abstain from giving API a rating.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Internal and external influencers may interfere with a Member's independent analysis.  For example, teammates in other departments may pressure analysts to give a certain opinion, as DiGravio does in this scenario by trying to influence Jorgensen's rating due to Belton Financial, Inc.'s investment banking business. To maintain her objectivity, Jorgensen should give clients factual updates based only upon publicly available information regarding Alpha Pharmaceuticals, Inc (API).  Furthermore, to avoid any appearance of a conflict, she should issue no recommendation (Choice B). (Choice A)  Transferring the responsibility of providing a recommendation on API to another individual does not eliminate the conflict of interest between investment banking and brokerage personnel.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Hans Mohr, CFA, manages the Matrix European Stock Index Fund at Matrix Ltd.  In his personal accounts, Mohr actively trades stocks, bonds, and mutual funds, but he does not invest in any fund that he manages.  Matrix does not require any disclosures regarding personal trading, and Mohr makes no disclosures.  Has Mohr violated Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts?
new_option_b: No, since Matrix does not have any disclosure requirements.
new_option_c: No, since Mohr does not invest in any fund that he manages.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." Conflicts of interest between investment professionals and their clients or employers may create the perception of compromised independence and objectivity.  One focus of Standard VI(A) is personal trading by investment personnel.  When analysts trade securities for a personal account, it may create incentives that bias them in their dealings with employers and/or clients. To address this concern, Members and Candidates should disclose to their employers any securities held in accounts in which they have a beneficial interest; once informed, employers may take appropriate steps to limit or prevent any conflicts of interest and to provide disclosure to clients. (Choices B)  Matrix should establish disclosure policies and require disclosure of employee trading in personal accounts. As a charterholder, Mohr should urge his employer do so to avoid even the appearance of conflicts. (Choices C)  Mohr should disclose all securities held in his personal account, regardless of whether he manages the investment.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Ishani Gupta works in the manufacturing industry and wants to transition into a financial services role.  She believes a CFA charter can help with this transition.  Gupta recently sat for Level III of the CFA exam and is excited to update her resume to send to potential employers, although she has not yet received her results.  Which of the following statements can she most appropriately use on her resume to adhere to the Standards?
new_option_a: "The knowledge gained from the CFA program makes me a superior candidate."
new_option_b: "I will be eligible for a CFA charter after completing my required work experience."
new_option_c: "My studies in the CFA program have enhanced my knowledge and skills in finance."
new_explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program regulates how Members and Candidates may use the CFA designation.  Stating objective facts about the benefits of achieving the CFA designation or the intensity and rigor of the CFA program is allowed.  This includes statements about knowledge and skills gained. However, the Standard forbids Members and Candidates from exaggerating the meaning or implication of their CFA charters, such as declaring superior competency as an investment professional or suggesting charter holders are more qualified than non–charter holders (Choice A). (Choice B)  Gupta sat for the Level III exam but has not yet received her results.  She does not yet know if she passed, and therefore saying that she will be eligible for the charter after completing the required work experience is a violation of the Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: A municipality hires Enzo Gianni, CFA, to design and manage its pension plan for a flat fee.  Gianni often uses Isabella Bellini of Bellini Capital, which specializes in short-term investments, as a subadvisor for clients.  Bellini speaks to Gianni about a new short-term investment portfolio to be specifically designed for the municipality.  If hired, Bellini will charge a 0.20% annual management fee to the municipality and offers to pay Gianni a 0.05% annual administration fee.  To comply with Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, which fee(s) is Gianni required to disclose to the municipality?
new_option_a: Both Bellini's management and administration fees.
new_option_b: Only Bellini's administration fee since it is the only hidden fee.
new_option_c: Only Bellini's management fee since the municipality does not pay the administration fee.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." Standard VI(A) requires Members and Candidates to be impartial when offering advice or making recommendations to clients.  However, certain fee structures can create conflicts of interest, which can compromise Members' or Candidates' impartiality.  Clients must be made aware of such conflicts so that they can determine whether an advisor's investment advice remains objective. In this example, Enzo Gianni must inform the municipality of both the management fee that Isabella Bellini receives and the administrative fee that Bellini pays to Gianni.  Bellini is effectively sharing fees paid by the municipality with Gianni, putting Gianni's objectivity at risk.  Gianni must disclose all fees so that the municipality can make its own decisions about Gianni's impartiality (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Stuart Grimaldi, CFA, is the compliance officer for a large hedge fund with several hundred employees.  Grimaldi has implemented a comprehensive set of rules for employees to comply with applicable laws and regulation.  He appropriately updates the rules and communicates all changes to the employees.  He also holds regular meetings to advise employees of different compliance issues. The fund permits employees to maintain investment accounts with outside firms but requires the employees to send Grimaldi duplicate confirmations for all trades.  The rule applies for accounts that the employee establishes in his or her own name as well as those for immediate family members such as a spouse, domestic partner, children, or parents.  About half of the employees have outside accounts.  Grimaldi does not regularly check the confirmations but believes that the employees are complying with the rule. Recently, an employee tried to circumvent the rule by having his neighbor open an account at another firm, with the employee directing the trades made in the account.  Grimaldi was not aware of this activity until the neighbor who "owned" the account was charged with insider trading.  The neighbor then implicated the employee who was directing the trades.  Of the following, the most appropriate statement is that Grimaldi violated Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors with respect to:
new_option_b: not taking appropriate actions to prevent the employee from circumventing the rule.
new_option_c: both not checking the confirmations and preventing the circumvention of the rule.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise other personnel to take reasonable steps to prevent and detect violations of laws and regulations.  The Guidance to the Standard indicates that compliance with the Standard, at a minimum, requires supervisors to: establish written compliance procedures; and perform regular reviews to ensure that employees are following the procedures. A supervisor who does not satisfy these requirements violates the Standard even if no laws were broken.  In this question, Grimaldi violated the Standard by not implementing a regular review to ensure that employees were complying with the requirement to provide confirmations for trades occurring in outside accounts. However, the concept of "reasonableness" does not make supervisors responsible for detecting all violations; employees may be able to evade compliance in ways that cannot be detected through reasonable efforts.  It is not reasonable to conclude that Grimaldi knew or should have known in advance that an employee would try to evade the requirement by establishing a hidden account (Choices B and C).  However, now that he knows it is possible, Grimaldi should update the fund's rules to prevent future occurrences.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Nahiya Salehi, CFA, helps manage the pension fund for Azhar, Inc.  One year ago, Azhar hired Yasir Kassem to lead the pension team, and since then the returns on Salehi's recommendations have lagged behind those of her colleagues.  One day, Kassem tells her, "I need you to develop relationships with managers at other companies for information to trade on.  Your colleagues have made friends with directors at other companies who provide them with strategic information."  Salehi feels that this constitutes insider trading, which is against local law.  She brings the conversation to the attention of Azhar's compliance manager and chief financial officer, who tell her not to worry since this is common practice and the pension fund returns have improved since Kassem joined the team.  To comply with Standard IV(A) Loyalty, Salehi's best course of action is to:
new_option_a: do nothing, since no clients are being harmed.
new_option_b: develop the relationships as Kassem suggests.
new_option_c: disclose the practice to local regulatory authorities.
new_explanation_en: "In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer." Standard IV(A) Loyalty requires Members and Candidates who are employees to protect their employers and refrain from conduct that could: injure the firm, deprive the firm of profit, or deprive the firm of the Member or Candidate's skills and abilities. However, employers' interests are secondary to clients' interests and the integrity of the capital markets.  Therefore, whistleblowing is permitted under the Standard, even when it is prohibited under a Member or Candidate's responsibilities to an employer under normal circumstances.  Nonetheless, whistleblowing is permitted only when the goal is to protect clients or market integrity, not for personal gain. In this scenario, Azhar, Inc. and Yasir Kassem are using inside information to increase the return on Azhar's pension fund.  However, acting on inside information is detrimental to overall investor confidence in the capital markets and is against local law.  Since market integrity supersedes Nahiya Salehi's loyalty to her employer, both doing nothing and collecting inside information would violate the Standard (Choices A and B). Salehi has already contacted Azhar's compliance manager and chief financial officer, who dismissed her concerns.  Therefore, she would be justified in disclosing the insider trading to local regulatory authorities.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Indra Kulkarni, CFA, runs a hedge fund.  Kulkarni wants to close out his short position in IPB Industrial (IPB), but the publicly traded stock's price keeps rising and Kulkarni wants to avoid taking a loss on the trade.  Kulkarni hires a public relations firm to distribute false reports of succession issues and erratic management at IPB following the recent death of IPB's respected CEO.  After the negative publicity causes the stock price to fall significantly, Kulkarni closes out his short position and realizes a large gain.  On the same day, after meeting regulatory filing requirements, Manjeet Jain, CFA, sells a large block of IPB stock that she had inherited from her mother, the late IPB CEO.  Jain knows the recent reports about IPB are false but does not know where they came from.  Although she fears her sale may further depress the stock price, she is anxious to sell the stock in order to diversify her portfolio and meet some immediate, personal liquidity needs.  Jain sells the stock at a loss but also realizes a large tax benefit.  Which of the parties most likely violates Standard II(B) Market Manipulation?
new_option_b: Kulkarni only
new_option_c: Both Jain and Kulkarni
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits behavior that undermines the integrity of markets by distorting trading volume or prices in a market in order to deceive those who rely on market information.  In this case, Kulkarni violates the Standard by hiring a public relations firm to mislead market participants with the intent of distorting the market price to his advantage.  This is an example of information-based manipulation. Market manipulation can be information-based or transaction-based: Information-based manipulation is the use of misleading or false information to distort market pricing or to induce others to trade based on such information. Transaction-based manipulation occurs when trading is used to distort market prices and volume. Jain does not violate the Standard since she trades only with the intent of meeting liquidity needs and diversifying her portfolio.  Although she trades at a price that reflects information that she "knows" is false, and she "fears" that her trade will affect the market price, her intent is not to deceive or defraud others by distorting market volume or price information.  It is also irrelevant that she derives some benefit from the trade (Choices A and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Christina Wilkerson, CFA, is a portfolio manager for a well-known asset management firm.  All managers include a brief biography on the firm's website.  Wilkerson's entry reads: "The CFA program afforded me a wide range of knowledge on diverse financial instruments and concepts.  I have held the CFA designation since 2011 and passed each level on my first attempt.  For each level, my scores in the topics of Fixed Income and Alternative Investments rated in the highest category in CFA Institute's grading system."  Assuming that all assertions in her entry can be verified, which of the following best describes whether Wilkerson's entry complies with Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program?
new_option_a: Her entry does not violate the Standard.
new_option_b: Her statement concerning her examination scores violates the Standard.
new_option_c: Her statement that she passed each level on her first attempt violates the Standard.
new_explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) governs how Members and Candidates may use the CFA designation.  One purpose of the Standard is to prevent charterholders from mispresenting the designation by implying that it gives them superior investment expertise or will result in better investment outcomes. An example of misrepresentation is a vague statement that a charterholder is better qualified to manage clients' money.  However, the Standard does not prohibit statements of objective facts. Wilkerson's assertion that she passed each level of the examination process on her first attempt can be verified.  Nothing in the statement implies that she is more qualified to manage investments than someone who required multiple attempts to pass one or more levels (Choice C). Similarly, her statement concerning her score category does not violate the Standard.  Candidates do not receive numerical scores; rather, the scores for each topic are placed into one of three categories.  Candidates receive a breakdown on each topic and are advised as to each score's category.  Again, Wilkerson is not exaggerating her ability or trying to mislead readers into concluding that her scores imply a superior ability (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Vanessa Van Eeden, CFA, is the director of investments at Consensus Investments (CI) and is responsible for equity management.  CI's specialty is small-cap stocks.  Due to the departure of several key employees, Van Eeden decides to make the following operational adjustments in the firm: The large-cap strategy will change from active to passive management. Management of the mid-cap strategy will be outsourced to an external manager. CI will continue its focus on actively managing small-cap stocks. To comply with Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, which of the following investment strategies must Van Eeden fully disclose to current and prospective clients?
new_option_b: The mid-cap and large-cap strategies
new_option_c: The mid-cap, large-cap, and small-cap strategies
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must disclose to clients and prospective clients the basic format and general principles of the investment processes they use to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios and must promptly disclose any changes that might materially affect those processes." According to Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, members and candidates must disclose the changes in the general underpinnings of investment processes (eg, strategies) to current and prospective clients.  The disclosure allows clients to decide whether the strategy changes still aligns with their risk and return objectives. Van Eeden alters the firm's investment process by moving from active to passive management in the large-cap strategy and by changing from internal to external management in the mid-cap strategy.  For both the large-cap mid-cap and strategies, Van Eeden should disclose the reasons behind changes and new risks and limitations associated with them to comply with the Standard.  A reasonable investor would want to know about this so they could determine if the new strategy meets their investment objectives (Choice A). (Choice C)  It is not required that Van Eeden disclose information surrounding the small-cap strategy since continuing to focus on the small-cap strategy is not a shift in strategy.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Beau Chamberlain, CFA, a manager at Flex Securities, is responsible for revamping Flex's compliance system.  His supervisor tells him, "The best way to eliminate conflicts of interest is to thoroughly review personal trades."  According to Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, which of the following is most likely a recommended practice?  Flex should:
new_option_a: receive duplicate trade confirmations from employees.
new_option_b: identify all employee client accounts to ensure nonemployee client accounts trade first.
new_option_c: disseminate notice of the blackout period to prevent client trades in restricted securities.
new_explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires employees to give clients ample time to act on an investment decision before transacting for themselves.  Employees' personal transactions should never harm a client's portfolio.  Personal transactions include activity in accounts of Employees Spouses, children, or other immediate family members Employees that have indirect beneficial financial interests (eg, trust) One recommended firm procedure is to require employees to deliver copies of trade confirmations to their employers.  This provides: Documentation of all purchases and sales Proof the firm monitors employees' trading Fewer conflicts due to personal trading (Choice B)  Employee and nonemployee client accounts trade simultaneously; nonemployee accounts do not trade first. (Choice C)  Blackout periods prevent employees, not clients, from placing any trades in a security just before the firm intends to transact for clients (ie, prevents front-running of restricted securities).  This usually applies to transactions of substantial size.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.03 Guidance For Standards I–VII - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Tony Fernandez, CFA, is an analyst who provides investment recommendations to clients of Johan Investment Management (JIM).  Mercedes Chevela, CFA, president of JIM, gives freedom to each analyst to develop diverse recommendations.  Chevela's philosophy is to be the first with new ideas, so she streamlined JIM's research operations and eliminated her review of the analysts' work.  All analysts deliver their recommendations to clients the same day they are made and are solely responsible for its content.  As part of Fernandez's research efforts, he sometimes checks certain websites to get a sense of how "hot" a stock currently is.  He also examines the company's financial statements, third- party research, and quantitative forecasts, which he believes cover all important issues.  Over the last year, most of his sell recommendations have proven to be wrong.  To ensure compliance with Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis, the most appropriate recommended action is that:
new_option_a: Fernandez should exclude internet rumors as part of his research.
new_option_b: Chevela should reinstate a review process to ensure diligence when making investment recommendations.
new_option_c: Fernandez should redesign his analysis since it lacks a reasonable basis, as proven by his consistently inaccurate recommendations.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must:

new_question_en: Regina Garcia, CFA, is the equity trader at Rushmore Advisors (RA), an institutional buy-side firm.  RA's normal business practice is to pay a standard commission rate of $0.02 per share for all stock trades.  This $0.02 commission pays for the cost of both research and trade execution. RA has trading relationships with two firms: Execution Only, Inc. (EO), where RA has committed to a minimum amount of soft dollar commissions to pay for research, and Integrated Brokers, for all other trades. Trading activity has been lower than expected, and Garcia determines that the standard $0.02 per share commission will be insufficient to cover the cost of RA's soft dollar commitments to EO for the year.  To prevent a shortfall, Garcia allocates most trades to EO and increases the commission rate paid to EO to $0.05 per share. According to Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, did Garcia most likely violate the Standards?
new_option_b: No, since Garcia has a duty of loyalty to her employer
new_option_c: No, since soft dollar arrangements are acceptable under the Code and Standards
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' best interests before their employer's or their own interests." Investment managers pay a commission to a broker to execute client trades.  Soft dollar brokerage is the practice of using a portion of brokerage commissions to purchase investment research and related services.  When a portion of the commission is used to purchase additional investment services (ie, soft dollars), the services "belong" to the client since the client indirectly "pays" the commission (ie, out of client assets).  The investment manager has a duty of loyalty to use such assets for the benefit of the client. In this instance, Garcia and the investment manager violated the duty of loyalty to the client by paying a higher-than-normal commission rate for the exclusive purpose of generating soft dollar commissions. The client will not receive any additional benefit from paying the higher commission since no additional research will be provided to Rushmore Advisors (RA). The only benefit of paying a higher commission was to satisfy RA's prior commitment to Execution Only, Inc., which is not the client's responsibility. (Choice B)  Garcia has a duty of loyalty to her employer (ie, ensure appropriate allocation of commissions) but not at the expense of the client. (Choice C)  Soft dollar arrangements are acceptable under the Code and Standards, but it is not acceptable for clients to pay a higher-than- normal brokerage commission without commensurate client benefit.

new_question_en: Matthew Beck, CFA, recently joined an investment management firm as a senior analyst after many years of working in the same role for a competitor.  Beck's spouse is a director of a publicly traded company that Beck will cover for his new employer.  His spouse has been a director for several years, and Beck wrote analyst reports about the company for his previous employer.  Beck also serves as a trustee for the youth soccer association in his town.  Part of his responsibilities as a trustee is to coordinate the association's fundraising efforts, but Beck does not directly solicit money.  The association is a relatively new entity, and Beck anticipates a significant time commitment for the next several months.  Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts most likely requires Beck to disclose to his new employer:
new_option_b: both his spouse's directorship and his soccer trusteeship.
new_option_c: neither his spouse's directorship nor his soccer trusteeship.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts defines a conflict as a matter that reasonably could be expected to "impair [members' or candidates'] independence or objectivity or interfere with their respective duties…."  Beck's spouse serves as a director of a company that Beck will be covering as an analyst.  This must be disclosed since it potentially interferes with Beck's objectivity.  It is irrelevant that Beck wrote reports on the company for his previous employer since he cannot assume the new employer is aware of the relevant facts. The Standard includes all conflicts, not just financial conflicts.  Beck's soccer trusteeship is a potential conflict since Beck will have to devote significant time to the association in the coming months.  This could interfere with his duties to his employer as well as to his clients.  The Standard does not require an actual conflict to exist to trigger disclosure, only that one could "reasonably be expected" to occur (Choice A). (Choice C)  Both Beck's spouse serving as a trustee of a company that Beck will be covering as an analyst and his soccer trusteeship pose actual or potential conflicts of interest, which Standard VI(A) requires him to disclose to his new employer.

new_question_en: According to Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information, which of the following best describes the concept of mosaic theory?  A manager complies with the Standards by recommending an investment using:
new_option_b: public and nonpublic material facts.
new_option_c: material public and nonmaterial nonpublic data.
new_explanation_en: "Member and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Information is deemed material if it is likely to change the price of a security or if a reasonable investor would use it to evaluate an investment. Information is considered nonpublic until it is widely disseminated.  Analysts may not act on material nonpublic information but may act on material public data or nonmaterial nonpublic data. The mosaic theory is a research approach that recognizes that analysts form conclusions from various sources of information.  Analysts may research collections of public and nonmaterial nonpublic data to piece together information (ie, a mosaic), leading to a conclusion.  An analyst using various sources of public and nonmaterial nonpublic information does not violate the Standard, even if the analyst reaches a conclusion that could have been reached using material nonpublic information. (Choices A and B)  An analyst acting on material nonpublic information would be in violation of Standard II(A).  Such action is an inappropriate application of the mosaic theory.

new_question_en: Patricia Murphy, CFA, is asked by her manager at the hedge fund firm Star Capital to create a marketing brochure for prospective clients.  The firm has achieved the following returns: Star Capital (actual) Star Capital (risk-adjusted) Market 20X3 5% 2% −4% 20X4 13% 12% 8% 20X5 24% 22% 13% 20X6 5% 5% 4% 20X7 16% 14% 6% In the brochure, Murphy writes, "Star Capital has consistently outperformed its benchmark on a risk-adjusted basis and has yet to have a loss in any year.  Clients can expect more of the same next year."  Which part of Murphy's statements most likely violates Standard I(C) Misrepresentation?  Stating that:
new_option_a: "Star Capital…has yet to have a loss in any year."
new_option_b: "Clients can expect more of the same next year."
new_option_c: "Star Capital has consistently outperformed its benchmark..."
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation focuses on avoiding both the use of false or misleading statements and the omission of facts, which can undermine investor trust.  This includes statements that guarantee clients a level of future performance or a specific return on risky investments (eg, stocks).  The Standard applies to information prepared as a verbal or published statement that is intended for clients, colleagues, or the public. In the marketing brochure, Murphy violates the Standard by implying that clients of Star Capital can expect to receive positive returns and to outperform the market next year.  Since the hedge fund's investments consist of risky assets, it is impossible for Murphy to know whether Star Capital can achieve these targets.  Past results are not guarantees of future performance and should not be presented as such. (Choice A)  Stating that Star Capital has not had a loss is not misrepresentation since it is a factual statement with no omissions. (Choice C)  Stating that returns have consistently outperformed the benchmark on a risk-adjusted basis is not misrepresentation since it, too, is a factual statement with no omissions.

new_question_en: Sarah Paxton, CFA, works as an investment adviser at a bank.  When a client is interested in buying a home, she refers them to Susan Jones, a friend and real estate agent.  Jones reciprocates by referring real estate clients to Paxton when appropriate.  Since Paxton and Jones are both skilled and respected professionals, each believes the referrals benefit their clients and are in the clients' best interest. According to Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, Paxton is most likely:
new_option_a: required to disclose this arrangement to both her employer and clients.
new_option_b: not required to disclose this arrangement because she believes the clients benefit.
new_option_c: not required to disclose this arrangement because no money is exchanged between Paxton and Jones.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services." Standard VI(C) Referral Fees requires Members and Candidates to notify their employers, existing clients, and prospective clients of benefits received for recommending a product or service.  Disclosing referral fee arrangements allows employers and clients to determine whether conflicts of interest exist and whether a recommendation is impartial.  Referral fees are broadly defined and include any cash or noncash rewards (eg, tickets to a sporting event). In this question, Paxton has entered into an agreement with Jones to mutually refer clients when appropriate, which is beneficial for both Paxton and Jones.  Therefore, Paxton is required to disclose this information to both her employer and clients although no direct money transfer is involved (Choice C). (Choice B)  The fact that Paxton believes the clients benefit from the arrangement does not preclude Paxton from the disclosure requirement of the Standard.

new_question_en: Marcos Silva, CFA, and Clara Neves, CFA, are analysts at Alpha Capital, an independent research firm.  Silva reads a blog post about Northwest Bank that details several fresh insights on company-specific growth.  After doing his own thorough research on Northwest, Silva agrees with the blogger's analysis, although he expects this growth to take longer than the blogger predicts. Silva then writes a research report on Northwest and includes a restatement of the blogger's insights.  Since he has changed some of the wording and the expected time horizon for growth, he does not reference the blog. Neves proofreads the report at Silva's request and agrees with his conclusion about the bank.  With Silva's approval, Neves adds a chart from the US Federal Reserve, which is not copyrighted, that shows expected growth in bank reserves over the next year.  She properly cites the US Federal Reserve as the source.  According to the Code and Standards:
new_option_a: both Silva and Neves have violated the Standards.
new_option_b: Silva has violated the Standards, but Neves has not.
new_option_c: Neves has violated the Standards, but Silva has not.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation protects investors against statements and information provided by the investing community that may undermine investor trust in the integrity of the profession.  Misrepresentation can include: Plagiarism:  quoting information without acknowledgment or citation of the source Omission:  presenting incomplete information or data in order to mislead Exaggeration:  inflating professional credentials or performance results The use of another's work without attribution is plagiarism, even if the work is not quoted verbatim from the original or slight changes have been made.  Others' work can be presented to clients as long as the original source is clearly identified. In this scenario, Marcos Silva restates an excerpt from a blog, changing only the time horizon of the expected growth while effectively copying important substance about the sources of that growth.  Silva does not make significant changes to the original author's work, nor does he attribute the work to that author; this is plagiarism, and Silva has violated the Standard (Choice C). (Choice A)  Clara Neves includes a chart from the US Federal Reserve, which is not her original work.  However, Neves does not commit plagiarism since the material is not copyrighted, allowing it to be repurposed without permission, and she properly cites the original source; therefore, she has not violated the Standard.

new_question_en: Clem Benson, CFA, is the chief investment officer at Sterling Hospital.  Sterling's board asks Benson for fundraising ideas.  Benson suggests that if Sterling refers past contributors to him, he will conduct a personalized investment review for a fee of $1,000.  In return, Benson will donate 50% of that fee to Sterling.  After receiving board approval, Sterling promotes the fundraising campaign to its past contributors, informs them of Benson's arrangement, and refers 50 clients to Benson.  The fundraiser raises $25,000 for Sterling.  According to Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, has Benson most likely violated the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, since Benson receives income from the referrals.
new_option_c: Yes, since Benson receives the tax deduction for the donation instead of the contributors.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services." Under Standard VI(C), Members and Candidates must notify clients of the benefits they obtain for receiving a referral.  When an adviser's referral arrangements are disclosed, prospective clients may evaluate the adviser's objectivity. All referral arrangements between an employee and employer or an employee and a third party must be disclosed.  Clem Benson does not violate the Standard since both Sterling Hospital and the past contributors being referred to Benson are aware of the referral structure. (Choice B)  Benson may receive cash from the referral arrangement since the clients are informed of the referral structure. (Choice C)  Benson is permitted to construct any legally allowable referral arrangement, including one that generates a tax benefit.  Since the referral structure is disclosed, he does not violate the Standard.

new_question_en: Gerry Walsh, CFA, trades only cryptocurrencies through an account at Mayday Securities.  Since the account was opened in January 20X7, Walsh has earned an average monthly return of 3.5%.  However, returns have been very volatile, and the monthly gains and losses often exceed 10%.  In January 20X8, Walsh starts a subscriber-based online investment newsletter providing information on his experience with cryptocurrencies and monthly returns.  In the newsletter, Walsh suggests similar long-term average returns are possible for others if they follow his strategies.  He states that cryptocurrency trading can generate large gains, but adds that it carries the potential for high volatility and significant losses.  Although Walsh wants more subscribers, he fully discloses the account's performance in 20X7 and notes that cryptocurrency investments may not be appropriate for all investors.  Based on the actions described, does Walsh violate Standard I(C) Misrepresentation by issuing the newsletter?
new_option_b: Yes, since he presents performance for only 20X7.
new_option_c: Yes, since he knows cryptocurrencies are not appropriate for all subscribers.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation concerns actions that may undermine investor trust in the integrity of the CFA profession and the financial markets.  The Standard applies to all information presented to clients, colleagues, or the public.  Misrepresentation can include: Omission: Presenting incomplete information or data in order to mislead Exaggeration: Inflating professional credentials or performance results Plagiarism: Quoting information without acknowledgment or citation In this scenario, Gerry Walsh has complied with the Standard by fully disclosing performance for the life of the account (Choice B).  The Standard prohibits Members and Candidates from guaranteeing clients specific returns on investments since all investments carry some degree of risk.  Although Walsh states that "similar long-term average returns are possible for others," he is not violating the Standard.  Walsh is not promising such returns will be achieved, and he warns investors about "the potential for high volatility and significant losses." (Choice C)  Walsh provides data conveying the risk of cryptocurrencies and advises they are not appropriate for all investors.  The Standard is not violated since there is no omission of information that might result in investors being misled.

new_question_en: Trevor Johnson, CFA, joins Pinnacle Advisors as an equity trader.  Pinnacle uses Research Market Brokers (RMB) for all trades from accounts that allow soft dollar arrangements and Cost Cutter Brokers (CCB) for those that do not.  RMB does not have the lowest execution price but offers research used for the benefit of Pinnacle's clients.  CCB offers the lowest price execution available for Pinnacle.  After a slow trading month, Pinnacle is below its soft dollar trading commitment to RMB.  RMB offers to temporarily lower the price of its trades to match CCB until the commitment is reached as long as all trades, including those on accounts that do not allow soft dollar arrangements, are made through their brokerage.  Based on the Code and Standards, Johnson:
new_option_a: can temporarily trade all accounts through RMB since it lowered its price.
new_option_b: can only trade stocks through CCB for all accounts since it is usually the lowest-priced.
new_option_c: cannot use trades for accounts that prohibit soft dollar arrangements to meet the commitment.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires Members and Candidates to seek best price and best execution for client trades.  "Best price" and "best execution" do not necessarily mean the lowest trading commission, but commissions paid to brokers to execute the trades must be commensurate with the value received. Soft dollar brokerage refers to the practice of using a portion of brokerage commissions to purchase investment services (eg, research). Since the client "pays" the commission out of client assets, these investment services are the property of the client, not the investment management firm, and must be used to benefit the client.  Typically, brokers that offer value-added investment services charge higher commissions.  Clients can choose not to have their accounts traded on a soft dollar basis if they do not feel the value is worth the cost. In this scenario, Johnson does not violate the Standard even though he directs all account trading to RMB.  RMB reduced its commissions to match CCB's commissions; therefore, the clients that do not allow soft dollars are not paying extra to subsidize the research used by clients that allow soft dollars (Choice C).  When RMB raises its prices, Johnson must switch accounts that do not allow soft dollars back to CCB. (Choice B)  Johnson is not required to trade through only CCB despite them having the lowest commissions since RMB adds value to Pinnacle's clients through the research they offer, so long as the research is used to benefit Pinnacle's clients.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Shweta Reddy, CFA, proctors the last day of the Level III CFA exam.  While conducting a walkthrough during the exam, she sees one Candidate glancing at another Candidate's monitor.  She notices that the question on the cheating Candidate's screen is about the portfolio management of pension funds.  After the exam, Shweta joins the other proctors for drinks at a local bar and runs into an old friend, a doctor who has no plans to take any CFA exam.  While chatting with the doctor, she mentions her proctoring experience and says, "I caught someone blatantly cheating on a pension fund question.  He wasn't even trying to hide it!"  Has Reddy most likely violated Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs?
new_option_b: No, since the last day of exams has been completed.
new_option_c: No, since she did not provide specific details about the question.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." CFA Institute strives to ensure that confidential information about its exams is not disclosed since this disclosure can create an unfair advantage for anyone who receives the information.  Therefore, Standard VII(A) prohibits Members and Candidates from disclosing any confidential information related to the exams or any behaviors that could undermine the integrity of CFA Institute or its programs. Members who serve as proctors may come across confidential information, including specific details about questions on the exams and the broad topical areas represented in those questions. A proctor does not violate the Standard by simply viewing exam materials.  However, sharing information about the materials is a violation.  All information contained in the exams must remain confidential unless CFA Institute eventually chooses to disclose it.  Until that time, revealing any of the information—even after the exam period has ended—constitutes a violation of the Standard (Choice B). (Choice C)  Although Shweta Reddy has not provided specific details about the question, she violates the Standard by revealing one of the broad topical areas on the exam (ie, pension funds).

new_question_en: Five years ago, Marlijn Wijngaards pled guilty to a finance-related felony.  She had previously earned the CFA designation, but her charter was revoked as a result of the plea.  Wijngaards has applied to CFA Institute to reinstate her charter and membership.  Her application is pending.  In her résumé, Wijngaards refers to herself as a "Former CFA Charterholder."  Does this reference violate Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program?
new_option_b: Yes, since she cannot refer to the CFA designation unless her application is successful.
new_option_c: Yes, since the revocation prohibits her from indicating that she ever held the designation.
new_explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) permits only CFA Institute members who have earned the CFA designation to refer to themselves as CFA charterholders. Wijngaards' guilty plea and the subsequent revocation of her charter mean that she forfeited her right to use the designation.  However, as interpreted by CFA Institute, Standard VII(B) does allow former charterholders to state that they previously held the designation. Nothing in the Code or Standards requires former charterholders to apply for reinstatement as a condition of stating that they are former charterholders (Choice B).  Furthermore, the Standards do not prohibit statements of objective fact.  Wijngaards can verify that she once held the CFA designation.  So long as Wijngaards's statement does not lead others to conclude that she expects to be reinstated, the Standards do not prevent her from stating that she previously was a charterholder (Choice C).

new_question_en: Eric Saul, CFA, is a portfolio manager with Skye Group.  He reads several social media posts from industry experts about the health benefits attributed to a new herbal tea made with rose petals.  Based on these posts, Saul reviews industry publications and finds several articles that speculate herbal rose tea will be the next big beverage craze.  Saul visits a senior vice president of Gamma Company, a conglomerate with a significant market share in the beverage industry, who confirms that the market for herbal tea has considerable potential.  After reviewing Gamma's financial statements and public disclosures, Saul uses industry-standard financial models to determine the intrinsic value of Gamma's stock.  He concludes that Gamma will introduce an herbal tea made with rose petals.  Based on this conclusion, Saul buys Gamma stock for all suitable client portfolios.  A few weeks later, Gamma announces a new line of herbal rose tea.  Did Saul most likely violate Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information?
new_option_b: Yes, by purchasing Gamma for clients
new_option_c: Yes, by acting on information from company management
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from trading on or recommending investments based on material nonpublic information.  However, analysts may piece together public and nonmaterial nonpublic data from multiple sources to form investment conclusions. This research approach is referred to as the mosaic theory, and it recognizes that analysts form conclusions from various sources of information. Conclusions formed through the mosaic process, even when based on information that would be considered material and nonpublic if it came directly from a reliable source (eg, the company), do not violate the Standard. In this scenario, Eric Saul used public information, including social media posts, industry publications, and financial statements.  His discussion at Gamma Company, although nonpublic, is not material since the senior vice president simply confirmed Saul's market research and indicated nothing about Gamma's intentions (Choice C). (Choice B)  Saul's purchase of Gamma did not violate the Standard since he did not use material nonpublic information to reach his conclusion regarding Gamma.  He also treated Skye's clients in an equitable manner by purchasing the stock for all suitable client portfolios.

new_question_en: Annika and Boris Goncharov are siblings, CFA charterholders, and investors of Bright Sky Capital (BSC).  Annika and Boris hold more than RUB 100 million each in BSC stock, and each plans to sell 10% to diversify their separate portfolios.  However, BSC is a lightly traded stock, and the siblings agree that large sales would likely cause the company's stock price to decline. Annika decides to break up her sales into small batches of limit orders and sell them over multiple days to minimize the impact on the stock's price.  Still, Annika's sales cause BSC's stock price to decline.  Boris similarly decides to sell his holdings in batches, but he simultaneously purchases half the amount he sells to ensure the stock price is unaffected by his trades.  Standard II(B) Market Manipulation is most likely violated by:
new_option_b: both Boris and Annika.
new_option_c: neither Boris nor Annika.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation requires Members and Candidates to avoid any practices that deceive market participants through the distortion of securities prices or trading volume.  Manipulation can occur through: information-based activities (eg, issuing misleading information) and transaction-based activities (eg, exaggerated trading between two accounts). The Standard is not meant to prevent the use of legitimate strategies that limit a trade's impact on the market when trading large positions or low- liquidity stocks.  The key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is whether the trading strategy is intended to deceive market participants.  If the strategy is intended to deceive investors, it violates the Standard. In this scenario, Annika Goncharov uses a legitimate strategy of breaking up a large position of a low-liquidity stock to limit the impact of the sale on the price.  Annika's strategy has not violated the Standard (Choice B).  Boris Goncharov intends to distort market prices by making market participants believe there are more buyers of Bright Sky Capital's stock than there are.  Since market participants cannot see that Boris is driving both the buying and the selling activity, the trading is deceptive and has violated the Standard (Choice C).

new_question_en: Stephanie Williams, CFA, is the portfolio manager of the Lantern Latin American Equity Fund (LLAEF).  LLAEF is a mutual fund that invests exclusively in stocks listed in Central and South America.  While attending her daughter's gymnastics practice, Williams discusses LLAEF with Jeffrey Jones, who also has a daughter in the class.  Jones states that he is a conservative investor, investing primarily in a balanced fund, and has never considered investing in Latin American equities before. Williams gives a very optimistic assessment of the economic conditions in the region and states that Latin American equities are among the most undervalued globally.  Williams says, "I believe Latin America is likely to be the best performing emerging market region in the world over the next few years.  This fund is a 'no brainer' and adds great diversification benefits to any portfolio."  Has Williams most likely violated Standard III(C) Suitability?
new_option_b: Yes, as Williams recommended a portfolio allocation
new_option_c: Yes, as Williams recommended a specific investment
new_explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are responsible for managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy, or style, they must make only investment recommendations or take only investment actions that are consistent with the stated objectives and constraints of the portfolio." Standard III(C) Suitability addresses Members' and Candidates' responsibilities to assess the suitability of investments for each client.  Members and Candidates that manage a pooled investment vehicle to a specific investment mandate have a responsibility to ensure the suitability of investments for the fund, specifically making sure investments adhere to the mandate.  Members and Candidates cannot be expected to ensure suitability for every investor in the fund; that is the responsibility of the investor or investor's advisor. In this instance, Stephanie Williams is an institutional portfolio manager, so her duty is to ensure suitability to the fund's mandate.  Since she is not in an advisory relationship with Jeffrey Jones, or any investor, she is not responsible for assessing the suitability of the fund for his investment portfolio (Choices B and C).  Therefore, Williams did not violate the Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Soomin Yoo, CFA, is helping grade the most recent Level 3 exam.  At dinner one evening, she discusses the grading process with a friend, Minsoo Han, CFA, who is not participating in the grading process. Yoo states "I'm surprised how many people are missing the question on fixed income investing strategies.  It didn't come across to me as that difficult." Han responds "If that's the case, candidates might be in trouble.  I read on a social media post that the multiple-choice section also had more fixed income questions than in other recent exams." According to the Standards, is it most likely that:
new_option_a: both Yoo and Han have violated the Standards.
new_option_b: Yoo has violated the Standards but Han has not.
new_option_c: Han has violated the Standards but Yoo has not.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) prohibits Members and Candidates from engaging in behavior that undermines the integrity of CFA Institute, its programs, and the public's confidence in the level of merit needed to achieve a CFA charter.  To uphold the integrity of the charter, the CFA Institute takes care to ensure that confidential information about exams is not shared by anyone.  For Members and Candidates, sharing such information is a violation of the Standard. Members may not disclose: questions that are set to appear on the exam or are under consideration, any parts of the deliberation process related to the exam, or information related to the grading of questions. Graders may not share information with anyone outside of the development or grading process.  Since Han is not part of the grading process, Yoo may not discuss any information relating to the grading of questions, whether it is specific details or general information.  By doing so, she violates the Standard.  If this information were shared with other participants in the grading process, it would not violate the Standard. (Choices A and C)  Han does not violate the Standard since he is not part of the exam's development, administering, or grading process and therefore does not know any information to disclose.  His only source of information is a social media post.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Vladimir Ivanov, CFA, is the portfolio manager of a separately managed account (SMA) that invests equally in 20 different large-cap international value stocks.  Most of Ivanov's personal investments are invested in the same strategy.  Since Ivanov's twin daughters are enrolling in college this year, he needs to sell a portion of his holdings to pay for their tuition.  To generate a tax loss, Ivanov sells the entire position of one holding instead of selling equal portions of all 20 positions in his account.  According to Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, did Ivanov most likely comply with the Standard?
new_option_b: No, by not informing his clients before the trade
new_option_c: No, by entirely divesting from a holding that is still held in client accounts
new_explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires members and candidates to place clients' and employers' financial interests before their own when investing.  It is not uncommon for a member or candidate to transact in the same investments as a client or even alongside the client.  This situation does not violate the Standard provided that: the client is not disadvantaged by the trade, the member or candidate does not benefit from the client transactions, and the member or candidate adheres to all applicable regulatory requirements. Likewise, a manager has no obligation to invest personal funds in the same strategy as clients do since the manager may have different risk and return objectives and different constraints (eg, liquidity needs) than the clients. In this scenario, Ivanov complied with the Standard.  Ivanov has no specific obligation to inform clients of his personal transactions (Choice B). His sale ran counter to the long-term advice given to clients, but since he did not violate the guidelines above, no infringement occurred (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Kathy Harriet, CFA, is the chief investment officer at PPG Investments.  Harriet hosts a video meeting where she speaks to all employees. During her live presentation, Harriet discusses PPG's top holdings, including Responsive Market Tech, Inc. (RMT).  Harriet explains why RMT is a top holding: existing barriers to entry and the current competitive landscape create a rare opportunity for accelerated earnings growth.  Sidney Fletcher, CFA and PPG employee, acts on Harriet's explanation and purchases 100,000 shares of RMT for PPG's trading account during the meeting.  After Fletcher's trades, RMT's price has not changed.  According to PPG's policies, Harriet sends the recorded meeting and its transcript to clients and employees right after the meeting.  According to Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, did Fletcher most likely comply with the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, since Fletcher did not impact RMT's price.
new_option_c: Yes, since Harriet sent the transcript directly after the meeting.
new_explanation_en: Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires Members and Candidates to place clients' interests ahead of their own.  The Standard mandates that, for a given security, the firm's or employee's trades must be placed after client trades.  There is no specific waiting period, but firms must give clients a reasonable amount of time to act on recommendations. Sidney Fletcher violated the Standard by trading Responsive Market Tech, Inc. for the firm's account before PPG Investments' clients had time to act upon Kathy Harriet's advice.  Fletcher should have postponed trading until clients could reasonably have acted on Harriet's recommendation. (Choice B)  The resulting price after Fletcher's trade does not mitigate his violation.  Fletcher is not exempted from violating the Standard just for having no price impact. (Choice C)  Harriet complied by delivering the meeting transcript and her recommendation as soon as possible, but Fletcher should have placed the firm's trades after clients could reasonably be expected to receive and use the recommendation.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Rahul Agarwal, CFA, is the Chief Investment Officer of Bagh Capital.  He is having lunch with a group of prospective clients and passes out a summary of the company's performance.  The summary mentions that the firm was able to generate returns of 25% last year, 18% annualized over the past three years, and 15% annualized over the past five years. The returns exclude several portfolios that Bagh closed last year due to underperformance.  The summary does not mention the exclusions but notes that it is limited in nature and that a detailed presentation is available upon request.  By distributing this summary to clients, does Agarwal most likely violate Standard III(D) Performance Presentation?
new_option_b: Yes, by excluding the closed portfolios
new_option_c: Yes, by distributing only the summary and not the detailed presentation
new_explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that this information is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires Members and Candidates to provide a fair, accurate, and complete performance record. Misrepresenting performance is a violation of the Standard, whether it is in the measurement or presentation.  Providing a complete performance record entails including all pertinent portfolios or composites when calculating the performance of a firm. Rahul Agarwal violates the Standard by excluding terminated portfolios from the firm's performance and not making any note that they were excluded (Choice A).  By excluding terminated portfolios, Agarwal misrepresents Bagh Capital's performance and fails to provide the prospective clients with an accurate and complete picture of historical returns. (Choice C)  Distributing a summary of performance is allowed under the Standard.  Best practices call for summaries to include a note about the limited nature of the presentation.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Shreya Batra, CFA, is an equity analyst for S&K Financial (SKF).  SKF creates an online forum solely for its paying clients and encourages its analysts to post their research reports following public dissemination so clients can discuss the reports among themselves.  Batra recommends that her clients join the forum so they can take part in the discussions.  However, she warns each client that posts on the forum can be seen by any SFK client and that they should avoid posting confidential or sensitive information.  Following the release of a new report about Fox Property Group, Batra posts the report to SFK's forum.  One client posts, "This has really got me thinking.  I should invest in Fox when I sell my company next year.  We can discuss it during our meeting next month."  Batra knows the sale of the client's company is confidential and deletes the post as soon as she sees it, an hour after it was posted.  Has Batra most likely violated Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality?
new_option_b: No, since the client – not Batra – posted the information on the forum
new_option_c: No, since Batra provided adequate warning to clients about posting confidential information
