new_question_en: Sonja Hossi, CFA, recently started her own investment research firm, Hossi Investor Research (HIR).  Throughout her career, Hossi has been a well-known analyst in the paper industry.  The chief financial officer (CFO) of Metsa, a company in the pulp sector of the industry, contacts Hossi and asks her if HIR will publish a Metsa-prepared research report that recommends Metsa as a "buy"; HIR currently rates Metsa as a "hold."  The CFO offers to pay Hossi her standard flat fee to publish the report under her name.  After conducting her own due diligence, Hossi believes that the upgrade is appropriate.  She makes some minor changes to the report's wording, but otherwise publishes it "as is" with herself as author and recommending Metsa as a "buy."  She also discloses that she was paid by Metsa.  Has Hossi most likely violated Standard I(C) Misrepresentation?
new_option_b: Yes, by accepting her full fee to issue the report
new_option_c: Yes, by representing the research report as her original work
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation concerns actions that may undermine investor trust in the integrity of the profession and financial markets.  The Standard applies whether the information is prepared for clients, colleagues, or the public.  Misrepresentation can include: Plagiarism:  quoting information without acknowledgement or citation Omission:  presenting incomplete information or data in order to mislead Exaggeration:  inflating professional credentials or performance results Here, Hossi violates the Standard by claiming she authored the report (ie, plagiarism).  The slight changes in wording she made are not enough to make it her work.  Although the chief financial officer granted verbal permission to use the report, this does not absolve Hossi of the need to disclose the original source (Choice A). (Choice B)  There is nothing in the Standards that prevents Hossi from collecting her full fee for this assignment.  By collecting only a flat fee that was neither based on her recommendation nor tied to the client's future stock performance, and by disclosing who paid for the report, Hossi has followed the recommendations under Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Sarah Cohen, CFA, is a portfolio manager at Mountain Peak Capital (MPC) and manages the firm's multi-cap equity growth fund.  Cohen often directs the firm's trading desk to place orders through certain brokerage firms that have assisted her in idea generation or in investment decision- making.  Cohen has recently agreed to enter into a new soft dollar relationship with Large-Cap Capital (LCC) for research services. Cohen sends a large order for a thinly traded small-cap stock to the firm's trading desk.  Cohen usually prefers small-cap stock trades to be directed to Small-Cap Specialists, Inc. (SCSI), as they are better able to source liquidity (ie, find buyers and sellers) to fill these trades than most of their competitors.  The trader suggests the order be routed through LCC to help satisfy MPC's new soft dollar commitment.  LCC can execute the order, but it would likely be at market prices, and the large order size will almost certainly negatively affect the execution.  After discussing the situation with the firm's trader, Cohen instructs the trader to send the order to LCC.  Cohen most likely violates Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, by:
new_option_a: entering into a soft dollar arrangement.
new_option_b: failing to achieve best price and execution.
new_option_c: actively directing orders to specific brokerage firms.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' best interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires Members and Candidates to seek best price and best execution for client trades.  "Best price" and "best execution" do not necessarily mean the lowest trading commission, but commissions must be commensurate with the value received.  Examples of sell-side factors to consider for best price and execution include: Idea generation Research and analysis Overall execution price Commission paid Charterholders must be especially diligent in applying best price and execution standards when there are soft dollar arrangements.  Soft dollar brokerage is the practice of using a portion of brokerage commissions to pay for investment research.  Such research is considered an asset of the client, not the manager, and must be used to benefit the client. In this instance, Sarah Cohen should have directed the large order of thinly traded small-cap stock to the firm that could best execute the trade, which is SCSI.  She violated the Standard by failing to obtain best price and best execution for the express purpose of satisfying the firm's soft dollar commitment and not for the client's benefit. (Choice A)  Soft dollar brokerage is not prohibited by the Standards, but the manager has a duty of loyalty to use this asset for the exclusive benefit of the client. (Choice C)  Directing trading activity to firms that provide decision-making value to the manager is not prohibited by the Standards.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Vanessa Pinto, CFA, an analyst at Force One Securities, uses fundamental research data supplied by Force One when she considers updating her investment recommendation on the stock of Bear Equipment, Inc.  Pinto also uses other sources, including a local college library, respected investment commentary, and blogs from other research firms.  After weeks of detailed research, Pinto makes no changes to her investment recommendation on Bear Equipment.  According to Standard V(C) Record Retention, for which data must Pinto most likely keep appropriate records?
new_option_b: None, since her recommendation is unchanged
new_option_c: Data provided by Force One and all independent sources
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must develop and maintain appropriate records to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications with clients and prospective clients." To comply with Standard V(C), Members and Candidates must keep well-organized records that demonstrate the extent of their investigative efforts and the motives for their recommendations.  Analysts must preserve the data used in their investigations regardless of whether the research results in changes to previous recommendations.  Vanessa Pinto is required to save the data and records obtained from all sources, including her employer (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Margareta Schiffrin, CFA, is an investment adviser at a firm that advises high-net-worth clients and has adopted the CFA Institute's Code and Standards.  Schiffrin informs the firm's compliance director that she just attended the World Cup alpine ski finals as a guest of one of the firm's long-standing clients, who had been pleased with his portfolio's superior performance.  Regarding Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity, did Schiffrin most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, by accepting the gift
new_option_c: Yes, by reporting the gift after she accepted it
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity focuses on avoiding any actions that would compromise the independence and objectivity of an investment professional.  A member or candidate is prohibited from accepting or offering a compromise to independence and objectivity. Inducements to do so may come from many sources (eg, employers, vendors, or firms that are the subject of research).  They may take many forms (eg, offers of gifts, entertainment, donations, or employment-related compensation). Gifts from clients with established compensation arrangements are not prohibited (Choice B).  They are considered supplementary compensation and unlikely to threaten the independence and objectivity of the adviser. Gifts from clients must be reported so that the employer can assess whether independence may have been compromised or firm policies violated.  Such gifts should be reported before they are accepted, but they may be reported after acceptance without violating the Standard (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Tim Green, CFA, is an investment advisor for Steady Hand Advisors (SHA).  While attending a charity function, Green runs into one of his clients, Dr. Walter Kowalski.  Kowalski tells Green about a small-cap biotechnology company developing a new process that could be a medical breakthrough.  Green says he is familiar with the company but considers its stock to be very speculative since the company has never been profitable or even produced a viable product. Nevertheless, Kowalski instructs Green to buy 10,000 shares of the stock when the market opens the next day.  Green advises against the trade: although an investment of this size will have an immaterial impact on Kowalski's portfolio, it does not meet his investment objectives and violates the constraints of his investment policy statement (IPS).  Still, Kowalski insists that Green execute the trade. The next morning, Green documents his rationale for why the trade is unsuitable on SHA's unsolicited trade request form.  Green emails the form to Kowalski to sign and return so the trade can be executed at the market open.  Do Green's actions comply with Standard III(C) Suitability?
new_option_b: No, the investment is unsuitable regardless of portfolio impact.
new_option_c: No, since Green is required update the investment policy statement.
new_explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must:… b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. c. Judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio.…" Standard III(C) Suitability addresses the adviser's responsibility to assess the suitability of investments for each client.  The adviser does this by researching a client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance, which together form the building blocks of the client's investment policy statement (IPS).  The IPS can be used to determine the suitability of proposed investments. Clients and advisors may disagree regarding investment suitability.  Best practices regarding unsolicited requests for unsuitable investments include: Refrain from making the trade until discussing it with the client. Educate the client regarding divergence from the IPS. Consider the trade's potential impact within the context of the client's entire portfolio. Be sure the client acknowledges being advised that the trade is unsuitable. Update the IPS if the trade is executed and its portfolio impact is material. In extreme cases, determine whether to continue the advisory relationship. In this scenario, Tim Green complies with the Standard since he: discusses the trade with the client, educates the client regarding the trade's conflict with the IPS, considers the trade's immaterial portfolio impact (Choice B), and has the client sign the unsolicited trade request form before the trade is executed. (Choice C)  Obtaining the client's acknowledgment of the discussion is a best practice, but the Standard does not require updating the IPS unless the trade has a material portfolio impact.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Stephanie Chang, CFA, is a financial advisor to individual clients for SMF Investments (SMF).  She also manages the account of her father, who is a client of SMF.  SMF secures a portion of shares for the oversubscribed initial public offering (IPO) of Trek Corp and assigns the IPO shares to its financial advisors to allocate to their clients' portfolios.  After reviewing Trek's suitability for her clients' portfolios, Chang concludes that she would allocate 2,500 shares to her clients, including 100 to her father.  She also likes Trek for her personal portfolio and wants to allocate 300 shares for herself.  However, she receives only 2,000 shares of Trek from SMF.  To avoid violating Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, Chang should most likely allocate IPO shares to her nonfamilial clients:
new_option_a: and herself, but not her father.
new_option_b: and her father, but not herself.
new_option_c: but not to herself or her father.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities." Standard III(B) Fair Dealing specifies that Members and Candidates must treat all clients fairly.  Investment actions must be taken based on each client's individual investment objectives and circumstances. When allocating shares of initial public offerings (IPOs), Members and Candidates should distribute the shares to all clients for which the offering is suitable.  If an IPO is oversubscribed, best practices dictate that the allocated shares be prorated for all applicable clients.  This includes family members who are clients.  Further, when issues are oversubscribed, managers should forgo any shares for themselves or family members who are not clients in order to provide as many shares to clients as possible. To comply with Standard III(B), since Stephanie Chang receives fewer Trek Corp shares from SMF Investments than planned, she should allocate shares only to her SMF clients and not to herself.  Since Chang's father is an SMF client, he should not be treated any differently than other SMF clients despite being family and should receive shares.  However, since Chang did not receive enough shares to fulfill her request for clients' portfolios, she should not keep any shares for herself (Choices A and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Gareth Irwin, CFA, recently retired after 30 years as a portfolio manager with a large asset-management firm.  Irwin is interested in obtaining freelance investment consulting engagements and creates a biography that lists his accomplishments.  Two entries in the biography are: Entry 1:  "As a CFA Charterholder for over 30 years, I have consistently achieved above-market returns" Entry 2:  "I am a retired CFA Charterholder." Irwin has sent a check to CFA Institute to pay for the upcoming year's membership dues.  He indicates on the check that he is paying as a "retired Charterholder" but has not completed any other membership paperwork. Based only on this information, which of the following concerning Irwin's biography most likely complies with Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA designation, and the CFA Program?
new_option_b: Only Entry 2
new_option_c: Neither Entry 1 nor Entry 2
new_explanation_en: When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program. Standard VII(B) addresses how Members and Candidates can use the CFA designation in written communications, which include Irwin's biography.  The Standard applies to both active and retired Members. Gareth Irwin can refer to himself as a retired Charterholder in his biography only if he is still a member of CFA Institute.  Membership requires that he pay the annual membership dues and complete the Professional Conduct Statement Agreement.  He has not submitted anything other than his dues payment.  Therefore, he cannot use the CFA designation in any capacity until he completes the Professional Conduct Statement and CFA Institute accepts it (Choice B). Standard VII(B) also governs how a Member or Candidate can use the CFA designation.  A Member can state facts but cannot misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning of being a Charterholder.  In this question, Irwin states that he achieved "above-market returns" but offers neither context (eg, how he defines the market) nor quantitative evidence to support the claim.  As such, Irwin's statement is not a statement of fact; using it in the biography misrepresents the meaning of the designation (Choice A).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Grace Chang, CFA, keeps two social media accounts: one for personal use and one firm-approved business account used for client engagement, which is monitored by her employer, Canyon Investments.  After three years at Canyon, during which Chang has connected with all her clients through her business account, Chang decides to leave Canyon for LVL Bank.  Canyon asks Chang to delete the business account before leaving.  However, Chang confirms that she has not signed a noncompete agreement with Canyon and, upon starting at LVL, Chang updates her business account to reflect her new employer and continues to maintain both accounts.  Has Chang most likely violated Standard IV(A) Loyalty?
new_option_b: No, since she did not sign a noncompete agreement with Canyon.
new_option_c: No, since all social media accounts operated by Chang are her property.
new_explanation_en: "In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer." Standard IV(A) Loyalty requires Members and Candidates to protect the interests of their employer.  This includes acting for the benefit of the employer even when one is planning to leave and refraining from taking property of that firm upon leaving unless given permission to do so. Social media accounts that are created solely for business use and contact with clients are considered property of the firm and should be treated similarly to other firm property (Choice C).  When leaving an employer, Members and Candidates should follow their firm's policies and procedures and transfer or delete the accounts if so directed.  When social media accounts include both personal contacts and clients, the Member or Candidate should discuss with the firm how those profiles should be treated. In this scenario, Chang created a social media account solely for client engagement.  Since this social media account is used solely for business, it is considered the property of Canyon Investments.  Even though Chang did not sign a noncompete agreement with Canyon, Chang must comply with the firm's request regarding its property.  Failure to delete the account disregards the firm's request and is a violation of the Standard (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Xu Liang, CFA, is an equity portfolio manager of a large mutual fund.  Liang's fund primarily invests in large-cap, dividend-paying stocks that tend to be less volatile than the broad equity market. Bernard Gerhardt is Liang's primary contact and salesperson at Trusted Brokers.  Liang's firm is Trusted Brokers' largest client, and Liang's fund generates significant commission business.  Gerhardt approaches Liang regarding a private placement in Smart AI, an artificial intelligence software company.  During their conversation, Gerhardt comments that "I know you don't normally buy these things for the mutual fund, but Smart AI is priced so cheap that it could easily double in just a few months!  You should consider investing personally." Liang conducts thorough due diligence and believes Smart AI is a great investment opportunity but not a good fit for the fund since it does not align with the fund's mandate and risk profile.  Therefore, Liang decides to personally invest in the private placement.  According to Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, Liang most likely:
new_option_a: violated the Standard by personally investing in the private placement.
new_option_b: did not violate the Standard since the investment was inappropriate for the fund.
new_option_c: did not violate the Standard since the fund was given the opportunity to invest first.
new_explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires Members and Candidates to place clients' and employers' financial interests before their own when conducting investment transactions and to avoid even the appearance of conflicts of interest.  A Member or Candidate's participation in private placements and initial public offerings (IPOs) requires an especially high standard of care. The potential for conflicts of interest is more significant for investment personnel at large investment firms.  Investment personnel (eg, Liang) may be offered special enticements, such as access to private placements or IPOs, as payback for doing business (eg, largest client) with the broker (eg, Trusted Brokers) offering the securities. Another concern is that once the private placement goes public, there is an incentive for the Member or Candidate who bought into the private placement and holds the now-public company's stock to offer and/or buy the securities for clients (or, in this case, for the fund) whether suitable or not. Participation in private placements should be strictly limited to special situations in which there is no potential for even the appearance of conflicts of interest.  Therefore, Liang violated the Standard by involving himself in a situation that potentially had the appearance of impropriety. (Choices B and C)  Liang appropriately considered the investment for the fund first and found it unsuitable.  However, this is not where the violation occurred.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Apurva Basu, CFA, is a highly respected analyst covering the mining industry for South India Investments (SII).  She has a list of 12 "star" clients who pay an extra fee for greater access to Basu and the other analysts at SII.  This service is disclosed and offered to all clients.  After sending her latest research report to all of her clients, Basu immediately calls the 12 on the list to discuss the report's conclusions in more detail. In regard to Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, based on Basu's research process, does she most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, by favoring one set of clients over others.
new_option_c: Yes, by not confirming that all her clients received the report before calling the "star" clients.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities." Standard III(B) Fair Dealing focuses on the responsibility of members and candidates to treat all clients fairly, specifically when disseminating investment recommendations and taking investment actions.  However, "fairly" does not mean "equally" since it is not possible to ensure that each client will receive investment recommendations at the same time.  Nor does each client have the same investment goals. Members and candidates must ensure each investment recommendation is disseminated in a way that provides all clients the ability to act on the recommendation.  The Standard allows firms to offer different levels of service to clients willing to pay a premium if those services: do not disadvantage or negatively affect other clients and the services are disclosed and available to all clients and prospective clients. In this scenario, since Basu disseminates her research report fairly to all clients before calling the "star" clients, and since her calls do not negatively impact the other clients, she does not violate the Standard (Choice B). (Choice C)  Basu is required by the Standard to ensure that her recommendations are disseminated fairly, but she is not required to wait for all of her clients to confirm that they received the report.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Giada Rossi, CFA, is a sell-side analyst at Hickory Capital, an integrated investment firm that offers trading, research, and investment banking services.  Rossi has covered Turtle Shell, Inc. (TSI) for several years and currently has a buy rating on the stock.  TSI has appreciated significantly in the past six months and is substantially above Rossi's price target.  Rossi prepares a research report downgrading TSI based on valuation, unaware that Hickory's investment banking group is preparing a secondary offering of TSI common stock. Hickory's head of investment banking, Peter Johnson, CFA, is concerned that a downgrade would be detrimental to the secondary offering and might cause Hickory to be left out of the deal.  Before Rossi disseminates her report, Johnson puts TSI on the firm's restricted list of investment banking clients and instructs Rossi to publish only factual news and corporate developments related to TSI.  Rossi agrees.  Has Rossi or Johnson most likely violated Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity?
new_option_b: Yes, Rossi violated the Standard by not properly disseminating her honest opinion.
new_option_c: Yes, Johnson violated the Standard by instructing Rossi to compromise her independence.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity mandates that Members and Candidates who are investment professionals avoid actions that compromise their independence and objectivity or create conflicts of interest.  Investment banking relationships often create conflict for sell- side firms since the firms may pressure analysts to provide favorable research reports for investment banking clients.  To minimize potential information sharing and conflicts of interest, firms should create firewalls between analysts and investment bankers. Firms are recommended to maintain a restricted list of investment banking clients and report only factual information, without analysts' opinions, for those companies.  If a firm's investment banking client is not on the restricted list and the firm will not disseminate unfavorable opinions, the firm should add the client to the list to maintain independence and objectivity. In this scenario, Giada Rossi does not violate the Standard since the firm restricted her ability to disseminate any investment opinion regarding Turtle Shell, Inc., in compliance with recommended practice (Choice B).  Peter Johnson does not violate the Standard since he added TSI to the restricted list, also in compliance with recommended practice (Choice C).  Therefore, the firm should publish only factual news and corporate developments related to TSI.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Shreya Bhatt, CFA, is an independent financial advisor who wants to grow her client base.  At a dinner with several prospective clients, she states, "The knowledge and skills I have gained in the CFA program have enhanced my abilities in portfolio management.  The rigor and intensity of the exams have trained me to work hard for my clients.  As a CFA charterholder, I am best qualified to manage your money.  My results speak for themselves.  My clients have achieved an annualized rate of return of 10% over the past ten years, compared with 6% for my benchmark." Assuming her return figures are accurate, has Bhatt violated Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program?
new_option_b: No, since her statements are backed by facts.
new_option_c: No, since her statements were made verbally.
new_explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program forbids Members and Candidates from exaggerating the meaning or implication of their CFA charters.  This includes overstating one's competency or ability to achieve superior performance.  Although other Standards prohibit Members and Candidates from generally promising the achievement of superior returns, Standard VII(B) specifies that these claims cannot be attributable to the CFA designation. Stating objective facts about the benefits of achieving the CFA designation or the intensity and rigor of the CFA program is allowed.  This includes statements about knowledge and skills gained.  However, such statements do not justify using the CFA designation to declare superior competency as an investment professional.  Shreya Bhatt violates the Standard by stating, "As a CFA charterholder, I am best qualified to manage your money" (Choice B).  Although her return figures are factual, she exaggerates the meaning of the CFA designation. (Choice C)  The Standard applies to any form of communication (eg, written, verbal).  It also applies to any audience (eg, employers, prospective clients, the public).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Rashid Miah, CFA, negotiates with his employer, Tenor Capital, to work only part-time as a financial advisor while finishing a graduate degree, with the understanding that he will return to full-time work after graduation.  After graduating, Miah remains employed part-time since Tenor does not have enough clients, and keeps him at a part-time status until more clients are obtained.  Miah looks for ways to increase his income and arranges to advise friends and family on investment decisions for a fee when not working for Tenor.  He also plans to work as a driver for a ridesharing company on weekends, when Tenor is closed.  To comply with Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Agreements, Miah should obtain written permission from Tenor before pursuing:
new_option_b: both the investment advisory and the ridesharing.
new_option_c: neither the investment advisory nor the ridesharing.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) addresses compensation arrangements from third parties that can challenge loyalty to an employer by competing with and/or creating a conflict with the employer's interests.  A Member or Candidate should receive written consent from all parties involved for any such compensation. In this scenario, Miah's investment advisory for friends and family can be reasonably seen as competing with Tenor's business, since Miah would be doing the same type of work that he currently does for Tenor.  Therefore, Miah needs to obtain written permission from Tenor and from his friends and family before he starts advising (Choice C).  The ridesharing role does not compete directly with Tenor's business, so Miah does not need to obtain written permission for this arrangement (Choice B). Standard IV(B) recommends that Members and Candidates make a written report to their employer detailing the compensation from any third- party sources before engaging in such activities.  However, obtaining written permission is only required before entering into arrangements that could be seen as competing or creating conflicts of interest.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Olga Ivanova, CFA, plans to leave her employer, Vector Advisors LLC ("Vector"), since they allow advisors to invest only in traditional assets. Ivanova plans to start her own investment advisory business where she can take riskier strategies.  She has not signed a noncompete agreement with Vector.  Before she leaves Vector, Ivanova: Searches for office space, on weekends, for the new company, Completes forms and begins the process to get the new company registered, and Calls Sergey Aslanov, her golf partner, to convince him to be her first client. Ivanova recently solicited Aslanov's business on behalf of Vector, but to date Aslanov has remained undecided about whether he will become a client.  Has Ivanova most likely violated Standard IV(A) Loyalty?
new_option_b: Yes, by contacting a prospective Vector client before leaving.
new_option_c: Yes, by preparing for her business on weekends before leaving Vector.
new_explanation_en: "In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer." Standard IV(A) Loyalty prohibits Members and Candidates from acting in ways that would harm their employer or deprive it of their skills and abilities.  When planning to leave an employer, Members and Candidates must continue to act in their employer's best interest.  This includes not contacting the firm's clients and prospective clients with the purpose of soliciting business for their own independent business or a new employer. In this scenario, Ivanova calls Aslanov before she leaves the firm to solicit his business for her independent advisory business.  Although Aslanov has not agreed to join Vector, Ivanova recently solicited his business on behalf of Vector, and he has not yet decided whether to become a client of the firm.  As such, he remains a prospective client for Vector, and Ivanova violates the Standard by soliciting his business for her independent practice (Choice A). (Choice C)  The Standard allows Ivanova to prepare her new business before leaving her current employer so long as preparation is done on her own time.  Since she works on her independent business on weekends, doing so does not violate the Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Bo Shun Zheng, CFA, is a journalist who writes articles on market sentiment for a major news organization.  She uses various sources, including social media, analyst interviews, and more conventionally published research.  In one article, she reproduces research published on social media by an analyst known only as "Big Alpha."  Since she does not know Big Alpha's real name, she includes the research without citation, noting only that it has been endorsed by "a leading investment expert."  Regarding Standard I(C) Misrepresentation, does Zheng most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_a: Yes, by not citing the source of the research.
new_option_b: Yes, by using research available only on social media.
new_option_c: No, because she protects Big Alpha's choice to hide his true identity.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation focuses on knowingly misrepresenting or misusing information, and as a result, undermining investor trust in the integrity of the profession and financial markets.  The standard applies whether information is prepared for clients, colleagues, or the public —and whether it is a verbal or published statement. Misrepresentation can consist of omission: not presenting complete information or data in order to mislead plagiarism: quoting information without acknowledgement or citation exaggeration: inflating professional credentials or performance results In this scenario, Zheng violates the standard in two ways.  First, by not citing the source of the research and by reproducing it as though it were her own, she engages in plagiarism.  Although she does not know the author's full name, she should not mislead her readers as to the information's source.  Second, she exaggerates the validity of the research by stating that it is endorsed by an "expert" when she does not know that to be the case. (Choice B)  Using research available on social media is not a violation of the Standard; social media is a legitimate outlet for information.  As with all sources, material from social media should be properly cited. (Choice C)  Although Zheng does not know the real name of the source of the research since the author chose not to share it, she should not reproduce the research without attribution.  Since she omits any citation, it is plagiarism.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Chen Hong, CFA, is an independent investment advisor.  Through a referral from an existing client, Chen contacts Zhao Qiuping.  Chen briefly meets with Zhao, who is leaving for vacation the next day.  Zhao agrees to be Chen's client and sends him money that is currently in her savings account.  They are not able to discuss the details of Zhao's financial circumstances and objectives at the meeting, but Zhao tells Chen that he can invest the money however he sees fit and agrees that they will meet again to create a detailed investment policy statement when Zhao returns. Chen invests a portion of Zhao's funds in several stocks of companies that Chen has invested in other clients' funds, since Chen believes the stock prices will increase and Chen does not want Zhao to miss out.  By the time Zhao returns, her investment portfolio is up 4%.  With regards to Zhao's investments, Chen:
new_option_a: was in full compliance with the Standards.
new_option_b: violated the Standards by not getting approval from Zhao for each investment.
new_option_c: violated the Standards by investing Zhao's funds before gathering appropriate information.
new_explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must:… a. Make a reasonable inquiry into a client's or prospective client's investment experience, risk and return objectives, and financial constraints prior to making any investment recommendation or taking investment action and must reassess and update this information regularly. b. Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action." Standard III(C) Suitability requires Members and Candidates that are advisors to properly assess the suitability of each potential investment for each client before making investment decisions.  To do this, an advisor must first gather information on each client's specific investment goals, constraints, and risk tolerance.  This information is used to develop an investment policy statement (IPS), which is then used to develop an appropriate investment program for the client. Without gathering and understanding the appropriate information, an advisor has no way of knowing if specific investments meet criteria for suitability for the client.  Therefore, investing a client's assets before gathering appropriate information violates the Standard.  In this scenario, Chen invests Zhao's assets before getting information on Zhao's financial circumstances and objectives.  Even though Zhao said to invest her assets however Chen saw fit, Chen had no way to know if the investments were suitable for Zhao.  Therefore, Chen violated the Standards (Choice A). (Choice B)  Members and Candidates do not need client approval for every specific investment to adhere to the Standard.  Once the IPS is created, the advisors can invest within the confines of the IPS without approval for each investment.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Christine Hansen, CFA, works as an investment advisor at a large regional bank.  Many of Hansen's larger clients can benefit from comprehensive estate planning, including the need for various trusts and insurance policies.  For the trust work, Hansen refers these clients to an outside law firm, and for their insurance needs, she refers them to the bank's internal insurance subsidiary.  Hansen receives a one-time $100 bonus for every insurance policy sold by the subsidiary on her referral.  The law firm is a corporate sponsor of the local professional basketball team and gives Hansen two courtside tickets for each referral.  With regard to Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, Hansen is required to disclose:
new_option_b: only the internal referral arrangement.
new_option_c: only the external referral arrangement.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services." Standard VI(C) Referral Fees requires members and candidates to notify employers and clients if they receive any benefit for recommending a product or service.  Such benefits can create a conflict of interest, so disclosing the potential conflict allows affected parties to determine whether the recommendation is impartial.  The Standard refers to "any compensation," so the size of the fee that Hansen receives is irrelevant.  She is required by the Standard to disclose both arrangements to her clients when making the referrals. (Choice B)  The outside referral arrangement is a form of noncash compensation and must also be disclosed to comply with the Standard. (Choice C)  The fact that a client being referred to the internal subsidiary is an existing client of the firm does not affect the need for full disclosure of the fee arrangement.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Liu Tengfei, CFA, manages a set of client portfolios.  Several of his portfolios are underperforming for the quarter.  Liu's boss tells him that Golden Peak, a pharmaceutical company, has a drug that is expected to receive regulatory approval soon, and the approval is likely to increase the price of the stock.  After analyzing Golden Peak's financials, Liu purchases Golden Peak stock for only his underperforming portfolios.  Two weeks later, the drug receives regulatory approval and the stock increases 35%.  Has Liu most likely violated Standard III(C) Suitability?
new_option_b: No, since Golden Peak's stock increased in value
new_option_c: No, since he allocated Golden Peak to only underperforming client portfolios
new_explanation_en: When Members and Candidates are in an advisory relationship with a client, they must: … b.  Determine that an investment is suitable to the client's financial situation and consistent with the client's written objectives, mandates, and constraints before making an investment recommendation or taking investment action. Standard III(C) Suitability addresses a Member's or Candidate's responsibilities in evaluating the appropriateness of every investment for each client.  A manager creates and maintains an investment policy statement for each client based on the client's goals, risk tolerance, and constraints.  The adviser should consider an individual client's situation before making an investment decision for the client. In this scenario, Liu violates the Standard by purchasing Golden Peak for clients based solely on the performance of their portfolios.  Liu must weigh the suitability of the stock's risk and return characteristics for each client's portfolio before making any purchases. (Choice B)  The increase in Golden Peak's stock price does not excuse Liu from evaluating the investment against each of his clients' investment parameters before making the investment decisions. (Choice C)  Liu conducts due diligence in regard to Golden Peak's financials, but he fails to evaluate the suitability of the investment for his clients.  Golden Peak's risk and return characteristics may not be suitable for each client with an underperforming portfolio, and they may be suitable for other clients' portfolios.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Ashton Griffiths, CFA, a world-renowned investor, is an adviser at TenSteps Investments.  On a popular podcast, Griffiths publicly recommends purchasing shares of Allthrift, a large online bank.  At Griffiths' direction, TenSteps has held Allthrift for over 7 years for clients and Griffiths is still confident that it is an excellent investment.  The next day, TenSteps buys 100,000 shares for clients.  After the trade, Allthrift price declines 2%. Two weeks later, after receiving preclearance, Griffiths sells 10,000 shares of Allthrift from his private account for tax purposes and to purchase a second home.  According to Standard VI(B) Priority of Transaction, does Griffith most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, by purchasing Allthrift for clients.
new_option_c: Yes, by selling Allthrift after recommending its purchase.
new_explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) requires Members and Candidates to put clients' interests ahead of their own.  This means clients should be financially unharmed by a Member's personal trades.  To comply with the Standard, for a given security, client trades should be placed before nonclient (eg, employee) trades.  If employees trade the same security before clients, employees may negatively impact the security's price (eg, higher prices for buys, lower prices for sells) for clients. The Standard allows Members and Candidate to make personal trades if they: Do not harm clients from their trades Do not receive an economic benefit from client trades Adhere to governing laws and regulations Even if the action contradicts previous investment recommendations (ie, selling after recommending a buy), investment professionals may invest according to their personal needs.  Ashton Griffiths publicly makes a recommendation, promptly makes purchases for clients, and sells after receiving preclearance.  He does not violate the Standard by selling Allthrift since clients are not harmed, he does not benefit from client trades, and he fulfills his regulatory obligations (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Meng Bo, CFA, is a research analyst for Grant Capital.  She currently has a hold rating on Spire Data Center Investments (SDCI).  SDCI is considering a secondary public offering.  Meng is approached by Hao Liang, an investment banker for Grant who is trying to win SDCI's business for its offering.  Hao tells Meng, "We'll have a better chance of winning SDCI's offering if we have a buy rating on them.  Can you take another look and see if you can upgrade them?" Meng reviews SDCI's business again and does not see any change to her base case, which she views as the most likely outcome.  However, Meng believes that, in a best-case scenario, SDCI could outperform its peers and be worthy of a buy rating.  She still views the best-case scenario as unlikely, but its probability increases with the funds from the secondary offering.  Meng writes a new report with a buy rating, stating that she expects SDCI to achieve its best-case scenario and outperform peers, and sends it to clients.  Has Meng most likely violated Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis?
new_option_b: No, since the new rating is backed by her best-case scenario
new_option_c: No, since she thoroughly reviewed SDCI's business before changing the rating
