pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Kyle Trainor, CFA, publishes a popular investing newsletter.  In the most recent edition he recommends that subscribers buy Ambit Holdings (AHC).  Trainor has owned AHC for many years and would like to sell it, but he believes that AHC is undervalued at its current price of $25 per share.  His recommendation is based on interviews with AHC's executives as well as his own independent research, and he believes that AHC's price will double when it releases its year-end earnings next month.  He includes a few details of his research, using phrases such as "I have heard that earnings will be very strong" and "Many people think that this stock will SOAR."  He also discloses his ownership of AHC stock.  Based on his recommendation, many subscribers buy AHC stock, which causes the price to rise.  Before AHC releases its year-end earnings, Trainor sells his entire AHC position at a price of $45 per share.  After AHC releases its earnings report, its price continues to rise, peaking at $64 per share before declining.  Did Trainor most likely violate Standard II(B) Market Manipulation?
new_option_b: Yes, since his recommendation was premised on opinion, not fact.
new_option_c: Yes, since he benefitted from the price increase caused by his recommendation.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants." Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits activities by members or candidates that distort securities prices.  Manipulation can occur through information-based activities, such as spreading false rumors, or transaction-based activities, such as exaggerated trading between two accounts. However, a key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is that the Member or Candidate must intend to deceive other market participants.  The Guidance emphasizes that intent is critical; there is no violation of the Standard without it.  Intent in each case must be inferred from relevant facts and circumstances. Here, no market manipulation occurred, as Trainor had no intent to deceive.  His recommendation was based on research from different sources, and while some of it could be characterized as rumor (eg, he heard that earnings would be "very strong"), he also offered details of the research, as well as disclosing his ownership in Ambit.  Since he engaged in no manipulative conduct, it is irrelevant that he benefitted from his recommendation (Choice C). (Choice B)  Trainor's recommendation was based on a combination of variables.  He formed an opinion based on a reasonable interpretation of those variables.  Nothing suggests any intent by Trainor to deceive his subscribers, which would have been the case had he based it on falsity or unsupportable conjecture.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Reem Gamal, CFA, is the owner of Osiris Partners.  She is working on the marketing pitch that she will give to the trustees of Horus University to have Osiris manage its endowment fund.  As part of her pitch, she plans to say: I: "Since Osiris hires only CFA charterholders, we are among the elite asset management firms, as proven by our performance: Our returns have outperformed the overall market in 9 of the past 10 years." II: "By passing such an intense and comprehensive study program, each of our analysts have enhanced their knowledge in portfolio management, including endowments." Which of the statements would most likely violate the Standards?
new_option_b: Only Statement II
new_option_c: Both Statement I and II
new_explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program forbids Members and Candidates from exaggerating the meaning or implication of having a CFA charter.  This includes overstating competency or the ability to achieve superior investment performance. Although Standard I(C) focuses generally on promises related to investment guarantees or ability to achieve superior returns, Standard VII(B) specifies that these claims cannot be attributable to the CFA designation.  However, statements of objective fact about the benefits (eg, knowledge and skills gained, credibility) of the CFA designation and the rigor of the program are allowed. In this question, Gamal's first statement violates the Standard by asserting that Osiris Partners is an elite asset management firm since the firm hires only CFA charterholders; by doing so, she attributes elite status to the charter.  Even though the statement compares the firm's performance against the market, the statement is still a violation since it implies superior performance can be expected going forward.  Gamal's second statement does not violate the Standard since it states only facts about the intensity of the exam and skills and knowledge earned (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Sumit Ahuja, CFA, is an investor with limited knowledge of the biotech industry.  Through an expert network, he calls a physician at a prestigious hospital regarding broad trends in the biotech industry.  The physician names several companies that have high-profile drugs in the final stages of the government's publicly disclosed approval process.  One of the companies is Orion Pharmaceuticals.  After the call, as part of his thorough research on Orion, Ahuja purchases a newly released research report from Vijaya Dayal, a respected biotech analyst who covers Orion. In her report, Dayal states that Orion's drug is likely to receive regulatory approval, based on her own opinion from thorough research.  As a result, Ahuja purchases stock in Orion.  Ahuja:
new_option_a: was in full compliance of the Standards.
new_option_b: violated the Standards by trading based on information received from the expert network.
new_option_c: violated the Standards by trading based on a research report that was not disseminated to the general public.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) requires Members and Candidates to abstain from investment actions if they have material nonpublic information (MNI).  Trading based on MNI erodes trust in the fairness of the capital markets and the investing profession by perpetuating the idea that insiders take deceitful advantage of the investing public.  MNI can come from many sources, including company management and expert networks.  A Member or Candidate must evaluate the information itself to decide whether it is MNI before acting on it. In this question, the physician whom Sumit Ahuja calls through an expert network provides information on broad industry trends, which is nonmaterial since it is not company specific.  The physician also provides the names of companies with drugs in the final stages of the government approval process, which is public information.  Therefore, Ahuja did not receive MNI through the expert network and did not violate the Standard by acting on it (Choice B). Although research reports from sell-side analysts, even those based on opinions, can be material and nonpublic, trading based on these reports does not violate the Standard if any investor can purchase them.  Such availability means that a report is public even if not publicly disseminated. Since the report Ahuja purchased from Vijaya Dayal is available to all investors, Ahuja did not violate the Standard by acting on it (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Trevor Collins, CFA, is a financial adviser for Starlight Advisory.  Some of his clients require additional services outside his expertise.  Collins refers clients who need life insurance to another department at Starlight.  The life insurance department gives Collins 10% of each client's initial life insurance payment as a referral fee.  Collins does not disclose this arrangement to clients since the referral is internal to his company.  Collins refers clients who need advanced tax services to Accounting Hub, a third-party accounting firm.  For every 10 referrals, Accounting Hub invites Collins to join the firm's managers in their corporate box for a professional football game.  Collins discloses to clients that he has a referral agreement with Accounting Hub but does not disclose the details.  Collins most likely violated the Standards with respect to:
new_option_a: only the internal life insurance referral.
new_option_b: only the third-party advanced tax services referral.
new_option_c: both the internal life insurance and third-party advanced tax services referrals.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services." Standard VI(C) Referral Fees requires Members and Candidates to notify their employers, existing clients, and prospective clients of any benefit they receive for recommending a product or service.  Disclosing referral arrangements allows employers and clients to determine if conflicts of interest exist and whether a recommendation is impartial.  A referral fee is broadly defined and includes any cash or noncash rewards. In this question, Trevor Collins violates the Standard for both referrals since the Standard stipulates that all referral agreements must be disclosed.  The referral for life insurance must be disclosed to clients since the referral fee can cause a conflict of interest for Collins whether it comes from an internal or external source (Choice B).  The referral for advanced tax services must be disclosed to clients with full details so clients can make informed judgments; it is not enough to simply disclose the existence of an agreement (Choice A).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Juan Castillo, CFA, is director of research at State Pension Fund (SPF).  SPF invests exclusively through subadvisors to construct the pension's portfolio.  While preparing for SPF's annual strategy session, Castillo contacts Macro Trade Research Advisors (MTRA) to get its latest research and views on the financial markets. MTRA has a correspondent brokerage relationship with Johnson Brothers Brokerage (JBB) in which JBB directs 50% of commissions to MTRA. Castillo instructs several subadvisors to send trades to JBB to pay for MTRA's research services.  Do Castillo's actions most likely comply with Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care?
new_option_b: No, since Castillo cannot direct other firms' trades.
new_option_c: No, since Castillo uses pension fund assets to pay for research services.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." A client practices directed brokerage by directing brokerage commissions for the purchase of goods or services that aid the beneficiaries of the client's account.  This practice is common among plan sponsors who outsource the responsibility of day-to-day investment decisions to subadvisors and do not directly generate commissions themselves. Trading commissions are considered an asset of the client—in this scenario, State Pension Fund (SPF), represented by Juan Castillo—not the subadvisor.  The client has the right to make beneficial use of that asset, and the subadvisor has a duty of loyalty to use the asset for the benefit of the client if so requested. Castillo, on behalf of SPF (ie, the client), instructs several subadvisors to direct trade commissions (ie, the asset) to Johnson Brothers Brokerage to pay for Macro Trade Research Advisors' research services.  Castillo complies with Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care by using directed brokerage to pay for investment research related directly to SPF's investment decisions and to SPF's benefit. (Choices B and C)  Castillo does not misuse his position or violate his duty of loyalty to the pension fund.  Since trading commissions are assets of the client, it is appropriate to sometimes request that those assets be used to acquire research services (ie, direct subadvisor trades) for the benefit of the client (ie, the pension plan).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Duane Wolfe, CFA, is a well-regarded equities analyst.  Advisors in his firm routinely forward his reports and other communications to their clients.  Wolfe covers a company called Western Aerospace, a major military contractor.  Western Aerospace is rumored to be close to signing a significant government contract and based on the rumors its stock price has steadily increased.  The company confirms only that contract talks are ongoing.  Many clients of Wolfe's firm own Western Aerospace stock. At a restaurant after work, Wolfe overhears two individuals he does not know talking about Western Aerospace's contract negotiations and implying that the deal will fall through.  Wolfe immediately calls a source at Western Aerospace, but the source neither confirms nor denies what Wolfe overheard. The next morning, Wolfe sends an email to the firm's client advisors that says, "Heads up: I may have information that could significantly affect Western Aerospace's stock price."  He provides no further details.  Several client advisors forward the email to their clients, many of whom interpret it to mean that the contract will not happen and therefore sell their stock.  Later that day, Western Aerospace announces that there will be no government contract, and its stock price declines significantly. Has Wolfe most likely violated Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information?
new_option_b: No, since the information Wolfe overheard was unreliable.
new_option_c: No, since Wolfe did not know that his email would cause clients to sell their stock.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from acting on or causing others to act on information that is both material and nonpublic.  The Standard applies only if both elements are present. Information is nonpublic if it is not available to the investing public in general.  In this scenario, Western Aerospace initially provides no information about the contract except to confirm that it is negotiating with the government.  It does not announce that the negotiations failed until after Duane Wolfe sent his email.  Therefore, prior to the announcement, information concerning the contract's status, including what Wolfe overheard, is nonpublic. Information is material if: a reasonable investor would consider it important to know before making an investment decision or the information would likely impact the stock price. With respect to materiality, information's reliability must be considered.  Wolfe cannot assess the veracity of what he overheard since he does not know the speakers.  In addition, his source at Western Aerospace cannot confirm what he overheard.  Therefore, the overheard conversation is unreliable, rendering the information immaterial (Choice A).  Although Wolfe may have violated Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis by sending his email, he did not violate Standard II(A). (Choice C)  Given Wolfe's stature as an analyst, it is reasonable to conclude that his email caused clients to act.  Had the email been based on material nonpublic information, Wolfe would have violated Standard II(A).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Emilia Cosgrove, CFA, is considering a job offer to work as an analyst for Juniper Securities.  It is the only offer she has received after five months of searching for employment.  Manuel Griggs, Cosgrove's close friend, was hired by Juniper six months ago and currently works there as an analyst.  In confidence, Cosgrove shares her offer with Griggs, who in turn shares his salary.  Griggs is paid 30% more than the salary offered to Cosgrove.  Cosgrove negotiates for higher compensation, but Juniper stands by its original offer.  She accepts the offer and begins working for Juniper.  Whenever she travels on assignments for Juniper, she requests reimbursement for amounts that exceed her actual expenses.  According to Standard I(D) Misconduct, do Griggs and/or Cosgrove most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, Cosgrove violates the Standard by compromising her integrity.
new_option_c: Yes, Cosgrove and Griggs violate the Standard by sharing salary information.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence." Members and Candidates must comply with Standard I(D) by abstaining from behaviors that diminish the individual's, firm's, or investment industry's reputation.  Deceitful or dishonest acts negatively impact a Member's or Candidate's integrity and violate the Standard. In this scenario, if Juniper Securities does not pay equitable wages to all employees, the matter should be pursued through the appropriate channels while maintaining compliance with the Standard.  Emilia Cosgrove violates the Standard by falsifying her travel expenses to Juniper regardless of her subjective belief that doing so is warranted.  Cosgrove diminishes her reputation and the reputation of the investment industry by dishonestly reporting her expenses (Choice A). (Choice C)  Cosgrove and Manuel Griggs may share personal information, including how much they earn, without violating the Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Walter Warner, CFA, is a research analyst covering the renewable energy sector.  He recently inherited 1,000 shares of Hast Renewal Energy (HRE).  Warner promptly informs his firm of his personal holding, and the firm does not restrict him from trading the stock.  Warner publishes a report with favorable coverage of the renewable energy industry, including HRE, without disclosing his ownership of HRE.  HRE stock, which Warner continues to hold, increases by more than 25% after the report's release.  With regard to Standard VI(A) Conflicts of Interest, did Warner's release of the report most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_a: Yes, by not disclosing his HRE stock in the report.
new_option_b: No, since he informed his employer of his holding.
new_option_c: No, since he did not sell the stock and realize a gain.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information." Personal ownership of stock recommended or held in client portfolios is a common potential conflict of interest that requires disclosure.  Here, Warner appropriately disclosed his ownership of HRE stock to his employer.  However, Standard VI(A) also requires disclosure of his personal ownership of HRE stock to clients and prospective clients.  This is meant to allow clients to decide for themselves whether the potential conflict of interest might influence a candidate's or member's objectivity (Choice B). (Choice C)  That Warner held the stock and did not sell it for a gain is not relevant to the requirement to disclose his personal holding in the published report.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Maya Levine, CFA, is a research analyst at a hedge fund.  Levine covers the global alternative energy industry and regularly uses an expert network to keep abreast of new developments.  During a recent expert network call with a junior scientific researcher at an electric car manufacturer, Levine asks about a new battery technology that was disclosed in the last earnings release.  The researcher echoes the optimistic tone of the press release, suggesting possible commercial development within a short period, but also notes that the rare earth elements needed for commercial production are in short supply. Based on this conversation, Levine begins researching rare earth mining stocks that could potentially benefit from large-scale commercialization were the technology adopted.  After conducting her research, Levine identifies and recommends the purchase for the hedge fund of an attractively valued rare earth mining company, believing that this new technology could provide an upside to her valuation estimate. According to the Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information, Levine:
new_option_b: violated the Standard by acting on material nonpublic information.
new_option_c: violated the Standard by not reporting the receipt of material nonpublic information to her supervisor or compliance staff.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from acting on or recommending investments based on material nonpublic information.  However, analysts may piece together public and nonmaterial nonpublic data from multiple sources to form an investment conclusion.  This process is referred to as mosaic theory.  Recommendations based on mosaic theory do not violate the Standard since, rather than rely on company insiders, the conclusions depend on the analyst's skill in synthesizing information from disparate sources. In this scenario, the researcher reiterates the company's already publicly released statement on the prospects and timeline for commercial development of a new battery technology, so no nonpublic information was disclosed.  The researcher's comments regarding rare earth elements being in short supply might provide some additional nonmaterial information since it can be reasonably assumed that the information is included in the company's publicly released forecasts or otherwise publicly available. Therefore, Maya Levine did not violate the Standard since she disclosed no material nonpublic information.  Levine used this information in applying mosaic theory to assist with the investment thesis for the rare earth mining company (Choice B). (Choice C)  Although it is recommended that Members and Candidates report the receipt of potentially material nonpublic information to their supervisor or compliance staff, it is not required in all circumstances, and Members and Candidates are urged to exercise their own judgment, as appropriate.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: David Landry, CFA, is director of investor relations at a small-cap industrial company and has been directed by the CEO to elevate the investment profile of the company.  Landry contacts independent research providers regarding writing an investment research report on the company for distribution to buy-side analysts. Landry obtains quotes from two analysts.  Nora O'Connor, CFA, proposes a variable fee structure based on the number of new buy-side investors.  George Novogratz, CFA, proposes a flat fee for the research report plus $2,500 for distributing the report to 10 of his buy-side contacts.  After evaluating both offers, Landry hires O'Connor. According to Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity, the Standard was violated by:
new_option_b: O'Connor and Novogratz only.
new_option_c: Landry, O'Connor, and Novogratz.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity requires Members and Candidates to avoid actions that compromise their independence and objectivity or create conflicts of interest. Producing issuer-paid research is an acceptable practice as long as the analyst conducts the research with due diligence, remains independent, and discloses all conflicts.  One way to maintain independence is to accept only a flat fee for this type of work, since a variable fee linked to conclusions, recommendations, or outcomes could inhibit the analyst's independence and objectivity.  In this scenario, Landry and O'Connor both violated the Standard by agreeing to tie compensation to outcomes (ie, new investors). (Choices B and C)  Novogratz did not violate the Standard by proposing his distribution arrangement since this compensation is not based on any specific outcome and cannot be seen as compromising his independence.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Nadine Pinot, CFA, is a fintech analyst.  To stay current on the latest technology, she hires Connective, Inc., a consulting firm that matches subject matter experts with investors.  Connective requires experts to pledge in writing that they will not share any confidential company information.  Through Connective, Pinot interviews Pierre Johann, head of technology at Advantage Securities Ltd.  During their conversation, Johann excitedly claims that his latest improvements in hardware and software technology, completed only a week earlier, will give Advantage the fastest trading speed in the market.  Johann also shares that although he is not sure, he believes Advantage will launch his technology in the current year.  Pinot realizes the launch could help Advantage gain more market share and improve its margins.  Based on Johann's information, she strongly recommends that her firm buy Advantage stock.  Does Pinot violate Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information?
new_option_b: No, since Johann pledged not to share private data.
new_option_c: No, since Pinot hired Connective to source new public information from experts.
new_explanation_en: Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) requires Members and Candidates to abstain from taking investment actions based on material nonpublic information (MNI) related to a security.  Buying and selling of the security may occur only after the information is publicly disclosed.  Members and Candidates who trade using MNI might generate short-term profits, but their actions diminish the integrity of capital markets and the investment profession over the long term. In this scenario, Nadine Pinot violates the Standard by basing her recommendation on MNI.  The new technology improvements could reasonably be expected to move the company's stock price, making the information material.  The information also has not been publicly disclosed by the company (Choices B and C). Pinot must evaluate her interaction with Pierre Johann and determine whether it provided her with MNI.  Pinot should conclude that the information she received is material, and since it has not been publicly disclosed, she should not use it in her recommendation.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Meiling Huang, CFA, is a well-respected independent real estate sell-side analyst.  The investor relations manager of MNC Properties, a real estate company that went public this year, reaches out to Huang to see if she will write a report on MNC.  MNC does not have significant cash on hand, so Huang agrees to be paid in stock options.  After evaluating MNC, Huang believes that the company is undervalued and worthy of a "buy" rating.  Huang writes her report on MNC and discloses that she was compensated by MNC but does not indicate the type of compensation.  Does Huang most likely violate Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity?
new_option_b: No, since her report's conclusion reflected her opinion
new_option_c: No, since she disclosed that she was compensated for her report
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity requires Members and Candidates to refuse any compensation that could reasonably be expected to compromise their independence and objectivity.  Sell-side analysts can be compensated by companies for writing research reports about the company.  However, analysts must be careful not let the compensation affect their judgement.  The report must reflect an independent opinion following diligent and thorough research. Compensation from the company should not be linked to the conclusion of the report.  Forms of compensation that violate that Standard are those that can reasonably be expected to bias the analyst's opinion directly (eg, payments based on the rating) or indirectly (eg, stock options, warrants).  Best practice calls for a flat fee paid by the company.  Analysts are required to disclose the compensation in their report, including the nature of the compensation, but disclosure does not offset a violation of accepting influential compensation (Choice C). (Choice B)  Although the report reflected Huang's independent opinion, this opinion can be reasonably viewed as biased by clients due to the nature of the compensation (ie, stock options) for writing the report, thus violating he Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Eugene Power, CFA, works with clients in Asia and the United States.  During his flight home from Asia to the US, he is unexpectedly upgraded to first-class and sits next to his college roommate Norm Brownstone.  While celebrating their chance meeting, they reminisce about college over several bottles of champagne.  Power knows that as soon as he gets back to the US, he must make personal trades, interview a potential client on the phone, and write an investment policy statement (IPS) for a client before getting some much-needed sleep.  Still intoxicated when he lands in the early morning, Power knows he should not drive and debates whether to hire a car for a short ride to his office or a longer ride to his home.  Power least likely violates Standard I(D) Misconduct if he:
new_option_a: writes the client IPS at the firm.
new_option_b: executes the personal trades at home.
new_option_c: interviews the potential client from home.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any professional conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, or deceit or commit any act that reflects adversely on their professional reputation, integrity, or competence" Under Standard I(D) Misconduct, Members and Candidates must refrain from conduct that diminishes the integrity, reputation, or competence of the industry, a firm, or themselves.  Although the CFA Institute recommends that Members and Candidates always act responsibly, the Standard focuses on how a Member's behavior impacts professional activities.  The integrity of the profession is founded on the belief that Members and Candidates act in a trustworthy manner; otherwise, the industry's overall reputation is diminished. In this scenario, to violate the Standard, Eugene Power must be intoxicated while working in a professional capacity.  He does not violate the Standard by being intoxicated and making personal trades.  The location of his work is irrelevant, but the nature of the work matters.  By itself, intoxication is not a violation of the Standard, but carrying out professional duties—such as interviewing potential clients or writing an investment policy statement while intoxicated—calls into question Power's judgment and competence and violates the Standard (Choices A and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Stella Smith, CFA, works for Aqua Investment Consulting.  She is invited to share her economic outlook at a conference hosted by Zenat Securities Corp., an investment management firm used by Aqua.  Zenat pays all speakers' travel expenses and entices speakers by offering a free spa day during the conference.  Smith most likely violates Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity if she accepts Zenat's offer for:
new_option_b: only the spa day.
new_option_c: both her travel and the spa day.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity mandates that Members and Candidates avoid actions that compromise their independence and objectivity or create conflicts of interest.  In many cases, Members and Candidates should refrain from accepting payment for travel expenses to avoid any appearance of compromised independence or objectivity. In this scenario, Stella Smith has been invited to speak on the economic outlook at an investment conference hosted by Zenat Securities Corp. Since she is not making any investment recommendations or endorsing Zenat in any way, accepting payment to cover her travel expenses in this case is not likely to compromise her independence or objectivity (Choices A and C). However, the spa day can be considered an extravagant gift.  Since Zenat has a vendor-client relationship with Smith's firm, Aqua Investment Consulting, this gift might be seen as an attempt to compromise Smith's independence and objectivity in making investment recommendations to Aqua's clients.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Nancy Bender, CFA, manages multigenerational clientele for Arch Investments, Inc.  Bender hosts a social media page that is exclusively for clients.  In January 20X5, she posts her quarterly investment review to the social media page, which states: "Wishing everyone a Happy New Year.  In 20X5, we expect monetary and fiscal policies will benefit the overall market and your investments.  If you have any questions, please let us know as we are here to help you.  Remember, as we discussed, do not post confidential information to this social media page." Leo Faber, one of Bender's clients, responds to Bender's social media review with the following post: "Nancy: Martha and I want to set up trusts of $1 million for each of our grandchildren.  Also, please see the attached tax forms detailing our income for 20X4.  Please forward this to your tax person we used last year." Bender immediately deletes Faber's post after reading it.  According to Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, does Bender most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, since Bender should prevent, not delete, Faber's post.
new_option_c: Yes, since Bender uses social media pages to communicate with clients.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must keep information about current, former, and prospective clients confidential unless: The information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client or prospective client, Disclosure is required by law, or The client or prospective client permits disclosure of the information." Standard III (E) Preservation of Confidentiality requires that Members and Candidates not disclose a client's information unless is it required by law or if the client gives explicit permission.  Conservative application of this Standard suggests that analysts should not disclose anything that the client may give or share with them unless the client gives authorization.  However, a client may accidentally share communications intended for only the advisor with others. To comply with the Standard, advisors must try to prevent accidental disclosures by instructing clients on the proper use of social media.  Since Bender reiterated instructions regarding the use of her social media page, she does not violate the Standard; immediately removing Faber's post also would align with meeting the Standard (Choice B). (Choice C)  The use of social media is common, and its use is not an immediate violation.  If an advisor chooses to contact clients using social media, the Member or Candidate must give clients clear instructions on its use to comply with the Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Aiko Nakamura, CFA, has worked as an investment adviser for the past 20 years and specialized in creating individual stock portfolios for her clients.  Recently her firm transitioned all clients to firm-approved model portfolios based on risk tolerance.  These model portfolios include only passively managed ETFs, a handful of actively managed mutual funds, and a few hedge funds.  Pat Smith, Nakamura's largest client and an old friend, is not happy with the new arrangement; she prefers to invest in individual stocks and threatens to take her business elsewhere.  To keep her client with the firm, Nakamura suggests that she could provide "informal" stock ideas to Smith on a quarterly basis at Nakamura's favorite restaurant, an expensive steakhouse, as long as Smith pays for dinner.  Smith could then execute the trades through an unrelated discount brokerage firm if she liked the ideas.  Smith is receptive to the idea, agreeing to the arrangement, and remains a client.  Does Nakamura's conduct violate Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements?
new_option_b: No, since Nakamura is just suggesting ideas over dinner with a friend.
new_option_c: No, since her firm no longer offers this service so she is not competing with her employer.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements notes that third-party, additional compensation is allowed.  However, if the arrangement could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with the employer, the Member or Candidate must obtain written permission from all parties involved. In this case, Nakamura cannot accept compensation for any investment advice that could be seen as conflicting with her firm's interests without written permission from all parties involved.  Since Nakamura is giving investment advice that differs from her firm's recommendations and proposing trade execution by another firm, this can reasonably be seen as a conflict with her employer's interests (Choice C).  Therefore, she has violated the Standards by not obtaining prior written permission. Additional compensation does not necessarily have to be cash compensation; it could be anything of value above a reasonable threshold, including a gift, tickets to a sporting event, or, as here, a series of expensive dinners.  By establishing this condition for sharing her investment ideas, Nakamura has created a compensation arrangement and is not just having dinner with a friend (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Grace Lee, CFA, is an investment advisor at Apex Investments.  After considerable research, Lee recommends the XYZ 130/30 long/short exchange traded fund (ETF) to her retail clients as their primary equity exposure, if it is suitable for their portfolios.  The XYZ fund invests in a selection of benchmark equity securities while employing leverage (130% long) and short positions (30% short) to arrive at an equivalent 100% long position. Lee is very comfortable recommending the ETF, as it has historically outperformed the benchmark index while exhibiting a similar level of volatility. When discussing the ETF with clients and prospects, Lee touts the relative outperformance and low tracking error versus the benchmark, referring to it as an "enhanced index fund."  Lee has most likely:
new_option_a: remained in full compliance with the Standards.
new_option_b: violated the Standards by not adequately disclosing the risks of the ETF.
new_option_c: violated the Standards by using the ETF as equity exposure for retail clients.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must: Use reasonable judgement in identifying which factors are important to their investment analyses, recommendations, or actions, and include those factors in communications with clients and prospective clients." Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients requires Members and Candidates to inform both clients and prospective clients about the limitations and risks of an asset or investment process.  The communications must use plain language that is easy for clients to understand but also conveys enough information for them to recognize the relevant risks and limitations. In this instance, Lee violated the Standard by oversimplifying the exchange traded fund (ETF) as an "enhanced index fund," which inappropriately downplays the underlying risks associated with the investment.  Specifically, the ETF is not an index fund and employs an active approach, leverage, and short positions, which should all be clearly acknowledged and detailed when communicating the risks of the investment with clients and prospects (Choice A). (Choice C)  The fact that Lee uses the ETF as primary equity exposure for retail clients does not specifically violate the Standard.  Lee conducted considerable research before recommending this investment and is acting in what she believes to be in the best interest of her clients.  The issue is in how she communicated the favorable aspects of the investment but failed to mention the considerable risks that a well-informed investor would want to know.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Harold Martin, CFA, is a senior wealth management strategist at Synergy Investment Advisors (SIA).  SIA does not manage funds but maintains a list of approved brokerage firms the advisors can suggest to clients for placing trades.  Recently, one of those firms asked Martin to recommend it exclusively to his clients.  In exchange, the firm offered to sell Martin tickets to a sold-out sporting event at the face value of $2,500 per ticket.  Martin would have been unable to acquire these tickets otherwise except at a significantly higher price.  The firm's commissions are slightly higher than others on the approved list, but it consistently provides better execution on its trades.  Martin subsequently recommends that his clients use this firm without advising them of its ticket incentive.  Does Martin most likely violate Standard VI(C) Referral Fees?
new_option_b: No, since he had to pay for the tickets and did not receive them as a gift
new_option_c: No, since his clients will receive enhanced value from the broker's better execution
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services." Standard VI(C) Referral Fees requires Members and Candidates to advise employers and clients if they receive any type of benefit for recommending a product or service.  These benefits can pose a conflict of interest, so disclosing the conflict allows affected parties to determine whether the recommendation was impartial.  Note that the Standard does not require that clients consent to the arrangement, only that they be made aware of it. In this question, Martin violated the Standard since he did not disclose the ticket arrangement to his clients.  The broker's offer to sell the tickets for a greatly reduced price confers a benefit to Martin.  CFA Institute defines "benefit" broadly to include both cash and noncash considerations.  It is irrelevant that Martin had to pay for the tickets; the ability to buy something for less than market value is still considered a benefit (Choice B). (Choice C)  It is irrelevant whether a client receives a benefit by following the recommendation.  The Standard does not excuse a Member or Candidate's failure to disclose a referral fee arrangement on the rationale that the client benefits by using the recommended product or service.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Choon-Hee Kim, CFA, a financial advisor, evaluates an attractive but risky initial public offering (IPO) for TTG, Inc.  After evaluating her clients' investment policies, Kim decides that TTG's stock is suitable for her risk-tolerant clients' portfolios but that it surpasses the risk threshold of her risk-averse clients.  Kim believes TTG's stock has a strong chance of appreciating quickly, so she allocates shares to her risk-tolerant clients.  Two months after the IPO, TTG stock has increased by 38%.  Regarding Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, did Kim most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, by allocating risky IPO shares to any of her clients.
new_option_c: Yes, by excluding clients from the allocation after concluding the stock would appreciate.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires Members and Candidates to be loyal to their clients and to use prudence and care when making investment decisions on a client's behalf.  Investment actions must be carried out for the sole benefit of the client and in the client's best interest.  Prudence includes adhering to the investment parameters established by the portfolio manager and the client.  Each client's individual needs should be considered. In this scenario, Kim acted with prudence and care when evaluating TTG, Inc.'s stock and deciding which accounts are appropriate for it, based on each client's risk tolerance.  Despite her belief in TTG's strong upside potential, Kim adhered to her clients' investment parameters by not allocating the stock to her risk-averse clients (Choice C).  Regardless of whether Kim's forecast proves accurate and the stock price continues to increase, the stock is still too risky for these clients. (Choice B)  Allocating risky shares to clients is not a violation of the Standard.  Such shares may be appropriate for clients with investment parameters that allow riskier assets.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Zhang Yong, CFA, is a CFA Institute volunteer who is helping create material for the upcoming Level III CFA exam.  Zhang meets with CFA Institute staff and other question writers and is assigned to write an essay question about portfolio management for a college endowment fund.  At dinner one night, Zhang tells his friend, Li Min, CFA, about the question he is working on.  Li manages the endowment fund of a local university, and Zhang believes that Li can provide helpful insight.  Has Zhang most likely violated Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs?
new_option_b: No, since Li is not a Candidate for an upcoming exam.
new_option_c: No, since the question is under deliberation and is not finalized.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) prohibits Members and Candidates from engaging in behavior that undermines the integrity of CFA Institute or its programs.  CFA Institute takes care to ensure that confidential information about exams is not shared by anyone.  For Members and Candidates, sharing such information is a violation of the Standard.  Members may not disclose: questions that are set to appear on the exam or are under consideration, any parts of the deliberation process related to the exam, or information related to the scoring of questions. In this scenario, Zhang Yong has confidential information about the deliberation process and questions under consideration, including one that he plans to write.  Per the Standard, he may not discuss this information with anyone, including Members and Candidates, regardless of whether the question he plans to write appears on the exam (Choices B and C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Trevor Halcott is a practicing lawyer and a CFA charterholder.  He meets with the legal team of a potential client, Smith & Smith, Inc., to discuss a case that involves derivatives and portfolio management.  At the beginning of the meeting, he hands out business cards that give his name as "Trevor Halcott, JD, CFA."  Later, he tells the legal team, "completing the CFA Program greatly improved my knowledge of portfolio management and derivatives."  Has Halcott violated most likely VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program?
new_option_b: Yes, by listing his JD before his CFA designation.
new_option_c: Yes, by stating that the CFA Program has increased his knowledge.
new_explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program designates when Members may use the CFA designation. CFA Institute takes special care to ensure that individuals who use the CFA designation meet all requirements to do so and use the designation properly. Although CFA Institute maintains specific rules about how to use the CFA designation, the Standard does not assign a mandatory order of credentials for Members who have multiple professional or academic certifications.  Therefore, in this scenario, Trevor Halcott does not violate the Standard by listing his JD before his CFA designation on his business card (Choice B). Standard VII(B) also governs how Members and Candidates reference the CFA Program.  Statements exaggerating the meaning or implication of having a CFA charter violate the Standard.  However, statements of objective fact about the benefits (eg, knowledge and skills gained) of the CFA designation are allowed.  In his meeting with a prospective client's legal team, Halcott states that the CFA Program enhanced his knowledge, which does not violate the Standard (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Bao Pham, CFA, is an investment adviser serving high–net worth retail clients.  Several of Pham's younger clients prefer using instant messaging to communicate with him.  Pham often receives requests and investment questions from clients via his personal phone and social media accounts.  Pham does not forward any of these items to his firm since he considers them personal.  The firm has no stated policy on data collection via personal devices or social media.  Does Pham's conduct most likely comply with Standard V(C) Record Retention?
new_option_b: Yes, since the firm has no stated policy on the issue.
new_option_c: Yes, since these are private messages received through personal devices and accounts.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must develop and maintain appropriate records to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications with clients and prospective clients." Standard V(C) Record Retention requires Members and Candidates to keep records that are considered property of their firms.  This requirement includes retaining and documenting all social media and instant messaging interactions that involve investment-related communication with clients and prospective clients. Although the Standard places some responsibility for record retention on firms, Members and Candidates must assist in the process, which includes capturing and forwarding documentation of work-related digital media (eg, text messages, blog posts, social media interactions). In this scenario, Bao Pham's failure to retain and document all of his client communications violates the Standard.  His concern that private information may be included does not override the requirement (Choice C). (Choice B)  Personal social media and instant messaging interactions that include any work-related content must be retained and submitted to the firm, even if the firm has no stated policy on the issue.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: One day after taking Level II of the CFA exam, Guyton Wyll visited a website used by several thousand CFA candidates and posted the following to a thread visible to candidates at all levels: "I can't believe that CFA Institute recommended that we study for more than 300 hours when they asked such easy questions on most topics.  But the Ethics questions were so subjective, and I can't remember that any of them dealt with the Standards...really unfair!"  Did Wyll's post most likely violate Standard VII(A)–Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs?
new_option_b: Yes, with his reference to the ethics questions
new_option_c: Yes, with his reference to CFA Institute's recommended study time
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) prohibits Members and Candidates from engaging in any conduct that would undermine the integrity of the CFA Institute or any CFA Institute program, including the CFA Program exams.  A specific requirement in connection with this Standard is a pledge that candidates must sign before taking any Level exam.  The pledge reads, in part, "After this exam, I will not disclose ANY portion of this exam…" Wyll, by referencing areas that the Ethics questions did not address, violated Standard VII(A) and the pledge.  It is immaterial that he did not discuss specific questions.  His statement that certain areas of the candidate body of knowledge were not tested, especially since it was posted soon after he took the exam, is considered assistance to future candidates.  This assistance undermines the integrity of the exam and is prohibited under the Standard. However, general opinions about the difficulty of an exam that do not address specific questions or topics or CFA Institute's policies and procedures do not violate the Standard.  Wyll's opinions that the exam was "easy" and that CFA Institute's recommendation is unwarranted regarding time needed to study for Level II do not violate the Standard (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Morena Villalba, CFA, and Franco Aquirre, a Level I CFA candidate, both work in the private wealth department of a major bank and often work with the same clients.  Villalba becomes aware that Aquirre receives compensation for each referral he makes to the bank's brokerage department that results in commissions but does not disclose that fact to clients.  Also, she learns that Aquirre and a colleague have been able to hide the arrangement and fees from the firm.  Villalba researches local law and believes that Aquirre's arrangement is illegal.  She reports the situation to her supervisor, but after some time has passed, Villalba notices that Aquirre continues to benefit from his referrals, and she is not sure what to do next.  According to Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, which of the following actions is Villalba's most appropriate next step?
new_option_a: Resign from her employment at the bank
new_option_b: Request a transfer to another department of the bank
new_option_c: Remain in her role to document stronger evidence to present later
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities.  In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation.  Members and Candidates must not knowingly participate or assist in and must dissociate from any violation of such laws, rules, or regulations." When a member or candidate becomes aware that violations of rules or laws are taking place, the Standard encourages the member or candidate first to report the situation to a supervisor or compliance department.  If that is unsuccessful, members and candidates should then attempt to dissociate (ie, separate themselves) from the activity, not necessarily resign from the firm. Here, Villalba's most appropriate next step is to dissociate from the activity by requesting reassignment.  She may need to resign if that request is not granted.  Note that although the Standard strongly encourages reporting, it does not require the member or candidate to report unethical or illegal activities by others to government authorities or regulators (Choice A). (Choice C)  Remaining in her current role is not an appropriate action.  The Standard implies that by both continuing to associate with and failing to act on a legal violation, Villalba could be considered as taking part in or assisting with the illegal conduct.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Matt Fabiano, CFA, is the senior portfolio manager at Marco Investment Advisors (MIA).  All of MIA's clients gave Fabiano discretion over their accounts and, as part of his service, he directs trades to a number of brokerage firms.  Fabiano discovers that if he trades exclusively with Strollo Brokerage Inc. (SB), MIA could participate in SB's client referral program, allowing MIA to serve more clients.  Based on MIA's analysis, Fabiano concludes that clients are neither harmed by nor benefit from using SB as a broker.  With respect to Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, if Fabiano trades exclusively with SB, most likely he:
new_option_a: does not violate the Standard since he has discretion.
new_option_b: violates the Standard since clients do not receive a benefit.
new_option_c: does not violate the Standard since he does not receive a benefit.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests." Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires members and candidates to be loyal to clients and use reasonable care.  This implies making prudent investment decisions based on the clients' best interests only.  One application of the Standard is how members and candidates direct trades on the clients' behalf. Here, Fabiano, who has discretion over client accounts, controls how client trades are executed.  If he trades exclusively with SB, he violates the Standard since clients do not benefit.  Fabiano and his firm reap the benefits (ie, financial reward from having more clients) by participating in the client referral program.  Being unharmed is not the same as receiving a benefit.  If there is any benefit derived from directing trades, it must be realized by the client (Choice C). (Choice A)  Having discretion indicates Fabiano makes day-to-day investment decisions without continually asking for the client's permission. However, having discretion does not exempt Fabiano from being loyal to his clients (ie, the Standards).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Hudson Bright, CFA, just received his certificate in quantitative finance.  As part of his studies, he developed training modules for financial modeling.  Soon after receiving his certificate, Bright joins QED Consulting, a quantitative analysis consulting firm, and posts news about his certificate and new job on social media.  The local CFA Society president sees his post and asks him to teach financial modeling classes.  After determining that the time commitment will not hinder his performance at QED, Bright agrees to teach a monthly, one-hour class for 6 months at €500 per class.  He advises QED of his plans in an email that states, "I am writing to inform you that I have agreed to partner with the local CFA Society to teach financial modeling classes.  Please contact me with any questions."  He does not receive a response and begins teaching the classes.  Has Bright most likely violated Standard IV(A) Loyalty to Employer?
new_option_b: Yes, since he started teaching prior to receiving approval from QED.
new_option_c: Yes, since his notice to QED left out required information on compensation and duration.
new_explanation_en: "In matters related to their employment, Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their employer and not deprive their employer of the advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or otherwise cause harm to their employer." Standard IV(A) Loyalty is one of the broader Duties to Employers addressed in Standard IV.  It places specific requirements on members or candidates who intend to engage in independent practice for compensation when that practice may conflict with the employer's interest or deprive the employer of business opportunities.  Members or candidates who plan to engage in such independent practice must notify their employer prior to offering the services. In this instance, there is no violation of the Standard since Bright's teaching does not compete with QED's business model.  Furthermore, based on the information provided, teaching the classes will not deprive his employer of any of his skills or time, and the teaching may benefit his employer by improving his skill set. (Choice B)  If Bright's independent practice competed with QED's business, he would have to wait for permission prior to teaching a class to comply with the Standard. (Choice C)  In this case, Bright is not required to provide notice.  When the Standard does apply, members and candidates are required to provide a description of the services to be offered, compensation to be received, and expected duration of services.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Tom Smith, CFA, is assigned a new client, Brigitte Duret, who is currently invested entirely in cash.  During a brief phone conversation with Smith, Duret says: "I'd like to earn a better return, but I don't want to take any risk.  I am going to work in the Amazon rainforest for about three months, so we will meet when I am back in the US."  Smith schedules a meeting with Duret three months from today.  Smith temporarily invests Duret's assets in the firm's Conservative Portfolio since he does not want Duret to miss out on at least some of the market's performance before their meeting.  Smith is the firm's leading expert on the Conservative Portfolio (shown in the table below) and has used it for many client portfolios with good results. Asset Class Percent Allocation Cash 45 Fixed Income 45 Developed Equity 5 Emerging Markets 5 According to Standard III(C) Suitability and based on the Conservative Portfolio's asset allocation, Smith most likely:
new_option_a: violates the Standard since he failed to perform due diligence before taking investment action.
new_option_b: violates the Standard since he invested the client's assets before understanding the client's risk and return objectives.
new_option_c: does not violate the Standard since he spoke to Duret, the investment is temporary, and it is consistent with what a prudent investor would expect.
new_explanation_en: "When Members and Candidates are responsible for managing a portfolio to a specific mandate, strategy, or style, they must make only investment recommendations or take only investment actions that are consistent with the stated objectives and constraints of the portfolio." Standard III(C) Suitability prescribes how the manager must act when investing on behalf of the client.  Suitability entails evaluating whether an investment's expected risk and return match the client's risk tolerance and return objectives.  Suitability cannot determine until the manager knows the client's investment objectives and constraints. (Choice A)  Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis states that managers must diligently exercise thoroughness when taking investment actions.  Given Smith's expertise with the Conservative Portfolio, it is reasonable to assume that the violation does not involve a lack of diligence. (Choice C)  The Conservative Portfolio has more risk than a cash portfolio since it has exposure to equities and emerging markets.  There is no prudent investor test to determine whether the portfolio is appropriate or not.  No matter how "temporary" the investment is intended to be, it does not excuse Smith from first assessing whether the investment is suitable for the client's risk and return objectives.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Erik Johansen, CFA, and Claire Olsen, CFA, decide to start their own fund.  They create a marketing brochure that includes the following: "Claire Olsen, CFA, a self-employed investor, has developed a proprietary model focused on growth stocks.  The model achieved a simulated annualized return of 15% over the past five years." "Erik Johansen, CFA, averaged a 12% annual return from 20X1 to 20X7 while working as a portfolio manager at his prior employer, Henderson Bank." Johansen received written approval from Henderson to use the return data.  Based on this information, have Johansen and Olsen most likely violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation?
new_option_b: Yes, by using Johansen's return data from a prior employer.
new_option_c: Yes, by using the simulated returns of Olsen's model and not the actual performance history.
new_explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires Members and Candidates to provide a fair, accurate, and complete record of their performance.  To avoid misrepresentation, a manager, firm, portfolio, or composite must provide full disclosure of all aspects of performance to all clients, prospective clients, and prospective employers. If the details are fully disclosed, the Standard allows the presentation of performance information from prior employers, accounts managed by multiple people, and simulations.  Performance data from a prior employer cannot be used without written permission from the employer.  In this scenario, Erik Johansen receives written approval from his prior employer, Henderson Bank, before presenting data on the returns he achieved there as a portfolio manager.  The marketing brochure fully discloses both this background and the fact that Claire Olsen's model returns are simulated, so the Standard is not being violated (Choices B and C).

new_question_en: Aline Costa, CFA, is a financial advisor for Solar Bank.  At a conference, Costa meets Juanita Carvalho, a portfolio manager for Lunar Financial.  Carvalho tells Costa about a propriety quantitative model developed by Lunar that aims to predict interest rate changes.  Costa reads Lunar's sales literature on the model to understand how it works, its assumptions, and its testing parameters, which included both extreme positive and negative scenarios.  Of the following, Costa can most appropriately begin integrating the model into her research process:
new_option_b: after thoroughly testing the model herself.
new_option_c: after taking the time to learn the technical aspects of the model.
