pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Bull Advisors, based in Country Y, expanded its operations to Country X, where securities laws and regulations are less strict than either CFA Institute's Code and Standards or Country Y's laws and regulations.  One of Bull's advisors, Joseph Telluci, CFA, travels to Country X to meet with a client.  In a rush to meet with the client before she leaves for vacation, Telluci does not familiarize himself with Country X's securities laws and regulations.  After the meeting, he begins the investment management process on behalf of the client based on the laws, regulations, and rules of Country Y and the Code and Standards.  Has Telluci most likely violated Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law?
new_option_b: No, since he follows the laws of Country Y.
new_option_c: No, since he adheres to CFA Institute's Standards of Professional Conduct.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must understand and comply with all applicable laws, rules, and regulations (including the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct) of any government, regulatory organization, licensing agency, or professional association governing their professional activities.  In the event of conflict, Members and Candidates must comply with the more strict law, rule, or regulation.  Members and Candidates must not knowingly participate or assist in and must dissociate from any violation of such laws, rules, or regulations." Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law requires members and candidates to understand local laws.  When members or candidates do business in more than one country, they are required to know and understand both the Standards of Professional Conduct and the laws and regulations of each country.  In all professional activities, they must follow the strictest of the applicable rules. Telluci does business in both Country Y (where Bull Advisors is based) and Country X (where the new client resides).  Before doing business with the client, Telluci must be familiar with the set of securities laws and regulations in Country X—in addition to those of Country Y and the Code and Standards—so that he knows which rules to apply if a conflict arises.  Without this knowledge, Telluci could not make an informed judgment. (Choices B and C)  Although the rules of Country X are less strict than those of Country Y or the Code and Standards, Telluci violated Standard I(A) by not familiarizing himself with and understanding all the applicable laws and regulations.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Dimitri Federov, CFA, is a financial adviser for Arrow Financial.  One of Federov's clients, Natasha Popova, offers Federov the use of her vacation home next January if her portfolio achieves 10% return this year.  Federov accepts Popova's offer without disclosing it to Arrow since it is only a nonmonetary offer.  Federov later joins the Safe Bank board of directors, which he discloses to Arrow.  As part of his compensation, Federov will receive Safe stock options for each of his clients that he enrolls as a client of Safe's trust services.  Federov does not disclose this arrangement to Arrow since he does not have any clients who currently need Safe's trust services and has not recommended them to anyone. Federov most likely violated the Standards:
new_option_a: only by accepting Popova's offer without disclosing it to Arrow.
new_option_b: only by failing to disclose the options compensation from Safe.
new_option_c: both by accepting Popova's offer and failing to disclose the options compensation from Safe.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or consideration that competes with or might reasonably be expected to create a conflict of interest with their employer's interest unless they obtain written consent from all parties involved." Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements allows additional compensation agreements with third parties, including clients.  However, Members and Candidates must disclose such agreements in full and obtain written permission from all parties involved before accepting compensation that could be reasonably seen as creating a conflict with their employers.  Gifts, benefits, and other compensation do not need to be monetary to require approval. In this scenario, Dimitri Federov's actions violate the Standard in both arrangements.  His options compensation agreement with Safe Bank must be disclosed to Arrow Financial in full before he accepts it.  The fact that he has not recommended Safe's trust services to his clients and has not received any options does not excuse him from disclosing the arrangement to Arrow, as it could create a conflict of interest later (Choice A). Likewise, his compensation agreement with Natasha Popova must be approved in writing by Arrow before he accepts it since the Standard applies to both monetary and nonmonetary compensation (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Chester Hall, CFA, manages a small hedge fund called Taurus Group.  Hall is currently seeking additional investors to grow assets under management and is approached by Kathy Walker, CFA, who manages a fund of hedge funds.  Walker tells Hall that being included in Walker's fund will increase Taurus's exposure, which in turn would increase assets.  However, there is intense competition to be included in the fund of hedge funds platform, and many hedge funds are under consideration.  Hall offers Walker box seats to a high-profile football game so they can further discuss Taurus.  Walker declines, telling Hall that she doesn't accept personal gifts.  Walker then mentions that her husband runs a charity that is having a fundraiser next month and says Hall should buy tickets so that they can discuss business at the event.  The Member(s) that most likely violates Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is:
new_option_b: only Walker.
new_option_c: both Hall and Walker.
new_explanation_en: Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity. Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity focuses on Members and Candidates maintaining their independence and objectivity so that their actions and advice to clients are unaffected by conflicts of interest.  The Standard applies to entities or individuals that seek to influence the decision-making process to the detriment of clients but does not apply to gifts from clients themselves. During the manager selection process, accepting, soliciting, or offering any gifts or donations that can be seen as compromising independence and objectivity violates the Standard.  The gift or donation does not need to be monetary or be directed at the manager.  Gifts to favorite charities or political candidates also violate the Standard. In this scenario, both Hall and Walker violate the Standard.  Walker, by suggesting that Hall purchase tickets to her husband's charity fundraiser, is soliciting a gift from Hall and attempting to influence the fund of hedge fund's decision-making process.  A donation to the charity run by Walker's husband may be seen as favorable to her and should be treated as a personal gift for the purposes of the Standard (Choice A).  Hall, by offering box seats to a high-profile football game, is attempting to influence Walker's decision and gain an unfair advantage in the fund selection process (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Krishan Patel, CFA, a senior analyst at CityStock, conducts due diligence of Specialty Products Corp. (SPC) and determines that it is a compelling buy and that the stock price will soon increase.  Patel hesitates to recommend SPC since CityStock places a five-day blackout period on all recommended stocks.  Instead, he purchases 300 shares of SPC for his account without sharing his analysis and recommendation with CityStock.  SPC's price subsequently drops by 30%.  Patel reviews his analysis and, still convinced that SPC is a great buying opportunity, submits his analysis and buy recommendation to the investment committee at CityStock. Patel most likely violates Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions:
new_option_b: only by withholding his recommendation.
new_option_c: both by withholding his recommendation and purchasing SPC.
new_explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions specifies the responsibility of members and candidates to place the interests of clients and employers ahead of their own.  An application of this Standard demands that personal trades for a given security be placed after clients' trades so as not to harm the clients' financial interests.  Withholding an investment recommendation to avoid this trading restriction violates the Standard. Since Patel has willfully not acted in his clients' best interests, his actions violate the Standard, even when his unshared determination proves to be wrong (ie, the stock declines by 30%).  The Standard is violated by Patel withholding his recommendation to purchase Specialty Products Corp. before clients can act (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Kevin Smith, Level I CFA Candidate, has just finished the exam.  Outside the test center, he posts on a popular CFA social media blog, "The Level I CFA mocks are a joke!", "Be sure to memorize ALL the convexity formulas!!!"  Hamza Bennani, who is also a Level I CFA Candidate, immediately responds by stating "I hope I passed!  The CFA Institute needs to provide better exam prep materials as there were too many questions that I wasn't prepared for!" Based on Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs, most likely:
new_option_b: only Bennani violated the Standard.
new_option_c: both Bennani and Smith violated the Standard.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs mandates that Members and Candidates maintain the reputation, integrity, validity, and security of CFA Institute exams and programs.  The Standard prohibits behavior that would compromise the public's confidence in the level of merit needed to achieve a CFA charter. Candidates taking the exam must sign the Candidate Pledge, which identifies behaviors that are prohibited before, during, and after the test. These behaviors include: giving or receiving information about the exam before or during the exam, and providing information regarding the exam to others after the exam, including broad topical areas and formulas tested, until that information is publicly released by CFA Institute. In this instance, Kevin Smith violated the Standard by providing specific information regarding which formulas were tested.  However, Hamza Bennani did not violate the Standard as he made a very generic comment without mentioning any areas of study or exam content. (Choices B and C)  Members and Candidates can express opinions about the exams or the CFA Institute without violating the Standard as long as the opinions do not reveal specific information about the exams.  Smith and Bennani did not violate the Standard by criticizing the CFA Institute.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Sofia Giordano, CFA, is a private tutor for Candidates taking the CFA exam.  Her marketing materials state that her program includes "tips and strategies to pass the CFA exam."  She continually works to make the program's practice exams more realistic.  The day after the end of the most recent CFA exam period, Giordano sends a follow-up email to her students, congratulating them on getting through the exam and asking them which specific topics, in each domain, were tested so she can improve next year's practice exams.  Giordano most likely violates Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs:
new_option_a: only by offering "tips and strategies" to pass the exam.
new_option_b: only by soliciting confidential information about the exam.
new_option_c: both by offering "tips and strategies" and soliciting confidential information.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not engage in any conduct that compromises the reputation or integrity of CFA Institute or the CFA designation or the integrity, validity, or security of CFA Institute programs." Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs requires Members and Candidates to refrain from conduct that undermines the integrity of CFA Institute or its programs.  Each Candidate taking the CFA exam must sign the Candidate Pledge, which specifies the types of conduct that violate the Standard, including: giving or receiving information about the exam before or during the exam, providing information about the exam to others after the exam, or violating CFA Institute rules and regulations. In addition, the Standard prohibits Members from soliciting confidential information gained prior to or during the exam.  Unless and until CFA Institute releases it publicly, Candidates must not divulge confidential information, including: specific details about questions on the exam and broad topical areas tested on the exam. In this scenario, Sofia Giordano solicits confidential information about the CFA exam from her students.  By doing so, she violates the Standard. Since the information has not been disseminated by CFA Institute, Candidates cannot disclose it.  If Giordano's students send her confidential information, they would also violate the Standard. (Choices A and C)  Offering tips and strategies to pass the CFA exam does not violate the Standard, as long as the tips and strategies do not include confidential information that CFA Institute has not publicly released.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Archer Clegg, CFA, manages a fund of illiquid distressed real estate that primarily consists of properties located in economically depressed areas.  Clegg does not report fund performance relative to a benchmark since there are no benchmarks based on distressed real estate.  Clegg uses two reputable appraisal firms to value each property annually.  Last year, a new appraisal firm was hired due to cost and timing concerns involving a previous appraiser.  Since then, Clegg has noticed that the new firm appears to consistently undervalue properties compared with the other firm doing appraisals.  Fund performance reports are prepared using the average of the two appraisals, a method that is disclosed to clients and potential clients.  Has Clegg most likely violated Standard I(C) Misrepresentation?
new_option_b: Yes, since he is not using only the lowest appraisal.
new_option_c: Yes, since he fails to compare performance to a benchmark.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation prohibits actions and statements by investment professionals that could undermine confidence in investment performance reporting.  Members and Candidates must provide accurate and reliable pricing information to enable informed investment decision-making by clients. Accurate values for distressed real estate are difficult to determine, and a wide range of appraised values is not uncommon.  Using the average from several appraisers is a reasonable method for estimating a property's fair value.  The method should be disclosed to clients and potential clients. (Choice B)  Using the lower estimates for asset values can lead to exaggerating the expected returns when undervalued assets are sold.  Archer Clegg potentially violates the Standard if he uses only the lowest appraisals since doing so could result in the estimates for future returns being upwardly biased. (Choice C)  The Standard recommends but does not require that Members and Candidates compare their performance results to comparable benchmarks.  CFA Institute recognizes that some assets, such as those Clegg manages, do not lend themselves to benchmark comparison.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Jalen Butler, CFA, is a research analyst for Principal Capital.  As part of his research, Butler uses aggregated data generated from a variety of social media websites to track trends.  Principal's compliance department updates its record retention policies annually, and therefore its most recent rules do not include several of the new websites used by Butler.  Butler does not retain the data generated from the websites outside of Principal's record retention list since the information is on the internet and therefore is easily accessible.  Has Butler most likely violated the Standards?
new_option_b: No, since certain sources are not on Principal's record retention list
new_option_c: No, since he is not required to retain records of information that can be found on the internet
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must develop and maintain appropriate records to support their investment analyses, recommendations, actions, and other investment-related communications with clients and prospective clients." Standard V(C) Record Retention requires members and candidates to keep records of their research and motives for their actions and recommendations.  Although records are considered property of the firm, and the Standard places some responsibility for record retention on the firm, Members and Candidates are ultimately responsible for assisting the firm in collecting and retaining this information, even if it is easily accessible to anyone via the internet.  Sources that require retention include: Client conversations Notes from earnings calls Statistical analyses (ie, spreadsheets) Written reports Electronic communications (eg, texts, emails) Media communications (eg, Twitter feeds, blogs) Given the frequent changes in digital media landscape, companies' record retention policies often lag the creation and popularization of new sources of information.  This puts the burden of retention regarding these types of media more heavily on the Member or Candidate than the company.  In this question, Jalen Butler is required to retain his records from all social media websites, whether on the company's retention list or not.  Failing to do so violates the Standard (Choice B). (Choice C)  Although media communication is often easily accessible on the internet, information can also be removed from a website, so Members and Candidates are required to retain this information.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Ross Farley, CFA, is the chief compliance officer at Prudent Advisors, Inc. (PA).  PA offers investment advisory services to retail investors. Farley monitors the activity of six financial advisors to ensure compliance with all applicable laws and regulations. Farley has provided all employees with the firm's code of ethics and a policies and procedures manual.  On an annual basis, Farley conducts educational training, sets expectations for behavior, and asks employees to sign a document attesting that they have received the code and manual and understand their contents.  In addition, employees are required to submit a quarterly transaction report detailing their trading of individual securities. Farley discovers that Greg Smith, an advisor at the firm, recently opened an unauthorized account at a discount brokerage firm and is conducting personal trades that have not been reported or approved.  According to Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, did Farley most likely violate the Standards?
new_option_b: Yes, for failing to set up and implement an effective compliance program
new_option_c: Yes, for failing to prevent Smith from trading in an unauthorized brokerage account
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, rules, regulations, and the Code and Standards." Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors requires Members and Candidates who supervise employees to make a reasonable effort to detect and prevent unethical behavior and violations of the law, rules established by their firm, and the Code and Standards.  However, failing to detect such behavior is not necessarily a violation of the Standard if the supervisor ensures that a proper compliance system is in place. The Guidance to the Standard indicates that compliance, at a minimum, requires supervisors to: establish written compliance procedures, and perform regular reviews to ensure that employees are following the procedures. A supervisor who does not satisfy these requirements violates the Standard even if no laws or codes were violated.  However, the concept of "reasonableness" does not make supervisors responsible for detecting all violations; employees may be able to evade compliance in ways that cannot be detected through reasonable efforts. In this instance, Ross Farley established and implemented an adequate compliance program (Choice B).  It is not reasonable to conclude that Farley should have known that an employee would try to evade the requirement (Choice C).  However, now that he knows it is possible, Farley should enhance the compliance systems to prevent future occurrences.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Miles McAllen, CFA, is a research analyst for Everhold Securities.  For the last several years, McAllen has analyzed 4Furniture, Inc. for Everhold.  McAllen joins 4Furniture's board of directors and receives 500 shares of 4Furniture's common stock as compensation, which is disclosed to and approved by Everhold.  According to Standard VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts, does McAllen's directorship most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_a: Yes, since McAllen's objectivity is compromised.
new_option_b: Yes, as McAllen must refuse external compensation.
new_option_c: No, but McAllen may not make investment decisions on 4Furniture.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and employer.  Members and Candidates must ensure that such disclosures are prominent, are delivered in plain language, and communicate the relevant information effectively." Members and Candidates who serve as directors have a conflict of interest between serving their employer's clients and the board's shareholders.  The existence of a conflict alone does not necessarily violate the Standard.  If an employee receives stock compensation as a director, the employee must: Disclose the compensation to the employer Disassociate from the investment decisions regarding the external company Since Miles McAllen's directorship is approved by Everhold Securities and McAllen discloses his compensation, McAllen does not violate the Standard (Choices A and B). Firms that allow employees to maintain directorships at external public companies must prevent them from making investment judgments on those companies since conflicts of interest exist.  Therefore, McAllen must not participate in analyzing or giving opinions about 4Furniture, Inc. to abide by the Standard.  A suggested solution is for firms to establish a firewall to mitigate the conflict.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Mina Pappas, CFA, is the sole proprietor of Milos Capital, providing financial advice to high-net-worth clients.  Pappas invests client's equity assets through a separately managed account strategy consisting of a portfolio of 20 equally weighted, large-cap stocks.  Part of Pappas' sales pitch to clients and prospects is that she invests "alongside" her clients by investing her own assets in the same strategy. Pappas decides to sell one of the holdings and replace it with her best new idea.  Pappas enters the buy and sell orders for all clients, including herself, and executes the trades.  All clients receive the same execution prices, including Pappas.  According to Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, Pappas most likely:
new_option_a: is in full compliance with the Standard.
new_option_b: violated the Standard by not adhering to a blackout period.
new_option_c: violated the Standard by not executing the client's trades first.
new_explanation_en: "Investment transactions for clients and employers must have priority over investment transactions in which a Member or Candidate is the beneficial owner." Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions requires members and candidates to place clients' and employers' financial interests before their own when conducting investment transactions.  It is not uncommon for a member or candidate to transact in the same investments as clients, or even alongside clients.  A Member or Candidate does not violate the Standard provided that: the client is not disadvantaged by the trade, the member or candidate does not benefit from the client transactions, and the member or candidate adheres to all applicable regulatory requirements. In this scenario, Pappas complied with the Standard. (Choice B)  Blackout periods are specifically intended to prevent "front-running," which is placing personal trades or a firm's proprietary trades ahead of client trades.  In this instance, by combining and executing all trades at once, Pappas is investing alongside her clients, as she has previously communicated.  Therefore, a blackout period is not applicable given the circumstances. (Choice C)  In this case, the client was not disadvantaged nor did Pappas benefit from the client transactions; therefore, Pappas did not violate the Standard by executing her trades alongside her clients' trades.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Anisa Bhandari recently received notice that she passed Level I of the CFA program.  She updates her credentials on a popular social media platform by stating, "CFA Candidate: Passed Level I of the CFA Program."  As Bhandari is looking for new full-time employment, she has decided not to enroll for the Level II exam until her work situation is more settled and she can be sure she can commit the time and energy needed to pass the exam.  Did Bhandari most likely violate the Standards?
new_option_b: Yes, by stating that she is a CFA Candidate.
new_option_c: Yes, by stating that she passed Level I of the CFA program.
new_explanation_en: "When referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, Members and Candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program." Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program regulates how Members and Candidates may use the CFA designation.  Candidates are those who have: registered with CFA Institute and are enrolled to sit for an exam, or sat for an exam and are awaiting results. Since Anisa Bhandari has received her results but has not registered for the next scheduled exam, she is no longer considered an active Candidate (Choice A).  When Bhandari successfully registers for Level II, she can consider herself a Candidate again. (Choice C)  Candidates may disclose their prior participation in the CFA program or may factually state that they passed a certain exam. Language such as "Passed Level I of the CFA Program" is acceptable.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: The CEO of PrimeHealth, Inc., a publicly traded pharmaceutical company, hosted a conference call for approximately 15 analysts from 10 different investment banks.  One of the listeners was Paula Pressly, Level II CFA candidate.  The CEO of PrimeHealth announces that the company has received regulatory approval to sell its latest cancer drug.  The CEO tells the assembled participants that he anticipates additional revenues of $3 billion this year, which he estimates will grow at 10% per year.  After the call, but before the CEO's information has been widely distributed, Pressly buys 100 shares of PrimeHealth for her account.  At the same time, she also calls her father and advises him to buy PrimeHealth stock, but he does not act on her advice.  Which of the following most accurately describes any violations by Pressly of Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information?
new_option_a: Pressly violated the Standard only by purchasing the stock.
new_option_b: Pressly violated the Standard only by recommending that her father purchase the stock.
new_option_c: Pressly violated the Standard both by her purchase and recommending that her father purchase the stock.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits members and candidates from trading on material nonpublic information.  "Material" refers to information that would be expected to cause a significant change in the market price of a security.  "Nonpublic" means that the information has not been disseminated to the general investing marketplace.  Information that is given only to a limited group of investors, such as to analysts on a conference call, does not make that information public. The Standard also prohibits members and candidates from recommending investments to others if the recommendation is based on material nonpublic information.  It is irrelevant whether the recipient acts on the recommendation. Pressly violated the Standard both by purchasing the stock and advising her father to buy it.  The CEO's information is clearly material since the expected boost to Prime Health's revenues from regulatory approval of the drug will likely affect PrimeHealth's stock price.  The information was also nonpublic since only a few analysts knew it when Pressly bought the stock.  Although Pressly's father did not act on her recommendation, it was based on material nonpublic information, so her recommendation alone violated the Standard (Choices A and B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Zoey Baines, CFA, works in the investment management division of a large bank.  As part of the bank's incentives for driving revenue growth, it offers Baines $300 for each investment management client she refers to either the bank's banking or financial planning divisions.  At year end, the employee with the most referrals receives an additional $5,000 bonus.  Baines does not share her compensation structure with her clients since she feels her compensation is a private matter.  Does Baines most likely violate Standard VI(C) Referral Fees?
new_option_b: No, since the incentive is considered compensation.
new_option_c: No, since the offer is for only referrals within the bank.
new_explanation_en: Members and Candidates must disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services Standard VI(C) addresses various types of conflicts of interest that Members and Candidates must avoid.  Under Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, Members and Candidates must notify clients of benefits they obtain for giving a referral.  By disclosing referral arrangements, clients may evaluate the employee's objectivity and a proposal's total cost.  All referral arrangements, whether with a third party or within the same firm, must be disclosed (Choice C). Zoey Baines violates the Standard by failing to inform clients about the financial reward she receives for referring customers to the bank's other divisions.  Even if Baines considers her compensation a private matter, it does not excuse her from disclosing any compensation associated with making internal or external referrals (Choice B).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Joseph Smith, CFA, is the head equity trader for an investment management firm and is responsible for the firm's soft dollar policies and brokerage relationships.  During a planning session, the investment management team agrees that the firm will use soft dollars to purchase new economic research from XYZ Economists, new performance attribution software, and new computers for the trading desk.  According to Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, Smith would most likely violate the Standard by using soft dollar brokerage to purchase the:
new_option_b: computers for the trading desk.
new_option_c: performance attribution software.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment.  Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' best interests before their employer's or their own interests." Investment managers pay a commission to a broker to execute client trades.  Soft dollar brokerage is the practice of using a portion of brokerage commissions to purchase investment services.  Since it is the client who ultimately "pays" (ie, out of client assets) the commission, when a portion of the commission (ie, soft dollars) purchases additional investment services, the services "belong" to the client. The investment manager has a duty of loyalty to use such assets for the benefit of the client.  Soft dollars can be used only to purchase research services that assist the manager in the investment decision-making process (ie, to make better decisions for the client).  Therefore, soft dollars cannot be used to cover the investment manager's operating expenses, such as computers, office supplies, or travel expenses. Investment managers may be tempted to generate excess soft dollar commissions to purchase additional research or to gain clout with brokerage firms by generating more commission revenue.  The investment manager cannot meet the Standard by paying a higher commission rate for the exclusive purpose of generating soft dollar commissions and must disclose soft dollar practices to clients. (Choices A and C)  Performance attribution software and economic research will assist the portfolio management team in making more informed investing decisions for the client and is therefore permissible under the Standard.

new_question_en: Anand Rana, CFA, a portfolio manager for Amethyst Investment Group, expects that political conflict between two developed countries will create turmoil for emerging markets.  He asks Rahul Kumar, CFA, a quantitative analyst at Amethyst, to develop a model to track various economic factors in each of the emerging markets.  Kumar creates a model, tests it with available data from the last two years when emerging markets expanded rapidly, then delivers it to Rana.  Unhappy with the finished product, Rana asks another quantitative analyst to create a model with different inputs.  The new model, upon thorough testing by Rana, delivers more helpful results.  Since this model delivers the results that Rana wants, he does not inquire how it uses the inputs or produces its results.  Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis is most likely violated by:
new_option_b: only Kumar.
new_option_c: both Rana and Kumar.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Rul Investing is a full-service investment firm that has adopted the CFA Institute Code and Standards.  As policy and practice, the firm prohibits communication between the research and investment banking departments.  An exception occurs when the firm forms teams that include both research analysts and investment bankers to work on joint projects.  For those projects, the entire team is eligible for a bonus based on the results of the project or transaction.  The firm is careful to disclose to clients those cases in which research analysts and investment bankers work together.  Does Rul's practice regarding these special project teams most likely comply with Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity?
new_option_b: No, since analysts can earn bonuses resulting from work on the special teams.
new_option_c: No, since the firm should not allow teams with both analysts and investment bankers.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." One potential threat to a member or candidate's independence and objectivity is pressure on research analysts from the investment banking department to issue more favorable recommendations.  Firms often establish firewalls between departments to mitigate this threat. One such firewall is establishing a compensation plan that rewards analysts for accuracy and objectivity, not the performance of other departments.  Rul's compensation for the joint teams directly conflicts with this requirement by making the analysts eligible for bonuses based on team results.  Thus, it is a violation of the Standard, whether or not it is disclosed to clients (Choice A). (Choice C)  The Standard recognizes that there may be efficiencies to having analysts and investment bankers work together (ie, more efficient risk assessment and pricing).  As a result, the Standard does not prohibit joint teams, such as those at Rul, but does recommend mitigating practices, such as ensuring that analysts' compensation plans that independent of investment banking results.

new_question_en: The endowment fund managers for Springvale University hire Omar Najjar, CFA, to provide investment advice.  During their conversation, the managers mention that the endowment is funding a new academic building that the University has not yet announced to the public.  Najjar tells the managers to call one of his clients, who just received an inheritance of $100,000 and disclosed that information to Najjar during a recent meeting. Later that night, Najjar has dinner with his friend, Farah Said, an alumna of Springvale University.  Najjar tells Said that the University is planning a new academic building and needs donations.  According to Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality, Najjar has most likely violated the Standard by disclosing:
new_option_a: his clients' inheritance to the endowment managers.
new_option_b: Springvale University's building plans and funding needs to Said.
new_option_c: both his client's inheritance and Springvale University's building plans and funding needs.

new_question_en: Enes Yilmaz, CFA, is a portfolio manager who is responsible for selecting emerging market subadvisors for a government pension fund. Yilmaz regularly evaluates third-party investment advisers and has developed an extensive due diligence checklist.  While screening for new managers, he identifies a particularly strong-performing hedge fund that provides excellent diversification benefits to the pension portfolio.  During his due diligence, Yilmaz discovers that: the fund is registered in an offshore jurisdiction with weak governance requirements, none of the firm's employees are CFA charterholders, and the company does not have an established code of ethics. The hedge fund's CEO explains that all employees are thoroughly vetted before hiring and that everyone at his firm "knows right from wrong." Although Yilmaz is concerned about the lack of a code of ethics, he confirms that the fund complies with local laws and is in good standing with regulators; therefore, he decides to invest.  Does Yilmaz's conduct comply with Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis?
new_option_b: Yes, since external advisory firms are not required to adopt a code of ethics.
new_option_c: Yes, since he performed thorough due diligence and investing in the hedge fund is in the plan's best interest.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must: Exercise diligence, independence, and thoroughness in analyzing investments, making investment recommendations, and taking investment actions. Have a reasonable and adequate basis, supported by appropriate research and investigation, for any investment analysis, recommendation, or action." Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis states that Members and Candidates must perform reasonable and standardized due diligence on external advisers.  In addition to reviewing an adviser's investment process, strategy, performance presentation, and internal controls, Members and Candidates must review the adviser's code of ethics. In this scenario, Enes Yilmaz conducts thorough due diligence and confirms that the hedge fund operates in compliance with local laws, as required by the Standard.  However, he also discovers that the company does not have an established code of ethics.  Without a code of ethics, Yilmaz cannot be confident that the firm will adhere to a high level of ethical standards.  Therefore, by investing with this manager, Yilmaz violates Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis. (Choice B)  Given the circumstances, the hedge fund is not required to conform to the Standards.  However, before investing, Yilmaz must ensure a minimum level of internal controls and decision-making protocols, including an established code of ethics. (Choice C)  Yilmaz has a fiduciary duty to the pension plan participants but also must adhere to the higher ethical standards imposed on CFA charterholders.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Lena Schmidt, CFA, is preparing an investment report on Fulcrum Industries while she waits for a plane at the airport.  While writing the report, she sees the CEO of Fulcrum boarding a flight to the city where Keel Manufacturing, one of Fulcrum's competitors, has its headquarters.  Based on her research of the companies' financial statements, Schmidt knows that Fulcrum and Keel have significant strategic and geographic overlap. She recalls that, on the company's latest earnings call, Fulcrum's CEO mentioned he was analyzing acquisition targets.  Based on this information, Schmidt concludes that Fulcrum may be preparing an offer to purchase Keel.  She revises her research report on Fulcrum to add her theory on the acquisition, citing the above information, and changes her recommendation from buy to hold.  She then sends the report to her clients.  Has Schmidt most likely violated Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information?
new_option_b: Yes, since she shared the information before the CEO announced his trip
new_option_c: Yes, since she shared her report only with clients and not the general public
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information." Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits Members and Candidates from trading on or recommending investments based on material nonpublic information.  However, analysts may piece together public and nonmaterial nonpublic data from multiple sources to form an investment conclusion. This research approach is referred to as the mosaic theory, and it recognizes that analysts form conclusions from various sources of information. Conclusions formed through the mosaic process, even when based on information that would be considered material and nonpublic if it were coming directly from a reliable source (eg, the company), do not violate the Standard. In this scenario, Lena Schmidt has used public information (eg, financial statements) and nonmaterial nonpublic information (ie, the CEO's flight) to form an investment conclusion using the mosaic approach.  Although Schmidt's conclusion, if true, would be the equivalent of material nonpublic information if disclosed directly to her by the company, her actions do not violate the Standard. (Choice B)  A CEO's travel plan is typically deemed a nonmaterial event (ie, by itself, it would not affect the company's stock price).  Therefore, Schmidt did not need to wait for the company to issue a press release to make the information public. (Choice C)  Analysts are not required to publicly disseminate their research reports.  As long as Schmidt's report was sent to clients in a fair manner, she has not violated the Standard.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: Aditi Kumar is a Level II Candidate and a performance measurement and attribution analyst for an investment manager.  On a quarterly basis, Kumar produces performance reports that include the firm's composites for each investment strategy. Raheem Khan, CFA, the portfolio manager of the firm's large-cap equity strategy approaches Kumar regarding the large-cap equity composite for the most recent quarter.  Kumar explains that several accounts in the composite should be excluded from this quarter's performance report due to a software issue that resulted in numerous accounts not being fully invested.  The resulting cash drag caused the composite to underperform the benchmark index for the quarter and year. Khan explains that he should not be held responsible for a software error.  Kumar agrees and produces new reports without the affected accounts.  According to Standard I(C) Misrepresentation, it is most likely that:
new_option_b: only Kumar violated the Standard.
new_option_c: both Kumar and Khan violated the Standard.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must not knowingly make any misrepresentations relating to investment analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities." Standard I(C) Misrepresentation protects investors against statements and information provided by the investing community that may undermine investor trust in the integrity of the profession.  Misrepresentation can include: Plagiarism:  quoting information without acknowledgment or citation of the source Omission:  presenting incomplete or misleading information Exaggeration:  inflating professional credentials or performance results Performance measurement and attribution is an area susceptible to selective disclosure and omission.  A prime example is the concept of "cherry picking," which involves choosing only the best funds or accounts or omitting the worst for performance reporting.  Omitting accounts or altering composite construction outside a clearly defined process may lead to misrepresenting composite performance. In this instance, Khan persuaded Kumar to alter the composite construction due to a one-time software issue, which improved the composite's performance.  Therefore, both Kumar and Khan violated the Standard by presenting incomplete or misleading information (Choices A and B). Although the software issue may not have been Khan's fault, changing the composite constituents to omit the affected accounts violates the Standard.  Also, the fact that Kumar is not yet a charterholder is irrelevant in this scenario since he, as a Candidate, is expected to uphold the Code and Standards.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\10. Ethics\11.05 Ethics Application - Answers.pdf
new_question_en: In 20X6, Shepherd Financial, Inc. (SFI), headed by founder Lillian Shepherd, CFA, is engaged by the Green Fund to manage part of the fund's assets.  SFI, with Shepherd as the advisor for the account, is one of 10 subadvisors hired by the Green Fund to select securities.  Two years later, in 20X8, the Green Fund terminates SFI.  In 20X9, Shepherd delivers performance reports to prospective clients that include the Green Fund's historical gross performance.  The reports also include the Green Fund's fee schedule and disclosures that SFI was one member of a 10- subadvisor team for the Green Fund from 20X6 to 20X8. According to Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, does Shepherd most likely violate the Standard?
new_option_b: Yes, since she reports the Green Fund's gross performance.
new_option_c: Yes, since she claims performance for a fund SFI no longer advises.
new_explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." To comply with Standard III(D) Performance Presentation, Members and Candidates must use credible return data when preparing performance information for current or potential clients.  Clients must receive performance information that is free from distorted data that may be misleading. To comply with the Standard, Members and Candidates need to fully disclose exceptions and avoid any disclosures that may misrepresent performance. Shepherd accurately portrays her work with the Green Fund and does not mislead her clients, who are made aware that she worked for the Green Fund from 20X6 to 20X8. (Choice B)  Shepherd does not violate the Standard by reporting the Green Fund's performance gross of fees since she discloses its fee schedule. (Choice C)  An advisor must report an account's returns even if the advisor is no longer associated with that account.  Otherwise, the advisor might conceal accounts that performed poorly, leading to the advisor's termination.

new_question_en: Calvin Wurtz, CFA, is the founder and CEO of Florenz Equities, an asset management firm specializing in small-cap stocks.  The firm's marketing materials display its average compounded returns over 5, 10, and 15 years.  The materials include the following statements: Statement 1:  "Average returns for each time period shown in these materials include returns from both currently active accounts and accounts that were terminated during that period." Statement 2:  "We present average return data gross of management fees." The materials do not specify the dates when accounts were terminated.  The materials state that the firm does not comply with Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS). Has Wurtz violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentation with respect to Florenz's marketing materials?
new_option_b: Yes, only regarding average return data.
new_option_c: Yes, regarding both terminated accounts and average return data.
new_explanation_en: "When communicating investment performance information, Members and Candidates must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, accurate, and complete." Standard III(D) Performance Presentation requires members and candidates to avoid misleading investors (and potential investors) when communicating investment performance.  The Standard applies to how performance is presented and measured.  Although compliance with the Global Investment Performance Standards® (GIPS) is recommended, a firm does not need to adopt GIPS to comply with this Standard. A firm must include both active and terminated accounts in its performance information.  The information must clearly indicate when accounts were terminated.  Failing to do so could mislead investors since the breakdown of returns for terminated accounts and active accounts cannot be easily determined. Firms must also indicate whether performance is calculated gross of (ie, before) or net of (ie, after) management fees.  In this scenario, Statement 2 clearly states that performance data are gross of fees, so the materials comply with the Standard.  Florenz Equities does not need to specify its management fees in its marketing materials (Choices B and C).

new_question_en: Which of the following is one of the six elements of the CFA Institute's Code of Ethics?  Members and candidates must:
new_option_a: judge the suitability of investments in the context of the client's total portfolio.
new_option_b: promote the integrity of the global capital markets for the ultimate benefit of society.
new_option_c: avoid misrepresentations relating to analysis, recommendations, actions, or other professional activities.
new_explanation_en: Code of Ethics Standards of Professional Conduct Aspirational Overarching expected behavior Conceptual Behavioral Ethical business practices Actionable CFA Charter holders and candidates are obligated to abide by and advocate for the Code of Ethics (ie, the Code) and the Standards of Professional Conduct (ie, the Standards), which provide guidance for appropriate ethical behavior.  The Code includes general principles to which members and candidates must adhere.  In contrast, the Standards address more specific applications of those principles that must be followed. To identify elements of the Code and the Standards, determine whether the task in question is actionable or is more conceptual.  "Promoting… integrity and viability…for the ultimate benefit of society" is one of the six principles of ethical behaviors in the Code.  Judging client suitability and avoiding misrepresentation are practical applications of the Standards (Choices A and C).

new_question_en: The CFA Institute's Professional Conduct staff (PCS) finds that Simon Perret, CFA, has violated the Standards.  Perret rejects the PCS's proposed sanctions.  Which of the following is most likely to occur?
new_option_b: The PCS issues Perret a cautionary letter.
new_option_c: The Disciplinary Review Committee reviews the PCS's investigative report.
new_explanation_en: The CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program is a framework for handling inquiries about members' and candidates' professional conduct.  The Professional Conduct staff (PCS) initiates an inquiry, which is based on an external complaint or internal investigations.  The PCS may question the accused member or anyone else associated with the inquiry.  The PCS records evidence relevant to the investigation, prepares a report, and determines if a violation occurred. If the PCS believes that a violation occurred and the member accepts this finding, then the PCS will either issue a cautionary letter or proceed with disciplinary action.  If the accused rejects the finding, then a panel of the Disciplinary Review Committee (DRC) becomes involved.  The panel reviews the PCS's report and further investigates the matter.  The DRC determines whether a violation occurred and sets the final disciplinary action. (Choices A and B)  The PCS imposes sanctions only when it believes a violation transpired and the member or candidate accepts the PCS's findings.

new_question_en: Based on Standard I Professionalism, Members and Candidates must:
new_option_a: have a duty of loyalty to their clients.
new_option_b: maintain independence and objectivity.
new_option_c: not compromise the reputation or the integrity of CFA Institute.
new_explanation_en: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.  Members and Candidates must not offer, solicit, or accept any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise their own or another's independence and objectivity." Standard I of the Standards of Professional Conduct addresses the professionalism of Members and Candidates.  Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity specifically states: "Members and Candidates must use reasonable care and judgment to achieve and maintain independence and objectivity in their professional activities.…" Standard I(B) specifically focuses on Members and Candidates achieving and maintaining independence and objectivity so that their actions and advice to clients are unaffected by conflicts of interest.  The Standard applies to situations wherein entities or individuals may seek to influence the decision-making process to the detriment of clients.  It does not apply to gifts from the clients themselves. In this question, all answer choices are directly from the Standards but only one is associated with Standard I. (Choice A)  Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care specifically addresses the duty of loyalty that Members and Candidates have toward their clients. (Choice C)  Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs requires Members and Candidates to act in a manner that does not compromise the reputation or the integrity of CFA Institute.

new_question_en: Standard VI(C) of the Standard of Professional Conduct on Conflicts of Interest most appropriately requires Members and Candidates to:
new_option_a: obtain their employers' written approval for outside compensation.
new_option_b: notify clients that they may receive a referral fee for recommending a product.
new_option_c: avoid sending more detailed recommendations to clients based on personal relationships.
new_explanation_en: This question highlights Standards that have similar language but address different ethical issues and/or requirements for compliance.  Although it is unlikely that a Candidate will see many of these "memorization" ethics questions, the Learning Outcome Statement requires Candidates to identify components of the Standards. Standard VI focuses exclusively on conflicts of interest.  Standard VI(C) Referral Fees requires Members and Candidates to notify clients that the Member or Candidate may receive a referral fee for recommending a product or service. (Choice A)  Standard IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements, not Standard VI, requires Members and Candidates to receive their employers' written approval for all outside compensation, which poses, or could reasonably pose, a conflict of interest.  Standard VI requires only that Members and Candidates notify affected parties of any conflict of interest, for which approval is not needed. (Choice C)  Standard III(B) Fair Dealing requires Members and Candidates to treat all clients impartially with respect to investment recommendations or opportunities.

new_question_en: The CFA Institute's Professional Conduct staff identifies a member as the subject of a written complaint.  According to the CFA Institute Bylaws and Rules of Procedure for Professional Conduct, which of the following is most likely the Professional Conduct staff's next step?
new_option_b: Issue the member a cautionary letter
new_option_c: Refer the inquiry to the Disciplinary Review Committee
new_explanation_en: The CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program manages inquiries about members and candidates.  One way the Professional Conduct staff (PCS) is informed about potential violations is through a written complaint from the public.  With this complaint, the PCS creates an inquiry.  Once an inquiry is opened, the PCS may question the accused member or anyone else associated with the inquiry (eg, the member's supervisor).  The PCS documents evidence relevant to the investigation and prepares a report. If the PCS believes that a violation occurred, it either issues a cautionary letter or proceeds with disciplinary action.  At this point, the member or candidate may reject or accept the charges and sanctions.  If the accused party rejects them, then a panel of the Disciplinary Review Committee (DRC) becomes involved.  The panel reviews the PCS's report and further investigates the inquiry.  It concludes whether the violation occurred and sets the final disciplinary action. (Choice B)  The PCS does not issue a cautionary letter until after the accused accepts the proposed sanctions. (Choice C)  The PCS refers the inquiry to the DRC only if the member or candidate rejects the PCS charges and sanctions.

new_question_en: A client names a Member in a written complaint involving potential misconduct and files the complaint with the Member's firm.  At a minimum, CFA Institute's Code and Standards require that the Member:
new_option_a: self-disclose the incident on the annual Professional Conduct Statement.
new_option_b: immediately disclose the incident to CFA Institute's Professional Conduct Program staff.
new_option_c: self-disclose the incident on the annual Professional Conduct Statement only if the firm finds wrongdoing.
new_explanation_en: Professional conduct All Members and Candidates must file an annual Professional Conduct Statement Any matter that questions professional conduct must be disclosed Written complaints sent directly to CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program staff can result in an investigation CFA Institute staff may also investigate if they become aware of questionable conduct The CFA Institute Professional Conduct Program provides a framework for handling inquiries about Members' and Candidates' professional conduct.  The Professional Conduct Program staff can initiate an inquiry based on either an external complaint or an internal investigation.  The staff works with the Disciplinary Review Committee to enforce the Code and Standards. Members and Candidates are required to submit a completed Professional Conduct Statement annually.  This statement is a pledge to adhere to the Code and Standards and the Professional Conduct Program.  It also provides an opportunity to self-disclose questionable behavior. When a Member or Candidate receives a written complaint that questions his or her professional conduct, the complaint must be disclosed to Professional Conduct Program staff.  CFA Institute encourages disclosure at the time of the event, but at a minimum the matter must be disclosed when filing the annual Professional Conduct Statement (Choice B). (Choice C)  Regardless of the outcome of any internal (ie, firm) investigation, the Member or Candidate must self-disclose the incident on the annual Professional Conduct Statement or directly to Professional Conduct Program staff.
